26S proteasome in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_proteasomeCONCRETE The 26S proteasome degrades proteins tagged with polyubiquitin chains. Its 20S core particle is a barrel of four stacked heptameric rings, two...
[more...][less] The 26S proteasome degrades proteins tagged with polyubiquitin chains. Its 20S core particle is a barrel of four stacked heptameric rings, two outer rings of alpha subunits that gate substrate entry and two inner rings of beta subunits, three of which (beta1, beta2 and beta5) are N-terminal threonine proteases with caspase-like, trypsin-like and chymotrypsin-like specificities. The 19S regulatory particle caps the core. Its base contains six AAA+ ATPases (Rpt1-Rpt6) that unfold substrates and open the core gate, together with the scaffolds Rpn1 and Rpn2. Ubiquitin receptors (Rpn10 and Rpn13) bind ubiquitylated substrates, the lid metalloprotease Rpn11 removes ubiquitin chains before degradation, and Uch-L5 bound to Rpn13 trims chains. Drosophila has a testis-specific 26S proteasome in which paralogs replace several alpha, beta, Rpt, Rpn and Uch-L5 subunits.

ABCE model of floral organ identity (MADS floral quartets)MODULE:floral_organ_identity_abceCONCRETE In the eudicot flower, four concentric whorls of organs (sepals, petals, stamens and carpels) get their identities from overlapping homeotic gene...
[more...][less] In the eudicot flower, four concentric whorls of organs (sepals, petals, stamens and carpels) get their identities from overlapping homeotic gene activities, as described by the ABC model and its later ABCE extension. In Arabidopsis thaliana the A function is supplied by APETALA1 (AP1, a MIKC-type MADS-domain transcription factor) and APETALA2 (AP2, an AP2/ERF-domain transcriptional repressor). The B function is supplied by the obligate MADS heterodimer APETALA3/PISTILLATA (AP3/PI) and the C function by AGAMOUS (AG). The E function is supplied redundantly by the four SEPALLATA MADS proteins (SEP1-SEP4). A alone specifies sepals (whorl 1), A+B petals (whorl 2), B+C stamens (whorl 3) and C carpels (whorl 4). E activity is required for B and C function: sep1 sep2 sep3 flowers make only sepals, and sep1 sep2 sep3 sep4 flowers make only leaf-like organs. At the molecular level, the floral quartet model proposes that each organ identity is set by a distinct tetrameric MADS complex. Two MADS dimers bind two CArG boxes and loop the DNA between them, with SEP proteins (above all SEP3) acting as the tetramerization hub. Expressing A or C together with B and E genes is enough to turn leaves into petal-like or stamen-like organs. A and C are mutually antagonistic. AP2 confines AG to the inner two whorls by recruiting the TOPLESS/HDA19 co-repressor, while AG excludes AP1 from the inner whorls. The SEP3-AG tetramer also terminates the floral meristem after carpel initiation. Floral meristem identity (LEAFY, AP1 meristem function, CAULIFLOWER, FRUITFULL, TERMINAL FLOWER1) is a separate, upstream module. LEAFY is cited here only as an activator of the B and C genes. The D-class ovule identity genes (STK/SHP) and the downstream organ differentiation programs are also outside this boundary.

AMP-activated protein kinase complex in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_ampk_complexCONCRETE AMP-activated protein kinase is a heterotrimeric energy sensor made of a catalytic alpha subunit, a scaffolding beta subunit with a...
[more...][less] AMP-activated protein kinase is a heterotrimeric energy sensor made of a catalytic alpha subunit, a scaffolding beta subunit with a glycogen-binding domain, and a gamma subunit whose CBS repeats bind AMP, ADP and ATP. Drosophila has a single gene for each subunit (AMPKalpha, alicorn and SNF4Agamma). When cellular energy falls, nucleotide binding to the gamma subunit promotes phosphorylation of the alpha activation loop by LKB1 and protects it from dephosphorylation. Active AMPK restores energy balance by inhibiting anabolic pathways, including TORC1 signaling and lipid synthesis, and promoting catabolism; in Drosophila it is also needed for epithelial polarity under energy stress and for normal lifespan and lipid storage.

Abscisic acid core signaling (PYR/PYL receptor - clade A PP2C - SnRK2 - ABF/ABI5 and SLAC1 outputs)MODULE:abscisic_acid_signalingABSTRACT The core abscisic acid (ABA) signalling pathway of land plants is a double-negative relay that converts ABA perception into transcriptional and...
[more...][less] The core abscisic acid (ABA) signalling pathway of land plants is a double-negative relay that converts ABA perception into transcriptional and ion-channel outputs. Soluble START-domain receptors of the PYR/PYL/RCAR family bind ABA in an internal cavity; a gate-latch-lock conformational change creates a surface that binds and occludes the active site of clade A type 2C protein phosphatases (PP2Cs such as ABI1, ABI2, HAB1 and PP2CA/AHG3). In the absence of ABA these PP2Cs bind subclass III SnRK2 protein kinases (SnRK2.2, SnRK2.3 and SnRK2.6/OST1 in Arabidopsis) and dephosphorylate their activation loop, keeping them inactive. ABA-bound receptors inhibit the PP2Cs and disrupt the PP2C-SnRK2 interaction, so the SnRK2s autophosphorylate and become active. Active SnRK2s phosphorylate the ABRE-binding bZIP transcription factors of the ABF/AREB/ABI5 group, which then activate ABA-responsive genes (for example RD29B and late embryogenesis-abundant genes), and in guard cells OST1 phosphorylates and activates the plasma-membrane S-type anion channel SLAC1, driving anion efflux, depolarisation and stomatal closure. ABA biosynthesis (including the NCED-catalysed committed step), ABA transport and catabolism, calcium-dependent kinase (CPK) branches, receptor turnover, and downstream transcriptional networks are outside this module's boundary.

Adrenal steroidogenesis — cholesterol to corticosteroids and adrenal androgens; STAR/CYP11A1/HSD3B2/CYP17A1/CYP21A2/CYP11B1/CYP11B2MODULE:adrenal_steroidogenesis Adrenal steroidogenesis converts cholesterol into the three classes of steroid hormone — glucocorticoids (cortisol), mineralocorticoids...
[more...][less] Adrenal steroidogenesis converts cholesterol into the three classes of steroid hormone — glucocorticoids (cortisol), mineralocorticoids (aldosterone) and adrenal androgens (DHEA, androstenedione) — through a branched network of mitochondrial and endoplasmic-reticulum enzymes. The acute, rate-limiting step is the delivery of cholesterol from the outer to the inner mitochondrial membrane by the steroidogenic acute regulatory protein STAR; there the side-chain-cleavage cytochrome P450 CYP11A1 (P450scc) makes pregnenolone, the common precursor of all steroid hormones. Pregnenolone is then routed by two ER enzymes whose order and combination select the branch: the 3beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/isomerase HSD3B2 (Delta5 -> Delta4, giving progesterone, 17-hydroxyprogesterone or androstenedione) and the bifunctional 17alpha-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase CYP17A1 (17-hydroxylation commits to cortisol; the 17,20-lyase reaction commits to androgens). 21-hydroxylase CYP21A2 then hydroxylates progesterone -> 11-deoxycorticosterone (mineralocorticoid branch) and 17-hydroxyprogesterone -> 11-deoxycortisol (glucocorticoid branch). The final oxidations return to the mitochondrion: CYP11B1 (11beta-hydroxylase) makes cortisol, while its close paralog CYP11B2 (aldosterone synthase), uniquely possessing 18-hydroxylase/18-oxidase activity, converts deoxycorticosterone through corticosterone and 18-hydroxycorticosterone to aldosterone in the zona glomerulosa. Inherited defects define the congenital adrenal hyperplasias and related disorders: STAR (congenital lipoid adrenal hyperplasia), CYP11A1 (adrenal insufficiency), HSD3B2 (3beta-HSD-deficiency CAH), CYP17A1 (combined 17alpha- hydroxylase/17,20-lyase deficiency), CYP21A2 (21-hydroxylase deficiency, >90% of CAH), CYP11B1 (11beta-hydroxylase-deficiency CAH) and CYP11B2 (aldosterone synthase / CMO deficiency; a CYP11B1/B2 chimera causes glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism).

Alcoholic fermentation of pyruvate to ethanolMODULE:alcoholic_fermentationABSTRACT Alcoholic fermentation is the two-step, NAD+-regenerating branch that follows glycolysis in yeasts and other fungi, in plants under hypoxia, and in...
[more...][less] Alcoholic fermentation is the two-step, NAD+-regenerating branch that follows glycolysis in yeasts and other fungi, in plants under hypoxia, and in a few bacteria such as Zymomonas mobilis. A thiamine-diphosphate-dependent pyruvate decarboxylase removes CO2 from pyruvate to give acetaldehyde. An NADH-dependent alcohol dehydrogenase then reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol. That second step reoxidises the NADH formed at the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step of glycolysis, so glycolysis can continue without respiration and the overall yield is two ATP per hexose. Two unrelated alcohol dehydrogenase families can carry out the reduction: zinc-dependent medium-chain dehydrogenases (fungal and plant ADH1) and the group III ("iron-containing") dehydrogenase family (Zymomonas ADH II and fungal ADH4-type enzymes), whose members differ in metal activation. Pyruvate decarboxylase also has a minor carboligase activity that joins acetaldehyde to a second acetaldehyde or to pyruvate, making acetoin. Acetoin can then be reduced to 2,3-butanediol. That side branch is modelled here as optional, together with the bacterial acetolactate route to the same product.

Aliphatic glucosinolate biosynthesis and myrosinase activation (glucosinolate-myrosinase defense system)MODULE:aliphatic_glucosinolate_myrosinase_defenseABSTRACT The glucosinolate-myrosinase system is the two-component chemical defense of the Brassicales. Methionine-derived (aliphatic) glucosinolates are...
[more...][less] The glucosinolate-myrosinase system is the two-component chemical defense of the Brassicales. Methionine-derived (aliphatic) glucosinolates are made in three phases: (1) side-chain elongation, a cycle recruited from leucine biosynthesis that runs partly in the cytosol and partly in the chloroplast: methionine is deaminated to its 2-oxo acid in the cytosol (BCAT4), and after import into the chloroplast the 2-oxo acid is condensed with acetyl-CoA (MAM), isomerized (IPMI), oxidatively decarboxylated (IPMDH1) and transaminated back to a chain-elongated methionine homolog (BCAT3), each turn adding one methylene group; (2) formation of the core glucosinolate structure, in which CYP79F converts the chain-elongated amino acid to an aldoxime, CYP83A1 activates the aldoxime for glutathione conjugation, the conjugate is trimmed by gamma-glutamyl peptidase (GGP1) and cleaved by the C-S lyase SUR1 to a thiohydroximate, which is S-glucosylated (UGT74C1/UGT74B1) and finally sulfated from PAPS by desulfoglucosinolate sulfotransferases (SOT16-18); and (3) side-chain modification, in which flavin monooxygenases (FMO GS-OX) S-oxygenate methylthioalkyl to methylsulfinylalkyl glucosinolates and the 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase AOP2 converts these to alkenyl glucosinolates such as allylglucosinolate (sinigrin). The intact glucosinolate is biologically inert. On tissue damage, thioglucosidases (myrosinases, TGG1/TGG2) hydrolyze it to an unstable aglucone that rearranges by default to an isothiocyanate; Fe(II)-dependent specifier proteins (ESP, NSPs, TFP) instead redirect the aglucone to epithionitriles, simple nitriles or organic thiocyanates. Natural variation at MAM, AOP and ESP loci accounts for much of the glucosinolate and breakdown-product diversity between accessions and species. Transcriptional regulation (MYB28/MYB29 with MYC2-4), glucosinolate transport (GTR1/GTR2), indole and aromatic glucosinolates, and sulfate activation to PAPS are outside this module's boundary.

Anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_anaphase_promoting_complexCONCRETE The anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) is a large multisubunit RING E3 ubiquitin ligase that drives mitotic exit by targeting securin and...
[more...][less] The anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) is a large multisubunit RING E3 ubiquitin ligase that drives mitotic exit by targeting securin and mitotic cyclins for proteasomal degradation, and that keeps APC/C substrate levels low in G1. Its catalytic core is formed by the cullin-like subunit Apc2 (Morula) and the RING subunit Apc11 (Lemming A). A platform of Apc1 (Shattered), Apc4 and Apc5 (Ida) supports the core and an arc of tetratricopeptide-repeat subunits (Cdc27/Apc3, Cdc16/Apc6, Apc7 and Cdc23/Apc8). Substrates are recognized by Apc10 together with a WD40 coactivator, Fizzy (Cdc20) in mitosis or Fizzy-related (Cdh1) at mitotic exit and during endocycles.

[more...][less] A reusable counter-defence module for suppression of a host CRISPR-Cas system by proteins encoded by phages, prophages, and other mobile genetic elements. Anti-CRISPR (Acr) proteins are small, unrelated in sequence, and act by mechanism rather than by homology, so the module is decomposed by the step of the host pathway each class attacks: blockade of crRNA-guided target recognition, neutralisation of the effector nuclease, and enzymatic destruction of a CRISPR component or signal. A fourth, optional part covers the Aca autoregulatory switch that limits acr transcription once the host system is disabled. Apical-basal polarity complexes (Par, Crumbs, Scribble) in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_epithelial_polarity_complexesCONCRETE Epithelial cells divide their plasma membrane into apical and basolateral domains using three conserved groups of polarity proteins that act on...
[more...][less] Epithelial cells divide their plasma membrane into apical and basolateral domains using three conserved groups of polarity proteins that act on each other. The Par complex, Bazooka (Par-3), Par-6 and atypical protein kinase C (aPKC), marks the apical side and the adherens junction; aPKC phosphorylates basolateral proteins to exclude them from the apical membrane. The Crumbs complex, the transmembrane protein Crumbs with Stardust (PALS1) and Patj, defines the apical membrane above the adherens junction. The Scribble module, Scribble, Discs large (Dlg1) and Lethal (2) giant larvae (Lgl), acts basolaterally and restricts apical determinants. Mutual antagonism between apical and basolateral proteins sets the boundary, and loss of the Scribble module causes neoplastic overgrowth.

Arabidopsis core circadian oscillator (CCA1/LHY - PRR - evening complex - ZTL)MODULE:plant_circadian_clock_oscillatorCONCRETE The core circadian oscillator of Arabidopsis thaliana is a network of interlocked transcriptional repressor loops that generates a roughly 24 h...
[more...][less] The core circadian oscillator of Arabidopsis thaliana is a network of interlocked transcriptional repressor loops that generates a roughly 24 h rhythm in the nucleus. It is reinforced by timed, light-gated proteolysis. At dawn, the single-MYB transcription factors CCA1 and LHY peak and repress evening-phased clock genes (TOC1, ELF4, LUX, ELF3) through evening elements in their promoters. Through the day, the pseudo-response regulators PRR9, PRR7, PRR5 and finally TOC1 (PRR1) accumulate in sequential waves. Each binds target promoters through its C-terminal CCT domain and represses CCA1 and LHY, recruiting TOPLESS/TPR corepressors with histone deacetylase, so that CCA1/LHY expression stays low until the end of the night. At dusk the evening complex (EC) assembles: the scaffold ELF3 bridges the DNA-binding MYB protein LUX and the small protein ELF4. The EC represses PRR9, PRR7, GI and LUX itself through the LUX binding site, closing the evening-to-morning connection and gating growth genes (PIF4/PIF5) to the end of the night. Post-translational control sets the pace. The LOV-domain F-box photoreceptor ZEITLUPE (ZTL), as the substrate adaptor of an SCF E3 ligase, targets phosphorylated TOC1 and PRR5 for proteasomal degradation, mainly in the dark. GIGANTEA binds ZTL in a blue-light-enhanced manner and stabilizes it during the day, so ZTL activity rises at dusk. Light input through phytochromes and cryptochromes, temperature input (sensed partly by the ELF3 prion-like domain), and output pathways such as photoperiodic flowering (GI-CO-FT, CDFs) are outside this module's boundary except where a component acts directly within the oscillator loops.

Arginine catabolism via arginase and ornithine aminotransferaseMODULE:arginine_catabolism_arginase_pathwayCONCRETE The arginase pathway degrades L-arginine to L-glutamate (or, without oxygen, to L-proline) and lets eukaryotes use arginine as a nitrogen source....
[more...][less] The arginase pathway degrades L-arginine to L-glutamate (or, without oxygen, to L-proline) and lets eukaryotes use arginine as a nitrogen source. Manganese-dependent arginase hydrolyzes L-arginine to L-ornithine and urea. Pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent ornithine aminotransferase then transfers the delta-amino group of ornithine to 2-oxoglutarate, forming L-glutamate and L-glutamate 5-semialdehyde, which cyclizes non-enzymatically to delta-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate (P5C). How P5C reaches glutamate depends on where the enzymes sit. In fungi, arginase and ornithine aminotransferase are cytosolic: P5C is first reduced to proline by P5C reductase, and proline is then oxidized back to P5C and on to glutamate by mitochondrial proline dehydrogenase and P5C dehydrogenase. Proline oxidation needs the respiratory chain, so under anaerobic conditions the pathway stops at proline. Where ornithine aminotransferase is mitochondrial (animals, plants), P5C dehydrogenase can oxidize the semialdehyde directly. Urea goes on to urea-degrading enzymes and is outside the module.

Arp2/3 complex in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_arp2_3_complexCONCRETE The Arp2/3 complex is a seven-subunit actin nucleator that binds the side of an existing actin filament and starts a new filament at a 70 degree...
[more...][less] The Arp2/3 complex is a seven-subunit actin nucleator that binds the side of an existing actin filament and starts a new filament at a 70 degree angle, producing branched actin networks. Two actin-related proteins, Arp2 and Arp3, form the template for the daughter filament, while the five ARPC subunits (ARPC1-ARPC5) hold them in place and contact the mother filament. The complex is intrinsically inactive and is switched on by nucleation-promoting factors such as SCAR/WAVE and WASp. In Drosophila, Arp2/3-driven branched actin is needed for lamellipodia, ring canal growth, myoblast fusion and many other processes. Drosophila has two ARPC3 paralogs, Arpc3A and Arpc3B, so two forms of the complex are possible.

Assimilatory sulfate reduction to sulfide (APS and PAPS routes)MODULE:aps_dependent_assimilatory_sulfate_reduction A reusable pathway that reduces inorganic sulfate to sulfide for incorporation into sulfur amino acids. Sulfate is first activated by ATP...
[more...][less] A reusable pathway that reduces inorganic sulfate to sulfide for incorporation into sulfur amino acids. Sulfate is first activated by ATP sulfurylase to adenosine 5'-phosphosulfate (APS), because the sulfate/sulfite couple is too electronegative for reduction by physiological donors. The activated sulfate is then reduced to sulfite by one of two routes: directly, by a thioredoxin-dependent APS reductase (many bacteria, and plants), or after phosphorylation of APS by APS kinase to 3'-phosphoadenosine 5'-phosphosulfate (PAPS), by a thioredoxin-dependent PAPS reductase that releases sulfite and adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate (enterobacteria and fungi). Finally a siroheme- and iron-sulfur-containing sulfite reductase performs the six-electron reduction of sulfite to sulfide, receiving electrons either from NADPH through a flavoprotein subunit (enterobacterial CysJ/CysI and the fungal Met10/Met5 alpha2beta2 enzyme) or from reduced ferredoxin. ATP sulfurylase itself is either a heterodimeric GTPase-coupled CysD/CysN enzyme (proteobacteria) or a homo-oligomeric enzyme (fungi, plants and many bacteria). Sulfate import is upstream; siroheme synthesis, thioredoxin regeneration, recycling of adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate, and incorporation of sulfide into homocysteine or cysteine are supporting or downstream biology outside the pathway boundary.

Autonomous flowering pathway repressing FLOWERING LOCUS C (Arabidopsis)MODULE:autonomous_flowering_pathwayCONCRETE The autonomous pathway is the set of photoperiod-independent Arabidopsis flowering promoters whose common output is quantitative repression of the...
[more...][less] The autonomous pathway is the set of photoperiod-independent Arabidopsis flowering promoters whose common output is quantitative repression of the MADS-box floral repressor FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC). It couples co-transcriptional RNA 3'-end processing to chromatin silencing. At FLC, the nuclear RRM/WW RNA-binding protein FCA binds the nascent antisense COOLAIR transcripts in liquid-like nuclear bodies and engages the CPSF subunit FY (WDR33/Pfs2p) through FY's C-terminal PPLPP motifs. This directs cleavage and polyadenylation to the promoter-proximal antisense poly(A) site. The spen-family RNA-binding protein FPA acts redundantly with FCA on poly(A) site choice. Proximal termination is handed over to a chromatin module made up of the LSD1-type H3K4 demethylase FLD, LUMINIDEPENDENS (LD, a Ref2/PNUTS-like subunit linked to an APRF1/TOPP4 CPF-like phosphatase module) and SDG26, which contacts FY. FLD/LD/SDG26 remove H3K4me1 over the FLC gene body, which reduces H3K36me3 and transcription and favours Polycomb (PRC2) H3K27me3. The RbAp48-like histone binding protein FVE (MSI4) promotes FLC repression as a shared subunit of HDA5/HDA6-FLD histone deacetylase complexes and of a CLF-PRC2. Repressed FLC releases its repression of the floral integrators FT and SOC1, so the pathway promotes flowering. FRIGIDA-mediated FLC activation, cold-induced vernalization silencing (VIN3/VRN-PRC2), photoperiod signalling and the FT/SOC1-triggered meristem identity program are outside this module. Here FLC, FT and SOC1 appear only as the regulated output.

[more...][less] Macroautophagy begins with formation of a cup-shaped phagophore that expands and closes to form the double-membrane autophagosome. The core Atg proteins act in conserved functional units. The Atg1 kinase complex (Atg1, Atg13, Atg17/FIP200 and Atg101) initiates phagophore formation in response to nutrient starvation and TOR inhibition. The class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase complex (Vps34/Pi3K59F, Vps15, Atg6/Beclin 1 and Atg14) produces phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate at the phagophore. Atg9 vesicles supply membrane and Atg9 has phospholipid scramblase activity, while Atg2, recruited with the PI3P-binding Atg18 proteins, transfers lipids to the expanding phagophore. Two ubiquitin-like conjugation systems act downstream: Atg7 and Atg10 conjugate Atg12 to Atg5, and the Atg12-Atg5-Atg16 complex promotes lipidation of Atg8 proteins with phosphatidylethanolamine by Atg7 and Atg3 after processing of Atg8 by the Atg4 proteases. In Drosophila, the fat body of starved larvae is the classic setting for studying this pathway.

Axonemal outer and inner dynein arms in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_axonemal_dynein_armsCONCRETE Axonemal dyneins are the motors that bend motile cilia and flagella. They are attached in rows along the doublet microtubules of the 9+2 axoneme as...
[more...][less] Axonemal dyneins are the motors that bend motile cilia and flagella. They are attached in rows along the doublet microtubules of the 9+2 axoneme as outer dynein arms, which mainly set beat frequency, and inner dynein arms, which mainly shape the waveform. Each arm contains one or more dynein heavy chains, the ATP-driven motor subunits, together with intermediate and light chains that anchor the arm and regulate it. In Drosophila, motile axonemes are found only in sperm flagella and in the cilia of chordotonal mechanosensory neurons, so axonemal dyneins act in male fertility and hearing. Several sperm-specific heavy chains are encoded by the Y-chromosome fertility factors kl-2, kl-3 and kl-5.

BBSome ciliary trafficking complex moduleMODULE:bbsome The BBSome is a conserved octameric protein complex that acts as a coat-like adaptor for ciliary membrane-protein trafficking. It is built from...
[more...][less] The BBSome is a conserved octameric protein complex that acts as a coat-like adaptor for ciliary membrane-protein trafficking. It is built from eight core subunits (BBS1, BBS2, BBS4, BBS5, BBS7, BBS8/TTC8, BBS9, and BBIP1/BBS18), assembled with the help of a dedicated chaperonin-like module (BBS6/MKKS, BBS10, BBS12 acting with the CCT/TRiC chaperonin). Once assembled, the BBSome is recruited to the ciliary membrane by the GTP-bound Arf-like GTPase ARL6/BBS3, where it polymerizes into a coat that recognizes signaling-receptor cargo (ciliary GPCRs and Hedgehog-pathway components) and couples them to the intraflagellar transport (IFT) machinery, mediating ciliary import and export of receptors out of the cilium. LZTFL1/BBS17 regulates BBSome ciliary trafficking, and CCDC28B is a BBSome-associated accessory factor. Loss of BBSome function causes Bardet-Biedl syndrome. This module models the BBSome as a cellular component / protein complex grounded in GO:0034464, capturing its composition, assembly, membrane recruitment, cargo trafficking, and regulation.

BLOC and BORC complexes in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_bloc_borc_complexesCONCRETE The biogenesis of lysosome-related organelles complexes BLOC-1, BLOC-2 and BLOC-3 are needed to form lysosome-related organelles such as...
[more...][less] The biogenesis of lysosome-related organelles complexes BLOC-1, BLOC-2 and BLOC-3 are needed to form lysosome-related organelles such as melanosomes in mammals and pigment granules in Drosophila eyes. BLOC-1 is an eight-subunit complex of small coiled-coil proteins (including dysbindin, pallidin, muted and snapin) that cooperates with endosomal sorting to deliver cargo to these organelles. BLOC-2 contains the HPS3, HPS5 and HPS6 subunits in mammals; the Drosophila HPS5 homolog is pink (p). BLOC-3, a heterodimer of HPS1 and HPS4, is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor for Rab32 and Rab38 in mammals. BORC is a related complex that shares Blos1, Blos2 and Snapin with BLOC-1 and adds BORCS5, BORCS6, BORCS7, BORCS8 and KXD1 subunits; it recruits Arl8 to lysosomes and controls their positioning.

BMP signaling pathway in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_bmp_signalingCONCRETE Bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signaling in Drosophila is triggered by the ligands Decapentaplegic (Dpp), Glass bottom boat (Gbb) and Screw...
[more...][less] Bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signaling in Drosophila is triggered by the ligands Decapentaplegic (Dpp), Glass bottom boat (Gbb) and Screw (Scw), which act as homo- or heterodimers. Ligands bind heteromeric complexes of type I receptor kinases (Thickveins, Saxophone) and type II receptor kinases (Punt, Wishful thinking). The activated type I receptor phosphorylates the receptor-regulated SMAD Mad, which forms a complex with the co-SMAD Medea and accumulates in the nucleus. With the zinc-finger protein Schnurri, the Mad-Medea complex represses brinker and activates other targets. The pathway patterns the dorsal-ventral axis of the embryo and the wing imaginal disc, maintains germline stem cells, and regulates synaptic growth at the neuromuscular junction, where Gbb and Wishful thinking act.

[more...][less] The bacterial nitrogen-regulatory (Ntr) system, which couples intracellular nitrogen status to the sigma-54-dependent nitrogen-scavenging regulon. A PII-family signal transduction protein integrates nitrogen and carbon/energy status through 2-oxoglutarate, ATP and ADP binding and through reversible uridylylation, and relays that status to the sensor histidine kinase NtrB by modulating its kinase/phosphatase balance. NtrB phosphorylates the conserved receiver aspartate of NtrC, and phosphorylated NtrC uses its AAA+ enhancer-binding module together with the sigma-54 holoenzyme to open -24/-12 promoters, inducing ammonium scavenging and ammonia assimilation. The module covers signal integration, His->Asp phosphotransfer, sigma-54-dependent activation, and the immediate assimilatory output.

Bacterial beta-aryl ether cleavage of lignin-derived dimersMODULE:bacterial_beta_aryl_ether_dimer_cleavageCONCRETE A reusable bacterial module for glutathione-dependent cleavage of the beta-O-4 (beta-aryl ether) interunit linkage of lignin-derived aromatic...
[more...][less] A reusable bacterial module for glutathione-dependent cleavage of the beta-O-4 (beta-aryl ether) interunit linkage of lignin-derived aromatic dimers, exemplified by guaiacylglycerol-beta-guaiacyl ether (GGE). The module has three reaction steps. An NAD+-dependent Calpha-dehydrogenase oxidizes the benzylic Calpha hydroxyl of the dimer to give the ketone alpha-(2-methoxyphenoxy)-beta-hydroxypropiovanillone (MPHPV). A glutathione S-transferase beta-etherase then displaces the aryloxy leaving group at Cbeta with glutathione, releasing guaiacol and alpha-glutathionyl-beta-hydroxypropiovanillone (GS-HPV). Finally a glutathione lyase removes the glutathione moiety using a second glutathione, yielding the achiral monomer beta-hydroxypropiovanillone (HPV) and glutathione disulfide. Because the lignin polymer is racemic at Calpha and Cbeta, each step is implemented by a set of stereochemically complementary enzymes, modeled as variants. Uptake of the dimer, downstream catabolism of HPV and guaiacol to vanillate and protocatechuate, glutathione regeneration, and pathways for other interunit linkages are outside the boundary.

Bacterial cyclic di-AMP second-messenger signallingMODULE:bacterial_c_di_amp_signalingABSTRACT A reusable second-messenger motif, predominantly of Gram-positive bacteria, in which cyclic di-AMP (c-di-AMP) reports ionic and osmotic...
[more...][less] A reusable second-messenger motif, predominantly of Gram-positive bacteria, in which cyclic di-AMP (c-di-AMP) reports ionic and osmotic sufficiency. Diadenylate cyclases condense two ATP molecules into c-di-AMP; the membrane-anchored CdaA/DacA class is the only cyclase in many Firmicutes, while DisA and CdaS are additional cytoplasmic classes in spore-formers. Degradation is two-tiered: DHH/DHHA1 phosphodiesterases of the GdpP class, and the unrelated 7TMR-HD PgpH class, open c-di-AMP to the linear dinucleotide pApA, and a second cytoplasmic DHH/DHHA1 enzyme (Pde2/NrnA class) clears pApA to AMP, which matters because pApA feedback-inhibits GdpP. Receptors convert c-di-AMP binding into inhibition of potassium and compatible-solute uptake: RCK_C-domain gating subunits of Ktr/Trk potassium systems and of cation/proton antiporters, the USP domain of the KdpD sensor kinase, the tandem CBS domains of the OpuC ATPase, and the PII-like receptors DarA/PstA. Because every characterised receptor restrains an uptake system, high c-di-AMP corresponds to restrained turgor and a reinforced envelope, and both depletion and accumulation impair fitness.

Bacterial cyclic di-GMP second-messenger signallingMODULE:bacterial_c_di_gmp_signalingABSTRACT A reusable bacterial second-messenger motif in which the intracellular level of cyclic di-GMP (c-di-GMP) is set by the opposing activities of...
[more...][less] A reusable bacterial second-messenger motif in which the intracellular level of cyclic di-GMP (c-di-GMP) is set by the opposing activities of synthesising and degrading enzymes and read out by dedicated receptor proteins. GGDEF-domain diguanylate cyclases condense two GTP molecules into c-di-GMP, usually as dimers and often under non-competitive product inhibition at an allosteric I-site in the GGDEF domain. Two unrelated phosphodiesterase families turn the signal over: EAL-domain enzymes hydrolyse c-di-GMP to linear pGpG, and HD-GYP-domain enzymes hydrolyse it via pGpG towards GMP. Receptors convert c-di-GMP binding into a change in the activity of a downstream target; well-characterised protein receptor classes are PilZ-domain proteins and proteins carrying catalytically degenerate GGDEF or EAL domains that retain c-di-GMP binding. The cyclases and phosphodiesterases typically carry N-terminal sensory domains, so the motif integrates many environmental inputs, and many receptors act on motility, adhesion, exopolysaccharide synthesis and virulence outputs that are modelled as separate modules.

Bacterial sulfoquinovose catabolism (sulfoglycolysis and sulfo-SMO)MODULE:bacterial_sulfoquinovose_catabolismCONCRETE A reusable bacterial module for breakdown of sulfoquinovose (SQ; 6-deoxy-6-sulfo-D-glucose), the polar head group of the plant and cyanobacterial...
[more...][less] A reusable bacterial module for breakdown of sulfoquinovose (SQ; 6-deoxy-6-sulfo-D-glucose), the polar head group of the plant and cyanobacterial sulfolipid sulfoquinovosyl diacylglycerol. An optional glycoside hydrolase first releases free SQ from sulfoquinovosyl glycerides. SQ is then consumed by one of several alternative, biochemically characterized routes. Three C-C bond cleavage (sulfoglycolytic) routes split the C6 sulfosugar into a non-sulfonated C3 unit used for growth and the C3 organosulfonate 3-sulfolactaldehyde (SLA), which is then reduced to 2,3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate (DHPS) or oxidized to 3-sulfolactate (SL) for excretion: the sulfo-EMP route (SQ isomerase, sulfofructose kinase, sulfofructose-1-phosphate aldolase), the sulfo-ED route (SQ dehydrogenase, sulfogluconolactonase, sulfogluconate dehydratase, KDSG aldolase), and the sulfo-SFT route (SQ isomerase and sulfofructose transaldolase). In the oxidative sulfo-SMO route a two-component flavin-dependent SQ monooxygenase cleaves the C-S bond, releasing sulfite and 6-dehydroglucose, which is reduced to glucose so that all six carbons are used. Uptake, regulation, and downstream mineralization of DHPS, SL or sulfite by other enzymes or community members are outside the module boundary.

The pathway has two converging branches: a hydroxymethylpyrimidine branch in which ThiC converts an AIR-derived precursor to HMP phosphate and ThiD phosphorylates it to the diphosphate, and a thiazole branch in which Dxs, alternative ThiO or ThiH routes, sulfur-relay proteins, and ThiG form the thiazole phosphate moiety. [more...][less] A species-neutral module for delivery of a passenger protein to the surface of a diderm bacterium by the type V route. The precursor crosses the inner membrane through Sec and is held in a translocation-competent, unfolded state in the periplasm by holdase chaperones. A beta-barrel translocator, which is either a domain of the passenger's own polypeptide or a separate partner protein, is installed in the outer membrane by the BAM complex. The passenger then crosses the outer membrane through that barrel and folds on the far side. No ATP or ion gradient is available at the outer membrane, so vectorial folding of the emerging passenger supplies the directionality. Sec translocation itself, the biological activity of the displayed passenger, and the general biogenesis of outer-membrane proteins unrelated to secretion lie outside this module.

Basement membrane laminin and collagen network in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_basement_membrane_networkCONCRETE Basement membranes are sheet-like extracellular matrices beneath epithelia and around muscles and organs. Their two self-assembling networks are...
[more...][less] Basement membranes are sheet-like extracellular matrices beneath epithelia and around muscles and organs. Their two self-assembling networks are made of laminin and type IV collagen. Drosophila has two laminin trimers, each made of one alpha chain (LanA or Wing blister) with the shared beta (LanB1) and gamma (LanB2) chains; laminins polymerise at the cell surface and initiate basement membrane assembly. Type IV collagen trimers of Col4a1 and Viking are made mainly by the fat body and hemocytes and then incorporated into basement membranes, where they form a cross-linked network that gives strength and shapes organs. Multiplexin (the collagen XV/XVIII homolog) and Pericardin (a collagen IV-like protein of the cardiac extracellular matrix) are additional collagens grouped with them.

Beta-cell glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (K-ATP triggering pathway)MODULE:beta_cell_glucose_stimulated_insulin_secretion The triggering pathway by which the pancreatic beta cell converts a rise in blood glucose into insulin release. Glucokinase phosphorylates glucose...
[more...][less] The triggering pathway by which the pancreatic beta cell converts a rise in blood glucose into insulin release. Glucokinase phosphorylates glucose at a rate that tracks the physiological glucose range and so sets the threshold of the pathway; glycolytic and mitochondrial oxidation of the resulting glucose 6-phosphate raises the cytosolic ATP/ADP ratio; the rise in ATP/ADP closes the ATP-sensitive potassium (K-ATP) channel formed by the Kir6.2 pore and the SUR1 regulatory subunit; the loss of K+ efflux depolarises the plasma membrane, opening L-type voltage-gated calcium channels; and the Ca2+ influx triggers exocytosis of insulin-containing dense-core granules. Glutamate dehydrogenase couples amino-acid (leucine/glutamine) oxidation into the same ATP/ADP signal, and the mitochondrial enzyme HADH restrains glutamate dehydrogenase; gain of the first and loss of the second both produce hyperinsulinism.

Beta-ketoadipate lower pathway from 3-oxoadipate to central metabolitesMODULE:beta_ketoadipate_lower_pathwayCONCRETE Species-neutral bacterial module for the shared lower beta-ketoadipate pathway that converts 3-oxoadipate and CoA to acetyl-CoA and succinate while...
[more...][less] Species-neutral bacterial module for the shared lower beta-ketoadipate pathway that converts 3-oxoadipate and CoA to acetyl-CoA and succinate while recycling a succinyl-CoA CoA donor. A two-subunit PcaIJ-like CoA-transferase first transfers CoA from succinyl-CoA to 3-oxoadipate, producing 3-oxoadipyl-CoA and succinate. A PcaF-like thiolase then cleaves 3-oxoadipyl-CoA with CoA to acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA, regenerating the donor consumed in the first reaction. The module begins after catechol- and protocatechuate-derived upper branches converge at 3-oxoadipate and excludes those branch-specific ring-cleavage reactions.

Bidirectional transsulfuration between homocysteine and cysteine (fungal)MODULE:fungal_sulfur_amino_acid_transsulfuration Interconversion of L-homocysteine and L-cysteine through the thioether intermediate L-cystathionine, catalysed by four pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP)...
[more...][less] Interconversion of L-homocysteine and L-cysteine through the thioether intermediate L-cystathionine, catalysed by four pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) dependent enzymes acting in two opposite directions. In the homocysteine-to-cysteine direction, cystathionine beta-synthase condenses L-homocysteine with L-serine to L-cystathionine, and cystathionine gamma-lyase cleaves cystathionine to L-cysteine, 2-oxobutanoate and ammonia; this transfers the sulfur atom of methionine-derived homocysteine onto the serine carbon skeleton and is the only transsulfuration route of mammals. In the cysteine-to-homocysteine direction, cystathionine gamma-synthase condenses L-cysteine with an O-acylated L-homoserine to cystathionine, and cystathionine beta-lyase cleaves cystathionine to L-homocysteine, pyruvate and ammonia; this is the main route to homocysteine in enteric bacteria and plants. Budding yeast and other fungi that assimilate reduced sulfur primarily into the four-carbon chain of homocysteine (by direct sulfhydrylation of O-acetylhomoserine) possess both directions, so they can make cysteine from homocysteine and can also use cysteine as a sole sulfur source for methionine synthesis. Other lineages carry only one direction, and the module is therefore satisfied by either direction or by both.

Bile acid synthesis I — ring modification (cholesterol -> 5-beta-cholestane intermediates); CYP7A1/CYP7B1/HSD3B7/AKR1D1MODULE:bile_acid_synthesis_ring_modification The first phase of bile-acid biosynthesis modifies the cholesterol steroid nucleus, producing the 7-alpha-hydroxylated, 3-oxo, 5-beta-reduced...
[more...][less] The first phase of bile-acid biosynthesis modifies the cholesterol steroid nucleus, producing the 7-alpha-hydroxylated, 3-oxo, 5-beta-reduced cholestane intermediates that are later shortened in the side chain to the C24 bile acids. Two entry routes converge: the CLASSIC (neutral) pathway begins with cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP7A1), the rate-limiting, feedback-regulated enzyme that hydroxylates cholesterol at C7-alpha; the ACIDIC (alternative) pathway begins when oxysterols (25- and 27-hydroxycholesterol, from CH25H/CYP27A1) are 7-alpha-hydroxylated by oxysterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP7B1). The 7-alpha-hydroxy sterols are then oxidised and isomerised by the 3-beta-hydroxy-Delta5-C27- steroid dehydrogenase HSD3B7 to the 3-oxo-Delta4 intermediate (7-alpha-hydroxy-4-cholesten- 3-one), and the Delta4 double bond is reduced to the 5-beta configuration by steroid 5-beta-reductase (AKR1D1), giving the cis-fused (5-beta) A/B ring junction characteristic of bile acids. (CYP8B1 branches here to specify cholic vs chenodeoxycholic acid.) Inherited defects: CYP7A1 deficiency (hypercholesterolemia/gallstones); CYP7B1 deficiency (hereditary spastic paraplegia type 5A and severe neonatal liver failure); HSD3B7 deficiency (congenital bile acid synthesis defect type 1); and AKR1D1 deficiency (bile acid synthesis defect type 2) — the HSD3B7/AKR1D1 defects present as neonatal cholestasis with fat-soluble-vitamin malabsorption.

Bile acid synthesis II — side-chain oxidation, peroxisomal shortening and amino-acid conjugation; CYP27A1/AMACR/ACOX2/SLC27A5/BAATMODULE:bile_acid_synthesis_sidechain_conjugation After the sterol nucleus of cholesterol has been hydroxylated (the ring-modification segment: CYP7A1/CYP7B1/HSD3B7/AKR1D1), the C27 side chain must...
[more...][less] After the sterol nucleus of cholesterol has been hydroxylated (the ring-modification segment: CYP7A1/CYP7B1/HSD3B7/AKR1D1), the C27 side chain must be oxidised and shortened by three carbons to give the mature C24 bile acids, which are then conjugated to an amino acid before secretion. Mitochondrial sterol 27-hydroxylase (CYP27A1) initiates side-chain oxidation, hydroxylating C27 of the 5beta-cholestane-3alpha,7alpha,12alpha-triol (and the 7alpha-hydroxy-diol) and further oxidising it to the C27 bile-acid intermediates 3alpha,7alpha,12alpha-trihydroxy-5beta-cholestanoic acid (THCA) and its 12-deoxy congener DHCA. These C27 acids are activated to their CoA thioesters and imported into the peroxisome, where alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase (AMACR) converts the (25R) diastereomer to the (25S) form required for beta-oxidation, and the peroxisomal branched-chain acyl-CoA oxidase ACOX2 catalyses the first (oxidase) step of one round of beta-oxidation; the downstream MFP2/SCPx steps release propionyl-CoA to give the C24 bile-acyl-CoAs choloyl-CoA and chenodeoxychenoyl-CoA. Bile acid-CoA:amino acid N-acyltransferase (BAAT) then transfers the C24 bile acid from CoA onto glycine or taurine, forming the glyco- and tauro-conjugated bile salts that are the major biliary species; the ER-membrane bile acyl-CoA synthetase SLC27A5 (cholate-CoA ligase / FATP5) re-activates free bile acids to their CoA esters, chiefly in the enterohepatic recycling loop, feeding BAAT for re-conjugation. Inherited defects across this segment cause cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (CYP27A1), AMACR deficiency (an adult sensorimotor neuropathy with bile-acid abnormalities), ACOX2 deficiency (a bile-acid synthesis defect with liver disease/dystonia) and familial hypercholanemia / bile acid conjugation defect (BAAT).

Bile-acid biosynthesis (classic + alternative pathways from cholesterol to conjugated bile acids)MODULE:bile_acid_biosynthesis Bile acids are the amphipathic end-products of hepatic cholesterol catabolism; their synthesis is the major route of cholesterol elimination and...
[more...][less] Bile acids are the amphipathic end-products of hepatic cholesterol catabolism; their synthesis is the major route of cholesterol elimination and produces the detergents that emulsify dietary lipids. Two pathways convert cholesterol to the primary bile acids cholic acid (CA) and chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA). In the CLASSIC (neutral) pathway, the rate-limiting ER cytochrome P450 CYP7A1 7-alpha-hydroxylates cholesterol; HSD3B7 then oxidises/isomerises the 3-beta-hydroxy-Delta5 sterol to a 3-oxo-Delta4 intermediate; the branch-point enzyme CYP8B1 (sterol 12-alpha-hydroxylase) 12-alpha-hydroxylates that intermediate to commit flux toward CA (its absence yields CDCA), setting the CA:CDCA ratio; AKR1D1 (Delta4-3-oxosteroid 5-beta-reductase) and AKR1C4 (3-alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase) then reduce the A/B-ring to the 5-beta-3-alpha-hydroxy configuration. In the ALTERNATIVE (acidic) pathway, the sterol side chain is oxidised first: the mitochondrial CYP27A1 (sterol 27-hydroxylase), the ER di-iron enzyme CH25H (25-hydroxylase) and the neuron-specific CYP46A1 (24-hydroxylase, the main route of brain cholesterol elimination) generate oxysterols, which the oxysterol 7-alpha-hydroxylases CYP7B1 (25-/27-OHC) and CYP39A1 (24S-OHC) route into bile-acid synthesis. Both pathways converge on side-chain shortening: CYP27A1 oxidises the C27 side chain to a C27 acid, AMACR racemises the (25R)- to the (25S)-acyl-CoA, and peroxisomal beta-oxidation (ACOX2 -> the D-bifunctional protein -> the SCPx thiolase, curated in the peroxisomal module) removes a propionyl unit to give the C24 bile-acyl-CoA. Finally the bile acid is activated by the CoA ligase SLC27A5 (BACS) and conjugated to glycine or taurine by BAAT. Inherited defects across the pathway cause bile-acid synthesis disorders: CYP7B1 (oxysterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency / SPG5), HSD3B7, AKR1D1, ACOX2, BAAT and SLC27A5 deficiencies, and CYP27A1 causes cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis.

Bioactive gibberellin (GA4/GA1) biosynthesis from geranylgeranyl diphosphateMODULE:gibberellin_biosynthesisABSTRACT Biosynthesis of the bioactive gibberellins GA4 and GA1 in vascular plants from the plastid diterpene precursor (E,E,E)-geranylgeranyl diphosphate...
[more...][less] Biosynthesis of the bioactive gibberellins GA4 and GA1 in vascular plants from the plastid diterpene precursor (E,E,E)-geranylgeranyl diphosphate (GGPP), decomposed into three compartment-defined stages that use three enzyme classes. (1) In the plastid stroma two terpene cyclases make the tetracyclic hydrocarbon ent-kaurene: the class II cyclase ent-copalyl diphosphate synthase (CPS) converts GGPP to ent-copalyl diphosphate (the first committed step) and the class I cyclase ent-kaurene synthase (KS) converts ent-CPP to ent-kaurene with release of diphosphate. (2) Two multifunctional cytochrome P450 monooxygenases at the plastid envelope and endoplasmic reticulum oxidize ent-kaurene to GA12: ent-kaurene oxidase (KO, CYP701A) performs three oxidations of C-19 to give ent-kaurenoic acid, and ent-kaurenoic acid oxidase (KAO, CYP88A) performs three further oxidations, including B-ring contraction, to give GA12, the first gibberellin. (3) Soluble 2-oxoglutarate/Fe(II)-dependent dioxygenases in the cytosol complete the pathway: GA 20-oxidase (GA20ox) oxidizes and removes C-20 of GA12 (via GA15 and GA24) to give the C19 gibberellin GA9, and GA 3-oxidase (GA3ox) 3beta-hydroxylates GA9 to bioactive GA4. The same two dioxygenases act on the 13-hydroxylated series (GA53 to GA20 to GA1). The early stages are encoded by single or few genes, whereas GA20ox and GA3ox are multigene families whose transcription is the main point of control of bioactive GA levels (feedback repression through DELLA signaling, light and developmental regulation). GGPP supply, GA 13-hydroxylation, GA 2-oxidase and other deactivation routes, GA transport, and GA perception/DELLA signaling are outside this module's boundary.

Biological nitrogen cycle moduleMODULE:nitrogen_cycle A taxon-neutral decomposition of the biological nitrogen cycle: the set of microbially driven redox transformations that interconvert dinitrogen,...
[more...][less] A taxon-neutral decomposition of the biological nitrogen cycle: the set of microbially driven redox transformations that interconvert dinitrogen, ammonia, hydroxylamine, nitrite, nitrate, nitric oxide, nitrous oxide, and hydrazine. The module is organized by transformation (fixation, nitrification, denitrification, DNRA, anammox, assimilatory reduction, and ammonification) rather than by organism, and uses variant sets where convergent enzyme chemistries (e.g. cd1 vs Cu nitrite reductase) implement the same step. Leaf steps are grounded to canonical reviewed Swiss-Prot exemplars where one exists; abstract function selectors are used where no reviewed exemplar is available (nitrite-oxidizer NXR). Companion to projects/NITROGEN_CYCLE.md and the GO:0071941 obsoletion project (projects/NITROGEN_CYCLE_OBSOLETION.md).

Biotin cycle — holocarboxylase synthetase and biotinidase (multiple carboxylase deficiency)MODULE:biotin_cycle The biotin cycle activates and recycles the cofactor biotin for the five human biotin-dependent carboxylases, and its two enzymes are the causes of...
[more...][less] The biotin cycle activates and recycles the cofactor biotin for the five human biotin-dependent carboxylases, and its two enzymes are the causes of multiple carboxylase deficiency. Holocarboxylase synthetase (HLCS, biotin-protein ligase) covalently attaches biotin to a specific lysine in the biotin-carboxyl-carrier domain of each apo-carboxylase — pyruvate carboxylase (PC), propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCCA/PCCB), 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase (MCCC1/MCCC2) and the cytosolic and mitochondrial acetyl-CoA carboxylases (ACACA, ACACB) — via a two-step reaction (biotin + ATP -> biotinyl-5'-AMP, then transfer to the carrier lysine), converting inactive apo-enzymes to active holo-carboxylases. When these holo-carboxylases are proteolytically degraded, the biotin remains bound as biocytin (biotinyl-lysine) or short biotinyl-peptides; biotinidase (BTD) hydrolyses these to liberate free biotin for reuse, and also releases dietary protein-bound biotin, making it bioavailable. Free biotin then re-enters the cycle as the HLCS substrate. Inherited deficiency of either enzyme produces multiple carboxylase deficiency (simultaneous functional loss of all biotin carboxylases, with lactic acidosis and organic aciduria): HLCS deficiency is the early-onset (neonatal) form, and BTD (biotinidase) deficiency is the late-onset form — a classic treatable, newborn-screened disorder rescued by biotin supplementation.

Brahma (SWI/SNF) chromatin remodeling complexes in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_brahma_complexesCONCRETE Brahma complexes are the Drosophila SWI/SNF-family ATP-dependent chromatin remodelers. They use the Brahma (brm) ATPase to slide or evict...
[more...][less] Brahma complexes are the Drosophila SWI/SNF-family ATP-dependent chromatin remodelers. They use the Brahma (brm) ATPase to slide or evict nucleosomes, making DNA accessible to transcription factors, and act as trithorax group regulators that oppose Polycomb silencing. All forms share a core of brm, Moira, Bap55, Bap60, Brd7-9 and actin. The BAP form contains the ARID protein Osa, the PBAP form instead contains Polybromo, Bap170 and e(y)3, and a non-canonical form (ncBAP) contains Bicra. Different forms control different target genes in development.

Branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) catabolism — transamination and the BCKDH complexMODULE:branched_chain_amino_acid_catabolism The committed, shared initial steps of the catabolism of the three branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs: L-leucine, L-isoleucine, L-valine), operating...
[more...][less] The committed, shared initial steps of the catabolism of the three branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs: L-leucine, L-isoleucine, L-valine), operating in the mitochondrial matrix. Branched-chain aminotransferase (BCAT2, the mitochondrial isozyme; BCAT1 is cytosolic) first reversibly transaminates each BCAA with 2-oxoglutarate to the corresponding branched-chain 2-oxo (alpha-keto) acid (BCKA: alpha-ketoisocaproate from Leu, alpha-keto-beta- methylvalerate from Ile, alpha-ketoisovalerate from Val) plus L-glutamate. The branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKDH) complex — a large mitochondrial multienzyme complex homologous to the pyruvate and 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes — then catalyses the irreversible, rate-limiting, committed oxidative decarboxylation of the BCKAs to the corresponding branched-chain acyl-CoA thioesters + CO2 + NADH. The complex has three catalytic components: E1 (a thiamine-pyrophosphate-dependent decarboxylase, an alpha2-beta2 heterotetramer of BCKDHA/E1-alpha and BCKDHB/E1-beta) which decarboxylates the BCKA and reductively acylates the lipoyl arm; E2 (DBT, dihydrolipoyllysine-residue (2-methylpropanoyl)transferase) which forms the structural core and transfers the acyl group to CoA; and E3 (DLD, dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase, an FAD flavoenzyme) which reoxidises the dihydrolipoyl arm and passes electrons to NAD+. E3/DLD is not BCKDH-specific: it is the common E3 shared with the pyruvate dehydrogenase, 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase and 2-oxoadipate dehydrogenase complexes and the glycine cleavage system. BCKDH flux is regulated by reversible phosphorylation of E1-alpha (inhibitory kinase BCKDK; activating phosphatase PPM1K). Inherited deficiency of BCKDHA, BCKDHB or DBT causes maple syrup urine disease (MSUD, from accumulation of BCAAs and their neurotoxic BCKAs); DLD deficiency causes a combined E3-deficiency phenotype (MSUD-like plus lactic acidosis / 2-oxoglutaric aciduria because PDH and OGDH are simultaneously impaired). Downstream, the branched-chain acyl-CoAs are degraded by substrate-specific dehydrogenases and hydratases (out of scope here) to acetyl-CoA, acetoacetate and/or succinyl-CoA (via propionyl-CoA/methylmalonyl-CoA for Ile and Val).

Brassinosteroid signal perception and relay to BZR1/BES1 transcription factorsMODULE:brassinosteroid_signalingCONCRETE Brassinosteroid (BR) signalling converts perception of a steroid hormone at the cell surface into a change in nuclear gene expression through a...
[more...][less] Brassinosteroid (BR) signalling converts perception of a steroid hormone at the cell surface into a change in nuclear gene expression through a chain of phosphorylation and dephosphorylation steps. In the absence of BR, the receptor kinase BRI1 is held inactive by its cytoplasmic inhibitor BKI1, and the constitutively active GSK3-like kinase BIN2 phosphorylates the BZR1 and BES1 transcription factors, which inhibits their DNA binding, promotes 14-3-3 binding and cytoplasmic retention, and targets them for degradation. Brassinolide binds the extracellular LRR domain of BRI1, which recruits the coreceptor kinase BAK1; transphosphorylation activates BRI1, which phosphorylates BKI1 (releasing it from the membrane) and the receptor-like cytoplasmic kinases BSK1 (and CDG1). Phosphorylated BSK1 binds the Kelch-repeat phosphatase BSU1, which (after CDG1 phosphorylation) dephosphorylates the conserved pTyr200 of BIN2 and inactivates it. With BIN2 off, PP2A dephosphorylates BZR1/BES1, which accumulate in the nucleus and bind BRRE and E-box elements to repress BR biosynthetic genes (feedback) and activate or repress thousands of growth-related genes. BR biosynthesis, receptor endocytosis/turnover, and downstream transcriptional networks are outside this module's boundary.

Budding yeast (S. cerevisiae) high-osmolarity (Ssk2-Pbs2-Hog1) MAPK cascade moduleMODULE:scer_hog1_cascade A decomposition of the Saccharomyces cerevisiae high-osmolarity glycerol (HOG) MAP kinase cascade, the osmostress-activated fungal realization of...
[more...][less] A decomposition of the Saccharomyces cerevisiae high-osmolarity glycerol (HOG) MAP kinase cascade, the osmostress-activated fungal realization of the generic three-tier MAP kinase relay (MODULE:mapk_relay). High external osmolarity is sensed by two functionally redundant upstream branches that converge on the single MAP2K Pbs2. In the Sln1 branch the hybrid histidine kinase Sln1 is constitutively active in the absence of stress and keeps phosphate flowing through the Hpt protein Ypd1 to the response regulator Ssk1, holding the cascade off; a drop in turgor silences Sln1, Ssk1 accumulates unphosphorylated and binds and activates the MAP3Ks Ssk2/Ssk22, so in this section of the pathway signalling output runs inversely to phosphorylation. In the Sho1 branch the tetraspan osmosensor Sho1, with the signalling mucins Msb2 and Hkr1 and the adaptor Ste50, assembles a membrane complex that brings the MAP3K Ste11 to Pbs2, which also acts as the scaffold of this branch. Pbs2 then dually phosphorylates the MAPK Hog1 on its TGY activation-loop motif. Active Hog1 translocates to the nucleus and activates transcription factors (Hot1, Msn2/Msn4, Sko1) that induce glycerol-biosynthesis and stress-response genes restoring osmotic balance. The kinase relay - Ssk2/Ssk22 -> Pbs2 -> Hog1 - is declared as an inner bundle that `conforms_to` mapk_relay, while the two osmosensing inputs and the Hog1 transcriptional output are this cascade's free extensions around the conforming core. Grounded in GO:0007231 (osmosensory signaling pathway).

Budding yeast (S. cerevisiae) pheromone-response (Ste11-Ste7-Fus3) MAPK cascade moduleMODULE:scer_mating_fus3_cascade A decomposition of the Saccharomyces cerevisiae pheromone-response (mating) MAP kinase cascade, the fungal realization of the generic three-tier...
[more...][less] A decomposition of the Saccharomyces cerevisiae pheromone-response (mating) MAP kinase cascade, the fungal realization of the generic three-tier MAP kinase relay (MODULE:mapk_relay). Mating pheromone (a-factor or alpha-factor) activates a G-protein-coupled receptor (Ste2/Ste3); the released G-protein beta-gamma dimer and the PAK kinase Ste20, organized on the scaffold Ste5, activate the MAP3K Ste11, which phosphorylates the MAP2K Ste7, which dually phosphorylates the MAPK Fus3 (and the partially redundant Kss1) on its TEY activation-loop motif. Active Fus3 phosphorylates the transcription factor Ste12 and the cell-cycle inhibitor Far1, driving the mating transcriptional program, G1 arrest, and polarized shmoo formation for conjugation. The kinase relay - Ste11 -> Ste7 -> Fus3 - is declared as an inner bundle that `conforms_to` mapk_relay, while the pheromone/GPCR input and the Ste12/Far1 output are this cascade's free extensions around the conforming core. Grounded in GO:0071507 (pheromone response MAPK cascade); the pre-composed term GO:0000750 (pheromone-dependent signal transduction involved in conjugation with cellular fusion) was obsoleted in GO release 2026-05-19 with replaced_by GO:0071507.

CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_ccr4_not_complexCONCRETE CCR4-NOT is the major cytoplasmic mRNA deadenylase in eukaryotes and also acts in transcription and translational repression. Its large scaffold...
[more...][less] CCR4-NOT is the major cytoplasmic mRNA deadenylase in eukaryotes and also acts in transcription and translational repression. Its large scaffold subunit Not1 binds two deadenylases, Pop2 (CAF1) and twin (CCR4), which shorten poly(A) tails, the first step of most mRNA decay. Not1 also binds Rcd-1 (CNOT9), Not10 and Not11, and a NOT module of Rga (Not2) and Not3. RNA-binding proteins, microRNA silencing complexes and translational repressors recruit CCR4-NOT to specific mRNAs; in Drosophila it controls maternal mRNA decay and germline stem cell maintenance.

CCT/TRiC chaperonin-mediated foldingMODULE:cct_chaperonin_foldingCONCRETE The chaperonin containing TCP-1 (CCT, also called TRiC) is the group II chaperonin of the eukaryotic cytosol. It is a double ring of two...
[more...][less] The chaperonin containing TCP-1 (CCT, also called TRiC) is the group II chaperonin of the eukaryotic cytosol. It is a double ring of two hetero-octameric rings, each made of one copy of eight paralogous subunits (CCT1/alpha to CCT8/theta), and this subunit set is conserved from yeast to nematodes and mammals. Each subunit has an equatorial ATP-binding domain, an intermediate hinge and an apical client-binding domain with a built-in lid, so CCT closes its folding chamber without a separate co-chaperonin. Cycles of ATP binding and hydrolysis drive lid closure and folding of clients held in the chamber. Nucleotide use is asymmetric: only four subunits (CCT1, CCT2, CCT4 and CCT5) bind ATP at physiological concentrations, and ATP binding by the other four is dispensable in vivo. The main obligate clients are actin and tubulin. Nascent actin and tubulin chains are captured by prefoldin (GimC in budding yeast), a jellyfish-shaped heterohexamer of two alpha-class and four beta-class subunits that binds non-native chains without ATP, docks on CCT and hands them over, raising the rate and yield of folding. In yeast, loss of prefoldin or CCT impairs actin- and tubulin-based cytoskeletal functions. In C. elegans, CCT depletion disrupts actin and microtubule organization and causes intestinal microvillus loss, prefoldin loss lowers alpha-tubulin levels and slows microtubule growth, and raising the CCT8 subunit level in somatic tissues extends lifespan in a CCT-dependent way.

CDP-diacylglycerol pathway of phospholipid synthesis (PS, PE, PC by methylation, PI, PG and cardiolipin)MODULE:cdp_dag_phospholipid_synthesisCONCRETE In the CDP-diacylglycerol (CDP-DAG) pathway, phosphatidic acid is activated with CTP to the liponucleotide CDP-DAG, which then donates its...
[more...][less] In the CDP-diacylglycerol (CDP-DAG) pathway, phosphatidic acid is activated with CTP to the liponucleotide CDP-DAG, which then donates its phosphatidyl group to a polar head-group acceptor, releasing CMP. Different CDP-alcohol phosphatidyltransferases use serine (phosphatidylserine synthase), myo-inositol (phosphatidylinositol synthase) and glycerol-3-phosphate (phosphatidylglycerophosphate synthase). In the aminophospholipid branch, phosphatidylserine (PS) is decarboxylated to phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) by pyruvoyl-dependent PS decarboxylases, and PE is converted to phosphatidylcholine (PC) by three successive S-adenosylmethionine-dependent N-methylations, performed by two enzymes in fungi or by a single PEMT enzyme in animals. In the mitochondrial branch, phosphatidylglycerophosphate is dephosphorylated to phosphatidylglycerol (PG), which is condensed with a second CDP-DAG by a eukaryotic CDP-alcohol phosphotransferase-type cardiolipin synthase to form cardiolipin. The pathway is distributed between compartments: CDP-DAG for PS and PI is made in the endoplasmic reticulum, whereas cardiolipin synthesis uses CDP-DAG made in the mitochondrial inner membrane by a distinct, Tam41-type CDP-DAG synthase; the major PS decarboxylase acts in the mitochondrial inner membrane and a second one in the endomembrane system, so PS and PE must move between the ER and mitochondria. In fungi this route makes PE and PC when ethanolamine and choline are not supplied, whereas the Kennedy pathway makes them from those precursors.

CLAVATA-WUSCHEL negative feedback loop in shoot apical meristem stem-cell homeostasisMODULE:shoot_meristem_clv_wus_feedbackCONCRETE The size of the stem-cell pool in the shoot apical meristem is held steady by a two-cell-layer negative feedback loop. The homeodomain...
[more...][less] The size of the stem-cell pool in the shoot apical meristem is held steady by a two-cell-layer negative feedback loop. The homeodomain transcription factor WUSCHEL (WUS) is made in the organizing center (OC), moves through plasmodesmata into the overlying central zone, and there both specifies stem-cell fate and directly activates CLAVATA3 (CLV3). CLV3 is processed and secreted as an arabinosylated 12/13-amino-acid CLE peptide. It is perceived at the plasma membrane of the underlying cells by parallel receptor systems: the LRR receptor kinase CLV1 and its paralogs BAM1/BAM2, which bind the peptide directly, and a heteromeric complex of the kinase-less LRR receptor-like protein CLV2 with the pseudokinase CORYNE (CRN). Whether CLV2/CRN binds the ligand directly is disputed; it acts at least as a co-receptor. Receptor signalling, relayed through CIK co-receptor kinases and PBL-type cytoplasmic kinases, represses WUS transcription and confines the OC. More stem cells therefore make more CLV3, which reduces WUS and so limits stem-cell number. When CLV1 is lost, BAM genes are de-repressed in the meristem centre and partly compensate. The KNOX homeodomain protein SHOOT MERISTEMLESS (STM), which keeps meristem cells undifferentiated and interacts genetically with the CLV genes, is shown only as optional context. RPK2, the CIK and PBL relay kinases, CLE processing, floral-meristem termination by AGAMOUS, and the root CLE40-ACR4 and CLE45-BAM3 pathways are outside this module boundary.

CNC/NRF oxidative and xenobiotic stress responseMODULE:nrf_oxidative_stress_responseCONCRETE A cross-species module for the oxidative and xenobiotic stress response driven by cap'n'collar (CNC) basic-leucine-zipper transcription factors:...
[more...][less] A cross-species module for the oxidative and xenobiotic stress response driven by cap'n'collar (CNC) basic-leucine-zipper transcription factors: NRF2 (NFE2L2) in vertebrates, CncC in Drosophila and SKN-1 in Caenorhabditis elegans. In unstressed cells the CNC factor is kept scarce by constitutive cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase-dependent degradation, and its nuclear activity is further restrained by glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3) phosphorylation. Two degradation arms are known. In vertebrates and insects the BTB-Kelch protein KEAP1 binds the CNC factor and presents it to a CUL3-RING ligase, and reactive KEAP1 cysteines act as sensors whose modification by oxidants and electrophiles stops degradation. Nematodes have no KEAP1; there the WD40 protein WDR-23, the ortholog of human DCAF11, restrains SKN-1 together with the CUL-4/DDB-1 (CRL4) ligase, and DCAF11 also targets human NRF2 for degradation through a separate degron. Stress-activated kinases promote nuclear accumulation of the factor; in C. elegans the NSY-1/SEK-1/PMK-1 p38 MAPK cascade phosphorylates SKN-1. Nuclear CNC factors then induce a phase II detoxification program that includes glutamate-cysteine ligase, the rate-limiting enzyme of glutathione synthesis, and glutathione S-transferases, and loss of the CNC factor makes animals sensitive to oxidative stress. NRF2 binds antioxidant response elements as a heterodimer with small MAF proteins, whereas SKN-1 binds DNA as a monomer through its Skn domain.

CRISPR-Cas adaptive immunityMODULE:crispr_cas_adaptive_immunityCONCRETE A reusable prokaryotic module for RNA-guided adaptive immunity against mobile genetic elements. The module has three obligate stages: adaptation,...
[more...][less] A reusable prokaryotic module for RNA-guided adaptive immunity against mobile genetic elements. The module has three obligate stages: adaptation, in which a Cas1-Cas2 integrase captures a protospacer from invading DNA and integrates it as a new spacer at the leader-proximal end of a CRISPR array; crRNA biogenesis, in which the transcribed array is processed into mature guides; and interference, in which a crRNA-loaded effector recognises a complementary target and destroys it. Effector architecture is the principal axis of variation and is modelled as alternative implementations rather than as separate modules: multi-subunit class 1 effectors (Cascade-Cas3, Csm/Cmr-Cas10) and single-protein class 2 effectors (Cas9, Cas12a, Cas13a) occupy the same structural slot in the pathway. Phage-encoded suppression of this module is a separate counter-defence module (MODULE:anti_crispr_suppression); host restriction-modification, BREX, retron, and other innate defence systems are outside the boundary, as is the laboratory use of Cas effectors as genome editors.

Camalexin biosynthesis (tryptophan-derived indole phytoalexin)MODULE:camalexin_biosynthesisCONCRETE Camalexin (3-thiazol-2'-yl-indole) is the main phytoalexin of Arabidopsis thaliana and is made from tryptophan after pathogen attack. The...
[more...][less] Camalexin (3-thiazol-2'-yl-indole) is the main phytoalexin of Arabidopsis thaliana and is made from tryptophan after pathogen attack. The ER-anchored cytochrome P450s CYP79B2 and CYP79B3 convert tryptophan to indole-3-acetaldoxime (IAOx), a branch point shared with indole glucosinolate and auxin biosynthesis. CYP71A13, with a minor contribution from its paralog CYP71A12, commits IAOx to the camalexin branch. It monooxygenates IAOx to an alpha-hydroxy-indole-3-acetonitrile (indole-3-cyanohydrin) intermediate and is proposed to dehydrate this to a reactive electrophile (dehydro-IAN) that is captured by the thiol of glutathione or cysteine. CYP71A13 also dehydrates IAOx to indole-3-acetonitrile (IAN), which may be largely an off-pathway product; CYP71A12 releases more of the cyanohydrin as its breakdown products indole-3-carbaldehyde and cyanide. Glutathione transferases, including GSTF6, are implicated in the conjugation, but many GSTs can support it, higher-order phi-class GST mutants make normal camalexin, and the electrophile can react with glutathione without an enzyme. The cytosolic gamma-glutamyl peptidases GGP1 and GGP3 remove the gamma-glutamyl residue of the glutathione conjugate (GS-IAN), and an unidentified peptidase removes glycine to give the cysteine conjugate Cys(IAN). The bifunctional P450 CYP71B15 (PAD3) then closes the thiazoline ring of Cys(IAN) with cyanide release to form dihydrocamalexic acid, and oxidatively decarboxylates it to camalexin. The pathway P450s associate with each other and with P450 reductase in an ER-anchored metabolon that channels intermediates. Pathogen-induced transcription of the biosynthetic genes depends on the MAP kinases MPK3 and MPK6, which phosphorylate the WRKY33 transcription factor; WRKY33 binds and activates the CYP71A13 and PAD3 promoters. These two components regulate the pathway and are not pathway enzymes.

Canonical JAK-STAT cytokine signaling pathway moduleMODULE:jak_stat_signaling A taxon-neutral decomposition of the canonical JAK-STAT signal transduction pathway, the principal route by which type I/II cytokines and many...
[more...][less] A taxon-neutral decomposition of the canonical JAK-STAT signal transduction pathway, the principal route by which type I/II cytokines and many hormones convert an extracellular signal into a direct change in gene transcription. The module is phrased as an ordered set of functions rather than a fixed gene list so it can represent the many receptor/JAK/STAT combinations that share the same mechanistic core: (1) a cytokine ligand binds and reorganizes a single-pass transmembrane receptor so that its intracellular domains are brought together; (2) receptor-associated Janus kinases (JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, TYK2) are juxtaposed and trans-activate by reciprocal tyrosine phosphorylation; (3) activated JAKs phosphorylate tyrosines on the receptor tails, creating phosphotyrosine docking sites; (4) latent cytoplasmic STAT transcription factors (STAT1-4, STAT5A, STAT5B, STAT6) are recruited via their SH2 domains and phosphorylated by the JAKs; (5) phosphorylated STATs dimerize through reciprocal SH2-phosphotyrosine contacts and translocate to the nucleus; (6) STAT dimers bind GAS/ISRE elements and drive transcription of cytokine-response genes; and (7) the response is terminated and tuned by SOCS/CIS proteins, protein tyrosine phosphatases (SHP1/SHP2, PTPN2), and PIAS SUMO ligases. Which JAKs and STATs are used is set by the receptor, captured here as variant sets along a receptor-class axis. The pathway is grounded in GO:0007259 (cell surface receptor signaling pathway via JAK-STAT).

Canonical Notch signaling pathway moduleMODULE:notch_signaling A cross-species decomposition of canonical (CSL-dependent) Notch signaling, a contact-dependent juxtacrine pathway present across eumetazoans. A...
[more...][less] A cross-species decomposition of canonical (CSL-dependent) Notch signaling, a contact-dependent juxtacrine pathway present across eumetazoans. A membrane-bound DSL-type ligand on a signal-sending cell is ubiquitylated by a Mind bomb or Neuralized E3 ligase and endocytosed; the resulting pulling force on the bound Notch receptor of the neighboring cell unfolds its negative regulatory region, exposing the S2 site to an ADAM10-family metalloprotease. The membrane-tethered remnant is then cut within its transmembrane segment by gamma-secretase, releasing the Notch intracellular domain (NICD). NICD enters the nucleus, binds the DNA-bound CSL transcription factor (RBPJ, Su(H), LAG-1), and together with a Mastermind-family coactivator converts CSL from a corepressor-bound repressor into an activator of target genes, prominently the HES/E(spl) and HEY bHLH repressors. Receptor competence is set beforehand in the ER and Golgi by POFUT1-type O-fucosylation and, in arthropods and vertebrates, by Fringe elongation of those O-fucose glycans, which tunes receptor responsiveness to Delta- versus Serrate/Jagged-type ligands. The module is written so that each role is a union over the lineage-specific implementations found in vertebrates, insects, nematodes, and cnidarians.

Cardiac specification transcriptional network moduleMODULE:cardiac_specification_network The evolutionarily conserved core transcriptional network that specifies cardiac progenitors in the mesoderm and launches their myocardial...
[more...][less] The evolutionarily conserved core transcriptional network that specifies cardiac progenitors in the mesoderm and launches their myocardial differentiation. An NK-2 class homeodomain factor (Drosophila Tinman, vertebrate NKX2-5) acts with a cardiogenic GATA zinc-finger factor (Pannier, GATA4) and T-box factors (Dorsocross, TBX5/TBX20) in a mutually cross-regulating set; these factors physically associate and synergistically activate cardiac enhancers. Together they activate the bHLH factor Hand and the MADS-box differentiation factor MEF2, which drives the cardiac muscle differentiation program. In the fly the network is deployed in dorsal mesoderm at the intersection of ectodermal Dpp and Wingless signals; in vertebrates its mammalian elaboration underlies first and second heart field development and chamber formation. No single factor is sufficient on its own: heart specification depends on their combination with signalling inputs.

Cardiolipin biosynthesis and remodelling in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_cardiolipin_biosynthesis_remodelingCONCRETE Cardiolipin is the signature phospholipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it supports respiratory chain complexes and cristae structure....
[more...][less] Cardiolipin is the signature phospholipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it supports respiratory chain complexes and cristae structure. It is made in mitochondria from CDP-diacylglycerol: Pgs1 forms phosphatidylglycerol phosphate, the phosphatase Ptpmt1 dephosphorylates it to phosphatidylglycerol, and cardiolipin synthase (Cls) joins phosphatidylglycerol with a second CDP-diacylglycerol to make nascent cardiolipin. Nascent cardiolipin is then remodelled: a lipase removes an acyl chain to form monolysocardiolipin, and the transacylase tafazzin (Taz) transfers an acyl chain from another phospholipid to monolysocardiolipin, giving cardiolipin its mature acyl composition. ABHD18 deacylates cardiolipin in flies and mice, and the calcium-independent phospholipase A2 iPLA2-VIA has also been implicated in cardiolipin deacylation. Loss of tafazzin causes monolysocardiolipin to accumulate and models Barth syndrome in flies.

Carnitine acyltransferase shuttle (mitochondrial import of acyl and acetyl units)MODULE:carnitine_shuttle The carnitine shuttle moves activated acyl groups across membranes that are impermeable to acyl-CoA. A carnitine acyltransferase on the donor side...
[more...][less] The carnitine shuttle moves activated acyl groups across membranes that are impermeable to acyl-CoA. A carnitine acyltransferase on the donor side transfers the acyl group from CoA to L-carnitine; the resulting acylcarnitine is carried across the mitochondrial inner membrane by a mitochondrial-carrier-family carnitine/acylcarnitine translocase in exchange for free carnitine; and a matrix carnitine acyltransferase reverses the transfer, regenerating acyl-CoA and releasing carnitine for recycling. The same chemistry serves different cargo in different lineages. In animals the shuttle imports long-chain fatty acids for mitochondrial beta-oxidation: carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 on the outer membrane catalyses the committed, malonyl-CoA-inhibited step and carnitine palmitoyltransferase 2 on the matrix side of the inner membrane regenerates long-chain acyl-CoA. In fungi such as budding yeast, where beta-oxidation is peroxisomal, the shuttle carries acetyl units: carnitine acetyltransferases in the peroxisome, cytosol and at the mitochondrial outer membrane form acetylcarnitine from acetyl-CoA produced by beta-oxidation or by cytosolic acetate and ethanol metabolism, and the mitochondrial isoform regenerates acetyl-CoA in the matrix for the tricarboxylic acid cycle. Cells take up carnitine through a plasma-membrane transporter; budding yeast cannot make carnitine and depends on uptake. Inherited defects of the animal components (SLC22A5, CPT1A, SLC25A20, CPT2) cause fatty-acid-oxidation disorders.

Carotenoid biosynthesis I — carotene backbone (GGPP -> phytoene -> lycopene -> cyclic carotenes)MODULE:carotene_backbone_biosynthesis The carotene backbone segment of carotenoid biosynthesis converts two molecules of the C20 isoprenoid geranylgeranyl diphosphate (GGPP) into the...
[more...][less] The carotene backbone segment of carotenoid biosynthesis converts two molecules of the C20 isoprenoid geranylgeranyl diphosphate (GGPP) into the C40 cyclic carotenes that seed every downstream carotenoid class. Phytoene synthase performs the head-to-head condensation that commits GGPP to carotenoids, giving 15-cis-phytoene. Phytoene is then desaturated to all-trans-lycopene by one of two mutually exclusive routes: a single FAD-dependent CrtI-type desaturase in most bacteria and fungi, or the four-enzyme poly-cis route of cyanobacteria and plants (PDS, Z-ISO, ZDS, CRTISO) in which two plastoquinone-dependent desaturases each introduce two double bonds and two isomerases convert the poly-cis intermediates to the all-trans product. Lycopene cyclases then form beta rings (giving gamma- and beta-carotene) or, in plants, one epsilon ring (giving delta- and alpha-carotene). Supply of GGPP, xanthophyll formation by ring hydroxylation and epoxidation, ketolation, and oxidative cleavage to apocarotenoids (retinal, abscisic acid, strigolactones, neurosporaxanthin) are outside this module.
