Catecholamine biosynthesis (Tyr -> L-DOPA -> dopamine -> noradrenaline -> adrenaline)MODULE:catecholamine_biosynthesis The catecholamine neurotransmitters and hormones - dopamine, noradrenaline (norepinephrine) and adrenaline (epinephrine) - are synthesised from the...
[more...][less] The catecholamine neurotransmitters and hormones - dopamine, noradrenaline (norepinephrine) and adrenaline (epinephrine) - are synthesised from the amino acid L-tyrosine by a linear four-enzyme pathway operating in catecholaminergic neurons and adrenal chromaffin cells. Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), the rate-limiting enzyme, hydroxylates L-tyrosine to L-DOPA using tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), O2 and a non-heme Fe(II) centre. Aromatic L-amino-acid decarboxylase (DDC/AADC), a pyridoxal-phosphate enzyme, decarboxylates L-DOPA to dopamine (and, on the parallel indoleamine branch, 5-HTP to serotonin). In noradrenergic and adrenergic cells, dopamine is imported into secretory (chromaffin) granules, where the copper- and ascorbate-dependent dopamine beta-hydroxylase (DBH) hydroxylates it to noradrenaline; finally, in adrenal medullary and some central adrenergic cells, the SAM-dependent phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT) N-methylates noradrenaline to adrenaline. Which product predominates depends on the cell type's enzyme complement (dopaminergic cells stop at dopamine; noradrenergic add DBH; adrenergic add PNMT). Inherited defects are severe neurological/autonomic disorders: TH deficiency causes DOPA-responsive dystonia / infantile parkinsonism, AADC (DDC) deficiency a global monoamine-neurotransmitter disease, and DBH deficiency autosomal-recessive orthostatic hypotension.

It is synthesized at the plasma membrane by chitin synthases: Krotzkopf verkehrt (kkv) makes chitin of the epidermal cuticle and trachea, and Chs2 is the second chitin synthase, expressed in the gut. Cholesterol biosynthesis I — sterol commitment (squalene -> lanosterol); FDFT1/SQLE/LSSMODULE:sterol_commitment_squalene_to_lanosterol The sterol-commitment segment of cholesterol biosynthesis converts the isoprenoid intermediate farnesyl diphosphate into the first cyclic sterol,...
[more...][less] The sterol-commitment segment of cholesterol biosynthesis converts the isoprenoid intermediate farnesyl diphosphate into the first cyclic sterol, lanosterol, committing carbon away from the branched isoprenoid pool (dolichol, ubiquinone, prenylation) and irreversibly toward sterols. Squalene synthase (FDFT1) performs the first committed step: a reductive head-to-head condensation of two farnesyl-diphosphate molecules (via presqualene diphosphate) to the C30 hydrocarbon squalene. Squalene monooxygenase / epoxidase (SQLE), an FAD flavoprotein and the second rate-limiting, cholesterol-feedback- regulated enzyme of the pathway, oxidises squalene to (S)-2,3-epoxysqualene using O2 and NADPH. Lanosterol synthase (LSS, oxidosqualene cyclase) then carries out the remarkable polycyclization of 2,3-epoxysqualene to lanosterol, the tetracyclic sterol scaffold from which cholesterol (and, in other tissues, downstream sterols) is made by the post-lanosterol demethylation/reduction steps. All three enzymes are endoplasmic-reticulum-membrane proteins. Inherited defects: FDFT1 deficiency (squalene synthase deficiency, a congenital cholesterol-biosynthesis disorder with dysmorphism/developmental delay) and LSS mutations (hypotrichosis with juvenile cataract / congenital cataract, and a palmoplantar keratoderma); SQLE is a validated antifungal/anticancer drug target rather than a Mendelian-disease gene.

Cholesterol biosynthesis II — lanosterol to cholesterol (post-lanosterol); SLOS, CDPX2, CHILD, lathosterolosisMODULE:cholesterol_synthesis_post_lanosterol The post-lanosterol segment of cholesterol biosynthesis converts lanosterol into cholesterol through a ~19-reaction sequence of demethylations,...
[more...][less] The post-lanosterol segment of cholesterol biosynthesis converts lanosterol into cholesterol through a ~19-reaction sequence of demethylations, isomerisation, desaturations and reductions carried out by endoplasmic-reticulum-membrane enzymes. The three lanosterol methyl groups are removed first: CYP51A1 (a cytochrome P450) removes the 14-alpha-methyl group, and the resulting Delta14 bond is reduced by TM7SF2 or LBR; then the two C4 methyls are removed in two rounds by the C4- demethylation machinery in which MSMO1 (a non-heme di-iron methylsterol oxidase) oxidises the C4 methyl to a carboxylate and NSDHL (a 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/ C4-decarboxylase) decarboxylates it (the 3-ketoreductase HSD17B7 then restores the 3-beta-ol). EBP (sterol Delta(8)-Delta(7) isomerase) shifts the ring double bond from Delta8 to Delta7; SC5D (lathosterol oxidase / sterol-C5-desaturase) introduces the C5-6 double bond; and DHCR7 (7-dehydrocholesterol reductase) reduces the C7-8 double bond to give cholesterol. The pathway runs as two interconvertible arms — the Bloch arm (retaining the side-chain Delta24 double bond until the end) and the Kandutsch-Russell arm (in which DHCR24 reduces the Delta24 bond early) — that differ only in the timing of the DHCR24 step. Isotope tracing shows that tissues mostly combine the Bloch arm with a modified Kandutsch-Russell arm, in which DHCR24 reduces zymosterol, rather than using the canonical Kandutsch-Russell route, in tissue-specific proportions. Inherited enzyme defects cause distinctive malformation/skeletal/skin disorders: DHCR7 -> Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome; SC5D -> lathosterolosis; EBP -> X-linked chondrodysplasia punctata 2 (Conradi-Hunermann-Happle); NSDHL -> CHILD syndrome; MSMO1 -> SC4MOL deficiency; and DHCR24 -> desmosterolosis.

In the endoplasmic reticulum, microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTTP, with protein disulfide isomerase as its small subunit) transfers neutral lipid onto apoB-48 as it is translated, producing a primordial lipoprotein that is then expanded into a pre-chylomicron. ApoB-48 is the non-exchangeable structural scaffold of the particle. The pre-chylomicron leaves the ER in a COPII-dependent carrier whose formation is started by the small GTPase SAR1B: GTP-bound SAR1B inserts into the ER membrane at exit sites and recruits the SEC23-SEC24 and SEC13-SEC31 coats. After Golgi maturation, the chylomicron is secreted basolaterally into lymph. The three steps correspond to three recessive fat-malabsorption disorders. Abetalipoproteinemia (MTTP) and homozygous familial hypobetalipoproteinemia 1 (APOB) block particle formation. Chylomicron retention disease (SAR1B) leaves particle formation intact but blocks ER exit.

Ciliary transition zone MKS, NPHP and CEP290 modulesMODULE:ciliary_transition_zoneCONCRETE The ciliary transition zone (TZ) is the proximal region of the cilium, just distal to the basal body, where Y-shaped links connect the axonemal...
[more...][less] The ciliary transition zone (TZ) is the proximal region of the cilium, just distal to the basal body, where Y-shaped links connect the axonemal microtubules to the ciliary membrane. It acts as a gate that controls which proteins enter and leave the cilium. In nematodes and mammals the TZ is built from the same set of conserved, ciliopathy-associated protein modules. An RPGRIP1L-family assembly hub (MKS-5 in C. elegans) is needed for essentially all other TZ proteins to reach the TZ. CEP290 is a large coiled-coil protein that binds microtubules and membranes; in C. elegans it is a core component of the central cylinder and is needed to localise the MKS module but not the NPHP module. The MKS module contains the three B9-domain proteins MKS1, B9D1 and B9D2, the C2-domain protein CC2D2A, the Tectonic proteins and several transmembrane proteins (TMEM67/meckelin, TMEM216, TMEM107, TMEM231, TMEM237, TMEM17, TMEM218). The NPHP module contains the nephrocystins NPHP1 and NPHP4. The MKS and NPHP modules are partially redundant. Loss of one module leaves cilia nearly normal, whereas combined loss of both causes severe defects in nematodes and mice: the basal body and TZ fail to attach to the membrane, Y-links are lost, axonemes are malformed and non-ciliary membrane proteins leak into the cilium. A further CEP290-dependent branch containing TMEM138 and CDKL1 belongs to neither module. Mutations in the human genes cause Meckel-Gruber syndrome, Joubert syndrome and nephronophthisis. In mammals the nephrocystins also act at epithelial cell-cell junctions, a role outside this module.

Cobalamin (B12) intracellular processing and trafficking; ABCD4/LMBRD1/MMACHC/MMADHCMODULE:cobalamin_intracellular_processing Once the transcobalamin-cobalamin complex has been endocytosed via CD320 and degraded in the lysosome, the freed cobalamin (vitamin B12) must be...
[more...][less] Once the transcobalamin-cobalamin complex has been endocytosed via CD320 and degraded in the lysosome, the freed cobalamin (vitamin B12) must be exported to the cytosol, stripped of its upper axial ligand, and routed to one of its two coenzyme forms. The lysosomal export step is carried out by a two-protein system: the ABC transporter ABCD4 (cblJ), which provides the ATP-dependent transmembrane cobalamin-transport activity, together with the lysosomal membrane protein LMBRD1 (cblF), which is required to target ABCD4 to the lysosome and acts as its escort subunit. In the cytosol the cblC protein MMACHC processes the cobalamin — reductive decyanation of cyanocobalamin and dealkylation of alkylcobalamins remove the beta-axial ligand to give cob(II)alamin. The cblD protein MMADHC then binds MMACHC-cob(II)alamin and acts as the branch-point/trafficking adaptor that directs cobalamin either to the mitochondrion for adenosylcobalamin synthesis (feeding methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, MMUT) or to the cytosolic methylcobalamin route (feeding methionine synthase, MTR). Defects in each step cause combined or isolated methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria: cblJ (ABCD4), cblF (LMBRD1), cblC (MMACHC) and cblD (MMADHC).

Cobalamin (vitamin B12) absorption and transport; TCN1/CBLIF/CUBN/AMN/TCN2/CD320MODULE:cobalamin_absorption_transport Dietary cobalamin (vitamin B12) reaches the cytoplasm of peripheral cells through a relay of binding proteins and endocytic receptors. In saliva...
[more...][less] Dietary cobalamin (vitamin B12) reaches the cytoplasm of peripheral cells through a relay of binding proteins and endocytic receptors. In saliva and the acidic stomach, cobalamin is first bound and protected by haptocorrin (TCN1); in the duodenum pancreatic proteases degrade haptocorrin and the cobalamin is transferred to gastric intrinsic factor (CBLIF/GIF), secreted by parietal cells. The intrinsic-factor-cobalamin complex is then recognised in the ileum by the cubam receptor, a complex of the large peripheral membrane protein cubilin (CUBN) and its transmembrane partner amnionless (AMN), which internalises it by receptor-mediated endocytosis; the cobalamin is released and exported to the blood. In plasma, newly absorbed cobalamin is bound by transcobalamin (TCN2), the physiologically essential delivery carrier, and the transcobalamin-cobalamin complex is taken up by peripheral cells through the cell-surface receptor CD320 (TCblR). Inherited defects along this route cause B12-deficiency disorders: CBLIF (hereditary intrinsic factor deficiency / juvenile pernicious anaemia), CUBN and AMN (Imerslund-Grasbeck syndrome, megaloblastic anaemia with proteinuria), TCN2 (transcobalamin deficiency, severe infantile megaloblastic anaemia with immunodeficiency) and CD320 (a usually mild/transient methylmalonic acidaemia detected on newborn screening).

Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) biosynthesis (PDSS1/2, COQ2-COQ9)MODULE:coenzyme_q10_biosynthesis Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone-10) is the lipophilic electron/proton carrier of the mitochondrial inner membrane that shuttles electrons from respiratory...
[more...][less] Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone-10) is the lipophilic electron/proton carrier of the mitochondrial inner membrane that shuttles electrons from respiratory Complexes I and II (and from electron-transfer flavoprotein, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase and others) to Complex III, and is a membrane antioxidant. Its biosynthesis has two arms that meet at the matrix face of the inner membrane. First, the C50 polyisoprenoid tail is built: the all-trans-decaprenyl-diphosphate synthase, a heterotetramer of PDSS1 and PDSS2, condenses (2E,6E)-farnesyl diphosphate with isopentenyl diphosphate units to all-trans- decaprenyl diphosphate. The polytopic inner-membrane prenyltransferase COQ2 then attaches this tail to the ring precursor 4-hydroxybenzoate, committing it to the pathway. A series of ring modifications, carried out by a membrane-associated multienzyme assembly (the "COQ synthome"/complex Q), converts the polyprenyl-hydroxybenzoate to ubiquinol: FAD-dependent C5 hydroxylation by COQ6, Zn-dependent C1 decarboxylation by COQ4 followed by C1 hydroxylation by COQ6, C2-methylation by the SAM-dependent methyltransferase COQ5, NADH-dependent di-iron C6 hydroxylation by COQ7 (whose lipophilic substrate is bound and presented by the lipid-binding protein COQ9), and the two O-methylation steps performed by COQ3 (not covered here). Assembly and activity of the synthome require the atypical UbiB-family kinase/ATPases COQ8A and COQ8B. The exact order of the head-group modifications in humans is not fully resolved (in particular, C1 decarboxylation by COQ4 can precede C5 hydroxylation by COQ6), and the enzymes act within the synthome complex rather than as free-standing steps. Defects in any of these genes cause primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency, a clinically heterogeneous mitochondrial disease (encephalomyopathy, cerebellar ataxia, steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, Leigh syndrome), some forms of which are partially responsive to oral CoQ10.

Core programmed cell death machinery in Caenorhabditis elegansMODULE:c_elegans_core_apoptosisCONCRETE Most somatic and germline apoptotic deaths in Caenorhabditis elegans are initiated by four proteins acting in a linear pathway. In living cells the...
[more...][less] Most somatic and germline apoptotic deaths in Caenorhabditis elegans are initiated by four proteins acting in a linear pathway. In living cells the BCL2-family protein CED-9 sits on mitochondria and binds an asymmetric dimer of the Apaf-1-like adaptor CED-4, holding it in an inactive state. A death signal raises the level of the BH3-only protein EGL-1, whose BH3 helix binds a hydrophobic groove on CED-9 and remodels it so that the CED-4 dimer is released. Free CED-4 dimers assemble into an ATP-bound octameric apoptosome that relocates to the nuclear periphery, recruits two molecules of the CED-3 caspase zymogen into its central hutch and drives their autocatalytic maturation. Active CED-3 then cleaves execution substrates such as DCR-1 and CED-8, which promote chromosome fragmentation and phosphatidylserine exposure for corpse engulfment. In the adult germline, DNA damage feeds into the same machinery through the p53-family transcription factor CEP-1, which induces transcription of egl-1 and of a second BH3-only gene, ced-13. CED-13 can also bind CED-9 and release CED-4, but its loss has only a small effect on DNA damage-induced germline death, so EGL-1 remains the main trigger on that route as well. Unlike the mammalian intrinsic pathway, the worm pathway has no known requirement for mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization or cytochrome c release; CED-9 inhibits by direct sequestration of CED-4 rather than by controlling a pore.

Creatine biosynthesis (vertebrate, two-step AGAT to GAMT)MODULE:creatine_biosynthesis De novo biosynthesis of creatine, the two-step pathway that supplies the phosphocreatine/creatine system used for cellular energy buffering in...
[more...][less] De novo biosynthesis of creatine, the two-step pathway that supplies the phosphocreatine/creatine system used for cellular energy buffering in tissues with high and fluctuating ATP demand (skeletal and cardiac muscle, brain). The pathway is short and committed: L-arginine and glycine are first condensed by L-arginine:glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT/GATM) to give guanidinoacetate (GAA) and L-ornithine, then guanidinoacetate is methylated by guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase (GAMT) using S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) as the methyl donor to yield creatine and S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH). The two activities are characteristically split both by subcellular compartment and, in mammals, by organ: AGAT/GATM is a mitochondrial intermembrane-space enzyme and catalyses the first, committed, feedback- regulated step (creatine represses GATM), whereas GAMT is a cytosolic enzyme and is the second, methylation step. The first step is most active in kidney and pancreas and the second predominates in liver, so guanidinoacetate is an inter-organ intermediate that is exported and taken up before methylation; finished creatine is distributed in the blood and imported into target tissues by the creatine transporter SLC6A8. GAMT is also the largest single consumer of SAM-derived methyl groups in the body, tying creatine synthesis to one-carbon / methionine-cycle metabolism. Inherited deficiency of either enzyme (and of the SLC6A8 transporter) causes cerebral creatine-deficiency syndromes. Creatine utilization by the creatine kinases (the phosphocreatine shuttle and the "futile creatine cycle") is downstream of this module and is not part of the biosynthetic pathway itself.

[more...][less] A navigational grouping for the biology that Reactome bundles as "Creatine metabolism" (R-HSA-71288), assembled here as an explicit biological *system* rather than as a single GO metabolic process. The grouping is deliberately not called "creatine metabolism": GO keys metabolism on the chemical entity, and this system spans more than one entity. It comprises (1) de novo synthesis of the creatine molecule (creatine biosynthetic process, GO:0006601; the AGAT/GATM -> GAMT pathway), (2) the creatine kinase energy-buffer that interconverts creatine and phosphocreatine (phosphocreatine metabolic process, GO:0006603; including phosphocreatine biosynthesis GO:0046314 and the thermogenic futile creatine cycle GO:0140651), (3) inter-organ and cellular distribution of creatine by the SLC6A8 transporter, and (4) non-enzymatic disposal of creatine and phosphocreatine to creatinine for excretion (creatinine metabolic process, GO:0046449). In strict GO terms (2) is phosphocreatine metabolism, not creatine metabolism, so the canonical GO umbrella creatine metabolic process (GO:0006600) covers only (1) and the creatinine-forming arm of (4). This node carries both GO:0006600 and GO:0006603 to make that cross-branch span explicit. The detailed, protein-grounded logic lives in the dedicated modules referenced by each part; this document holds no annotons of its own and exists only to relate them.

Cuproptosis (copper-induced cell death) moduleMODULE:cuproptosis A decomposition of cuproptosis: the regulated cell-death program in which excess intracellular copper, reduced to Cu(I) by the mitochondrial...
[more...][less] A decomposition of cuproptosis: the regulated cell-death program in which excess intracellular copper, reduced to Cu(I) by the mitochondrial ferredoxin FDX1, binds the lipoyl moieties of lipoylated tricarboxylic-acid-cycle enzymes (chiefly the pyruvate dehydrogenase E2 subunit DLAT), driving their disulfide-dependent oligomerization/aggregation while destabilizing iron-sulfur cluster proteins. The resulting proteotoxic stress kills the cell. Cuproptosis is mechanistically distinct from apoptosis, necroptosis, ferroptosis, and pyroptosis. This module is framed for the mammalian in-vivo pathway, with concrete human gene products grounded to UniProt where they are used as representatives of the mammalian implementation. Design intent: the module is organized as an upstream copper-homeostasis layer that sets the death threshold (importer, chaperone, exporters), a copper- reduction trigger (FDX1), the protein-lipoylation machinery that builds the copper "bait", the lipoylated TCA-cycle targets/effectors (the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, with DLAT as the aggregation-prone effector), and the execution node (cuproptosis proper). Protective and modulatory regulators (MTF1, GLS, CDKN2A) and the non-substituting paralog FDX2 are kept as an optional regulatory sub-module. Genes are grounded to UniProt only where verified; GO ids are grounded only to verified, non-obsolete terms in the matching aspect (MF in function, BP in processes/concepts, CC in locations).

Cuticle tanning and pigmentation in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_cuticle_tanning_pigmentationCONCRETE After each molt and at eclosion, the insect cuticle is hardened (sclerotized) and pigmented using dopamine made by tyrosine hydroxylase (Pale) and...
[more...][less] After each molt and at eclosion, the insect cuticle is hardened (sclerotized) and pigmented using dopamine made by tyrosine hydroxylase (Pale) and DOPA decarboxylase. Dopamine is used in three branches. Arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase (Speck, Aanat1) acetylates it to N-acetyldopamine (NADA), the precursor of colourless sclerotin. Ebony conjugates dopamine with beta-alanine to N-beta-alanyldopamine (NBAD), the precursor of yellow-tan sclerotin, and Tan hydrolyses NBAD back to dopamine, so the Ebony-Tan balance sets cuticle colour. Oxidation of dopamine and DOPA by phenoloxidases yields quinones and chromes that polymerize into black and brown melanins; the Yellow family proteins Yellow-f and Yellow-f2 convert dopachrome and Yellow-h converts dopaminechrome, and Yellow itself is needed for black melanin. Beta-alanine for NBAD comes from decarboxylation of aspartate by Black (Adc) and from uracil degradation through dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase, dihydropyrimidinase and beta-ureidopropionase.

Cyanobacterial septal junction moduleMODULE:septal_junction The septal junction (SJ) is a proteinaceous, gap-junction-like cell-cell junction of filamentous, heterocyst-forming cyanobacteria (e.g....
[more...][less] The septal junction (SJ) is a proteinaceous, gap-junction-like cell-cell junction of filamentous, heterocyst-forming cyanobacteria (e.g. Nostoc/Anabaena sp. PCC 7120). SJs traverse the shared septal peptidoglycan (PG) through nanopores and directly connect the cytoplasms of adjacent cells in a filament, mediating and gating the intercellular diffusion of small molecules (metabolites and signaling compounds) — a prerequisite for multicellular behavior and for diazotrophic growth, in which heterocysts exchange fixed nitrogen for photosynthate with neighboring vegetative cells. In situ cryo-electron tomography with subtomogram averaging resolves the SJ as a five-fold-symmetric assembly with four structural modules: a cytoplasmic cap (five arches), a membrane-embedded plug, a septum-spanning tube, and a transmembrane/periplasmic anchor. This module represents the SJ as a structural cell-cell junction: its two molecularly identified core components — SepN (the plug) and FraD (the membrane/periplasmic anchor) — the still molecularly-unidentified cap and (partly lipidic) tube modules, the cell-wall amidases that drill the septal PG nanopore array the SJ passes through, and the additional septal proteins (SepJ/FraG, FraC, FraE) that influence SJ architecture and filament integrity.

Cytokinin two-component (His-Asp phosphorelay) signaling in ArabidopsisMODULE:cytokinin_two_component_signalingCONCRETE The cytokinin signal transduction pathway of Arabidopsis thaliana is a eukaryotic multistep His-Asp phosphorelay. Cytokinins bind the...
[more...][less] The cytokinin signal transduction pathway of Arabidopsis thaliana is a eukaryotic multistep His-Asp phosphorelay. Cytokinins bind the extracytosolic CHASE domains of three partially redundant hybrid sensor histidine kinase receptors (AHK2, AHK3 and CRE1/AHK4), located mainly in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane. Ligand binding activates autophosphorylation of a conserved histidine in the transmitter domain; the phosphoryl group passes to an aspartate in the receptor's receiver domain and then to a conserved histidine of the small, nucleocytosolic histidine phosphotransfer proteins (AHP1, AHP2, AHP3, AHP5). AHPs deliver the phosphoryl group to the receiver aspartate of nuclear type-B response regulators (principally ARR1, ARR10 and ARR12), which are Myb-related (GARP) DNA-binding transcription factors; receiver phosphorylation activates them to bind AGAT(T)-containing cis-elements and induce cytokinin primary-response genes. Among these targets are the type-A response regulators (e.g. ARR5), receiver-only proteins that are themselves phosphorylated and stabilized through the relay and attenuate the pathway, closing a negative feedback loop. Without ligand, CRE1/AHK4 can reverse the relay and dephosphorylate AHPs. The phosphorelay core (receptor -> AHP -> type-B ARR) conforms to the generic two-component relay motif; transcriptional output and type-A feedback are this pathway's extensions. Cytokinin biosynthesis, transport and degradation, the cytokinin-independent histidine kinase CKI1, CRFs, and downstream developmental targets are outside the module boundary.

Cytoplasmic (80S) ribosome in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_cytoplasmic_ribosomeCONCRETE The cytoplasmic 80S ribosome translates nuclear-encoded mRNAs. It consists of a 40S small subunit, which binds mRNA and decodes it, and a 60S large...
[more...][less] The cytoplasmic 80S ribosome translates nuclear-encoded mRNAs. It consists of a 40S small subunit, which binds mRNA and decodes it, and a 60S large subunit, which carries the peptidyl transferase centre and the polypeptide exit tunnel. Each subunit is built from ribosomal RNAs and dozens of ribosomal proteins named by the universal (u) and eukaryote-specific (e) nomenclature. In Drosophila several ribosomal proteins are encoded by duplicated genes, and some paralogs are expressed mainly in the germline or testis (for example RpL22-like). FlyBase therefore also defines testis-specific variant compositions of both subunits, in which RpS28-like, RpL22-like and RpL37-2 appear only in the testis variants.

Cytoplasmic dynein and dynactin in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_cytoplasmic_dynein_dynactinCONCRETE Cytoplasmic dyneins are multi-subunit minus-end-directed microtubule motors. Cytoplasmic dynein 1, built around the heavy chain Dhc64C, moves...
[more...][less] Cytoplasmic dyneins are multi-subunit minus-end-directed microtubule motors. Cytoplasmic dynein 1, built around the heavy chain Dhc64C, moves organelles, vesicles, mRNAs and chromosomes toward microtubule minus ends and acts in spindle assembly, nuclear positioning and oocyte polarity. It contains intermediate chains (Short wing, sw), light intermediate chains (Dlic) and LC8, Tctex and roadblock families of light chains. Dynein 1 is processive only when bound to dynactin and a cargo adaptor. Dynactin is a large complex with a short filament of Arp1 capped at the barbed end by capping protein and at the pointed end by a complex including Arp10 (Arp11), plus a projecting shoulder and arm formed by p150Glued (DCTN1-p150), p50 dynamitin (DCTN2-p50) and p24 (DCTN3-p24). Cytoplasmic dynein 2, with the heavy chain Beethoven (btv), drives retrograde intraflagellar transport in the cilia of sensory neurons.

Cytosolic NADPH regeneration in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_cytosolic_nadph_regenerationCONCRETE NADPH supplies reducing power for fatty acid synthesis and for antioxidant systems such as glutathione and thioredoxin reduction. In Drosophila, as...
[more...][less] NADPH supplies reducing power for fatty acid synthesis and for antioxidant systems such as glutathione and thioredoxin reduction. In Drosophila, as in other animals, it is regenerated outside mitochondria by three sets of NADP-dependent dehydrogenases. The oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway produces two NADPH per glucose 6-phosphate through glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6pd, Zw) and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (Pgd). NADP-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase (Idh) oxidizes isocitrate to 2-oxoglutarate, and NADP-dependent malic enzyme (Men) decarboxylates malate to pyruvate, each reducing NADP+. Studies of fly mutants and allozyme variants link these enzymes to lipid accumulation.

D-erythroascorbate (dehydro-D-arabinono-1,4-lactone) biosynthesisMODULE:erythroascorbate_biosynthesisABSTRACT In fungi, D-erythroascorbate, the five-carbon analogue of L-ascorbate, is made from D-arabinose in two oxidations. The IUBMB and ChEBI name for it...
[more...][less] In fungi, D-erythroascorbate, the five-carbon analogue of L-ascorbate, is made from D-arabinose in two oxidations. The IUBMB and ChEBI name for it is dehydro-D-arabinono-1,4-lactone. First, a cytosolic aldo-keto-reductase-type D-arabinose 1-dehydrogenase oxidises D-arabinose to D-arabinono-1,4-lactone, using NAD+ or NADP+. Second, a membrane-bound, FAD-dependent D-arabinono-1,4-lactone oxidase in the mitochondria oxidises the lactone with O2, giving dehydro-D-arabinono-1,4-lactone and hydrogen peroxide. The terminal oxidase belongs to the aldonolactone oxidoreductase group of the vanillyl alcohol oxidase flavoprotein superfamily. Its homologs make L-ascorbate in animals (L-gulono-1,4-lactone oxidase) and plants (L-galactono-1,4-lactone dehydrogenase), and the yeast enzyme can also oxidise L-gulono- and L-galactono-1,4-lactone. Erythroascorbate is thought to act as an antioxidant: yeast cells lacking the oxidase are more sensitive to oxidative stress, although its importance under normal conditions is debated.

DAF-2 insulin/IGF-1-like signaling to DAF-16/FOXO in Caenorhabditis elegansMODULE:c_elegans_daf2_insulin_signalingCONCRETE In Caenorhabditis elegans a large family of insulin-like peptides, secreted mainly by neurons, acts through a single insulin/IGF-1 receptor...
[more...][less] In Caenorhabditis elegans a large family of insulin-like peptides, secreted mainly by neurons, acts through a single insulin/IGF-1 receptor tyrosine kinase, DAF-2. Active DAF-2 signals through the class I PI3K catalytic subunit AGE-1 to generate phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3), which the PTEN lipid phosphatase DAF-18 removes. PIP3 supports activation of the 3-phosphoinositide-dependent kinase PDK-1, which in turn activates a kinase complex of AKT-1, AKT-2 and SGK-1. These kinases phosphorylate the FOXO transcription factor DAF-16, and phosphorylated DAF-16 is bound by the 14-3-3 protein FTT-2 and held in the cytoplasm. When ligand input falls, as in poor food or high pheromone conditions, or when the pathway is genetically reduced, DAF-16 enters the nucleus and regulates a broad transcriptional program that includes stress-resistance genes such as the mitochondrial manganese superoxide dismutase sod-3, as well as antimicrobial and metabolic genes. The pathway controls the dauer diapause decision, adult lifespan, stress resistance and fat storage, and DAF-16 is its major output.

DBL-1 BMP-like Sma/Mab signaling in Caenorhabditis elegans body size controlMODULE:c_elegans_dbl1_body_size_signalingCONCRETE In Caenorhabditis elegans the BMP2/4-related ligand DBL-1 is secreted mainly by neurons and acts on the epidermis (hypodermis) to promote...
[more...][less] In Caenorhabditis elegans the BMP2/4-related ligand DBL-1 is secreted mainly by neurons and acts on the epidermis (hypodermis) to promote postembryonic growth and to pattern the male tail. DBL-1 signals through a receptor pair of the type I serine/threonine kinase SMA-6 and the type II kinase DAF-4, and then through the Smads SMA-2 and SMA-3 together with the co-Smad SMA-4. Loss of any of these components gives small (Sma) animals with abnormal male tails (Mab), and the DBL-1 dose sets body length, so overexpression makes animals longer. SMA-3 is the principal receptor-regulated Smad. Signaling is tuned at the cell surface: the glypican LON-2 restrains it, apparently through the matricellular protein SMOC-1, which binds both LON-2 and DBL-1, rather than by binding DBL-1 directly; and the LRIG-family transmembrane protein SMA-10, which binds both receptors and supports SMA-6 endocytic trafficking, enhances it. In the nucleus the Schnurri-family zinc finger protein SMA-9 acts as a transcriptional cofactor that mainly represses targets in body size control. One downstream target is lon-1, which encodes a secreted CAP/CRISP-family protein made in the hypodermis. The pathway represses lon-1, and LON-1 limits body size, binds sterol in vitro and feeds back to dampen pathway output. The same ligand, receptors and SMA-3 also act in epidermal antifungal defense, lipid storage and other outputs.

De novo UMP biosynthesis and conversion to UTP and CTPMODULE:de_novo_pyrimidine_synthesis The conserved six-reaction pathway that builds UMP from glutamine, hydrogencarbonate, ATP, aspartate, and PRPP, followed by phosphorylation of UMP...
[more...][less] The conserved six-reaction pathway that builds UMP from glutamine, hydrogencarbonate, ATP, aspartate, and PRPP, followed by phosphorylation of UMP to UTP and amination of UTP to CTP. Carbamoyl phosphate is formed first, followed by assembly and oxidation of the pyrimidine ring, attachment to phosphoribose, and decarboxylation to UMP. UMP kinase and nucleoside-diphosphate kinase then make UTP, and CTP synthase transfers the glutamine amide nitrogen to UTP to make CTP. Enzyme architecture varies: bacteria commonly use separate CarA, CarB, PyrB, PyrC, PyrE, and PyrF proteins, whereas animals fuse the first three activities in CAD and the final two activities in UMPS; fungi fuse the carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase and aspartate carbamoyltransferase in one protein that also carries an inactive dihydroorotase-like domain, and use separate dihydroorotase, orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and OMP decarboxylase proteins. These fusions do not change the chemical leaves represented by the module. Dihydroorotate oxidation has two implementations: membrane-associated quinone-dependent (class 2) enzymes, which in eukaryotes sit on the mitochondrial inner membrane and couple pyrimidine synthesis to respiration, and soluble fumarate-dependent (class 1A) enzymes, acquired by Saccharomyces yeasts from bacteria, which allow pyrimidine synthesis without oxygen. Bacteria phosphorylate UMP with a PyrH-type UMP kinase, eukaryotes with a UMP/CMP kinase of the adenylate kinase family.

De novo biotin biosynthesis (pimelate-thioester supply and BioF-BioA-BioD-BioB ring assembly)MODULE:biotin_biosynthesis De novo synthesis of biotin in bacteria, fungi and plants. A seven-carbon pimelate thioester (pimeloyl-ACP or pimeloyl-CoA) is first made by a...
[more...][less] De novo synthesis of biotin in bacteria, fungi and plants. A seven-carbon pimelate thioester (pimeloyl-ACP or pimeloyl-CoA) is first made by a lineage-specific route, and four conserved reactions then assemble the two rings of biotin. In many bacteria, BioC methylates malonyl-ACP, the shared fatty-acid-synthase reactions extend the masked intermediate to pimeloyl-ACP methyl ester, and BioH removes the methyl group. Filamentous fungi make pimeloyl-CoA by peroxisomal beta-oxidation, and Saccharomyces yeasts need the oxygen-dependent BIO1 protein, whose reaction is not known. The pimelate thioester is condensed with L-alanine to 8-amino-7-oxononanoate (KAPA) by a PLP-dependent KAPA synthase: bacterial BioF, a peroxisomal BioF in filamentous fungi, or, in Saccharomyces, a step that requires the BIO6 protein, a paralogue of the BioA aminotransferase. BioA then transfers an amino group from S-adenosylmethionine to give 7,8-diaminononanoate (DAPA), BioD closes the ureido ring with CO2 and ATP to give dethiobiotin, and the radical-SAM enzyme BioB inserts sulfur to form biotin. In fungi BioB is mitochondrial, and in filamentous fungi and plants BioD and BioA are fused in one protein. Biotin attachment to carboxylases, biotin uptake and regulation are outside the module.

De novo deoxyribonucleoside triphosphate synthesis by class I ribonucleotide reductaseMODULE:dntp_de_novo_synthesis De novo formation of the four DNA precursors dATP, dGTP, dCTP and dTTP from ribonucleoside diphosphates in eukaryotes and other organisms with a...
[more...][less] De novo formation of the four DNA precursors dATP, dGTP, dCTP and dTTP from ribonucleoside diphosphates in eukaryotes and other organisms with a class I (oxygen-dependent) ribonucleotide reductase. The reductase replaces the 2'-hydroxyl of ADP, GDP, CDP and UDP with hydrogen using electrons from thioredoxin or glutaredoxin; its large (alpha) subunit binds substrates and the allosteric effectors that balance the four products, and its small (beta) subunit carries the di-iron tyrosyl radical cofactor. In budding yeast the active enzyme is an alpha2 homodimer of Rnr1 (or the damage-induced Rnr3) with a beta heterodimer of the radical-bearing Rnr2 and the catalytically inactive but essential Rnr4. Nucleoside-diphosphate kinase then phosphorylates dADP, dGDP and dCDP to the triphosphates. dTTP cannot be made by direct reduction: dUMP is produced either by hydrolysis of dUTP by dUTP diphosphatase, which also keeps dUTP out of DNA, or by deamination of dCMP by dCMP deaminase; thymidylate synthase then methylates dUMP to dTMP with 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate, dTMP kinase makes dTDP and nucleoside-diphosphate kinase makes dTTP. Activity and subunit levels are tightly controlled by the cell cycle and the DNA damage checkpoint. Class II (adenosylcobalamin) and class III (anaerobic, glycyl-radical) reductases of prokaryotes, deoxynucleoside salvage and the mitochondrial dNTP supply pathway of animals are outside the module.

The module represents ten ordered reaction positions and separates reaction roles from lineage-specific protein fusions. It includes alternative folate-dependent PurN and ATP/formate-dependent PurT routes for GAR formylation, and alternative two-enzyme and direct routes for AIR carboxylation. Enzyme architecture varies widely: bacteria commonly use separate PurF, PurD, PurN/PurT, PurL, PurM, PurK, PurE, PurC, PurB and PurH proteins; animals fuse PurD, PurM and PurN in GART and direct AIR carboxylase with SAICAR synthetase in PAICS; fungi fuse PurD with PurM in a bifunctional GAR synthetase-AIR synthetase and PurK with PurE in a bifunctional AIR carboxylase that works through the N5-carboxyaminoimidazole ribonucleotide intermediate. In eukaryotes the pathway is cytosolic. The first enzyme, amidophosphoribosyltransferase, is feedback-inhibited by adenine nucleotides. IMP-to-AMP and IMP-to-GMP branches are outside the module, although PurB also has a second physiological role in AMP synthesis.

De novo riboflavin biosynthesis and flavin cofactor activationMODULE:riboflavin_biosynthesis De novo synthesis of riboflavin (vitamin B2) from GTP and ribulose 5-phosphate, followed by conversion of riboflavin to the active flavin cofactors...
[more...][less] De novo synthesis of riboflavin (vitamin B2) from GTP and ribulose 5-phosphate, followed by conversion of riboflavin to the active flavin cofactors FMN and FAD, as found in bacteria, fungi and plants. The ring pathway has two converging branches. In the GTP-derived pyrimidine branch, GTP cyclohydrolase II opens the imidazole ring of GTP; the product then undergoes deamination of the pyrimidine ring and reduction of the ribosyl side chain, and the resulting phosphorylated intermediate is dephosphorylated. The order of deamination and reduction differs by lineage: bacteria deaminate first and then reduce, usually with one bifunctional RibD protein, whereas fungi reduce first and then deaminate, with two separate proteins. The ribulose-5-phosphate branch makes the four-carbon donor 3,4-dihydroxy-2-butanone 4-phosphate. The two branches converge at lumazine synthase, and riboflavin synthase then forms riboflavin by a dismutation of two lumazine molecules. Riboflavin kinase converts riboflavin to FMN and FMN adenylyltransferase converts FMN to FAD. In many bacteria both activation steps are carried out by one bifunctional RibF protein, whereas eukaryotes use a monofunctional riboflavin kinase and a separate FAD synthase.

[more...][less] De novo L-serine biosynthesis and its immediate use as a one-carbon donor form a central node of intermediary metabolism, supplying the building blocks and methyl groups for nucleotide synthesis, methylation and redox balance — a pathway on which proliferating and neural cells especially depend. Serine is made from the glycolytic intermediate 3-phospho-D-glycerate by the "phosphorylated pathway": PHGDH (D-3-phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase) oxidises 3-phosphoglycerate to 3-phosphonooxypyruvate using NAD+; PSAT1 (phosphoserine aminotransferase, PLP-dependent) transaminates it with glutamate to O-phospho-L-serine; and PSPH (phosphoserine phosphatase, Mg2+-dependent) hydrolyses the phosphate to release L-serine, the committed final step. The newly made serine then feeds one-carbon (folate) metabolism through serine hydroxymethyltransferase, which reversibly transfers a one-carbon unit from serine to tetrahydrofolate, producing glycine and 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate. Humans have two SHMT isozymes running this reaction in parallel compartments: cytosolic SHMT1 (supplying one-carbon units for cytosolic thymidylate/purine synthesis and the methylation cycle, with a nuclear role in the thymidylate-synthesis complex) and mitochondrial SHMT2 (the principal entry to mitochondrial one-carbon metabolism, exporting formate/one-carbon units to the cytosol and supplying glycine). Inherited defects cause serine deficiency: PHGDH — Neu-Laxova syndrome 1 / serine-deficiency with microcephaly and seizures; PSAT1 — Neu-Laxova syndrome 2; PSPH — phosphoserine phosphatase deficiency.

De novo sphingolipid biosynthesis (ceramide core, with fungal inositol-phosphorylceramide head groups)MODULE:sphingolipid_de_novo_synthesis De novo sphingolipid synthesis builds ceramide, the hydrophobic backbone of all complex sphingolipids, from serine and fatty acyl-CoA on the...
[more...][less] De novo sphingolipid synthesis builds ceramide, the hydrophobic backbone of all complex sphingolipids, from serine and fatty acyl-CoA on the endoplasmic-reticulum membrane. The committed, rate-limiting first step is catalysed by serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT), a pyridoxal-5'-phosphate-dependent membrane complex built on a heterodimer of two homologous subunits (SPTLC1/LCB1 and SPTLC2/LCB2). A small, lineage-specific activating subunit is also required: SPTSSA/B in animals, which sets acyl-CoA specificity, and the unrelated Tsc3 in fungi. SPT condenses L-serine with palmitoyl-CoA to 3-ketodihydrosphingosine. 3-ketodihydrosphingosine reductase (KDSR, yeast Tsc10) then reduces this, using NADPH, to dihydrosphingosine (sphinganine). Ceramide synthases of the TLC/Lag1 family N-acylate the sphingoid base with a fatty acyl-CoA. Each animal isoform prefers a different acyl chain length: CERS1 makes C18 ceramide (brain/muscle), CERS2 very-long-chain C22-C24 ceramide (broadly expressed), and CERS3 ultra-long-chain C26+ (acyl)ceramides for the skin barrier. Fungal Lag1 and Lac1 act with the accessory subunit Lip1 and use C26-CoA. The sphingoid base is then modified at C4 by one of two related di-iron enzymes. The dihydroceramide desaturase DEGS1 introduces the 4,5-trans double bond, an O2- and iron-dependent oxidation that converts dihydroceramide to ceramide; this is the predominant route in animals. The sphingoid-base C4-hydroxylase (yeast Sur2) instead converts sphinganine or dihydroceramide to the phyto (4-hydroxy) form, which is the predominant route in fungi and plants. Fungal ceramides are also hydroxylated at C2 of the very long acyl chain (Scs7). Fungi then build their characteristic complex sphingolipids in the Golgi. The Aur1-Kei1 inositol phosphorylceramide (IPC) synthase transfers inositol phosphate from phosphatidylinositol to ceramide. IPC is mannosylated by Csg1/Csh1-Csg2 complexes to MIPC, and in budding yeast Ipt1 adds a second inositol phosphate to make M(IP)2C. Animals instead make sphingomyelin and glycosphingolipids, which are covered by separate modules. Inherited defects of the human ceramide core include HSAN1 (SPTLC1/SPTLC2), spastic paraplegia (SPTSSA), erythrokeratodermia/thrombocytopenia (KDSR), progressive myoclonic epilepsy 8 (CERS1), congenital ichthyosis ARCI9 (CERS3) and hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 18 (DEGS1). The fungal IPC synthase is the target of the antifungal aureobasidin A.

De novo tetrahydrofolate and folylpolyglutamate biosynthesisMODULE:tetrahydrofolate_biosynthesis De novo synthesis of tetrahydrofolate (THF) and its polyglutamylated forms, as found in bacteria, fungi, plants and many protists but absent from...
[more...][less] De novo synthesis of tetrahydrofolate (THF) and its polyglutamylated forms, as found in bacteria, fungi, plants and many protists but absent from animals, which must take up preformed folate. The pathway joins two branches. In the pterin branch, GTP cyclohydrolase I opens the GTP imidazole ring to give 7,8-dihydroneopterin triphosphate; the triphosphate is removed (a Nudix-type pyrophosphatase followed by a phosphatase) to give 7,8-dihydroneopterin; dihydroneopterin aldolase releases glycolaldehyde to give 6-hydroxymethyl-7,8-dihydropterin; and 6-hydroxymethyl-7,8-dihydropterin pyrophosphokinase activates it as the diphosphate. In the p-aminobenzoate (pABA) branch, chorismate is aminated by glutamine-dependent aminodeoxychorismate synthase and 4-amino-4-deoxychorismate is cleaved by aminodeoxychorismate lyase to pABA and pyruvate. Dihydropteroate synthase condenses the pterin diphosphate with pABA to 7,8-dihydropteroate, dihydrofolate synthase adds the first L-glutamate to give 7,8-dihydrofolate, and dihydrofolate reductase reduces it with NADPH to THF. Folylpolyglutamate synthase then adds further gamma-linked glutamates, which retain folates in cells and organelles and make them preferred cofactors of folate-dependent enzymes. The reaction chain is conserved, but enzyme architecture varies: dihydroneopterin aldolase, pyrophosphokinase and dihydropteroate synthase are separate proteins in many bacteria and a single trifunctional polypeptide in fungi; aminodeoxychorismate synthase is a two-subunit PabA-PabB enzyme in many bacteria and a fused polypeptide in fungi and plants; and dihydrofolate synthase and folylpolyglutamate synthase are one bifunctional FolC protein in many bacteria but separate proteins in fungi and plants. In eukaryotes the steps are split between compartments (for example, the fungal trifunctional pterin enzyme and plant dihydrofolate synthase are mitochondrial). Chorismate supply, folate salvage and transport, and the interconversion and use of one-carbon-substituted THF are outside the module.

Diadenosine tetraphosphate (Ap4A) turnoverMODULE:diadenosine_tetraphosphate_turnover A reusable metabolic module for the production and removal of diadenosine 5',5'''-P1,P4-tetraphosphate (Ap4A), a dinucleoside polyphosphate that...
[more...][less] A reusable metabolic module for the production and removal of diadenosine 5',5'''-P1,P4-tetraphosphate (Ap4A), a dinucleoside polyphosphate that accumulates under stress and has been proposed to act as an intracellular signal. Ap4A is made as a side reaction of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, either by transfer of the aminoacyl-adenylate AMP to ATP (as in lysyl-tRNA synthetase) or by direct condensation of two ATP molecules (as in glycyl-tRNA synthetase). It is removed by one of three unrelated enzyme chemistries: asymmetrical Nudix hydrolases that yield ATP + AMP (animals and other eukaryotes), symmetrical ApaH-type hydrolases that yield two ADP (proteobacteria), and Ap4A phosphorylases that yield ADP + ATP by phosphorolysis (fungi). Downstream Ap4A effectors (for example HINT1 or transcription factors) and the related Ap3A/FHIT system are outside the module boundary.

[more...][less] Biosynthesis of DIF-1, the chlorinated polyketide morphogen that induces prestalk/stalk cell differentiation in the social amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum. The pathway builds and tailors a hexanoyl-primed acylphloroglucinol in three enzymatic stages: (1) the hybrid type I/type III "steely" polyketide synthase StlB condenses a hexanoyl-CoA starter with malonyl-CoA extender units to make the acylphloroglucinol backbone THPH (1-(3,5-dihydroxy-... phloro- caprophenone); (2) the flavin-dependent halogenase ChlA chlorinates THPH, first to 3-chloro-THPH and then to 3,5-dichloro-THPH (des-methyl-DIF-1); and (3) the O-methyltransferase DmtA methylates des-methyl-DIF-1 to yield mature DIF-1. DIF-1 is then secreted and read out by the prestalk transcriptional machinery (DimA/DimB). This module is Dictyostelium-specific but phrased over enzyme functions and family selectors with D. discoideum representative members rather than a fixed gene list, so a related steely-PKS / halogenase / O-MT route in another dictyostelid could be substituted. OUT OF SCOPE: the DIF-1 RESPONSE (DimA/DimB-driven prestalk/prespore patterning; a separate module), DIF-1 dechlorination/inactivation (the DIF catabolic arm), and the additional O-methylation intermediates upstream of chlorination — only the three named, reviewed enzymes StlB, ChlA and DmtA are grounded here.

DIF-1 (the chlorinated acylphloroglucinol produced by the dicty_dif1_biosynthesis module) is perceived by the basic-region leucine-zipper (bZIP) transcription factors DimA and DimB, which translocate to the nucleus and reprogram cell-type gene expression: DimA/DimB activate prestalk/stalk genes (the extracellular-matrix markers ecmA and ecmB) and repress prespore genes, so a cell exposed to DIF-1 commits to the prestalk pathway. The two bZIPs are partly redundant and heterodimerise, with DimB the principal activator of ecmB. This module is the RESPONSE arm; its input is the DIF-1 made by the separate biosynthesis module. OUT OF SCOPE: DIF-1 biosynthesis (dicty_dif1_biosynthesis module), the STATa/CudA culmination circuit (CudA is only indirectly DIF-1-linked), and DIF-1 catabolism. Dictyostelium SDF-2 spore-encapsulation relay (AcbA-TagC-DhkA-RegA-PKA)MODULE:dicty_sdf2_encapsulation_relay The non-cell-autonomous signalling relay that triggers rapid, synchronous encapsulation of prespore cells into spores during culmination in...
[more...][less] The non-cell-autonomous signalling relay that triggers rapid, synchronous encapsulation of prespore cells into spores during culmination in Dictyostelium discoideum. The acyl-CoA-binding protein AcbA is unconventionally secreted by prespore cells and cleaved at the prestalk cell surface by the ABC-transporter/ serine-protease TagC to release the peptide signal SDF-2. SDF-2 binds the membrane sensor histidine kinase DhkA and INHIBITS its phosphorelay; because DhkA (through the histidine-phosphotransfer protein RdeA) normally keeps the response-regulator cAMP phosphodiesterase RegA active, inhibiting DhkA lowers RegA activity, so intracellular cAMP rises and activates cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA-C released from PKA-R), which drives spore encapsulation. The net logic is a double negative — SDF-2 inhibits DhkA, DhkA activates RegA, RegA suppresses cAMP/PKA — so SDF-2 ultimately ACTIVATES encapsulation. The relay is self-amplifying (encapsulating cells release more AcbA). Phrased over functions and family selectors with D. discoideum representatives rather than a fixed gene list. OUT OF SCOPE: the parallel GABA/GrlE input that also triggers AcbA release (a separate module), the ACR/PKA culmination cAMP source, and spore-coat assembly. The histidine-phosphotransfer intermediate RdeA is described in the DhkA->RegA connection but is NOT separately grounded here because it has not yet been reviewed.

Dictyostelium counting-factor group-size controlMODULE:dicty_counting_factor_size_control The secreted-signal feedback system that sets the number of cells per aggregate (and hence fruiting-body size) in Dictyostelium discoideum....
[more...][less] The secreted-signal feedback system that sets the number of cells per aggregate (and hence fruiting-body size) in Dictyostelium discoideum. Aggregating cells secrete "counting factor" (CF), a large multisubunit complex whose principal component is Countin (CtnA); high CF activity decreases cell-cell adhesion and the size of cAMP-relay streams, breaking large aggregation territories into smaller groups. The cytosolic protein SmlA negatively regulates the secretion of counting factor: smlA-null cells oversecrete CF and form many small aggregates, whereas countin-null cells undersignal and form few large ones. The module is thus a two-element size rheostat — SmlA restrains CF output, CtnA is the secreted size-limiting signal. Phrased over the reviewed D. discoideum proteins. OUT OF SCOPE: the other CF subunits (CF45-1, CF50) which are not yet reviewed, and the downstream glucose/adhesion effectors of CF.

[more...][less] The developmentally staged cell-cell adhesion systems of Dictyostelium discoideum, culminating in tgr-locus allorecognition. As starving cells enter development they deploy successive adhesion molecules: (1) the Ca2+-dependent adhesion molecule ddCAD-1 (cadA), which mediates EDTA-sensitive homophilic adhesion at the loose-aggregate stage; (2) the contact-sites-A glycoprotein csA/gp80 (csaA), which mediates EDTA-resistant (Ca2+-independent) homophilic adhesion during tight aggregation; and (3) the polymorphic Tiger proteins TgrC1 (the ligand) and TgrB1 (the receptor), a heterophilic self-recognition pair required for post-aggregation adhesion and kin discrimination — cells bearing matching tgrB1/tgrC1 alleles cooperate, enabling coordinated multicellular development and excluding non-kin. This is a set of parallel, developmentally ordered adhesion systems rather than a linear pathway, so it is modelled as staged PRECEDES steps. OUT OF SCOPE: the intracellular actin cytoskeleton coupling of adhesion, and the other ~12 tgr paralogs at the tgr locus (only the reviewed tgrB1/tgrC1 pair is grounded). Note tgrC1 = lagC/gp150.

Dictyostelium extracellular cAMP relay / aggregation oscillatorMODULE:dicty_extracellular_camp_relay The defining Dictyostelium discoideum aggregation system — a self-organising extracellular cAMP oscillator that propagates chemotactic waves so...
[more...][less] The defining Dictyostelium discoideum aggregation system — a self-organising extracellular cAMP oscillator that propagates chemotactic waves so that starving amoebae stream together into a mound. Secreted cAMP is detected by the seven-transmembrane receptor cAR1 (carA), which couples through the heterotrimeric G protein Galpha2 (gpaB); receptor activation recruits the PH-domain adaptor CRAC (dagA) that is required to activate the aggregation adenylyl cyclase ACA (acaA), which synthesises cAMP. The newly made cAMP is secreted and activates cAR1 on neighbouring cells (the RELAY, a positive feedback), while the extracellular phosphodiesterase PdsA degrades secreted cAMP and the intracellular response-regulator phosphodiesterase RegA degrades internal cAMP — the negative feedback / adaptation that lets the system oscillate and produce propagating waves rather than saturate. This is the extracellular-cAMP CHEMOTACTIC oscillator, distinct from the generic intracellular GPCR->cAMP->PKA cassette. OUT OF SCOPE: the downstream PKA-driven developmental gene expression (cAMP effector; see the pkaC review and the SDF-2 relay module), the actin/PI3K chemotaxis motor, and the later adenylyl cyclases ACG/ACR. Phrased over functions and family selectors with D. discoideum representatives.

Dictyostelium starvation / growth-to-development initiationMODULE:dicty_starvation_initiation The switch that commits starving Dictyostelium discoideum cells to development. Two inputs converge. (1) Density sensing: growing and...
[more...][less] The switch that commits starving Dictyostelium discoideum cells to development. Two inputs converge. (1) Density sensing: growing and early-starving cells secrete conditioned-medium factor (CMF, cmfA); only when CMF accumulates above a threshold (i.e. enough cells are present) can cells respond to cAMP pulses and aggregate, coupling cell density to developmental onset. (2) The growth-to-development kinase: on starvation the DYRK-family dual-specificity kinase YakA arrests the cell cycle and drives developmental initiation, in part by down-regulating the Pumilio-family translational repressor PufA; PufA normally binds the pkaC (PKA catalytic subunit) mRNA and represses its translation, so relieving PufA de-represses PKA-C, and rising PKA activity turns on early developmental gene expression and the cAMP-signalling machinery. The net YakA -| PufA -| pkaC logic is a double negative — YakA activates PKA. OUT OF SCOPE: the downstream cAMP relay (dicty_extracellular_camp_relay) and PKA's many later developmental roles; the CMF receptor CMFR1 (not yet reviewed). Phrased over functions and family selectors with D. discoideum representatives.

Diphthamide biosynthesis on translation elongation factor 2MODULE:diphthamide_biosynthesisABSTRACT Diphthamide is a post-translationally modified histidine residue found only on archaeal and eukaryotic translation elongation factor 2 (EF2), at...
[more...][less] Diphthamide is a post-translationally modified histidine residue found only on archaeal and eukaryotic translation elongation factor 2 (EF2), at the tip of domain IV. It is the target of diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A, which ADP-ribosylate it and so inactivate EF2. The modification is built on the folded EF2 protein in the cytosol in four enzymatic steps. First, a [4Fe-4S]-cluster enzyme cleaves S-adenosyl-L-methionine at the methionine C(gamma)-S bond, unlike canonical radical-SAM enzymes, and transfers the 3-amino-3-carboxypropyl (ACP) group to C2 of the histidine imidazole ring. In archaea this enzyme is a Dph2 homodimer; in eukaryotes it is a Dph1-Dph2 heterodimer that also needs the CSL-zinc-finger protein Dph3, which reduces its iron-sulfur clusters, and the J-domain protein Dph4. Second, the SAM-dependent methyltransferase Dph5 trimethylates the amino group and methylates the carboxylate, giving diphthine methyl ester. Third, the WD40-repeat methylesterase Dph7 hydrolyses the ester to diphthine. Fourth, the ATP-binding diphthine-ammonia ligase Dph6 amidates the carboxylate with ammonium to form diphthamide. Diphthamide is not essential in yeast, but its loss reduces translational fidelity (more -1 ribosomal frameshifting) and confers resistance to diphtheria toxin and the antifungal sordarin.

Dolichol / dolichyl-phosphate biosynthesis (cis-PT -> DHRSX -> SRD5A3 -> DHRSX -> DOLK)MODULE:dolichyl_phosphate_biosynthesis Dolichyl phosphate (Dol-P) is the essential polyprenol lipid carrier on which the eukaryotic glycosylation machinery assembles and delivers...
[more...][less] Dolichyl phosphate (Dol-P) is the essential polyprenol lipid carrier on which the eukaryotic glycosylation machinery assembles and delivers glycans: it anchors the lipid-linked oligosaccharide for N-linked glycosylation, the mannose/glucose donors (Dol-P-Man, Dol-P-Glc) for N-glycan, O-mannose, GPI-anchor and C/O-mannosylation, and it is regenerated after each transfer cycle. Its biosynthesis begins where the isoprenoid-diphosphate trunk ends: the ER-membrane cis-prenyltransferase (cis-PT) complex — catalytic subunit DHDDS plus the non-catalytic partner NUS1 (NgBR) — elongates (2E,6E)-farnesyl diphosphate (FPP) by many cis (Z)-condensations of isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) to the long-chain dehydrodolichyl diphosphate (dehydro-Dol-PP). This polyprenyl diphosphate is dephosphorylated to polyprenol by a phosphatase that has not been identified in humans. Polyprenol is then converted to dolichol by a three-step detour rather than by a single reduction. DHRSX oxidizes polyprenol to polyprenal (NAD+), SRD5A3 reduces the alpha-isoprene double bond of polyprenal to give dolichal (NADPH), and DHRSX reduces dolichal to dolichol (NADPH). Dolichol kinase DOLK then phosphorylates dolichol (CTP-dependent) to Dol-P, completing the carrier pool. The dolichyl-diphosphate phosphatase DOLPP1 regenerates Dol-P from the Dol-PP released after oligosaccharyltransferase moves the glycan onto protein. The cis-PT subunits, SRD5A3, DOLK and DOLPP1 are endoplasmic reticulum membrane proteins, whereas DHRSX has been localized to lipid droplets. Defects across this module cause congenital disorders of glycosylation (DHDDS-CDG/RP59, NUS1-CDG/epileptic encephalopathy, DHRSX-CDG, SRD5A3-CDG, DOLK-CDG) and inherited retinal dystrophy.

Dolichol phosphate and lipid-linked sugar-donor supply for glycosylation; SRD5A3/DHRSX/DOLK/DPM1/DPM2/DPM3/ALG5/MPDU1MODULE:dolichol_phosphate_sugar_donor_supply Assembly of the dolichol-linked oligosaccharide (and of GPI anchors, O- and C-mannosylation) depends on a dolichyl-phosphate lipid carrier and on...
[more...][less] Assembly of the dolichol-linked oligosaccharide (and of GPI anchors, O- and C-mannosylation) depends on a dolichyl-phosphate lipid carrier and on two lipid-linked monosaccharide donors, dolichyl-phosphate-mannose (Dol-P-Man) and dolichyl-phosphate-glucose (Dol-P-Glc). This module curates their supply at the endoplasmic-reticulum membrane. The last steps of de novo dolichol synthesis go through aldehyde intermediates. SRD5A3 reduces the alpha-isoprene double bond of polyprenal to give dolichal, and DHRSX reduces dolichal to dolichol (DHRSX also makes polyprenal from polyprenol upstream). Dolichol kinase DOLK then phosphorylates dolichol (using CTP) to dolichyl phosphate (Dol-P), the essential carrier. Dol-P is charged with sugars by two systems: the dolichol-phosphate-mannose (DPM) synthase, a three-subunit complex in which DPM1 is the GDP-mannose-utilising catalytic subunit and DPM2 (regulatory/stabilising) and DPM3 (membrane anchor for the TM-less DPM1) are non-catalytic, produces Dol-P-Man from GDP-mannose and Dol-P; and ALG5 (dolichyl-phosphate beta-glucosyltransferase) produces Dol-P-Glc from UDP-glucose and Dol-P. The utilisation factor MPDU1 (Lec35) is then required for these lipid-linked donors to be used by the lumenal glycosyltransferases. Because they feed the whole glycosylation system, defects in every gene here cause a congenital disorder of glycosylation: SRD5A3-CDG (CDG-Iq), DHRSX-CDG, DOLK-CDG (CDG-Im, dilated cardiomyopathy), DPM1-CDG (CDG-Ie), DPM2-CDG (CDG-Iu) and DPM3-CDG (CDG-Io) — the latter two dystroglycanopathies — MPDU1-CDG (CDG-If) and ALG5-CDG.

EGFR signaling pathway in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_egfr_signalingCONCRETE Drosophila has a single EGF receptor (Egfr), a receptor tyrosine kinase activated by the TGF-alpha-like ligands Spitz, Keren and Gurken and the...
[more...][less] Drosophila has a single EGF receptor (Egfr), a receptor tyrosine kinase activated by the TGF-alpha-like ligands Spitz, Keren and Gurken and the neuregulin-like ligand Vein. Spitz, Keren and Gurken are made as inactive membrane-bound precursors; the chaperone Star carries them from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi, where rhomboid intramembrane proteases cleave them to release the secreted ligand. Ligand-bound Egfr recruits the adaptor Drk (Grb2) and the guanine nucleotide exchange factor Son of sevenless, which activates Ras85D. Ras triggers the Raf, Dsor1 (MEK) and Rolled (ERK) kinase cascade, assisted by the scaffolds KSR, CNK and Aveugle. ERK changes nuclear gene expression by activating the ETS factor Pointed and promoting the degradation or export of the repressors Yan (Aop) and Capicua. The pathway acts in oogenesis axis formation, photoreceptor recruitment, wing vein formation, and cell survival and proliferation in many tissues.

ERK1/2 (Ras-RAF-MEK-ERK) MAPK cascade moduleMODULE:erk_cascade A taxon-neutral decomposition of the canonical Ras-RAF-MEK-ERK mitogen-activated protein kinase cascade, the concrete ERK1/2 realization of the...
[more...][less] A taxon-neutral decomposition of the canonical Ras-RAF-MEK-ERK mitogen-activated protein kinase cascade, the concrete ERK1/2 realization of the generic three-tier MAP kinase relay (MODULE:mapk_relay). The cascade converts receptor-proximal tyrosine-phosphorylation events into ERK1/ERK2 activity and a proliferative/differentiation transcriptional program, and is deployed downstream of many distinct receptor systems: receptor tyrosine kinases (EGFR, FGFR, PDGFR, insulin/IGF), cytokine receptors signaling through JAKs, G-protein-coupled receptors, and integrins. The module captures six parts, numbered as in `parts`: (1) recruitment of SH2/SH3 adaptors (GRB2, SHC) to a receptor phosphotyrosine, with GRB2-mediated recruitment of the Ras guanine nucleotide exchange factor SOS; (2) the Ras nucleotide switch (SOS GEF -> Ras GTPase -> RasGAP), declared as an inner bundle that `conforms_to` gtpase_switch; (3) the conforming ERK kinase relay - Ras-driven RAF(MAP3K) -> MEK1/2(MAP2K) -> ERK1/2(MAPK) on the TEY motif - declared as an inner bundle that `conforms_to` mapk_relay; (4) ERK action on nuclear (ELK1/Ets, RSK, MSK) and cytoplasmic substrates to drive transcription, proliferation, and differentiation; (5) DUSP/MKP negative feedback on ERK; and (6) optional Sprouty/SPRED feedback inhibition at the SOS-Ras-RAF level. Grounded in GO:0000165 (MAPK cascade) / GO:0070371 (ERK1 and ERK2 cascade).

[more...][less] The endosomal sorting complexes required for transport (ESCRTs) sort ubiquitylated membrane proteins into intralumenal vesicles of multivesicular bodies and drive membrane scission that buds away from the cytoplasm. ESCRT-0 (Hrs, Stam) binds ubiquitylated cargo on endosomes; ESCRT-I and ESCRT-II bind cargo and membrane and nucleate ESCRT-III, whose subunits polymerize into spirals that constrict the bud neck. The AAA ATPase Vps4, with its cofactor Vta1, disassembles ESCRT-III and recycles it. Early metazoan development moduleMODULE:early_metazoan_development A top-level developmental module that organises the conserved early events of animal (metazoan) embryogenesis into an ordered set of sub-programs,...
[more...][less] A top-level developmental module that organises the conserved early events of animal (metazoan) embryogenesis into an ordered set of sub-programs, from the fertilised egg to a patterned, three-germ-layer embryo with a segregated germline. The trunk is a temporal sequence of four sub-programs, each detailed in its own dedicated module document: (1) the maternal-to-zygotic transition, which hands control from maternal factors to the embryo's own genome; (2) body axis specification, which converts graded morphogens into the AP, DV, and LR body axes; (3) germ layer specification during gastrulation, which partitions the embryo into endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm; and (4) primordial germ cell specification, which sets aside the gamete lineage. All four are wired by a small, deeply conserved "developmental toolkit" of signalling pathways - Wnt, TGF-beta/Nodal/BMP, Hedgehog, Notch, and RTK/FGF - captured here as a cross-cutting variant set that points to the existing signalling module documents. Grounded in GO:0009790 (embryo development).

The vitelline membrane, the innermost layer, is laid down first from vitelline membrane proteins (Vm26Aa, Vm26Ab, Vm26Ac, Vm32E, Vm34Ca and Vml) that are cross-linked into an insoluble layer. The chorion is secreted afterwards and is built from chorion proteins encoded mainly by two clusters: an X-linked cluster at 7F (Cp36, Cp38 and Cp7Fa-c) and an autosomal cluster at 66D (Cp15, Cp16, Cp18 and Cp19). Ehrlich pathway (amino acid catabolism to fusel alcohols and fusel acids)MODULE:ehrlich_pathwayCONCRETE Catabolic route by which yeasts and other fungi degrade the branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine), the aromatic amino acids...
[more...][less] Catabolic route by which yeasts and other fungi degrade the branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine), the aromatic amino acids (phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan) and methionine when these are used as nitrogen sources. Only the amino group is retained by the cell; the carbon skeleton is excreted. The pathway has three steps. A pyridoxal-phosphate aminotransferase first transfers the amino group to an acceptor 2-oxo acid (2-oxoglutarate for the branched-chain aminotransferases; pyruvate or phenylpyruvate for the inducible aromatic aminotransferase), giving the corresponding 2-oxo acid. A thiamine-diphosphate-dependent 2-oxo-acid decarboxylase then irreversibly converts the 2-oxo acid to an aldehyde with one carbon fewer; this is the first step specific to the pathway. Finally, depending on the redox state of the cell, the aldehyde is reduced by NADH alcohol dehydrogenases to a fusel alcohol (isoamyl alcohol, 2-methylbutanol, isobutanol, 2-phenylethanol, tyrosol, tryptophol) or oxidized by aldehyde dehydrogenases to a fusel acid. All three steps are carried out by sets of overlapping isozymes whose use depends on the amino acid, the carbon source and the growth stage. In budding yeast the aminotransferase and decarboxylase of the aromatic branch are co-induced by aromatic amino acids. Oxidative degradation of the 2-oxo acids by the mitochondrial branched-chain 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase complex, the catabolic route that dominates in animals, is outside this module.

Electron-transfer flavoprotein (ETF) system — electron sink for mitochondrial FAD dehydrogenasesMODULE:electron_transfer_flavoprotein_system The electron-transfer flavoprotein (ETF) system is the shared electron-relay that couples a large set of mitochondrial matrix FAD-dependent...
[more...][less] The electron-transfer flavoprotein (ETF) system is the shared electron-relay that couples a large set of mitochondrial matrix FAD-dependent dehydrogenases to the respiratory chain. At least a dozen matrix flavoenzymes — the acyl-CoA dehydrogenases of fatty-acid beta-oxidation (ACADVL, ACADM, ACADS, ACAD9, etc.), the branched-chain and other acyl-CoA dehydrogenases of amino-acid catabolism (IVD, GCDH, etc.), sarcosine and dimethylglycine dehydrogenases, and others — do not pass their electrons directly to the respiratory chain. Instead they reduce a common, soluble matrix heterodimeric flavoprotein, ETF (the ETFA alpha subunit, which carries the FAD, plus the ETFB beta subunit, which carries AMP and provides the docking surface for the partner dehydrogenases). Reduced ETF then diffuses to the inner-membrane iron-sulfur flavoprotein ETF-ubiquinone oxidoreductase (ETFDH / ETF-QO), which reoxidises ETF and transfers the electrons to ubiquinone (CoQ) in the respiratory chain, linking these oxidations to oxidative phosphorylation. Because ETF/ETFDH is the common electron sink for so many dehydrogenases, its inherited deficiency (ETFA, ETFB or ETFDH) causes multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (MADD / glutaric acidemia type 2), a severe fatty-acid-oxidation and amino-acid-oxidation disorder; the ETFDH form is frequently riboflavin-responsive and can present as a myopathy with secondary coenzyme-Q10 deficiency.

Endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein responseMODULE:er_unfolded_protein_responseCONCRETE The endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response (UPR-ER) matches the folding capacity of the ER to the load of client proteins entering it. In...
[more...][less] The endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response (UPR-ER) matches the folding capacity of the ER to the load of client proteins entering it. In animals ER stress is sensed by three ER-membrane transducers. The kinase-endoribonuclease IRE1 removes a small intron from the XBP1 mRNA, and the spliced mRNA encodes the active bZIP transcription factor XBP1s, which induces chaperone, folding and ER-associated degradation genes, including the BiP gene. The eIF2alpha kinase PERK phosphorylates eIF2alpha to attenuate general translation and so reduce client load; reduced ternary complex favours translation of the uORF-containing ATF4 mRNA, and ATF4 then activates cytoprotective genes. ATF6 is an ER-membrane-anchored bZIP factor that is released by intramembrane proteolysis and enters the nucleus. The ER HSP70 BiP is both a luminal folding chaperone and a UPR target, and its binding to the luminal domains of the transducers keeps them inactive until misfolded proteins compete it away. The IRE1 arm is the ancestral eukaryotic core: budding yeast has only Ire1 and its spliced-mRNA target Hac1, an unrelated bZIP factor that plays the XBP1 role, while the PERK and ATF6 arms are animal additions. The arms are partly redundant; in C. elegans, loss of the IRE1-XBP1 arm together with PERK or ATF6 causes larval arrest, and neuronal XBP1s can activate the UPR-ER in distant tissues.

Enterocyte apical sterol uptake and efflux — NPC1L1 uptake opposed by ABCG5/ABCG8 exportMODULE:intestinal_sterol_absorption_and_efflux Net absorption of dietary and biliary sterols across the small intestine is set at the enterocyte brush-border membrane by two opposing transport...
[more...][less] Net absorption of dietary and biliary sterols across the small intestine is set at the enterocyte brush-border membrane by two opposing transport activities. Niemann-Pick C1-like 1 (NPC1L1) binds free cholesterol through its luminal N-terminal domain and takes it up into the cell by sterol-induced, clathrin/AP2-dependent endocytosis of NPC1L1 with cholesterol-enriched membrane; NPC1L1 favours cholesterol over plant sterols and is the target of the absorption inhibitor ezetimibe. The ATP-binding cassette heterodimer ABCG5/ABCG8 exports neutral sterols, especially plant sterols such as sitosterol and part of the absorbed cholesterol, from the apical membrane back into the lumen; the same transporter on the hepatocyte canalicular membrane secretes sterols into bile. The balance of uptake and efflux limits net sterol absorption and keeps plant sterols out of the circulation. NPC1L1 loss-of-function variants lower LDL cholesterol, whereas biallelic loss of ABCG5 or ABCG8 causes sitosterolaemia, with plant-sterol accumulation and premature atherosclerosis.

Enterohepatic bile salt cycling transport relay; BSEP/ASBT/FABP6/OSTalpha-beta/NTCPMODULE:enterohepatic_bile_salt_cyclingCONCRETE Conjugated bile salts are not consumed by the digestion they enable: they are secreted into bile, act as detergents in the intestinal lumen, and...
[more...][less] Conjugated bile salts are not consumed by the digestion they enable: they are secreted into bile, act as detergents in the intestinal lumen, and are then reclaimed and returned to the liver, so that the whole bile salt pool recirculates many times a day and only a small fraction is lost in faeces. The relay is carried out by a small set of membrane transporters acting in a fixed order around a closed loop, each at a defined pole of a polarised epithelium: ATP-driven export across the hepatocyte canalicular (apical) membrane into bile (BSEP/ABCB11); sodium-coupled uptake across the apical brush border of the terminal ileal enterocyte (ASBT/SLC10A2); cytosolic shuttling across the enterocyte by a soluble bile acid binding protein (FABP6); basolateral efflux into portal blood by an obligate heteromeric facilitative transporter (OSTalpha/OSTbeta, SLC51A/SLC51B); and sodium-coupled reuptake across the hepatocyte basolateral (sinusoidal) membrane (NTCP/SLC10A1), closing the cycle. The hepatic uptake step has two parallel implementations - the sodium-dependent SLC10A1 route for conjugated bile salts and the sodium-independent OATP route for unconjugated and some conjugated species - which is modelled here as a variant set. Two paralogous members of one family (PANTHER:PTHR10361) supply the two sodium-coupled steps at opposite epithelial poles, and PAINT resolves this as a sub-branch split: the apical ileal node and the basolateral hepatic node are distinct ancestral nodes within the family. Loss of any single step produces a recognisable human disorder, which is the clearest evidence that the steps are required parts rather than redundant routes.

Ergosterol biosynthesis (squalene -> lanosterol -> ergosterol)MODULE:ergosterol_biosynthesisCONCRETE Fungal sterol synthesis converts farnesyl diphosphate from the isoprenoid trunk into ergosterol, the principal sterol of fungal membranes, through...
[more...][less] Fungal sterol synthesis converts farnesyl diphosphate from the isoprenoid trunk into ergosterol, the principal sterol of fungal membranes, through about twenty reactions on the endoplasmic-reticulum membrane. The first half is shared with animal cholesterol synthesis. Squalene synthase reductively joins two farnesyl diphosphates into squalene, squalene epoxidase oxidises it to 2,3-oxidosqualene, and lanosterol synthase cyclises that to lanosterol. The cytochrome P450 sterol 14alpha-demethylase (CYP51) then removes the C-14 methyl, a Delta14-reductase saturates the resulting double bond, and a C-4 demethylation complex removes both C-4 methyls in two rounds: a C-4 methylsterol oxidase oxidises the methyl to a carboxylate, a 3beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/C-4 decarboxylase releases it as CO2, and a 3-ketosteroid reductase restores the 3beta-hydroxyl. A membrane scaffold (Erg28) tethers the three C-4 demethylation enzymes, yielding zymosterol. The ergosterol-specific tail follows. A sterol C-24 methyltransferase adds the C-28 methyl group that animals lack. A C-8 sterol isomerase that is unrelated to the animal EBP isomerase moves the Delta8 bond to Delta7. A C-5 desaturase homologous to animal SC5D adds the Delta5 bond, a cytochrome P450 C-22 desaturase (CYP61) adds the side-chain Delta22 bond, and a C-24(28) reductase completes ergosterol. The P450 steps take electrons from NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase, and the C-4 oxidase and C-5 desaturase use cytochrome b5, which can also support CYP51. The pathway is the target of the main antifungal drug classes: azoles (CYP51), allylamines such as terbinafine (squalene epoxidase) and morpholines (Delta14-reductase and C-8 isomerase).
