HSF-driven cytosolic heat shock responseMODULE:heat_shock_responseCONCRETE The heat shock response couples proteotoxic stress to transcriptional induction of the cytosolic chaperone network. Its driver is heat shock factor...
[more...][less] The heat shock response couples proteotoxic stress to transcriptional induction of the cytosolic chaperone network. Its driver is heat shock factor (HSF), a winged helix-turn-helix transcription factor found across eukaryotes. HSF binds heat shock elements (HSEs), inverted nGAAn pentamer repeats, as a homotrimer and activates RNA polymerase II transcription of chaperone genes. How HSF is held in check differs between lineages. In metazoans, exemplified by human HSF1, HSF is kept as an inert monomer in complexes with HSP90 and HSP70. Proteotoxic stress titrates these chaperones away, and HSF1 then trimerizes, binds HSEs and concentrates in nuclear stress granules. The induced chaperones feed back to switch HSF1 off. In budding yeast, Hsf1 is constitutively trimeric and nuclear. Its essential job is to maintain basal expression of the Hsp70 and Hsp90 genes, and stress raises its activity further. The chaperone output falls into three activities. Hsp70 family foldases refold non-native clients by ATP-driven cycles. J-domain co-chaperones deliver clients and stimulate the Hsp70 ATPase, and HSP110- and BAG-family nucleotide-exchange factors reset the cycle. HSP90 is an ATP-dependent chaperone for metastable signaling and structural clients and is also the main repressor of metazoan HSF1. Small heat shock proteins are ATP-independent holdases that keep heat-denatured proteins soluble and refolding-competent for the ATP-dependent chaperones. Nematodes add an HSF-1/DAF-16-co-regulated branch of atypical 12-kDa small HSPs that contributes to longevity rather than to the acute response. In C. elegans the capacity of the response also falls sharply at the onset of reproduction, when repressive chromatin at stress loci blocks HSF-1 binding.

Hedgehog signaling pathway in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_hedgehog_signalingCONCRETE Hedgehog (Hh) is a secreted morphogen that is autoprocessed and modified with cholesterol and, by the acyltransferase Rasp, with palmitate. The...
[more...][less] Hedgehog (Hh) is a secreted morphogen that is autoprocessed and modified with cholesterol and, by the acyltransferase Rasp, with palmitate. The transmembrane protein Dispatched releases lipid-modified Hh from producing cells. In receiving cells Hh binds its receptor Patched together with the co-receptors Ihog and Boi. In the absence of Hh, Patched keeps the seven-pass transmembrane protein Smoothened inactive, and the Hedgehog signaling complex of the kinesin-like protein Costal-2 (Cos), the kinase Fused and the zinc-finger transcription factor Cubitus interruptus (Ci) promotes processing of Ci into a repressor form. Hh binding relieves Patched inhibition, Smoothened accumulates at the plasma membrane and recruits the Cos-Fused complex, Ci processing is blocked and full-length Ci activates Hh target genes. The pathway patterns embryonic segments and the anterior-posterior axis of imaginal discs.

Heme degradation (heme -> biliverdin -> bilirubin)MODULE:heme_degradation Heme (iron-protoporphyrin IX), released chiefly from senescent-erythrocyte hemoglobin, is both an essential cofactor and, when free, a pro-oxidant;...
[more...][less] Heme (iron-protoporphyrin IX), released chiefly from senescent-erythrocyte hemoglobin, is both an essential cofactor and, when free, a pro-oxidant; its controlled catabolism recovers iron, produces the signalling gas carbon monoxide, and generates the antioxidant bile pigments. Degradation proceeds in two enzymatic steps. First, heme oxygenase — the highly inducible, cytoprotective HMOX1 (HO-1/HSP32) and the constitutive HMOX2 (HO-2, an oxygen sensor in brain and vasculature) — uses molecular O2 and electrons from NADPH--cytochrome P450 reductase to oxidatively cleave the alpha-methene bridge of heme, releasing biliverdin IX-alpha, carbon monoxide (CO) and free ferrous iron (Fe2+); this is the rate-limiting step, and the iron is recaptured by ferritin while CO acts as a vasodilatory/anti-inflammatory messenger. Second, biliverdin reductase reduces the green biliverdin to the yellow, lipophilic, potently antioxidant bilirubin: the cytosolic NAD(P)H-dependent BLVRA acts on the major IX-alpha isomer (and additionally moonlights as a signalling kinase/scaffold), while the broad-specificity NADPH flavin reductase BLVRB reduces the IX-beta isomer (prominent in fetal heme catabolism) as well as flavins and other substrates. Bilirubin is subsequently glucuronidated (UGT1A1) for biliary excretion. Inherited defects cause severe systemic inflammation with hemolysis (HMOX1 deficiency) and green jaundice / hyperbiliverdinemia (BLVRA deficiency).

[more...][less] Heparan sulfate and chondroitin sulfate chains are built in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi on serine residues of core proteins such as the glypicans Dally and Dally-like, Syndecan and Perlecan. Both start on a shared tetrasaccharide linker (xylose-galactose-galactose-glucuronic acid) made by Oxt, beta4GalT7, beta3GalTII and GlcAT-I. The chain is modified by the N-deacetylase/N-sulfotransferase Sulfateless (Sfl), the C5-epimerase Hsepi and the 2-O-, 6-O- and 3-O-sulfotransferases (Hs2st, Hs6st, Hs3st-A, Hs3st-B). Addition of N-acetylgalactosamine by Csgalnact instead starts chondroitin chains, which are polymerized by Chsy and Chpf and sulfated by C4st. Heparan sulfate made by this pathway is required for Wingless, Hedgehog, Dpp and FGF signaling in Drosophila.

Heparan sulfate lysosomal degradation (the mucopolysaccharidoses); IDS/IDUA/SGSH/HGSNAT/NAGLU/GNS/GUSBMODULE:heparan_sulfate_lysosomal_degradation Heparan sulfate is degraded in the lysosome by an ordered, strictly sequential exolytic cascade that removes one monosaccharide or sulfate group at...
[more...][less] Heparan sulfate is degraded in the lysosome by an ordered, strictly sequential exolytic cascade that removes one monosaccharide or sulfate group at a time from the non-reducing end of the chain; each enzyme can act only after the preceding one has exposed its substrate, so a deficiency of any single step blocks the whole pathway and causes a mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS) with lysosomal heparan-sulfate storage. Iduronate-2-sulfatase (IDS) first removes the 2-O-sulfate from a terminal iduronate-2-sulfate; alpha-L-iduronidase (IDUA) then hydrolyses the exposed iduronate; sulfamidase (SGSH) removes the N-sulfate from the terminal N-sulfoglucosamine; the lysosomal-membrane transacetylase HGSNAT then N-acetylates the freed glucosamine (using cytosolic acetyl-CoA) so that alpha-N-acetylglucosaminidase (NAGLU) can hydrolyse it; N-acetylglucosamine-6-sulfatase (GNS) removes a 6-O-sulfate; and beta-glucuronidase (GUSB) hydrolyses the terminal glucuronate — regenerating a substrate for IDS/IDUA as the cycle repeats. The three sulfatases (IDS, SGSH, GNS) additionally require the formylglycine catalytic residue generated by SUMF1. Each enzyme defines a distinct disease: MPS II (IDS, Hunter), MPS I (IDUA, Hurler-Scheie), MPS IIIA (SGSH, Sanfilippo A), MPS IIIC (HGSNAT, Sanfilippo C), MPS IIIB (NAGLU, Sanfilippo B), MPS IIID (GNS, Sanfilippo D) and MPS VII (GUSB, Sly).

Histamine synthesis and recycling in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_histamine_metabolismCONCRETE Histamine is the neurotransmitter of Drosophila photoreceptors and some central neurons. Histidine decarboxylase (Hdc) makes histamine from...
[more...][less] Histamine is the neurotransmitter of Drosophila photoreceptors and some central neurons. Histidine decarboxylase (Hdc) makes histamine from histidine, and LOVIT, a putative vesicular histamine transporter, maintains histamine in photoreceptor synaptic terminals. After release, histamine is taken up by surrounding epithelial glia, in part by the histamine-specific transporter HisT. In glia, Ebony conjugates histamine with beta-alanine to form carcinine (beta-alanyl-histamine), which returns to photoreceptors through the carcinine transporter CarT. Tan then hydrolyses carcinine, releasing histamine for reuse. This glia-photoreceptor recycling loop sustains visual transmission when de novo synthesis is limiting.

Homocysteine metabolism (remethylation and transsulfuration)MODULE:homocysteine_metabolism The two competing cytosolic fates of L-homocysteine, the branch-point metabolite of the methionine cycle. Homocysteine is generated from...
[more...][less] The two competing cytosolic fates of L-homocysteine, the branch-point metabolite of the methionine cycle. Homocysteine is generated from S-adenosylhomocysteine after SAM-dependent methylation reactions, and its two disposal routes determine methionine/one-carbon homeostasis and sulfur-amino-acid supply. (1) Remethylation regenerates L-methionine: methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) reduces 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate to 5-methyl-THF, the methyl donor that cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase (MTR) uses to transfer a methyl group to homocysteine (via an enzyme-bound methylcobalamin cofactor), producing methionine and regenerating tetrahydrofolate. Because MTR's cobalamin is periodically oxidised to inactive cob(II)alamin, methionine synthase reductase (MTRR), an NADPH-dependent diflavin oxidoreductase, reductively reactivates it; and the upstream cobalamin-processing enzyme MMACHC (cblC) decyanates/dealkylates incoming cobalamin to the cob(II)alamin precursor that supplies both methylcobalamin (to MTR) and adenosylcobalamin (to methylmalonyl-CoA mutase). (2) Transsulfuration commits homocysteine's sulfur to cysteine: the PLP-dependent cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS) condenses homocysteine with L-serine to cystathionine, which cystathionine gamma-lyase (CTH/CSE) then cleaves to L-cysteine (plus 2-oxobutanoate and ammonia); CBS and CTH are also the principal enzymatic sources of the gasotransmitter hydrogen sulfide. Inherited defects all cause homocystinuria / hyperhomocysteinemia with distinct biochemistry: CBS → classic homocystinuria (with hypermethioninemia); MTHFR → homocystinuria with low methionine; MTR → cblG and MTRR → cblE homocystinuria; MMACHC → cblC (combined methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria); CTH → (largely benign) cystathioninuria.

Imd signaling pathway in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_imd_signalingCONCRETE The immune deficiency (Imd) pathway is the main Drosophila defense against Gram-negative bacteria and some Gram-positive bacilli. It is triggered...
[more...][less] The immune deficiency (Imd) pathway is the main Drosophila defense against Gram-negative bacteria and some Gram-positive bacilli. It is triggered when DAP-type peptidoglycan binds the transmembrane receptor PGRP-LC or the intracellular receptor PGRP-LE. The receptors recruit the death-domain protein Imd, which assembles a complex with the adaptor Fadd and the caspase Dredd. Dredd cleaves Imd, and the E3 ligase Diap2, with the E2 enzymes Bendless and Effete and the E2 variant Uev1A, attaches K63-linked ubiquitin chains. These chains recruit the Tak1-Tab2 kinase complex, which activates the IKK complex (IKKbeta and Kenny). IKK phosphorylates the NF-kappa-B factor Relish, Dredd cleaves it, and the Rel homology domain enters the nucleus to induce antimicrobial peptide genes. Tak1 also activates the JNK branch (Hemipterous, Basket) that acts through AP-1 (Jra, Kayak).

Intracellular triacylglycerol lipolysis (ABHD5-ATGL, HSL, MGLL)MODULE:triacylglycerol_lipolysis Neutral (cytoplasmic) lipolysis is the stepwise hydrolysis of triacylglycerol stored in cytoplasmic lipid droplets to glycerol and three fatty...
[more...][less] Neutral (cytoplasmic) lipolysis is the stepwise hydrolysis of triacylglycerol stored in cytoplasmic lipid droplets to glycerol and three fatty acids. Adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL/PNPLA2) catalyzes the first, rate-limiting step, hydrolyzing triacylglycerol to diacylglycerol on the lipid droplet surface; its activity is strongly stimulated by the non-catalytic co-activator ABHD5 (CGI-58). Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL/LIPE) then hydrolyzes diacylglycerol to monoacylglycerol, and monoglyceride lipase (MGLL) completes the pathway by hydrolyzing monoacylglycerol to glycerol and a fatty acid. The pathway operates in adipocytes, where it supplies fatty acids to other tissues during fasting, and in most other cells including skeletal and cardiac muscle. Biallelic loss of ABHD5 causes neutral lipid storage disease with ichthyosis (Chanarin-Dorfman syndrome) and biallelic loss of PNPLA2 causes neutral lipid storage disease with myopathy; both show triacylglycerol accumulation in cytoplasmic droplets of many tissues.

Intraflagellar transportMODULE:intraflagellar_transportCONCRETE Intraflagellar transport (IFT) is the bidirectional, motor-driven movement of large protein trains along the ciliary axoneme that builds and...
[more...][less] Intraflagellar transport (IFT) is the bidirectional, motor-driven movement of large protein trains along the ciliary axoneme that builds and maintains cilia. It is ancestral in ciliated eukaryotes and has been lost along with cilia in lineages such as most fungi, flowering plants and Dictyostelium. IFT trains are polymers of two multisubunit complexes. IFT-B (including IFT88, IFT52, IFT57, IFT80, IFT70, IFT38, IFT46, IFT54, IFT56, IFT172, IFT20 and the IFT74/IFT81 tubulin-binding module) is needed to extend the axoneme and carries tubulin and other axonemal precursors. IFT-A (IFT140, IFT122, IFT144, IFT139, IFT121 and IFT43) is needed for retrograde transport and for ciliary import of membrane proteins. Heterotrimeric kinesin-II (two kinesin-2 motor subunits and a non-motor KAP subunit) carries trains from the ciliary base through the transition zone toward the tip. Some lineages add a homodimeric kinesin-2 accessory motor. In Caenorhabditis elegans sensory cilia, OSM-3 takes trains over from kinesin-II in a handover zone and alone builds the distal singlet segment, and the IFT-B subunit DYF-1 is required for OSM-3 to dock onto trains. At the tip trains turn around and are returned to the base by IFT-dynein (cytoplasmic dynein-2), whose heavy chain is DYNC2H1 (worm CHE-3). Ciliary kinases of the MAK/CILK1 family (worm DYF-5, human CILK1) regulate motor behaviour, train turnaround and cilium length; DYF-5 phosphorylates the tubulin-binding module of IFT-74 to promote tubulin unloading, and CILK1 phosphorylates the kinesin-II subunit KIF3A. The BBSome couples IFT-A and IFT-B and regulates IFT assembly at the base and turnaround at the tip. Loss of IFT-B, IFT-A, kinesin-II or dynein-2 function causes absent, truncated or malformed cilia; in worms this prevents dye uptake by sensory neurons, and in humans IFT gene mutations cause skeletal and renal ciliopathies.

Intraflagellar transport complexes A and B in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_intraflagellar_transportCONCRETE Intraflagellar transport (IFT) moves protein cargo along the axoneme between the ciliary base and tip. IFT trains are built from two multi-subunit...
[more...][less] Intraflagellar transport (IFT) moves protein cargo along the axoneme between the ciliary base and tip. IFT trains are built from two multi-subunit complexes: IFT-B, which is carried toward the tip by kinesin-2 and is required for anterograde transport and axoneme assembly, and IFT-A, which is needed mainly for retrograde transport by cytoplasmic dynein 2 and for import of membrane proteins. In Drosophila, cilia occur only on type I sensory neurons and on sperm. IFT is required to build the sensory cilia of chordotonal and external sensory neurons, and mutants such as nompB (IFT88) lack mechanosensory potentials, whereas most of the sperm axoneme is assembled without IFT.

Isoprenoid (prenyl) diphosphate biosynthesis (IPP/DMAPP -> GPP -> FPP -> GGPP)MODULE:isoprenoid_diphosphate_biosynthesisCONCRETE The isoprenoid-diphosphate trunk converts the universal five-carbon isoprene units produced by the mevalonate pathway (or, in bacteria and...
[more...][less] The isoprenoid-diphosphate trunk converts the universal five-carbon isoprene units produced by the mevalonate pathway (or, in bacteria and plastids, the MEP pathway; both curated separately) into the linear trans-prenyl diphosphates that seed the major downstream isoprenoid classes. Isopentenyl- diphosphate delta-isomerase (type 1 IDI) reversibly interconverts isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) and its allylic isomer dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP), supplying the allylic primer. Farnesyl diphosphate synthase then carries out two sequential head-to-tail (trans, 1'-4) condensations: DMAPP + IPP -> geranyl diphosphate (GPP, C10), and GPP + IPP -> farnesyl diphosphate (FPP, C15). FPP is the central branch point: it feeds sterol synthesis (cholesterol in animals, ergosterol in fungi, via squalene), heme A, ubiquinone side chains, dolichol (cis-prenyltransferases) and protein farnesylation. A geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthase adds one more IPP to FPP giving geranylgeranyl diphosphate (GGPP, C20), the donor for protein geranylgeranylation. The GGPP step has two architectures: a dedicated homomeric GGPP synthase (human GGPS1, budding-yeast BTS1), or, in fission yeast, which lacks a GGPS1/BTS1 homolog, a heteromer of the FPP synthase Fps1 with an inactive FPP-synthase-like subunit Spo9. All enzymes are soluble Mg2+-dependent isomerases/prenyltransferases (animal IDI1/IDI2 also peroxisomal). The pathway is the pharmacological target of nitrogen bisphosphonates (FDPS); human GGPS1 loss-of-function causes a muscular dystrophy / sensorineural hearing loss / ovarian insufficiency syndrome.

JAK-independent STAT signaling in Caenorhabditis elegansMODULE:c_elegans_jak_independent_stat_signalingCONCRETE Caenorhabditis elegans has no Janus kinase, no interferon system and no cytokine receptors that dock JAKs, yet both of its STAT-family...
[more...][less] Caenorhabditis elegans has no Janus kinase, no interferon system and no cytokine receptors that dock JAKs, yet both of its STAT-family transcription factors act in immune gene regulation. Each paralog is wired into a different upstream input and controls transcription in the opposite direction. STA-1 binds promoters in intestinal cells and acts mainly as a constitutive repressor of genes induced by Orsay virus. Its repressive function genetically requires the ACK-family non-receptor tyrosine kinase SID-3, and repression is relieved during infection. STA-2 acts in the epidermis. It is held at apical hemidesmosomes by the matrix receptor MUP-4, physically associates with the SLC6 transporter SNF-12, and is the point of convergence for a fungal-infection and wounding p38 MAPK cascade and for hemidesmosome or cuticle-collagen damage. STA-2 is required to induce antimicrobial peptide genes of the nlp-29 cluster. STA-2 lacks the conserved C-terminal phosphotyrosine motif that JAKs target in canonical STATs.

JAK-independent STAT signaling in Dictyostelium discoideumMODULE:dicty_jak_independent_stat_signalingCONCRETE The social amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum has four STAT-family transcription factors (STATa to STATd) but no Janus kinase and no kinases of the...
[more...][less] The social amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum has four STAT-family transcription factors (STATa to STATd) but no Janus kinase and no kinases of the tyrosine-kinase group. Its STATs are instead tyrosine phosphorylated by tyrosine kinase-like (TKL) kinases, and they dimerize, accumulate in the nucleus and regulate transcription during multicellular development and stress. The two best-studied paralogs are wired to different inputs. STATc is activated by the prestalk morphogen DIF-1 and by hyperosmotic and other stresses. Its activating Tyr922 is phosphorylated by the TKL kinases Pyk2 and Pyk3, which bind the STATc SH2 domain through autophosphorylated tyrosines. The kinase activity is largely constitutive, so the signal is set mainly by the tyrosine phosphatase PTP3: DIF-1 and stress induce serine phosphorylation of PTP3 (in part by the TKL kinase Phg2), which inhibits it and shifts STATc toward the phosphorylated state. Nuclear STATc activates stress-response genes and restricts graded expression of the prestalk gene ecmA. STATa is tyrosine phosphorylated on Tyr702 within seconds of extracellular cAMP binding the serpentine receptor cAR1, apparently without the G-beta subunit. The receptor-like TKL kinase DrkA phosphorylates STATa in vitro and is a candidate STATa kinase. STATa stays nuclear in the prestalk cells of the slug tip, where it represses the stalk gene ecmB and directly activates cudA, a transcription factor needed for culmination.

Environmental stress and inflammatory cytokines signal through upstream MAP3Ks (MEKK1/MAP3K1, ASK1, MLK family) to the dual-specificity MAP2Ks MKK4 (MAP2K4) and MKK7 (MAP2K7), which dually phosphorylate the JNK MAPKs (JNK1/2/3) on their TPY activation-loop motif. Active JNK phosphorylates the transcription factor c-Jun (and JunD, ATF2), assembling the AP-1 transcriptional program that controls stress responses, apoptosis, and proliferation. The kinase relay - MAP3K -> MKK4/7 -> JNK - is declared as an inner bundle that `conforms_to` mapk_relay, while the stress/cytokine input and the JNK/AP-1 output and DUSP-mediated feedback are this cascade's free extensions around the conforming core. Grounded in GO:0007254 (JNK cascade) / GO:0051403 (stress-activated MAPK cascade).

Jasmonate perception and JAZ derepression (JAR1-COI1-JAZ-NINJA/TPL-MYC module)MODULE:jasmonate_coi1_jaz_signalingABSTRACT Jasmonate signaling in vascular plants works by hormone-triggered derepression. Jasmonic acid is activated by the GH3-family jasmonoyl-amino acid...
[more...][less] Jasmonate signaling in vascular plants works by hormone-triggered derepression. Jasmonic acid is activated by the GH3-family jasmonoyl-amino acid conjugate synthetase JAR1, which adenylates JA and conjugates it to L-isoleucine to form jasmonoyl-L-isoleucine (JA-Ile), the bioactive hormone. JA-Ile is perceived by a co-receptor formed by the F-box/LRR protein COI1 and a JAZ (JASMONATE ZIM-domain) repressor: the hormone sits in an open pocket of the COI1 leucine-rich-repeat domain, is trapped by the Jas-motif degron of JAZ, and the complex is potentiated by inositol phosphate. COI1 is the substrate adaptor of an SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase (COI1-ASK1/ASK2-CUL1-RBX1), so hormone-dependent JAZ binding leads to JAZ polyubiquitination and 26S proteasome-dependent degradation. In the resting state, JAZ proteins bind the N-terminal JAZ-interaction domain of the bHLH transcription factors MYC2, MYC3 and MYC4 through their Jas motif, competitively blocking MYC recruitment of the Mediator subunit MED25; through their TIFY/ZIM domain they bind the adaptor NINJA, whose EAR motif recruits the Groucho/Tup1-type corepressor TOPLESS (TPL) and TPL-related proteins. JA-Ile-triggered JAZ degradation therefore removes both the MYC-blocking and the corepressor-recruiting activities, releasing MYC factors to activate jasmonate-responsive genes that control defense against insects and necrotrophic pathogens, wound responses, secondary metabolism and growth inhibition. Many JAZ genes are themselves MYC targets, providing negative feedback. Jasmonate biosynthesis upstream of JA (13-LOX, AOS, AOC, OPR3 and beta-oxidation), JA-Ile catabolism and JAZ-independent COI1 functions are outside this module.

[more...][less] The constitutive nine-enzyme Raetz pathway that builds Kdo2-lipid A, the minimal essential lipopolysaccharide anchor, at the cytoplasmic face of the Gram-negative inner membrane. LpxA reversibly transfers an (R)-3-hydroxyacyl chain from acyl carrier protein (ACP) to UDP-GlcNAc; the zinc deacetylase LpxC then irreversibly removes the N-acetyl group, the committed step that sets pathway flux. LpxD adds the second (R)-3-hydroxyacyl chain, LpxH cleaves part of the UDP-diacylglucosamine pool to lipid X, LpxB condenses lipid X with UDP-diacylglucosamine to the beta-1',6-linked disaccharide, and LpxK phosphorylates the 4' position to give lipid IVA. The bifunctional Kdo transferase WaaA adds two Kdo residues from CMP-Kdo, and the late acyltransferases LpxL and LpxM add laurate and myristate to the Kdo2-lipid IVA acceptor to give hexa-acylated Kdo2-lipid A. Flux is set at LpxC by FtsH-mediated proteolysis tuned by the adaptor LapB and the anti-adaptor YejM (PbgA), represented here as an optional regulatory part rather than as pathway chemistry.

Kennedy pathway (CDP-choline / CDP-ethanolamine synthesis of PC and PE)MODULE:kennedy_pathway_phospholipid_synthesisCONCRETE The Kennedy pathway is the principal de-novo route to the two most abundant membrane glycerophospholipids, phosphatidylcholine (PC) and...
[more...][less] The Kennedy pathway is the principal de-novo route to the two most abundant membrane glycerophospholipids, phosphatidylcholine (PC) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE). It runs as two parallel three-step branches that converge on a common diacylglycerol (DAG) acceptor. In the CDP-choline branch, choline kinase (CHKA/CHKB) phosphorylates choline to phosphocholine; the rate-limiting, membrane-regulated CTP:phosphocholine cytidylyltransferase (PCYT1A/PCYT1B) converts phosphocholine + CTP to CDP-choline; and a CDP-alcohol phosphotransferase (CHPT1, or the dual-specificity CEPT1) transfers phosphocholine from CDP-choline onto DAG to make PC + CMP. In the parallel CDP-ethanolamine branch, ethanolamine kinase (ETNK1/ETNK2) makes phosphoethanolamine, the rate-controlling CTP:phosphoethanolamine cytidylyltransferase (PCYT2) makes CDP-ethanolamine, and the ethanolaminephosphotransferases (the selenoprotein SELENOI/EPT1, or CEPT1) transfer phosphoethanolamine onto DAG to make PE + CMP. The two branches are linked by phosphatidylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PEMT), an ER enzyme (liver-enriched) that performs three sequential SAM-dependent methylations of PE to PC — the only way to make PC without preformed choline, and a major consumer of methyl groups. The amphitropic cytidylyltransferase PCYT1A senses membrane PC content, making it the key regulatory node. Inherited defects span a striking phenotypic range: PCYT1A congenital lipodystrophy / spondylometaphyseal dysplasia with cone-rod dystrophy, CHKB megaconial congenital muscular dystrophy, and PCYT2 and SELENOI hereditary spastic paraplegia. The same three-step branches operate in fungi, where the kinases are cytosolic, the cytidylyltransferases associate with the nuclear/ER membrane, and the two CDP-alcohol phosphotransferases overlap in specificity (the yeast ethanolaminephosphotransferase also uses CDP-choline, and fission yeast has a single dual-specificity enzyme). In fungi the Kennedy pathway runs in parallel with the CDP-diacylglycerol pathway, which makes PE by phosphatidylserine decarboxylation and PC by PE methylation when ethanolamine and choline are not supplied.

[more...][less] Keratan sulfate and the galactose/N-acetylhexosamine termini of chondroitin, dermatan and keratan sulfate are degraded in the lysosome by an ordered exolytic cascade that complements the heparan-sulfate pathway. Keratan sulfate is a repeating -Gal-GlcNAc- polymer with 6-O- sulfates on both sugars: N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase / galactose-6-sulfatase (GALNS) removes the 6-O-sulfate from a terminal galactose-6-sulfate (and, in chondroitin-6-sulfate, from GalNAc-6-sulfate), and GlcNAc-6-sulfatase (GNS, in the heparan-sulfate module) removes it from GlcNAc-6-sulfate; lysosomal acid beta-galactosidase (GLB1) then hydrolyses the exposed terminal beta-galactose; and lysosomal beta-hexosaminidase — the alpha-beta heterodimer hexosaminidase A (HEXA+HEXB) and the beta-beta homodimer hexosaminidase B (HEXB) — removes the terminal beta-N-acetylhexosamine, regenerating a substrate for the next round. These enzymes are broadly specific: GLB1 also degrades the GM1 ganglioside, and hexosaminidase A (with the GM2-activator) degrades the GM2 ganglioside, so the same genes underlie both mucopolysaccharide and glycosphingolipid storage diseases. Disorders: MPS IVA (GALNS, Morquio A), GM1 gangliosidosis / MPS IVB (GLB1, Morquio B), Tay-Sachs (HEXA) and Sandhoff (HEXB) GM2 gangliosidoses.

Ketogenesis (hepatic ketone body synthesis)MODULE:ketogenesis Ketogenesis is the mitochondrial pathway, operating chiefly in liver during fasting, starvation, prolonged exercise and low-carbohydrate states,...
[more...][less] Ketogenesis is the mitochondrial pathway, operating chiefly in liver during fasting, starvation, prolonged exercise and low-carbohydrate states, that converts acetyl-CoA (mostly from fatty-acid beta-oxidation) into the circulating ketone bodies acetoacetate and (R)-3-hydroxybutyrate, which supply oxidizable fuel to brain, heart and muscle when glucose is scarce. Four mitochondrial-matrix steps: mitochondrial acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase (thiolase, ACAT1) condenses two acetyl-CoA to acetoacetyl-CoA; the rate-limiting, fasting-induced mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase (HMGCS2) adds a third acetyl-CoA to give 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA); HMG-CoA lyase (HMGCL) cleaves HMG-CoA to acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA; and the inner-membrane NAD+-dependent D-3-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (BDH1) reversibly reduces acetoacetate to (R)-3-hydroxybutyrate, the predominant blood ketone. The pathway shares the HMGCL step with leucine catabolism and shares BDH1 (run in reverse) with ketolysis; liver exports the ketone bodies because it lacks the ketolytic enzyme OXCT1/SCOT. Inherited defects: HMGCS2 deficiency and HMGCL deficiency cause fasting hypoketotic hypoglycemia; ACAT1 (beta-ketothiolase) deficiency affects both ketone-body and isoleucine metabolism. (Ketone-body UTILIZATION/ketolysis in peripheral tissues — BDH1 -> OXCT1 -> ACAT1 -> 2 acetyl-CoA — is modelled separately in MODULE:ketone_body_oxidation.)

Ketone-body uptake and oxidationMODULE:ketone_body_oxidationCONCRETE A reusable pathway for use of D-3-hydroxybutyrate as a carbon and energy source. D-3-hydroxybutyrate is oxidized to acetoacetate, acetoacetate is...
[more...][less] A reusable pathway for use of D-3-hydroxybutyrate as a carbon and energy source. D-3-hydroxybutyrate is oxidized to acetoacetate, acetoacetate is activated to acetoacetyl-CoA, and a thiolase can cleave acetoacetyl-CoA to acetyl-CoA. Organisms differ in the activation reaction: animal ketolysis generally uses a succinyl-CoA-dependent CoA transferase, whereas some bacteria use an ATP-dependent acetoacetate-CoA ligase. Substrate import is an optional upstream role for organisms that consume extracellular ketone bodies. Intracellular D-3-hydroxybutyrate released from storage-polymer metabolism can enter at the oxidation step. Pseudomonas putida KT2440 provides candidate exemplars for import, oxidation, and ATP-dependent activation; their pathway dominance and the terminal thiolase remain to be resolved experimentally.

Kynurenine pathway / de novo NAD+ biosynthesis from tryptophan (TDO2/IDO1/AFMID/KMO/KYNU/HAAO/ACMSD/QPRT)MODULE:kynurenine_nad_de_novo The kynurenine pathway is the major route of L-tryptophan catabolism and the sole de novo source of NAD+ in humans, converting tryptophan through a...
[more...][less] The kynurenine pathway is the major route of L-tryptophan catabolism and the sole de novo source of NAD+ in humans, converting tryptophan through a series of ring-opening and modification steps to quinolinate and then to nicotinate mononucleotide (NaMN), which enters the common NAD+ pathway. It also generates neuroactive branch metabolites (kynurenic acid, quinolinic acid) and is central to immune regulation. The committed first step — oxidative ring cleavage of L-tryptophan to N-formyl-L-kynurenine — is catalysed by two heme dioxygenases with distinct physiology: the hepatic, rate-limiting TDO2 (tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase) and the broadly IFN-gamma-inducible, immunoregulatory IDO1 (indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase). The formamidase AFMID then hydrolyses N-formyl-kynurenine to L-kynurenine. Flux toward NAD+ requires the FAD-dependent, outer-mitochondrial-membrane kynurenine 3-monooxygenase KMO to hydroxylate kynurenine to 3-hydroxykynurenine (diverting away from the kynurenic-acid branch made by the aminotransferases AADAT/GOT2), followed by the PLP-dependent kynureninase KYNU, which cleaves 3-hydroxykynurenine to 3-hydroxyanthranilate. The Fe(II)-dependent dioxygenase HAAO opens the aromatic ring of 3-hydroxyanthranilate to 2-amino-3-carboxymuconate semialdehyde (ACMS), which spontaneously cyclises to quinolinate — unless the zinc enzyme ACMSD decarboxylates ACMS instead, diverting flux away from NAD+ toward full oxidation (picolinate/ acetyl-CoA). Finally quinolinate phosphoribosyltransferase QPRT condenses quinolinate with PRPP to NaMN, completing de novo NAD+ synthesis and detoxifying excitotoxic quinolinate. Inherited HAAO and KYNU deficiencies cause a congenital NAD-deficiency malformation syndrome (niacin-preventable in models); the pathway's enzymes (IDO1, TDO2, KMO, ACMSD) are drug targets in cancer immunotherapy, neurodegeneration and metabolic disease.

[more...][less] De novo L-arginine biosynthesis from L-glutamate through N-acetylated intermediates and L-ornithine, as found in bacteria, archaea, fungi and plants. The module includes the linear route, in which ArgA initiates acetylation and ArgE hydrolyses N-acetyl-L-ornithine, and the cyclic (acetyl-cycle) route, in which bifunctional ArgJ (ornithine acetyltransferase) recycles the acetyl group from N-acetyl-L-ornithine to L-glutamate and can also initiate the pathway; the cyclic route is the one used by fungi, where a structurally distinct fungal-type N-acetylglutamate synthase supplies anaplerotic N-acetylglutamate. After ornithine formation, ornithine carbamoyltransferase, argininosuccinate synthase and argininosuccinate lyase convert it through L-citrulline and argininosuccinate to L-arginine. In fungi the pathway is split between compartments: the five ornithine-forming reactions take place in the mitochondrial matrix, where acetylglutamate kinase and acetylglutamyl-phosphate reductase are made as a single precursor polyprotein that is cleaved into two enzymes after import, and the argininosuccinate reactions are cytosolic. Ornithine carbamoyltransferase is cytosolic in budding yeast, which exports ornithine from mitochondria, but mitochondrial in fission yeast and Neurospora, which export citrulline. Fungi also have a carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase dedicated to arginine biosynthesis (CPS-A), distinct from the pyrimidine-pathway enzyme, and it is modelled as an optional part; where carbamoyl phosphate comes from a synthetase shared with pyrimidine biosynthesis, as in many bacteria, that supply lies outside the module boundary. Succinylated-intermediate, N-acetylcitrulline, and LysW-dependent arginine pathways are distinct implementations not expanded in this module.

L-arginine metabolism in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_arginine_metabolismCONCRETE Three conserved urea-cycle enzymes interconvert citrulline, arginine and ornithine in Drosophila. Argininosuccinate synthase (Ass) condenses...
[more...][less] Three conserved urea-cycle enzymes interconvert citrulline, arginine and ornithine in Drosophila. Argininosuccinate synthase (Ass) condenses citrulline with aspartate to form argininosuccinate, argininosuccinate lyase (Argl) cleaves it to arginine and fumarate, and arginase (Arg) hydrolyses arginine to ornithine and urea. Together the first two steps regenerate arginine from citrulline, and arginase links arginine to ornithine, the precursor of proline and polyamines. Insects are not known to run a complete urea cycle, so the three enzymes act as a branch of amino acid metabolism rather than as the main route of nitrogen excretion.

L-aspartate, L-asparagine and L-alanine formation and turnoverMODULE:aspartate_asparagine_metabolism Formation and turnover of the amino acids that lie one step from the central-carbon 2-oxoacids oxaloacetate and pyruvate, in eukaryotes. Aspartate...
[more...][less] Formation and turnover of the amino acids that lie one step from the central-carbon 2-oxoacids oxaloacetate and pyruvate, in eukaryotes. Aspartate aminotransferase reversibly transaminates oxaloacetate with L-glutamate to give L-aspartate and 2-oxoglutarate. Eukaryotes carry a cytosolic and a mitochondrial isozyme; in budding yeast the cytosolic enzyme supplies most cellular aspartate, whereas the mitochondrial one acts in the matrix. L-aspartate is then amidated by glutamine-dependent asparagine synthetase, which uses ATP and the glutamine amide nitrogen to form L-asparagine and releases glutamate, AMP and diphosphate. Asparaginases hydrolyse L-asparagine back to L-aspartate and ammonium, which lets asparagine serve as a nitrogen source; fungi can have an intracellular asparaginase and, in some lineages, a cell-wall asparaginase regulated by nitrogen availability. The aspartate made by transamination feeds the aspartate family (threonine, methionine, isoleucine), arginine and pyrimidine synthesis, and the malate-aspartate shuttle. In the same way, alanine aminotransferase reversibly transaminates pyruvate with L-glutamate to give L-alanine and 2-oxoglutarate, and so serves both alanine synthesis and alanine use as a nitrogen source. All of these reactions use L-glutamate as amino donor or acceptor and so connect the ammonium-assimilation hub to carbon metabolism.

L-fucose degradation (mammalian non-phosphorylative pathway)MODULE:mammalian_l_fucose_degradationCONCRETE Catabolism of free cytosolic L-fucose to pyruvate and L-lactate by a five-reaction, non-phosphorylative (oxidative) route described biochemically...
[more...][less] Catabolism of free cytosolic L-fucose to pyruvate and L-lactate by a five-reaction, non-phosphorylative (oxidative) route described biochemically in pig and rabbit liver and kidney and in human. beta-L-Fucose is oxidized by NAD+-dependent L-fucose dehydrogenase (HSD17B14) to L-fucono-1,5-lactone, which rearranges non-enzymatically to L-fucono-1,4-lactone; a lactonase that has not been molecularly identified in mammals hydrolyses the lactone to L-fuconate; L-fuconate dehydratase (ENOSF1, the rTS-gamma isoform) forms 2-keto-3-deoxy-L-fuconate; an NAD+-dependent 2-keto-3-deoxy-L-fuconate 4-dehydrogenase (BDH2 is the leading candidate) forms 2,4-diketo-3-deoxy-L-fuconate; and an unidentified hydrolase cleaves this to pyruvate and L-lactate. Two of the five steps therefore have no assigned gene and a third has a candidate whose physiological role is unsettled. The route is chemically analogous to the bacterial non-phosphorylative pathway (Xanthomonas, Burkholderia, Herbaspirillum) and is distinct from the phosphorylative FucI/FucK/FucA route of Escherichia coli, from the salvage of L-fucose to GDP-L-fucose, and from lysosomal release of L-fucose from glycoconjugates. The pathway is not universal in mammals: rats oxidize little L-fucose and rat HSD17B14 has negligible L-fucose dehydrogenase activity.

[more...][less] De novo biosynthesis of L-histidine from PRPP and ATP through the conserved ten-reaction His pathway found in bacteria, archaea, fungi and plants. The module begins at the first committed ATP phosphoribosyltransferase reaction; PRPP production is shared upstream metabolism and is intentionally outside the module boundary. The pathway returns the ATP-derived purine ring to nucleotide metabolism as AICAR during the imidazole-glycerol-phosphate synthase reaction, which couples histidine and purine biosynthesis. The reaction chain is invariant, but its enzyme architecture varies widely across lineages: ATP phosphoribosyltransferase exists as a short-form catalytic subunit with a separate HisZ regulatory subunit or as a long-form single chain; the phosphoribosyl-ATP diphosphatase and phosphoribosyl-AMP cyclohydrolase can be separate proteins, a bifunctional HisIE protein, or domains of a trifunctional protein that also carries histidinol dehydrogenase (as in budding yeast); the glutaminase and cyclase halves of imidazole-glycerol-phosphate synthase can be separate HisH and HisF subunits or a single fused HisHF chain (as in fungi); and histidinol-phosphate phosphatase activity has arisen in several unrelated families (IMPase-like, HAD and PHP). The terminal histidinol dehydrogenase performs two successive NAD+-dependent oxidations through histidinal to produce L-histidine.

L-lysine biosynthesis via alpha-aminoadipateMODULE:lysine_biosynthesis_aminoadipateCONCRETE De novo biosynthesis of L-lysine from 2-oxoglutarate and acetyl-CoA through the C6 intermediate L-2-aminoadipate (alpha-aminoadipate, AAA). This...
[more...][less] De novo biosynthesis of L-lysine from 2-oxoglutarate and acetyl-CoA through the C6 intermediate L-2-aminoadipate (alpha-aminoadipate, AAA). This route is chemically unrelated to the diaminopimelate pathway of most bacteria and plants. Its first half extends the carbon chain by one methylene unit through reactions homologous to the citrate-to-2-oxoglutarate segment of the tricarboxylic acid cycle and to leucine biosynthesis: homocitrate synthase condenses acetyl-CoA with 2-oxoglutarate, homocitrate is isomerised to homoisocitrate in two aconitase-family steps (homocitrate dehydration to cis-homoaconitate, then hydration to homoisocitrate), homoisocitrate dehydrogenase oxidatively decarboxylates homoisocitrate to 2-oxoadipate, and a transaminase produces L-2-aminoadipate. The second half diverges by lineage. In fungi, a large phosphopantetheinylated alpha-aminoadipate reductase reduces AAA to its 6-semialdehyde, which is reductively condensed with L-glutamate to saccharopine and then cleaved to L-lysine and 2-oxoglutarate. In Thermus and in Sulfolobus and other archaea, AAA is instead ligated to the C-terminal glutamate of the small carrier protein LysW and converted to lysine by ArgB/C/D-like enzymes before a hydrolase releases free lysine. In fungi the early steps are split between compartments, with homocitrate isomerisation and homoisocitrate oxidation in the mitochondrial matrix and the final steps in the cytosol and peroxisome.

[more...][less] The main (saccharopine) pathway of L-lysine degradation in humans, a mitochondrial route that also handles L-hydroxylysine and the final steps of L-tryptophan catabolism, converging on glutaryl-CoA and ultimately acetyl-CoA. The bifunctional alpha-aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase (AASS) catalyses the first two committed steps: its lysine-2-oxoglutarate reductase (saccharopine dehydrogenase, NADP+) activity condenses L-lysine with 2-oxoglutarate to saccharopine, and its saccharopine dehydrogenase (NAD+) activity then oxidises saccharopine to L-2-aminoadipate-6-semialdehyde + L-glutamate. Downstream (semialdehyde -> L-2-aminoadipate by ALDH7A1; L-2-aminoadipate -> 2-oxoadipate by the aminotransferase AADAT — not modelled here) yields 2-oxoadipate, which the 2-oxoadipate dehydrogenase complex (OADHC) oxidatively decarboxylates to glutaryl-CoA. The OADHC is a paralogous sibling of the 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex: a dedicated E1 (DHTKD1, TPP-dependent) plus the shared E2 succinyltransferase core (DLST, acting as a glutaryltransferase here) and the shared E3 (DLD). Finally the FAD-dependent glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase (GCDH) oxidatively decarboxylates glutaryl-CoA to crotonyl-CoA + CO2, passing electrons to the electron-transfer flavoprotein system (ETF -> ETFDH -> respiratory chain). Inherited defects: AASS deficiency causes (largely benign) hyperlysinemia / saccharopinuria; DHTKD1 deficiency causes 2-aminoadipic/2-oxoadipic aciduria (and is linked to Charcot-Marie-Tooth 2Q); and GCDH deficiency causes glutaric aciduria type 1 (GA1), a serious encephalopathy with striatal injury.

L-methionine biosynthesis (from homoserine)MODULE:methionine_biosynthesis De novo biosynthesis of L-methionine from L-homoserine through three ordered stages: homoserine activation, sulfur incorporation to form...
[more...][less] De novo biosynthesis of L-methionine from L-homoserine through three ordered stages: homoserine activation, sulfur incorporation to form L-homocysteine, and methylation of L-homocysteine. Bacteria can activate homoserine with an acetyl or succinyl group, incorporate sulfur through two-step trans-sulfuration or one-step direct sulfhydrylation, and complete the pathway with a cobalamin-independent or cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase. Substrate-matched alternatives are retained explicitly because enzyme-family membership alone does not reliably distinguish acetyl from succinyl chemistry or forward biosynthetic from related PLP-dependent lyase reactions. Fungi such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe activate homoserine with an acetyl group, rely mainly on direct sulfhydrylation of O-acetylhomoserine with sulfide from sulfate assimilation, can also make homocysteine from cysteine by trans-sulfuration, and finish with a cobalamin-independent methionine synthase that requires a polyglutamylated 5-methyltetrahydrofolate. Plants use a cobalamin-independent synthase and a trans-sulfuration route whose cystathionine gamma-synthase takes O-phospho-L-homoserine rather than an acylated homoserine.

L-methionine salvage from 5'-methylthioadenosine (MTA cycle)MODULE:methionine_salvage_mta_cycle The methionine salvage pathway, or 5'-methylthioadenosine (MTA) cycle, regenerates L-methionine from MTA, the by-product of S-adenosylmethionine...
[more...][less] The methionine salvage pathway, or 5'-methylthioadenosine (MTA) cycle, regenerates L-methionine from MTA, the by-product of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) use in polyamine synthesis (and, in plants, ethylene synthesis). The methylthio group of MTA and carbons 2-5 of its ribose become the methionine skeleton, so the cycle recovers reduced sulfur that is costly to assimilate, and it also clears MTA, which inhibits spermidine synthase. MTA is first converted to S-methyl-5-thio-alpha-D-ribose 1-phosphate (MTR-1-P), either directly by MTA phosphorylase (eukaryotes and many bacteria) or by MTA nucleosidase followed by ATP-dependent MTR kinase (many bacteria, plants). MTR-1-P isomerase converts MTR-1-P to the ribulose phosphate, which MTRu-1-P dehydratase converts to the 2,3-diketo phosphate. An enolase and a phosphatase then form the acireductone 1,2-dihydroxy-5-(methylthio)pent-1-en-3-one. Fungi and animals do this with one bifunctional enolase-phosphatase (E1); Bacillus uses a RuBisCO-like enolase (MtnW) and a separate phosphatase (MtnX). An Fe(II)-dependent acireductone dioxygenase then oxidises the acireductone to 4-methylthio-2-oxobutanoate (KMTB) and formate. A final transamination converts KMTB to methionine. This step is redundant and is carried out by broad-specificity aromatic and branched-chain amino acid transaminases, not a dedicated enzyme. The cycle needs dioxygen and is largely cytosolic.

L-methionine salvage pathway in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_methionine_salvageCONCRETE The methionine salvage pathway recycles the methylthio group of 5'-methylthioadenosine (MTA), a by-product of polyamine synthesis, back into...

MTA phosphorylase (Mtap) cleaves MTA to adenine and 5-methylthioribose-1-phosphate, which is isomerised to methylthioribulose-1-phosphate (Mri1) and dehydrated to a diketo phosphate (CG11134). The bifunctional enolase-phosphatase Enoph converts this to acireductone, which acireductone dioxygenase (Adi1) oxidises to 4-methylthio-2-oxobutanoate. A final transamination regenerates methionine. As in other animals, the pathway in flies lacks the methylthioribose kinase step used by bacteria and plants, because MTA is cleaved phosphorolytically.

L-phenylalanine and L-tyrosine biosynthesis from chorismateMODULE:phenylalanine_tyrosine_biosynthesis Branch of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis that converts chorismate to L-phenylalanine and L-tyrosine in bacteria, fungi and plants. Chorismate...
[more...][less] Branch of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis that converts chorismate to L-phenylalanine and L-tyrosine in bacteria, fungi and plants. Chorismate mutase rearranges chorismate to prephenate; this committed step is the main point of feedback control, typically inhibited by tyrosine (and in fungi and plants activated by tryptophan). Prephenate is then converted by one of two routes. In the prephenate route used by fungi and most bacteria, prephenate dehydratase gives phenylpyruvate and prephenate dehydrogenase gives 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate, and aromatic aminotransferases convert these keto acids to phenylalanine and tyrosine. In the arogenate route that predominates in plants, prephenate aminotransferase first gives arogenate, which arogenate dehydratase and arogenate dehydrogenase convert to phenylalanine and tyrosine. In enteric bacteria chorismate mutase is fused to the dehydratase (P-protein) or the dehydrogenase (T-protein); in fungi and plants it is a separate allosteric enzyme. Synthesis of chorismate, the tryptophan branch and the hydroxylation of phenylalanine to tyrosine are outside this module.

L-threonine biosynthesis from L-aspartateMODULE:aspartate_family_threonine_biosynthesis De novo biosynthesis of L-threonine from L-aspartate in five reactions, as found in bacteria, fungi and plants; animals lack the pathway. The first...
[more...][less] De novo biosynthesis of L-threonine from L-aspartate in five reactions, as found in bacteria, fungi and plants; animals lack the pathway. The first three reactions form the aspartate-family trunk that produces L-homoserine: aspartate kinase phosphorylates L-aspartate to 4-phospho-L-aspartate, aspartate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase reduces it with NADPH to L-aspartate 4-semialdehyde, and homoserine dehydrogenase reduces the semialdehyde with NAD(P)H to L-homoserine. L-homoserine is a branch point: homoserine kinase commits it to threonine as O-phospho-L-homoserine, and threonine synthase, a pyridoxal-phosphate enzyme, converts O-phospho-L-homoserine to L-threonine. The chemistry is conserved but the enzyme architecture varies. Aspartate kinase and homoserine dehydrogenase are separate monofunctional proteins in fungi, whereas bacteria such as Escherichia coli and plants also carry bifunctional aspartate kinase-homoserine dehydrogenase fusion proteins. The threonine synthases of plants are allosterically activated by S-adenosylmethionine, whereas the bacterial and fungal enzymes are not. In plants O-phospho-L-homoserine is also the substrate of cystathionine gamma-synthase, so the methionine branch diverges after the kinase. In bacteria and plants L-aspartate 4-semialdehyde also feeds the diaminopimelate lysine pathway; fungi make lysine by the unrelated alpha-aminoadipate pathway, so in fungi the trunk serves only threonine, isoleucine and methionine. Threonine feedback-inhibits the trunk, chiefly at aspartate kinase.

L-tryptophan biosynthesisMODULE:tryptophan_biosynthesis De novo biosynthesis of L-tryptophan from chorismate, the branch-point precursor of the aromatic amino acids, as found in bacteria, archaea, fungi...
[more...][less] De novo biosynthesis of L-tryptophan from chorismate, the branch-point precursor of the aromatic amino acids, as found in bacteria, archaea, fungi and plants. Five ordered reactions convert chorismate to L-tryptophan, drawing in L-glutamine (amide nitrogen), PRPP (5-phospho-alpha-D-ribose 1-diphosphate) and L-serine, and releasing pyruvate, CO2 and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate along the way. The reaction chain is invariant, but the enzymes that carry it out are fused in different combinations in different lineages. Anthranilate synthase is a glutamine amidotransferase built from a synthase component (TrpE) and a glutaminase component (TrpG); TrpG can be a separate protein, fused to anthranilate phosphoribosyltransferase (TrpGD of enteric bacteria), fused to indole-3-glycerol-phosphate synthase (budding yeast TRP3, TrpG-TrpC), or the first domain of a trifunctional TrpG-TrpC-TrpF protein (Neurospora trp-1, fission yeast trp1). Phosphoribosylanthranilate isomerase (TrpF) is a standalone enzyme in many bacteria and in budding yeast, but is fused to indole-3-glycerol-phosphate synthase in TrpCF proteins and in the fungal trifunctional protein. The terminal tryptophan synthase is an alpha-2-beta-2 complex of TrpA and TrpB in bacteria and plants and a single fused TrpA-TrpB chain in fungi; in both forms indole made at the TrpA (alpha) active site is channelled through an intramolecular tunnel to the PLP-dependent TrpB (beta) site, where it condenses with L-serine, so free indole is not released. The pathway is feedback-regulated by L-tryptophan at anthranilate synthase and, in many bacteria, also transcriptionally by attenuation and the TrpR repressor.

L-valine, L-leucine, and L-isoleucine biosynthesisMODULE:branched_chain_amino_acid_biosynthesis De novo biosynthesis of the three branched-chain amino acids in bacteria, archaea, fungi and plants; the pathway is absent from animals....
[more...][less] De novo biosynthesis of the three branched-chain amino acids in bacteria, archaea, fungi and plants; the pathway is absent from animals. L-isoleucine synthesis begins with threonine deamination to 2-oxobutanoate. An acetohydroxy-acid synthase (a catalytic large subunit with a regulatory small subunit), ketol-acid reductoisomerase and dihydroxy-acid dehydratase then form a shared catalytic trunk that processes either the valine precursor derived from two pyruvate molecules or the isoleucine precursor derived from pyruvate plus 2-oxobutanoate. The valine intermediate 2-oxoisovalerate also enters a three-reaction leucine extension (2-isopropylmalate synthase, isopropylmalate isomerase and 3-isopropylmalate dehydrogenase). A branched-chain amino-acid aminotransferase performs the terminal transamination for all three products. The reaction chain is conserved, but two features vary by lineage. First, isopropylmalate isomerase is a heteromeric LeuC-LeuD enzyme in bacteria and plants but a single fused polypeptide in fungi. Second, in fungi the pathway is split between compartments: threonine deaminase, the shared trunk, most 2-isopropylmalate synthase and a biosynthetic aminotransferase are in the mitochondrial matrix, 2-isopropylmalate is exported to the cytosol by a mitochondrial carrier, and the isomerase and dehydrogenase are cytosolic. In budding yeast, mitochondrial BAT1 and cytosolic BAT2 are paralogous aminotransferases, with BAT1 favoured for biosynthesis and BAT2 for catabolism.

LDL receptor-mediated endocytic uptake — apoB-100 ligand, LDLR internalization and recycling, PCSK9 degradation controlMODULE:ldl_receptor_mediated_endocytosis Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) carries most plasma cholesterol and is cleared mainly by hepatocyte LDL receptors. Each LDL particle contains one...
[more...][less] Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) carries most plasma cholesterol and is cleared mainly by hepatocyte LDL receptors. Each LDL particle contains one apolipoprotein B-100 molecule, whose receptor-binding region is the ligand for the cysteine-rich ligand-binding repeats of the LDL receptor (LDLR) at the cell surface. LDLR-LDL complexes cluster in clathrin-coated pits through the LDLR cytoplasmic NPxY motif (with the adaptor LDLRAP1/ARH in liver) and are internalized by receptor-mediated endocytosis. In the acidic early endosome the receptor releases LDL, which proceeds to lysosomes where cholesteryl esters are hydrolysed and free cholesterol is delivered to the cell; the empty receptor recycles to the plasma membrane for further rounds. Secreted PCSK9 binds the LDLR EGF-A repeat and, after co-internalization, prevents the receptor's acid-induced conformational change so that it is routed to lysosomes and degraded instead of recycling, lowering receptor number and LDL clearance (IDOL/MYLIP provides an intracellular, ubiquitin-dependent degradation route). Loss of LDLR, of the apoB-100 receptor-binding region, or of LDLRAP1, or gain of function of PCSK9, causes familial hypercholesterolaemia; PCSK9 loss of function lowers LDL cholesterol and is the target of PCSK9-inhibitor therapy.

LINC complex (SUN-KASH nuclear envelope bridge) moduleMODULE:linc_complexABSTRACT The LINC (linker of nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton) complex is a transmembrane bridge across the nuclear envelope. It connects the cytoskeleton to...
[more...][less] The LINC (linker of nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton) complex is a transmembrane bridge across the nuclear envelope. It connects the cytoskeleton to the nuclear interior. Inner-nuclear-membrane SUN-domain proteins form trimers whose C-terminal SUN domains project into the perinuclear space. Each trimer binds the C-terminal KASH peptides of three outer-nuclear-membrane KASH proteins, and the pair is reinforced by a conserved intermolecular disulfide. On the nucleoplasmic side, SUN proteins bind the nuclear lamina and, in meiosis, telomeres. On the cytoplasmic side, different KASH proteins engage different cytoskeletal systems: nesprin-1 and nesprin-2 bind actin through calponin-homology domains and bind microtubule motors (dynein-dynactin through BICD2, and kinesin-1); nesprin-3 binds plectin and so intermediate filaments; nesprin-4 binds kinesin-1; and the meiosis-specific KASH5 recruits dynein-dynactin. The bridge transmits force for nuclear migration and anchorage, centrosome-nucleus coupling, meiotic telomere-led chromosome movement, and sperm head-tail attachment. Disruption causes muscular dystrophy, cerebellar ataxia, hearing loss, infertility and neuronal migration defects.

Lactate fermentation and the Rapoport-Luebering (2,3-BPG) shunt — GSD XI, BPGM deficiencyMODULE:lactate_fermentation_and_bpg_shunt Two branch reactions of glycolysis, prominent in anaerobic tissue and in erythrocytes (which depend entirely on glycolysis and lack mitochondria)....
[more...][less] Two branch reactions of glycolysis, prominent in anaerobic tissue and in erythrocytes (which depend entirely on glycolysis and lack mitochondria). (1) Lactate fermentation: lactate dehydrogenase (a tetramer of the LDHA/M and LDHB/H subunits) reduces the glycolytic end-product pyruvate to L-lactate using NADH, regenerating the NAD+ that glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase needs to sustain glycolytic flux when oxidative phosphorylation is unavailable or saturated; the LDHA-rich isoenzymes favour pyruvate to lactate (anaerobic/glycolytic tissue) while LDHB-rich isoenzymes favour the reverse oxidation of lactate to pyruvate (oxidative tissue). (2) The Rapoport-Luebering shunt: bisphosphoglycerate mutase (BPGM) diverts 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (and hydrolyses it onward to 3-phosphoglycerate), bypassing the ATP-generating phosphoglycerate-kinase step; 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate is the principal allosteric effector that binds deoxyhemoglobin and lowers its oxygen affinity, tuning O2 delivery to tissues. Both branches feed off glycolytic intermediates (pyruvate and 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate respectively). Inherited defects: LDHA deficiency causes glycogen storage disease type XI (exertional myopathy, myoglobinuria, skin lesions); LDHB deficiency is usually clinically silent; and BPGM deficiency lowers 2,3-BPG, raising hemoglobin oxygen affinity and causing secondary erythrocytosis.

[more...][less] Arabidopsis leaf trichomes (unicellular epidermal hairs) are spaced by a cell-autonomous activator complex and mobile inhibitors. In the leaf primordium epidermis an MYB-bHLH-WD40 (MBW) activator complex forms from the R2R3-MYB GLABRA1 (GL1; MYB23 acts partially redundantly), the redundant bHLH proteins GLABRA3 (GL3) and ENHANCER OF GLABRA3 (EGL3), and the WD40-repeat protein TRANSPARENT TESTA GLABRA1 (TTG1); GL3/EGL3 bridge GL1 and TTG1. The active complex binds and activates the promoters of the HD-ZIP IV transcription factor GLABRA2 (GL2), which executes trichome differentiation, and of the single-repeat R3 MYB inhibitors CAPRICE (CPC), ENHANCER OF TRY AND CPC1 (ETC1) and TRIPTYCHON (TRY). The R3 MYB proteins lack an activation domain; they move into neighbouring epidermal cells, bind GL3/EGL3 and compete with GL1, so that inactive complexes form there and those cells remain pavement cells (lateral inhibition). TRY also represses its own promoter, and TTG1 depletion from cells surrounding a trichome by GL3-dependent trapping contributes a second, trapping/depletion patterning mechanism. TRY suppresses trichome clustering, CPC mainly sets trichome density, and try cpc double mutants convert all cells contacting a trichome into trichomes. Jasmonate (JAZ) and gibberellin (DELLA) repressors bind GL1 and GL3/EGL3 and modulate the complex; these hormone inputs, the root epidermis WER-GL3/EGL3-TTG1 module that specifies non-hair cells, and the seed coat/anthocyanin MBW complexes built on TT8 and TT2/PAP MYBs share components with this module but are outside its boundary.

Lysine catabolism (saccharopine pathway; AASS/ALDH7A1/AADAT/DHTKD1/GCDH)MODULE:lysine_catabolism_saccharopine The saccharopine pathway is the main route of L-lysine degradation in mammals, converting lysine to acetyl-CoA through 2-aminoadipate and...
[more...][less] The saccharopine pathway is the main route of L-lysine degradation in mammals, converting lysine to acetyl-CoA through 2-aminoadipate and glutaryl-CoA, predominantly in liver and brain mitochondria. The bifunctional enzyme AASS (2-aminoadipic-6-semialdehyde synthase) catalyses the first two steps: its lysine-ketoglutarate reductase domain condenses L-lysine with 2-oxoglutarate to saccharopine, and its saccharopine dehydrogenase domain then cleaves saccharopine to L-2-aminoadipate 6-semialdehyde (AASA) plus L-glutamate. AASA (in equilibrium with delta-1-piperideine-6-carboxylate, P6C) is oxidised to L-2-aminoadipate by the NAD-dependent aldehyde dehydrogenase ALDH7A1 (antiquitin); a block here causes accumulation of P6C, which inactivates pyridoxal-5'-phosphate and produces pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy. The PLP-dependent aminotransferase AADAT (KAT2) then transaminates 2-aminoadipate with 2-oxoglutarate to 2-oxoadipate (AADAT is also kynurenine aminotransferase II, linking to tryptophan metabolism). 2-oxoadipate is oxidatively decarboxylated to glutaryl-CoA by the 2-oxoadipate dehydrogenase DHTKD1 (with DLST and DLD), and glutaryl-CoA is dehydrogenated/decarboxylated to crotonyl-CoA by GCDH (glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase), which continues to two acetyl-CoA. Inherited defects cause aminoadipic/oxoadipic aciduria (DHTKD1), pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (ALDH7A1) and glutaric aciduria type 1 (GCDH).

Lysosomal glycogen degradation (acid alpha-glucosidase) — Pompe disease (GSD II)MODULE:lysosomal_glycogen_degradation Lysosomal glycogen degradation is the acid-hydrolase route for breaking down the glycogen that is delivered to lysosomes by autophagy (glycophagy),...
[more...][less] Lysosomal glycogen degradation is the acid-hydrolase route for breaking down the glycogen that is delivered to lysosomes by autophagy (glycophagy), complementing the cytosolic glycogenolysis pathway (phosphorylase/debranching). Its single enzyme is lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA, acid maltase), a glycoside-hydrolase-family-31 enzyme that works at the acidic pH of the lysosomal lumen to completely hydrolyse glycogen to free glucose, cleaving the alpha-1,4-glucosidic bonds (and, more slowly, the alpha-1,6 branch linkages). GAA is synthesised as a precursor, N-glycosylated and mannose-6-phosphate-tagged for delivery to the lysosome, and proteolytically matured to its active forms. Because this route continuously clears autophagocytosed glycogen, its loss is not compensated by cytosolic glycogenolysis: inherited GAA deficiency causes Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II) — lysosomal glycogen accumulation producing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and profound hypotonia in the infantile-onset form, and a progressive limb-girdle and respiratory myopathy in late-onset disease. It is one of the few glycogenoses treatable by enzyme replacement therapy (recombinant human GAA, e.g. alglucosidase/avalglucosidase alfa).

[more...][less] Glycoproteins delivered to the lysosome are proteolysed to glycopeptides whose glycans are then dismantled by lumenal exoglycosidases working from both ends. From the non-reducing end, N-glycan antennae are trimmed residue by residue: capping sialic acid (NEU1), terminal galactose (GLB1), antennal N-acetylglucosamine (beta-hexosaminidase, HEXA/HEXB), alpha-linked mannoses (MAN2B1) and the core beta-mannose (MANBA); terminal alpha-N-acetylgalactosamine of blood group A and mucin-type determinants is removed by NAGA. From the reducing end, the core alpha1,6-fucose is removed by FUCA1, which is required because core fucosylation blocks aspartylglucosaminidase (AGA); AGA then cleaves the N-glycosidic GlcNAc-Asn bond, separating the glycan from the asparagine residue. Loss of any step causes a glycoproteinosis (oligosaccharidosis) with lysosomal storage and urinary excretion of the corresponding oligosaccharides or glycoasparagines: sialidosis, GM1 gangliosidosis, Sandhoff disease, alpha- and beta-mannosidosis, fucosidosis, aspartylglucosaminuria and NAGA deficiency.

Lysosome-to-nucleus lipid signaling in Caenorhabditis elegansMODULE:c_elegans_lysosomal_lipid_signalingCONCRETE In the Caenorhabditis elegans intestine, lysosomes send lipid signals to the nucleus that adjust fat metabolism and extend lifespan. The TFEB...
[more...][less] In the Caenorhabditis elegans intestine, lysosomes send lipid signals to the nucleus that adjust fat metabolism and extend lifespan. The TFEB ortholog HLH-30 is a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that moves into the nucleus during fasting, after germline loss or when TOR signalling falls. It turns on autophagy and lysosome genes, and with the Max-like factor MXL-3 it links lysosomal lipolysis to nutrient supply. The lysosomal acid lipase LIPL-4, a homolog of human LIPA, is induced in these conditions and hydrolyses lipids at acidic pH inside the lysosome. Its activity raises the levels of omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids, which promote autophagy, and of the N-acylethanolamine oleoylethanolamide (OEA). The intestinal fatty acid-binding protein LBP-8 sits on lysosomes and binds OEA and oleic acid with high affinity. When LIPL-4 activity is high, LBP-8 enters the nucleus through an N-terminal nuclear localization signal. There, OEA binds the HNF4-family nuclear receptor NHR-80 directly. NHR-80 works with its partner NHR-49, which does not bind OEA, to switch on genes for fatty acid desaturation (fat-5, fat-6, fat-7) and mitochondrial beta-oxidation (acs-2), as well as lbp-8 itself. The pathway is needed for the long life of animals that overexpress LIPL-4 or LBP-8. It is independent of dietary restriction.

Major (U2-type) spliceosome in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_spliceosomeCONCRETE The major spliceosome removes U2-type introns from nuclear pre-mRNAs. It is assembled stepwise on each intron from the U1, U2, U4/U6 and U5 small...
[more...][less] The major spliceosome removes U2-type introns from nuclear pre-mRNAs. It is assembled stepwise on each intron from the U1, U2, U4/U6 and U5 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particles (snRNPs) and many non-snRNP proteins. Each snRNP contains a small nuclear RNA; the U1, U2, U4 and U5 snRNAs carry a heptameric ring of Sm proteins, whereas U6 snRNA binds the related LSm proteins. U1 snRNP recognizes the 5' splice site, and the U2 snRNP auxiliary factor (U2AF) together with SF1 recognizes the 3' splice site region, allowing U2 snRNP to pair with the branch site (complex A). Joining of the U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP forms the precatalytic complex B; release of U1 and U4 and recruitment of the Prp19 complex and associated proteins create the catalytic spliceosome, which carries out the two transesterification steps (complex C) and then releases the spliced mRNA (post-catalytic complex P) with an exon junction complex deposited upstream of the exon-exon junction.

Malate-aspartate shuttle (MDH1/MDH2/GOT1/GOT2 + SLC25A11/SLC25A12)MODULE:malate_aspartate_shuttle The malate-aspartate shuttle is the principal mechanism by which reducing equivalents (cytosolic NADH generated in glycolysis) are transferred into...
[more...][less] The malate-aspartate shuttle is the principal mechanism by which reducing equivalents (cytosolic NADH generated in glycolysis) are transferred into the mitochondrial matrix for oxidation by the respiratory chain, in tissues such as heart, liver and brain. Because NADH itself cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane, the shuttle moves the electrons as malate: in the cytosol, malate dehydrogenase 1 (MDH1) reduces oxaloacetate to malate, consuming a cytosolic NADH; the malate is imported by the oxoglutarate/malate carrier (SLC25A11, OGC) in exchange for 2-oxoglutarate; in the matrix, malate dehydrogenase 2 (MDH2) re-oxidises malate to oxaloacetate, regenerating matrix NADH that feeds Complex I. Oxaloacetate cannot cross the membrane either, so it is transaminated with glutamate to aspartate by mitochondrial aspartate aminotransferase (GOT2, PLP-dependent); the aspartate is exported by the Ca2+-regulated aspartate-glutamate carrier (SLC25A12, AGC1/aralar) in exchange for cytosolic glutamate, and cytosolic aspartate aminotransferase (GOT1) regenerates oxaloacetate and 2-oxoglutarate to close the cycle. The AGC1 antiport, being electrogenic and effectively unidirectional, gives the shuttle its net direction. Defects in these components cause disease: SLC25A12/AGC1 deficiency causes a hypomyelinating encephalopathy (global cerebral hypomyelination / epilepsy), MDH2 and GOT2 deficiencies cause early infantile epileptic encephalopathy, and the shuttle is a key node in cancer redox metabolism.

Mammalian cerebellum development moduleMODULE:cerebellum_developmentCONCRETE A mammalian developmental program that builds the cerebellum from dorsal rhombomere 1. The program begins with allocation of the cerebellar anlage...
[more...][less] A mammalian developmental program that builds the cerebellum from dorsal rhombomere 1. The program begins with allocation of the cerebellar anlage by the midbrain-hindbrain (isthmic) organizer, followed by segregation of two principal germinal-zone programs: an ATOH1-positive rhombic-lip program that generates glutamatergic lineages and a PTF1A-positive ventricular-zone program that generates GABAergic lineages. Reelin-dependent reorientation of an early/posterior-born Purkinje-cell subset initiates early plate formation. As Purkinje cells differentiate, they provide Sonic hedgehog (SHH) to expand granule-cell precursors in the transient external granule layer. Partly overlapping granule-neuron migration and Bergmann-glial differentiation assemble the cortical layers, while Engrailed-dependent regional patterning coordinates foliation of the vermis and hemispheres. The module ends with formation of the layered, foliated cerebellum; mature synaptic physiology, motor learning, adult homeostasis, and tumorigenesis are outside its boundary.

Mannose 6-phosphate tagging of lysosomal hydrolases — Golgi GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase (GNPTAB) and its retention factor LYSETMODULE:mannose_6_phosphate_lysosomal_targeting Newly synthesised soluble lysosomal acid hydrolases are sorted away from the secretory pathway by a mannose 6-phosphate (M6P) recognition marker on...
[more...][less] Newly synthesised soluble lysosomal acid hydrolases are sorted away from the secretory pathway by a mannose 6-phosphate (M6P) recognition marker on their N-glycans. In the cis-Golgi the GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase complex (alpha2beta2gamma2; catalytic alpha/beta subunits encoded by GNPTAB, gamma by GNPTG) recognises a conformational protein determinant shared by lysosomal hydrolases and transfers GlcNAc-1-phosphate from UDP-GlcNAc to C6 hydroxyls of mannose residues of their high-mannose N-glycans. The Golgi membrane protein LYSET (TMEM251) binds the GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase, stabilising it and supporting its site-1 protease activation and Golgi retention, and is required for M6P tagging. In the trans-Golgi network the uncovering enzyme NAGPA removes the covering GlcNAc to expose M6P, and the M6P receptors (cation-dependent M6PR and cation-independent IGF2R) bind the tagged hydrolases and deliver them to endosomes, from which the receptors recycle. Loss of GNPTAB causes mucolipidosis II (I-cell disease) and MLIII alpha/beta, GNPTG loss causes MLIII gamma, and LYSET deficiency causes a mucolipidosis-like disorder, all with hypersecretion of lysosomal enzymes and lysosomal storage.

[more...][less] The earliest developmental hand-off in metazoan embryos, in which control of development passes from maternally deposited factors to the embryo's own genome. The module has two coupled, ordered arms: (1) clearance of maternal mRNAs and proteins, executed by sequence-specific RNA-binding factors and maternal/zygotic small RNAs that target maternal transcripts for deadenylation and decay; and (2) zygotic genome activation (ZGA), in which pioneer and pluripotency transcription factors (e.g. POU5F1/Oct4, Nanog/NANOG, SOX2, and lineage-specific activators such as DUX/DUX4 and Nr5a2) open embryonic chromatin and switch on the first zygotic transcripts. Maternal patterning determinants deposited during this window feed forward into modules/body_axis_specification.yaml.

Metaphase/anaphase transition and mitotic exit (APC/C-driven)MODULE:metaphase_anaphase_transition_and_mitotic_exitCONCRETE A taxon-neutral decomposition of the two coupled proteolytic switches that end mitosis. (1) The anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C), a...
[more...][less] A taxon-neutral decomposition of the two coupled proteolytic switches that end mitosis. (1) The anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C), a cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase, is activated by CDK1 phosphorylation and by binding of its substrate-adaptor coactivator Cdc20 (Slp1). (2) Until every kinetochore is attached, the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) - Mps1/Mph1 kinase at unattached kinetochores, Mad1-Mad2 templating, and the Bub1/Bub3 scaffold - assembles the mitotic checkpoint complex (Mad2-BubR1/Mad3-Bub3-Cdc20) that sequesters and inhibits APC/C-Cdc20. (3) Once the SAC is satisfied, APC/C-Cdc20 ubiquitinates securin (PTTG1, Pds1, Cut2), releasing separase (ESPL1, Esp1, Cut1) to cleave the cohesin kleisin subunit (RAD21, Scc1/Mcd1, Rad21) and trigger sister-chromatid separation, the metaphase/anaphase transition proper. (4) APC/C-Cdc20 and then APC/C-Cdh1 (FZR1, Hct1/Cdh1, Ste9/Srw1) ubiquitinate the mitotic cyclins, extinguishing CDK1 activity. (5) A CDK-counteracting phosphatase - Cdc14 released by the mitotic exit network in budding yeast, Clp1/Flp1 and the septation initiation network in fission yeast, and reactivated PP2A-B55 in metazoa - reverses CDK phosphorylation to complete mitotic exit and reset G1. Representative members are drawn from human, Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe. Grounded in GO:0007091 (metaphase/anaphase transition of mitotic cell cycle) and GO:0010458 (exit from mitosis).

Metazoan autophagosome biogenesis and maturationMODULE:metazoan_autophagosome_biogenesisCONCRETE In animals, macroautophagy builds a double-membrane autophagosome around cytoplasmic cargo and delivers it to lysosomes. The core steps are shared...
[more...][less] In animals, macroautophagy builds a double-membrane autophagosome around cytoplasmic cargo and delivers it to lysosomes. The core steps are shared with yeast, but several are wired differently. An initiation complex of the Atg1/ULK kinase, ATG13 and ATG101 marks the site of formation, which in animals lies on endoplasmic reticulum (ER) subdomains called omegasomes. The class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase complex I (VPS34, the pseudokinase VPS15, Beclin 1 and ATG14) makes phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) on this membrane. Two kinds of WD40 PROPPIN read PI3P. WIPI1/2-type proteins recruit the conjugation machinery, and WIPI3/4-type proteins partner the ATG2 rod in an ATG2-ATG18 complex. ATG2 carries lipids from the ER to the growing phagophore, and the ATG9 scramblase spreads them between the two leaflets. Atg8-family proteins are primed by ATG4 and conjugated to phosphatidylethanolamine by the E1 ATG7, the E2 ATG3 and the E3-like ATG12-ATG5-ATG16 complex, with ATG16 setting where conjugation happens. Animals have two Atg8 subfamilies, GABARAP-type and LC3-type, and the stage at which each acts differs between lineages: in nematodes the GABARAP-type protein acts early and the LC3-type protein late, whereas in mammalian cells the GABARAP subfamily dominates autophagosome-lysosome fusion. Cargo receptors such as p62/SQSTM1 link ubiquitinated cargo to Atg8-family proteins. Fusion with late endosomes and lysosomes needs EPG5, a metazoan-specific RAB7 effector that binds Atg8-family proteins and SNAREs and makes sure autophagosomes fuse with the correct partner.

Methionine (S-adenosylmethionine) cycle moduleMODULE:methionine_cycle A taxon-neutral decomposition of the methionine / S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) cycle, the core methyl-group-cycling pathway that interconverts...
[more...][less] A taxon-neutral decomposition of the methionine / S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) cycle, the core methyl-group-cycling pathway that interconverts methionine, S-adenosyl-L-methionine, S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine, and homocysteine, with exits to transsulfuration (via cystathionine beta-synthase) and remethylation inputs from folate (via methionine synthase) and choline/betaine (via BHMT). This module is intentionally structured in two layers. The CATALYTIC layer (enzymatic steps) grounds each step to a GO molecular-function term, the same EC <-> GO MF alignment used by the gluconeogenesis module. The REGULATORY layer is captured as connections of type POSITIVELY_REGULATES / NEGATIVELY_REGULATES whose predicate is grounded to a Systems Biology Ontology (SBO) term that distinguishes the MECHANISM (competitive vs allosteric), with the effector represented as a ChEBI-grounded metabolite-pool node. This regulatory wiring (small-molecule effector -> enzyme, with mechanism and sign) is information GO cannot express: GO annotations attach to gene products, the effectors here are metabolites, and GO has no competitive-vs-allosteric distinction. The regulatory structure is transcribed from the biosustain Maud kinetic model `data/methionine/methionine_cycle.toml`. A notable showcase is METAT, where two isozyme forms of methionine adenosyltransferase catalyse the SAME reaction but are OPPOSITELY regulated by SAM: MAT-I is competitively product-inhibited by SAM, whereas MAT-III is allosterically activated by SAM. Isozyme-specific regulation of this kind is the central thing GO flattens away. The core chemistry (SAM synthesis, transmethylation, SAH hydrolysis, homocysteine remethylation) is universal; the lineage-specific pieces are modelled as optional parts or variants. Fungi such as budding and fission yeast run the cycle with single-chain SAM synthetases (two paralogues in S. cerevisiae), a single adenosylhomocysteinase, and a cobalamin-independent (MetE-type) methionine synthase that uses 5-methyltetrahydropteroyl triglutamate; they have no glycine N-methyltransferase or betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase, whereas mammals use the cobalamin-dependent MetH-type enzyme plus hepatic BHMT and GNMT. The 5'-methylthioadenosine (MTA) salvage route back to methionine is a separate module (methionine_salvage_mta_cycle).
