Mevalonate pathway (acetyl-CoA -> isopentenyl diphosphate)MODULE:mevalonate_pathwayCONCRETE The eukaryotic (classical) mevalonate pathway converts acetyl-CoA into the universal five-carbon isoprenoid building block isopentenyl diphosphate...
[more...][less] The eukaryotic (classical) mevalonate pathway converts acetyl-CoA into the universal five-carbon isoprenoid building block isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP), the precursor of sterols (cholesterol in animals, ergosterol in fungi), dolichol, ubiquinone (CoQ), heme A and the farnesyl/geranylgeranyl groups used for protein prenylation. A cytosolic acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase condenses two acetyl-CoA to acetoacetyl-CoA; HMG-CoA synthase adds a third acetyl-CoA to give 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA); HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting, sterol-feedback-regulated enzyme and target of the statin drugs, reduces HMG-CoA to mevalonate with two NADPH on the endoplasmic-reticulum membrane; mevalonate kinase and phosphomevalonate kinase then doubly phosphorylate mevalonate to mevalonate 5-diphosphate; and diphosphomevalonate decarboxylase decarboxylates it to IPP in an ATP-dependent reaction. The reaction chain is conserved across animals, fungi and plants, but the phosphomevalonate kinase step is carried out by two unrelated protein families: a GHMP-kinase-type enzyme (ERG8 type) in fungi, plants and bacteria, and a small P-loop kinase (PMVK type) that displaced it early in animal evolution. Fungi may carry two HMG-CoA reductase isozymes (budding yeast HMG1 and HMG2). Mevalonate kinase is a second, metabolite-level control point, competitively feedback-inhibited by downstream prenyl diphosphates. In humans, inherited defects cause mevalonate kinase deficiency (MVK; hyper-IgD/periodic fever syndrome to mevalonic aciduria) and porokeratosis (MVD and MVK); HMGCR and HMGCS1 are pharmacologic (statin), autoimmune and rare-myopathy loci rather than classic enzymopathies.

Microsomal fatty-acid elongation cycle (ELOVL or KCS -> KAR -> HACD -> ECR)MODULE:fatty_acid_elongation_cycle Most fatty acids longer than the C16 palmitate made by cytosolic fatty-acid synthase are produced by the microsomal elongation system, a...
[more...][less] Most fatty acids longer than the C16 palmitate made by cytosolic fatty-acid synthase are produced by the microsomal elongation system, a four-reaction cycle on the cytosolic face of the endoplasmic-reticulum membrane that adds two carbons per turn. Each round begins with the rate-limiting, substrate-selective condensation of an acyl-CoA with malonyl-CoA to a 3-oxoacyl-CoA (releasing CO2), catalysed by one of seven fatty-acid elongases (ELOVL1-7) whose chain-length and saturation preferences define which fatty acids a cell makes: ELOVL1/3/6 handle saturated and monounsaturated substrates (ELOVL6 the C16->C18 lipogenic step, ELOVL1 the C22->C26 very-long-chain step for sphingolipids/myelin, ELOVL3 skin/brown-fat lipids), ELOVL2/5 the C20/C22 polyunsaturated fatty acids en route to DHA, ELOVL7 C18-C20 substrates, and ELOVL4 the unique ultra-long-chain (C26-C38) fatty acids of retina, skin and brain. The 3-oxoacyl-CoA is then reduced by the NADPH-dependent 3-ketoacyl-CoA reductase HSD17B12 (KAR) to (3R)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA, dehydrated by the 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydratases HACD1/HACD2 to (2E)-enoyl-CoA, and reduced by the NADPH-dependent trans-2-enoyl-CoA reductase TECR to the two-carbon-extended saturated acyl-CoA, which re-enters the cycle. The reductase/dehydratase/reductase enzymes are shared across all ELOVLs; substrate specificity resides in the elongase. Inherited defects span the products: ELOVL1 (IKSHD ichthyosis/spastic quadriplegia), ELOVL4 (Stargardt-like macular dystrophy, SCA34, ichthyosis), HACD1 (congenital myopathy), TECR (intellectual disability), reflecting the roles of very-long-chain and ultra-long-chain fatty acids in skin barrier, myelin, retina and muscle. Fungi use ELO-family elongases homologous to the ELOVLs, whose paralogs divide the chain-length range from medium-chain (C12-C14) to C26 substrates, together with orthologous reductase, dehydratase and enoyl reductase; the C26 product is the fatty acid of fungal sphingolipids. Plants run the same four-step cycle but use an unrelated condensing enzyme, the thiolase-fold 3-ketoacyl-CoA synthases (KCS; e.g. FAE1/KCS18 for seed erucic acid, CER6/KCS6 for cuticular wax), while the downstream steps are carried out by orthologs of the animal enzymes (KCR1, PAS2, ECR/CER10 in Arabidopsis). The condensation step is therefore modelled as alternative enzyme families, and the three shared steps list animal and plant exemplars.

Mitochondrial ADP/ATP and phosphate carriers (ATP synthasome substrate carriers); SLC25A4/A5/A6 + SLC25A3MODULE:oxphos_adenine_nucleotide_phosphate_carriers Oxidative phosphorylation is completed not only by the five respiratory complexes but by the inner-membrane carriers that supply ATP synthase...
[more...][less] Oxidative phosphorylation is completed not only by the five respiratory complexes but by the inner-membrane carriers that supply ATP synthase (Complex V) with its substrates and export its product. Because the inner membrane is impermeable to adenine nucleotides and phosphate, two SLC25 mitochondrial-carrier activities are essential: the ADP/ATP translocase (adenine nucleotide translocator, ANT) and the phosphate carrier (PiC). The ADP/ATP translocase is an electrogenic antiporter that imports cytosolic ADP into the matrix in exchange for newly synthesised ATP, exporting the ATP made by Complex V; humans express three near-identical isoforms with tissue-specific distribution — ANT1/SLC25A4 (heart and skeletal muscle), ANT2/SLC25A5 (proliferative and glycolytic tissues) and ANT3/SLC25A6 (ubiquitous). The phosphate carrier SLC25A3 (PiC) imports inorganic phosphate into the matrix in symport with a proton, providing the Pi consumed by ATP synthase. ANT, PiC and ATP synthase physically associate as the "ATP synthasome", coupling substrate delivery to ATP synthesis. The ADP/ATP translocase also forms part of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore and participates in apoptosis (curated as non-core roles). Disorders: ANT1 (SLC25A4) mutations cause autosomal-dominant progressive external ophthalmoplegia and mitochondrial myopathy/cardiomyopathy; SLC25A3 defects cause a mitochondrial phosphate-carrier deficiency with lactic acidosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

[more...][less] Beyond its 14 conserved "core" subunits, mitochondrial respiratory Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) carries ~30 nuclear-encoded accessory (supernumerary) subunits that form a shell around the core L-shaped enzyme. These subunits are stable constituents of the mature holoenzyme (unlike the transient assembly factors) but are non-catalytic — they carry no redox cofactor and do not themselves perform the NADH:ubiquinone reaction. Their roles are structural: they stabilise and shield the core, seal the membrane arm, and are required for assembly and stability of a fully active complex. This module groups the human accessory subunits by which arm they decorate. The peripheral (matrix) arm accessory subunits — NDUFA2 (thioredoxin-fold), NDUFA5, NDUFA6, NDUFA12 (near the N/Q junction) and NDUFA13/GRIM-19 — buttress the flavoprotein and Q modules; NDUFA13 additionally has a well-documented moonlighting role as a negative regulator of STAT3 signalling and in apoptosis, curated separately from its structural role. The membrane arm accessory subunits — NDUFA1 (MWFE), NDUFA8 (twin-CX9C), NDUFA10, NDUFA11 (Tim17-like fold), NDUFB3, NDUFB7, NDUFB8, NDUFB9, NDUFB10 and NDUFB11 (several imported and disulfide-folded by the MIA40/CHCHD4 relay), and NDUFC2 — clamp the hydrophobic ND subunits. Loss of individual accessory subunits destabilises the holoenzyme and causes isolated mitochondrial complex I deficiency (Leigh syndrome, cardiomyopathy, leukoencephalopathy; NDUFB11 is X-linked, causing histiocytoid cardiomyopathy / MLS-like disease).

This module groups the human Complex I assembly factors by the step they serve. A set of factors covalently modify or metallate specific core subunits before they can be incorporated: NDUFAF5 hydroxylates a conserved arginine of NDUFS7, NDUFAF7 symmetrically dimethylates an arginine of NDUFS2, NUBPL (IND1) delivers the [4Fe-4S] clusters, and the FAD-dependent oxidoreductase-fold protein FOXRED1 is required for maturation of the late ~815 kDa intermediate (its substrate, if any, is unknown). Synthesis of the central MT-CO1 subunit is activated by the matrix RNA-binding translational activator TACO1 (which binds the MT-CO1 mRNA on the mitoribosome), and the nascent MT-CO1 is captured and stabilised by the MITRAC module (COA3/CCDC56 with COX14) that couples its translation to assembly. MT-CO2 itself is threaded into the membrane by the OXA1L-family insertase COX18 (with COX20). Finally, PET100 and PET117 are small chaperones that promote incorporation of the early nuclear-encoded subunits (COX7/COX8) to complete the holoenzyme. [more...][less] Translation in mitochondria uses the 22 tRNAs encoded by mitochondrial DNA, which are charged with their amino acids in the mitochondrial matrix by a separate set of nuclear-encoded aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (the "2" synthetases, for example AARS2, DARS2 and TARS2). Each synthetase activates its amino acid with ATP and transfers it to the cognate mitochondrial tRNA. A single mitochondrial tRNA(Met) serves both initiation and elongation; the fraction destined for initiation is formylated on its methionyl group by methionyl-tRNA formyltransferase (MTFMT), using 10-formyltetrahydrofolate, to give fMet-tRNA(Met), which is recognized by the mitochondrial initiation factor and used to start synthesis of the 13 mtDNA-encoded respiratory-chain subunits. Biallelic variants in the mitochondrial synthetases cause tissue-selective disorders (for example DARS2 leukoencephalopathy with brainstem and spinal cord involvement and lactate elevation, AARS2 infantile cardiomyopathy or adult leukoencephalopathy with ovarian failure, TARS2 combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency), and MTFMT variants cause Leigh syndrome and combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 15.

[more...][less] Iron-sulfur (Fe-S) clusters are cofactors of respiratory complexes, the TCA cycle, DNA replication and repair enzymes and many other proteins. In eukaryotes all clusters depend on the mitochondrial iron-sulfur cluster (ISC) machinery. In the matrix, the cysteine desulfurase Nfs1, stabilised by Isd11 (bcn92) and acyl-ND-ACP, supplies sulfur and frataxin (fh) stimulates assembly of a [2Fe-2S] cluster on the scaffold IscU, with electrons from ferredoxin (Fdx1) and ferredoxin reductase (dare). The Hsc20-Hsc70-5 chaperone pair with glutaredoxin 5 transfers the cluster to client proteins, and the ISA proteins (MagR, CG13623) with IBA57 (CG8043) convert [2Fe-2S] into [4Fe-4S] clusters for mitochondrial targets. A sulfur-containing compound made by the ISC machinery is exported by the ABC transporter Abcb7 and used by the cytosolic iron-sulfur protein assembly (CIA) system: the diflavin reductase CG13667 and anamorsin (Ciapin1) supply electrons, the Nubp1-Nubp2 scaffold builds [4Fe-4S] clusters, and the CIA targeting complex (Ciao1, CG17683, galla2 and Mms19) inserts them into cytosolic and nuclear apoproteins.

[more...][less] Many essential enzyme cofactors and coenzymes are synthesised (wholly or partly) in the cytosol but are required by enzymes inside the mitochondrial matrix, which the inner membrane keeps impermeable. A set of SLC25 mitochondrial-carrier proteins solves this by importing specific cofactors into the matrix. This module groups the human cofactor/coenzyme carriers. SLC25A19 imports thiamine pyrophosphate (ThPP), the cofactor of the matrix 2-oxo-acid dehydrogenases (pyruvate dehydrogenase, 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase) and transketolase-like enzymes; SLC25A26 is the only carrier that imports S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the methyl donor for matrix methyltransferases (mtDNA/RNA methylation and cofactor maturation), exchanging it for the product S-adenosylhomocysteine; SLC25A32 imports FAD (and is linked to mitochondrial folate/one-carbon metabolism); and SLC25A42 imports coenzyme A (CoA), needed for matrix acyl-CoA metabolism (fatty-acid oxidation and the TCA cycle), in exchange for intramitochondrial adenine nucleotides. Loss-of-function of these carriers causes cofactor-specific mitochondrial diseases: SLC25A19 — Amish lethal microcephaly and bilateral striatal necrosis/polyneuropathy (THMD3/4); SLC25A26 — combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 28; SLC25A32 — riboflavin/folate-responsive exercise intolerance and myopathy; SLC25A42 — a mitochondrial myopathy with episodic metabolic crises.

Mitochondrial dNTP supply for mtDNA maintenance — MNGIE and mtDNA depletion syndromesMODULE:mitochondrial_dntp_supply Faithful replication of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), including in post-mitotic tissues, requires a balanced supply of the four deoxyribonucleoside...
[more...][less] Faithful replication of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), including in post-mitotic tissues, requires a balanced supply of the four deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) inside mitochondria. Because mitochondria cannot rely on the cell-cycle-regulated cytosolic de novo machinery, they use a dedicated salvage pathway plus a p53-inducible de novo input, and depend on cytosolic enzymes that keep nucleoside pools balanced. The mitochondrial deoxyribonucleoside kinases phosphorylate imported deoxyribonucleosides to dNMPs: thymidine kinase 2 (TK2) handles the pyrimidines (thymidine, deoxycytidine, deoxyuridine) and deoxyguanosine kinase (DGUOK) the purines (deoxyguanosine, deoxyadenosine). The p53-inducible ribonucleotide reductase small subunit RRM2B (p53R2), with RRM1, provides de novo deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates (dNDPs) by reducing NDPs — the main dNTP source for quiescent cells and mtDNA. Cytosolic thymidine phosphorylase (TYMP) governs systemic thymidine/deoxyuridine levels; its loss floods the dNTP pool with thymidine-derived nucleotides and destabilises mtDNA. Together these enzymes maintain the mitochondrial dNTP balance; imbalance (excess or deficiency) causes mtDNA depletion/deletions. Inherited defects are the classic mtDNA-maintenance disorders: TYMP -> MNGIE; TK2 -> myopathic mtDNA depletion; DGUOK -> hepatocerebral mtDNA depletion; RRM2B -> encephalomyopathic mtDNA depletion and dominant progressive external ophthalmoplegia.

Mitochondrial di-/tricarboxylate and glutamate carriers (SLC25A1 citrate, SLC25A10 dicarboxylate, SLC25A21 oxodicarboxylate, SLC25A22 glutamate)MODULE:mitochondrial_dicarboxylate_tricarboxylate_carriers The tricarboxylic-acid (TCA) cycle both consumes and generates carbon skeletons that must move between the mitochondrial matrix and the cytosol for...
[more...][less] The tricarboxylic-acid (TCA) cycle both consumes and generates carbon skeletons that must move between the mitochondrial matrix and the cytosol for anabolism (lipogenesis, gluconeogenesis) and amino-acid metabolism. A set of SLC25 mitochondrial carriers exchanges these di- and tricarboxylate intermediates and related amino acids across the impermeable inner membrane. This module groups four such carriers. The citrate carrier SLC25A1 (CIC/CTP) exports matrix citrate in exchange for cytosolic malate, feeding cytosolic citrate lysis into acetyl-CoA (and NADPH) for fatty-acid and cholesterol synthesis. The dicarboxylate carrier SLC25A10 (DIC) exchanges malate or succinate for inorganic phosphate, supplying dicarboxylates for gluconeogenesis and lipogenesis and linking to sulfur metabolism. The oxodicarboxylate carrier SLC25A21 (ODC) transports the C5-C7 2-oxodicarboxylates 2-oxoadipate and 2-oxoglutarate, serving the mitochondrial steps of lysine and tryptophan degradation. The glutamate carrier SLC25A22 (GC1) imports L-glutamate in symport with a proton, feeding glutamate catabolism and ammonia handling (and, in neurons, glutamate metabolism). Loss-of-function causes distinct metabolic diseases: SLC25A1 — combined D-2- and L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria and a congenital myasthenic syndrome; SLC25A22 — early infantile epileptic encephalopathy with migrating partial seizures; and SLC25A21 has been linked to a 2-oxoadipate/2-oxoglutarate-dehydrogenase-related phenotype.

Mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation spiral (cross-species)MODULE:fatty_acid_beta_oxidation The core four-step spiral of mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation, by which saturated fatty acyl-CoA esters are degraded two carbons at a time,...
[more...][less] The core four-step spiral of mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation, by which saturated fatty acyl-CoA esters are degraded two carbons at a time, releasing one acetyl-CoA and a chain-shortened acyl-CoA per turn that re-enters the cycle. The four obligate reactions are (1) FAD-dependent alpha,beta-dehydrogenation of acyl-CoA to (2E)-enoyl-CoA by an acyl-CoA dehydrogenase; (2) hydration of the trans double bond to (3S)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA by an enoyl-CoA hydratase; (3) NAD+-dependent oxidation to 3-ketoacyl-CoA by a 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase; and (4) thiolytic cleavage by a 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase to yield acetyl-CoA plus an acyl-CoA shortened by two carbons. Each step is carried out by a family of chain-length-specific isozymes: as the acyl chain shortens through successive turns of the spiral, the enzyme that acts changes. The long-chain steps 2-4 are performed by the membrane-bound mitochondrial trifunctional protein (MTP, an alpha2-beta2 heterotetramer whose alpha subunit carries the hydratase and dehydrogenase activities and whose beta subunit carries the thiolase), whereas the medium- and short-chain steps are carried out by separate soluble matrix enzymes. This module is built cross-species: each catalytic role is grounded with both the human enzyme(s) and the Drosophila melanogaster ortholog(s), so the conserved enzymatic logic and the species-specific gene complement can be compared directly. The chain-length axis is modelled as a variant set at each step; "use MF specific for chain length" where such a molecular-function term exists, with a fall-back to the general activity where it does not. This module covers the SATURATED spiral. Degradation of UNSATURATED fatty acids additionally requires an auxiliary-enzyme cassette - a delta(3),delta(2)-enoyl-CoA isomerase (fly mitochondrial CG4592/CG4594/CG4598 vs peroxisomal Dci), a delta(3,5),delta(2,4)-dienoyl-CoA isomerase (fly Ech1), and a 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase (DECR1, for which no clean Drosophila ortholog is currently assignable) - which are curated in the project but not modelled as variant sets here; see the Fatty Acid beta-Oxidation project page (unsaturated cassette section) for details.

Mitochondrial fission and fusionMODULE:mitochondrial_dynamicsCONCRETE In animals and fungi, mitochondrial shape is set by a balance between fission and fusion carried out by three classes of dynamin-family GTPases....
[more...][less] In animals and fungi, mitochondrial shape is set by a balance between fission and fusion carried out by three classes of dynamin-family GTPases. Fission of the outer membrane is driven by a dynamin-related protein (DNM1L/Drp1 in mammals, Dnm1 in budding yeast, DRP-1 in nematodes) that is recruited from the cytosol to constriction sites on the outer membrane. There it assembles into helices and uses GTP hydrolysis to constrict and sever the organelle. The same dynamin also divides peroxisomes. Recruitment depends on outer-membrane receptors whose identity differs between lineages: the tail-anchored adaptor MFF in animals, and Fis1 with the adaptors Mdv1 and Caf4 in budding yeast. In nematodes, the two MFF paralogs promote fission but are not essential for recruiting DRP-1. Fusion happens in two membrane-specific steps. Mitofusins (MFN1/MFN2, Fzo1, FZO-1) tether and fuse outer membranes. OPA1 and its orthologs (Mgm1 in yeast, EAT-3 in nematodes) fuse inner membranes; human L-OPA1 does this together with cardiolipin on the opposing membrane. When fusion is lost, unopposed fission fragments the mitochondrial network, and this fragmentation needs the fission dynamin. When fission is lost, the network becomes hyperconnected. The balance between the two is used in stress responses and in segregating damaged mitochondria for mitophagy.

SLC25A24 (APC1/SCaMC-1) is a Ca2+-regulated ATP-Mg/phosphate carrier that exchanges cytosolic Mg-ATP (or ADP) for matrix inorganic phosphate, adjusting the total matrix adenine-nucleotide pool in response to cytosolic calcium via its N-terminal EF-hand domain. Mitochondrial protein import machinery in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_mitochondrial_protein_importCONCRETE Most mitochondrial proteins are made on cytosolic ribosomes and imported post-translationally. Nearly all enter through the TOM complex of the...
[more...][less] Most mitochondrial proteins are made on cytosolic ribosomes and imported post-translationally. Nearly all enter through the TOM complex of the outer membrane, whose channel is formed by Tom40. Beta-barrel outer membrane proteins are then handed by the small TIM chaperones of the intermembrane space to the SAM complex for insertion. Carrier-type inner membrane proteins are inserted by the TIM22 complex, and presequence-bearing precursors are translocated by the TIM23 complex, driven into the matrix by the presequence translocase-associated motor (PAM) built around mitochondrial Hsp70 (Hsc70-5). Matrix presequences are removed by the mitochondrial processing peptidase, and some intermembrane space-sorted precursors are further cleaved by the inner membrane peptidase. Cysteine-rich intermembrane space proteins are imported and oxidatively folded by the Mia40-Alr disulfide relay. Drosophila has testis-specific paralogs of several subunits (for example tomboy40, tomboy20 and several Tim17 and Tim50 paralogs).

Mitochondrial respiratory Complex I core (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) — catalytic N and Q modules and membrane-arm core; NDUFV1/NDUFV2/NDUFS1-3/NDUFS6-8/NDUFA9, MT-ND1/MT-ND5/MT-ND6MODULE:mitochondrial_complex_i_core Respiratory Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) is the largest enzyme of the electron transport chain and its main entry point: it oxidises...
[more...][less] Respiratory Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) is the largest enzyme of the electron transport chain and its main entry point: it oxidises NADH, passes the electrons through a chain of flavin and iron-sulfur cofactors to reduce ubiquinone, and uses the energy released to pump four protons across the inner membrane. This module covers the catalytic core of the L-shaped peripheral (matrix) arm — the seven conserved "core" nuclear subunits plus the closely associated flavoprotein subunits — together with representative mtDNA-encoded core subunits of the membrane arm, organised into three functional modules. The N-module (NADH-oxidising) holds the flavin site: NDUFV1 (51 kDa) binds FMN and the NADH substrate, NDUFV2 (24 kDa) carries the first [2Fe-2S] cluster (N1a), and NDUFS1 (75 kDa) provides further Fe-S clusters, forming the flavoprotein (FP) subcomplex with the accessory NDUFS6. The Q-module (ubiquinone-reducing) forms the wire to the quinone site: NDUFS2 (49 kDa) and NDUFS3 (30 kDa) are cofactor-less core subunits shaping the ubiquinone cavity, NDUFS7 (PSST) coordinates the terminal [4Fe-4S] cluster N2 that donates electrons to ubiquinone, NDUFS8 (TYKY) carries the N6a/N6b [4Fe-4S] clusters of the electron-transfer wire, and the accessory NDUFA9 (SDR-fold, structural NADPH) stabilises the Q-module/membrane-arm junction; NDUFS4 is an accessory subunit required for assembly and stability of the whole peripheral arm. The P-module (membrane arm, proton-pumping) is represented by three of its seven mtDNA-encoded core subunits: MT-ND1 lines the quinone-channel exit and begins the E-channel, MT-ND6 forms part of the E-channel, and MT-ND5 is the distal antiporter-like subunit; each contributes to proton translocation within the assembled complex. Inherited defects in these core subunits are among the commonest causes of mitochondrial complex I deficiency — typically Leigh syndrome, leukoencephalopathy, fatal infantile lactic acidosis or encephalocardiomyopathy.

Mitochondrial respiratory Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) + assembly factors; SDHA/SDHB/SDHC/SDHD + SDHAF1/SDHAF2MODULE:mitochondrial_complex_ii Respiratory Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase, SDH) is the only enzyme shared between the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and the mitochondrial...
[more...][less] Respiratory Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase, SDH) is the only enzyme shared between the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and the mitochondrial electron transport chain. It oxidises succinate to fumarate in the matrix and feeds the released electrons into the ubiquinone pool, without pumping protons. The holoenzyme is a heterotetramer anchored in the inner membrane: the flavoprotein subunit SDHA carries a covalently bound FAD and the succinate-oxidising active site; the iron-sulfur subunit SDHB relays the electrons through three Fe-S clusters ([2Fe-2S], [4Fe-4S], [3Fe-4S]); and the two integral-membrane subunits SDHC and SDHD form the membrane anchor, bind a single heme b and provide the ubiquinone-reduction site. Two dedicated matrix assembly factors build the soluble catalytic head before it docks onto the membrane anchor: SDHAF2 (SDH5) promotes the covalent attachment of FAD to SDHA (flavinylation), and SDHAF1 — a LYR-motif protein acting with the HSC20/HSPA9 Fe-S co-chaperone system — delivers and inserts the iron-sulfur clusters into SDHB. Germline defects in the SDH subunits and assembly factors cause hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma syndromes and, when biallelic, mitochondrial complex II deficiency (Leigh syndrome, leukoencephalopathy, cardiomyopathy).

Mitochondrial respiratory Complex III (cytochrome bc1) — subunits and assembly; UQCRC1/UQCRC2/UQCRB/UQCRQ/UQCRH/UQCRFS1/CYC1 + BCS1L/LYRM7/TTC19/UQCC2/UQCC3MODULE:mitochondrial_complex_iii Respiratory Complex III (ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase, the cytochrome bc1 complex) is the central proton-pumping enzyme of the...
[more...][less] Respiratory Complex III (ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase, the cytochrome bc1 complex) is the central proton-pumping enzyme of the mitochondrial electron transport chain: it oxidises ubiquinol and reduces cytochrome c through the protonmotive Q cycle, contributing to the transmembrane proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis. The functional complex is a homodimer, each protomer built from cytochrome b (mtDNA-encoded MT-CYB) and ten nuclear-encoded subunits. The three redox centres reside in cytochrome b (the two b-hemes and the Qo/Qi ubiquinone sites), the Rieske iron-sulfur protein UQCRFS1 (the [2Fe-2S] cluster), and cytochrome c1 (CYC1); the hinge protein UQCRH mediates the cytochrome c1-cytochrome c electron-transfer interface. The two large "core proteins" UQCRC1 and UQCRC2 (peptidase-M16-fold but non-catalytic) and the small subunits UQCRB and UQCRQ are structural, providing the scaffold and the ubiquinone-binding environment. Assembly is stepwise and requires dedicated factors: UQCC2 (with UQCC1) stabilises and promotes translation of MT-CYB to nucleate the complex; UQCC3 stabilises the cytochrome-b assembly intermediate and (via cardiolipin binding) supports supercomplex organisation; LYRM7 is a matrix chaperone that holds apo-UQCRFS1 before [2Fe-2S] insertion; BCS1L is the AAA-ATPase translocase that inserts the matured Rieske protein into the nearly complete complex; and TTC19 clears the UQCRFS1 N-terminal fragments generated during Rieske maturation. Inherited defects in the subunits or assembly factors cause mitochondrial complex III deficiency (a spectrum of encephalopathy, leukoencephalopathy, lactic acidosis, tubulopathy and — for BCS1L — GRACILE syndrome).

Mitochondrial respiratory Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) — nuclear subunits and MT-CO1/CO2 assembly; COX5A/COX6A2/COX7B/COX8A + COX14/COX20MODULE:mitochondrial_complex_iv Respiratory Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase, COX) is the terminal enzyme of the mitochondrial electron transport chain: it accepts electrons from...
[more...][less] Respiratory Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase, COX) is the terminal enzyme of the mitochondrial electron transport chain: it accepts electrons from reduced cytochrome c and uses them to reduce molecular oxygen to water, coupling this to proton pumping across the inner membrane. The three catalytic core subunits — MT-CO1 (the heme a/a3-CuB binuclear centre), MT-CO2 (the CuA centre) and MT-CO3 — are encoded by mitochondrial DNA; around ten nuclear-encoded structural subunits (COX4, COX5A, COX5B, COX6A/B/C, COX7A/B/C, COX8) surround and stabilise this core and modulate activity. Because the catalytic subunits are mtDNA-encoded and membrane-embedded, COX assembly is a highly ordered process guided by dedicated inner-membrane factors: COX14 (with COA3/MITRAC) couples MT-CO1 translation to its stepwise assembly, and COX20 chaperones the newly-made MT-CO2 through membrane insertion (with COX18) and copper (CuA) metallation by SCO1/SCO2, before the nuclear subunits are added. Inherited defects in the nuclear subunits or the assembly factors cause mitochondrial complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) deficiency — a clinically heterogeneous group including Leigh syndrome, cardiomyopathy (COX6A2), X-linked linear skin defects with multiple congenital anomalies (COX7B) and encephalopathy/ataxia.

Mitochondrial respiratory Complex V (F1Fo ATP synthase) — subunits and F1 assembly; ATP5F1A/ATP5F1B/ATP5F1D/ATP5F1E/ATP5PO/ATP5MC3/ATP5MD + ATPAF2/TMEM70MODULE:mitochondrial_complex_v Complex V, the F1Fo ATP synthase, is the terminal enzyme of oxidative phosphorylation: it uses the proton-motive force generated by the electron...
[more...][less] Complex V, the F1Fo ATP synthase, is the terminal enzyme of oxidative phosphorylation: it uses the proton-motive force generated by the electron transport chain (Complexes I-IV) to drive the synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. It is a rotary molecular motor with two coupled sectors. The membrane-embedded Fo sector — the c-ring (ATP5MC1/2/3), the a-subunit (mtDNA-encoded MT-ATP6) and small membrane subunits including DAPIT (ATP5MD) and 6.8PL — conducts protons and rotates the central stalk; the matrix-facing F1 sector is the catalytic head, an alpha3-beta3 hexamer (ATP5F1A/ATP5F1B) whose three catalytic nucleotide sites are turned through their conformational cycle by the rotating central stalk (gamma/ATP5F1C, delta/ATP5F1D, epsilon/ATP5F1E). The peripheral (stator) stalk, anchored at the top by OSCP (ATP5PO), holds the F1 head stationary against the rotor so that rotation is converted into ATP synthesis rather than futile spinning. Assembly is factor-dependent: ATPAF2 (ATP12) is a matrix chaperone that binds the F1 alpha subunit to build the alpha3-beta3 catalytic core, and TMEM70 is an inner-membrane scaffold that promotes incorporation of subunit c into the Fo c-ring rotor. Neither factor is a subunit of the mature enzyme or carries its catalytic activity. Inherited defects in the subunits or assembly factors cause mitochondrial complex V (ATP synthase) deficiency — commonly a neonatal encephalopathy with 3-methylglutaconic aciduria, lactic acidosis and cardiomyopathy.

Mitochondrial ribosome in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_mitochondrial_ribosomeCONCRETE The mitochondrial ribosome (mitoribosome) translates the small set of mitochondrial-DNA-encoded mRNAs, which in animals encode core subunits of the...
[more...][less] The mitochondrial ribosome (mitoribosome) translates the small set of mitochondrial-DNA-encoded mRNAs, which in animals encode core subunits of the respiratory chain and ATP synthase. It consists of a small subunit built on the mitochondrially encoded 12S-type rRNA (mt:srRNA) and a large subunit built on the 16S-type rRNA (mt:lrRNA), together with nuclear-encoded mitochondrial ribosomal proteins. Animal mitoribosomes are protein-rich: they contain bacterial-type ribosomal proteins plus many mitochondria-specific proteins. In Drosophila, loss of the small-subunit protein tko (mRpS12) causes the technical knockout phenotype of bang sensitivity.

Mitochondrial sulfide oxidation in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_sulfide_oxidationCONCRETE Hydrogen sulfide produced by cysteine catabolism and gut microbes is detoxified in the mitochondrial matrix. Sulfide:quinone oxidoreductase (Sqor)...
[more...][less] Hydrogen sulfide produced by cysteine catabolism and gut microbes is detoxified in the mitochondrial matrix. Sulfide:quinone oxidoreductase (Sqor) oxidises sulfide to a protein-bound persulfide, passing the electrons to ubiquinone in the respiratory chain. The persulfide sulfur is then oxidised to sulfite by the persulfide dioxygenase ETHE1 (CG30022 in flies) or transferred to sulfite to form thiosulfate. Sulfite oxidase (shop) oxidises sulfite to sulfate, and the mitochondrial dicarboxylate carrier (Dic1) can export thiosulfate and sulfate in exchange for other anions.

Mitochondrial type II fatty acid synthesis in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_mitochondrial_fatty_acid_synthesisCONCRETE Mitochondria carry their own type II fatty acid synthesis (mtFAS) system, in which separate enzymes act on acyl chains attached to the...
[more...][less] Mitochondria carry their own type II fatty acid synthesis (mtFAS) system, in which separate enzymes act on acyl chains attached to the mitochondrial acyl carrier protein (ND-ACP). Malonyl groups are loaded onto ACP by the malonyl transacylase (beg), condensed by a beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthase (CG12170), reduced by a 3-ketoacyl-ACP reductase, dehydrated and then reduced by the enoyl-ACP reductase Mecr. The main product, octanoyl-ACP, is the precursor of lipoic acid; acylated ACP also binds and supports assembly of respiratory complex I and the iron-sulfur cluster assembly machinery.

Mitochondrial unfolded protein responseMODULE:mitochondrial_uprCONCRETE The mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt) is a mitochondria-to-nucleus signaling pathway that raises the expression of nuclear genes...
[more...][less] The mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt) is a mitochondria-to-nucleus signaling pathway that raises the expression of nuclear genes encoding mitochondrial chaperones and proteases when mitochondrial protein homeostasis is disturbed. Its executing transcription factor is a bZIP protein of the ATF4/ATF5 family that is partitioned between mitochondria and the nucleus: nematode ATFS-1 and its mammalian functional counterpart ATF5 both carry a mitochondrial targeting sequence, are kept in mitochondria in unstressed cells, and activate chaperone and protease genes when mitochondrial function fails; ATF5 rescues UPRmt signaling in atfs-1 mutant worms. The induced matrix chaperones, the HSP60 chaperonin and the mitochondrial HSP70, are both the classic reporters and the protective output of the response. How mitochondrial stress is relayed to the transcription factor differs between lineages. In Caenorhabditis elegans, where the pathway was defined, the key regulatory point is the import efficiency of ATFS-1: misfolded matrix proteins are degraded by the ClpP protease CLPP-1, the inner-membrane ABC transporter HAF-1 exports the resulting peptides and attenuates protein import under moderate stress, and ATFS-1 that escapes import reaches the nucleus. A nematode chromatin arm (DVE-1/UBL-5 together with the MET-2/LIN-65 H3K9 methylation machinery and the JMJD-3.1 H3K27 demethylase) acts alongside ATFS-1. In mammals, mitochondrial stress such as depolarization, import defects or iron deficiency activates the inner-membrane protease OMA1, which cleaves DELE1; the released DELE1 fragment activates the eIF2alpha kinase HRI (EIF2AK1) in the cytosol, and the resulting integrated stress response raises translation of ATF4 and ATF5. Mammalian CLPP is not required for the UPRmt, so the ClpP peptide signal is not a conserved part of the pathway.

MitophagyMODULE:mitophagyCONCRETE Mitophagy is the selective macroautophagy of mitochondria. In animals, damaged or unwanted mitochondria are marked on their outer membrane and...
[more...][less] Mitophagy is the selective macroautophagy of mitochondria. In animals, damaged or unwanted mitochondria are marked on their outer membrane and captured by phagophores decorated with Atg8-family proteins (LC3 and GABARAP in mammals, LGG-1 in nematodes). Two kinds of mark are used. In the ubiquitin-dependent route, the kinase PINK1 accumulates on the outer membrane of depolarized or import-defective mitochondria and phosphorylates ubiquitin and the ubiquitin-like domain of the RBR E3 ligase Parkin at Ser65. Activated Parkin builds ubiquitin chains on outer-membrane proteins, and in mammals these chains are read by soluble ubiquitin-binding receptors such as optineurin and NDP52, which also bind LC3/GABARAP and recruit the autophagy initiation machinery. In the receptor-mediated route, integral outer-membrane proteins bind Atg8-family proteins directly through LC3-interacting regions. BNIP3 and NIX (BNIP3L) act in hypoxia-induced and developmental mitophagy, such as mitochondrial clearance in maturing reticulocytes, and FUNDC1 acts in hypoxia-induced mitophagy. These receptors are conserved in nematodes, where the BNIP3/NIX ortholog DCT-1 acts in stress-induced somatic mitophagy together with PINK-1 and the Parkin ortholog PDR-1, and the FUNDC1 ortholog FNDC-1 acts in hypoxia-reoxygenation mitophagy. Nematodes also have lineage-specific components. Paternal mitochondria and membranous organelles in the C. elegans embryo are cleared by the nematode-specific receptor ALLO-1 (allophagy), and in worm muscle the FIS1-family proteins FIS-1 and FIS-2 act at a late step to complete orderly disposal of fission-derived mitochondrial fragments.

Mitotic and meiotic cohesin complexes in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_cohesin_complexesCONCRETE Cohesin is a ring-shaped SMC complex that holds sister chromatids together from DNA replication until anaphase and also organizes interphase...
[more...][less] Cohesin is a ring-shaped SMC complex that holds sister chromatids together from DNA replication until anaphase and also organizes interphase chromatin into loops. The ring is built from the SMC1-SMC3 heterodimer, whose ATPase heads are bridged by a kleisin subunit, which in turn binds a stromalin (SA) subunit. In mitotic cells the kleisin is Rad21, encoded in Drosophila by verthandi (vtd), and the SA subunit is SA1; separase cleavage of Rad21 opens the ring at anaphase. Drosophila meiosis uses meiosis-specific cohesion proteins: C(2)M, a kleisin-family protein required for synaptonemal complex formation, and Solo and Sunn, which are required for meiotic centromeric cohesion.

Mitotic cell cycle progression (phase-transition control)MODULE:cell_cycle_progressionCONCRETE An umbrella module that composes the three irreversible, cyclin-CDK-gated phase transitions of the mitotic cell cycle into one cycle: (1) the G1/S...
[more...][less] An umbrella module that composes the three irreversible, cyclin-CDK-gated phase transitions of the mitotic cell cycle into one cycle: (1) the G1/S transition (Start / restriction point), at which growth-coupled G1 cyclin-CDK releases the G1/S transcription program and SCF-dependent destruction of the CDK inhibitor commits the cell to S phase (MODULE:g1_s_transition); (2) the G2/M transition, at which the Wee1 / Cdc25 switch activates cyclin B-CDK1 and commits the cell to mitosis (MODULE:g2_m_transition); and (3) the metaphase/anaphase transition and mitotic exit, at which SAC-gated APC/C-Cdc20 destroys securin and the mitotic cyclins, separase cleaves cohesin, and a CDK-counteracting phosphatase resets the G1 state (MODULE:metaphase_anaphase_transition_and_mitotic_exit). The unifying logic is a single oscillator of cyclin-dependent kinase activity - rising from Start through mitotic entry and collapsing at mitotic exit - whose thresholds are made irreversible by positive-feedback proteolysis (SCF at G1/S, APC/C at M/A and exit) and by mutual antagonism between CDK and its inhibitors (CKIs, Wee1, PP2A-B55). Each part here is a compact summary node that names the phase-specific cyclin-CDK holoenzyme and the proteolytic switch; the detailed decompositions live in the three referenced modules. Representative members are drawn from human, Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe. Grounded in GO:0044772 (mitotic cell cycle phase transition).

Recruited to endosomes by Rab5 and phosphoinositides, it activates Rab7 and thereby drives Rab5-to-Rab7 conversion during endosome maturation, and it also acts on autophagosomes. Mutator foci 22G-RNA amplification in Caenorhabditis elegansMODULE:c_elegans_mutator_22g_rna_amplificationCONCRETE In the Caenorhabditis elegans germline, silencing guided by primary small RNAs is weak, and is made effective by a second round of small RNA...
[more...][less] In the Caenorhabditis elegans germline, silencing guided by primary small RNAs is weak, and is made effective by a second round of small RNA synthesis. A primary Argonaute such as RDE-1 recognizes a target transcript and recruits the NYN-domain endoribonuclease RDE-8, which cuts it. The ribonucleotidyltransferase RDE-3 (MUT-2) gives the 5' fragment a poly(UG) tail, and RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRPs) then use the tailed RNA as a template to synthesize abundant 22-nucleotide, 5'-guanosine secondary siRNAs (22G-RNAs). Most of this amplification takes place in Mutator foci. These are perinuclear, phase-separated condensates that lie next to P granules at nuclear pores. The intrinsically disordered Q/N-rich protein MUT-16 is the scaffold of the foci. Distinct regions of MUT-16 recruit the RdRP RRF-1; MUT-15 (RDE-5), which in turn recruits RDE-8; the DEAD-box RNA helicase MUT-14, which acts redundantly with SMUT-1 to start amplification; RDE-3; and, through the adaptor RDE-2 (MUT-8), the 3'-5' exoribonuclease MUT-7. The 22G-RNAs made in this way are loaded into worm-specific Argonautes (WAGOs) that lack slicer residues, such as WAGO-1, and silence transposons, pseudogenes and other germline-repressed genes. A second germline RdRP, EGO-1, makes most of the 22G-RNAs bound by the catalytic Argonaute CSR-1, which target most germline-expressed genes and protect them from WAGO-mediated silencing instead of silencing them. The two RdRP systems are not fully separate: EGO-1 also contributes, partly redundantly with RRF-1, to WAGO-class 22G-RNAs.

[more...][less] MuvB is a conserved core of five proteins (Mip130, Mip120, Mip40, Lin-52 and Caf1-55) that assembles with different partners to repress or activate cell-cycle and differentiation genes. With E2F2, Dp and the retinoblastoma-family proteins Rbf or Rbf2 it forms dREAM, which represses E2F target genes and developmentally regulated genes. [more...][less] N-linked glycosylation begins with the stepwise assembly of the dolichol-linked oligosaccharide (LLO, or dolichol-PP-oligosaccharide) on the cytoplasmic face of the endoplasmic-reticulum membrane. Using nucleotide-sugar donors from the cytosol, the pathway builds a Man5GlcNAc2 glycan on the polyprenol carrier dolichyl phosphate before the intermediate is flipped into the ER lumen. DPAGT1 (GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase, the first and committed step, and the tunicamycin target) transfers GlcNAc-1-P from UDP-GlcNAc onto dolichyl phosphate to give GlcNAc-PP-dolichol; the bipartite UDP-GlcNAc transferase ALG13/ALG14 (ALG13 catalytic, ALG14 membrane-anchoring) adds the second GlcNAc to form the chitobiose core GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol; ALG1 (beta-1,4-mannosyltransferase) adds the first mannose; the bifunctional ALG2 (alpha-1,3 and alpha-1,6 mannosyltransferase) adds the second and third mannoses to give Man3GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol; and ALG11 (alpha-1,2-mannosyltransferase) adds the fourth and fifth mannoses to complete Man5GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol, the final cytoplasmic-face intermediate (subsequently flipped to the lumen by the RFT1 flippase, and extended by the lumenal ALG enzymes). All the mannose-addition steps in this segment use GDP-mannose. Inherited defects in each step cause a congenital disorder of glycosylation (CDG type I): DPAGT1-CDG (and a congenital myasthenic syndrome), ALG13-CDG (an X-linked developmental/epileptic encephalopathy), ALG14-CDG (congenital myasthenic syndrome), ALG1-CDG, ALG2-CDG (and CMS14) and ALG11-CDG.

[more...][less] After the Man5GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol intermediate is flipped from the cytoplasmic to the lumenal face of the endoplasmic-reticulum membrane (by the RFT1 flippase), the dolichol-linked oligosaccharide (LLO) is completed inside the ER lumen to the mature Glc3Man9GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol donor for protein N-linked glycosylation. Unlike the cytoplasmic-face steps, the lumenal glycosyltransferases use lipid-linked donors: dolichyl-phosphate-mannose (Dol-P-Man) for the mannose additions and dolichyl-phosphate-glucose (Dol-P-Glc) for the glucose additions. Four mannoses are added: ALG3 (alpha-1,3) adds the sixth mannose, ALG9 (alpha-1,2) adds the seventh and, later, the ninth mannose, and ALG12 (alpha-1,6) adds the eighth, giving Man9GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol. Three glucoses then cap the glycan: ALG6 (alpha-1,3) adds the first glucose, ALG8 (alpha-1,3) the second, and ALG10 (alpha-1,2) the third and terminal glucose, producing the mature Glc3Man9GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol. The terminal glucose is the recognition signal for efficient transfer of the glycan to nascent proteins by the oligosaccharyltransferase (and, after transfer, for glucosidase trimming and calnexin/calreticulin quality control). Inherited defects in each step cause a congenital disorder of glycosylation (CDG type I): ALG3-CDG (CDG-Id), ALG9-CDG (CDG-Il / Gillessen-Kaesbach-Nishimura syndrome), ALG12-CDG (CDG-Ig), ALG6-CDG (CDG-Ic, one of the commonest CDG-I subtypes) and ALG8-CDG (CDG-Ih).

N-glycan trimming and processing in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_n_glycan_processingCONCRETE After oligosaccharyltransferase transfers Glc3Man9GlcNAc2 to asparagine residues of nascent proteins, the N-glycan is trimmed in the endoplasmic...
[more...][less] After oligosaccharyltransferase transfers Glc3Man9GlcNAc2 to asparagine residues of nascent proteins, the N-glycan is trimmed in the endoplasmic reticulum and then remodelled in the Golgi apparatus. In the ER, glucosidase I (Gcs1) removes the outer glucose and the glucosidase II heterodimer (Gcs2alpha catalytic and Gcs2beta regulatory subunits) removes the two inner glucoses; these steps also control entry into and exit from the calnexin-calreticulin folding cycle. Class I alpha-1,2-mannosidases trim mannoses in the ER and cis-Golgi. In the Golgi, GlcNAc transferase I (Mgat1) adds GlcNAc to the alpha-1,3 arm, which allows alpha-mannosidase II to remove two further mannoses. In insects most N-glycans are then converted to paucimannose glycans by the Golgi beta-N-acetylglucosaminidase Fused lobes (fdl), while a smaller fraction is extended to hybrid and complex glycans by GlcNAc transferase II, core fucosyltransferases, galactosyl-, GalNAc-, glucuronyl- and sialyltransferases.

Each complex pairs a catalytic subunit with one or more auxiliary subunits that anchor it to the ribosome and shape substrate choice. NatA (catalytic Naa10, vnc in flies, with auxiliary Naa15-16) acetylates N termini exposed after removal of the initiator methionine; Naa50 (san) associates with NatA. NADP+ synthesis (NAD kinases NADK/NADK2) and nicotinamide riboside salvage (NMRK1/NMRK2)MODULE:nadp_synthesis_and_nr_salvage Two committed reactions that complete the cellular NAD(P) cofactor network beyond the core NAD+ biosynthesis hub. First, the nicotinamide riboside...
[more...][less] Two committed reactions that complete the cellular NAD(P) cofactor network beyond the core NAD+ biosynthesis hub. First, the nicotinamide riboside (NR) salvage entry: nicotinamide riboside kinases NMRK1 (ubiquitous) and NMRK2 (muscle-enriched) phosphorylate the dietary/circulating NAD+ precursor nicotinamide riboside (and nicotinic acid riboside, and the reduced vitamers) with ATP to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) / nicotinic acid mononucleotide (NaMN). NMN then enters the NMNAT step of the NAD+ biosynthesis hub (see MODULE:nad_biosynthesis_salvage), making NR the shortest two-step route to NAD+ and the basis for NR/NMN nutraceutical supplementation. Second, the NADP+ branch: NAD kinases phosphorylate the 2'-hydroxyl of the adenine ribose of NAD+ with ATP to give NADP+, the sole de novo source of the NADP(H) pool that drives reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defence (glutathione and thioredoxin regeneration). Humans have two compartment-specific NAD kinases from distinct families: cytosolic NADK supplies the cytosolic/nuclear NADP(H) pool, and mitochondrial NADK2 supplies the matrix NADP(H) pool required for proline biosynthesis (feeding NADPH to ALDH18A1/P5CS), mitochondrial one-carbon metabolism and fatty-acid oxidation. NADK2 deficiency causes a severe metabolic encephalopathy (hyperlysinemia, 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase deficiency); NADK activity is itself redox- and growth-signal-regulated.

NADPH-driven glutathione/glutaredoxin and thioredoxin systems with peroxide and superoxide scavengingMODULE:glutathione_thioredoxin_redox_systemsCONCRETE Cells keep their thiols reduced and remove reactive oxygen species with two parallel NADPH-driven thiol-disulfide relays and a set of...
[more...][less] Cells keep their thiols reduced and remove reactive oxygen species with two parallel NADPH-driven thiol-disulfide relays and a set of thiol-independent scavengers. In the glutathione/glutaredoxin system, the FAD enzyme glutathione reductase uses NADPH to reduce glutathione disulfide to glutathione, and glutathione in turn reduces dithiol glutaredoxins, which reduce protein disulfides and glutathione-protein mixed disulfides. In the thioredoxin system, thioredoxin reductase uses NADPH to reduce thioredoxin, which reduces protein disulfides, supplies electrons to biosynthetic reductases such as ribonucleotide reductase and PAPS reductase, and reduces the thiol peroxidases. Thioredoxin reductase is a low-molecular-weight flavoenzyme in fungi, plants and bacteria and a high-molecular-weight selenoprotein related to glutathione reductase in animals. Hydrogen peroxide and organic hydroperoxides are reduced by several families of thioredoxin-dependent thiol peroxidases (typical 2-Cys peroxiredoxins, glutathione-peroxidase-like peroxiredoxins, atypical 2-Cys and BCP-type peroxiredoxins). Superoxide dismutases convert superoxide to hydrogen peroxide (Cu/Zn enzyme in the cytosol and mitochondrial intermembrane space, Mn enzyme in the mitochondrial matrix), and haem catalases dismutate hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen without thiol reductant. The two thiol systems overlap: in budding yeast at least one cytosolic thioredoxin or dithiol glutaredoxin is required for viability.

NLRP3 inflammasome activation and pyroptotic execution moduleMODULE:nlrp3_inflammasomeCONCRETE A decomposition of the canonical NLRP3 inflammasome: the cytosolic sensor-adaptor-protease platform that converts a diffuse cellular perturbation...
[more...][less] A decomposition of the canonical NLRP3 inflammasome: the cytosolic sensor-adaptor-protease platform that converts a diffuse cellular perturbation into active caspase-1, and the lytic execution arm that caspase-1 then triggers. The chain is linear and each hand-off is a change of molecular currency rather than of chemistry: NLRP3 senses a perturbation indirectly and presents a pyrin-domain filament (GO:0044546), that filament nucleates ASC polymerisation into the one-per-cell speck (GO:0061703), the clustered ASC CARDs recruit procaspase-1 and permit proximity-induced autoprocessing (GO:0061702), the autoprocessed protease cleaves gasdermin D and the interleukin-1-family precursors, the released GSDMD N-terminal fragment oligomerises into wide plasma-membrane pores (GO:0141201), and NINJ1 finally ruptures the membrane. Four of the five steps contribute no catalysis at all - NLRP3, ASC and NEK7 all supply geometry - so the module is best read as a geometry cascade with a single proteolytic step in the middle and two independent membrane-acting effectors at the end. Design intent: one ordered chain of parts, like necroptosis and unlike the redundant-suppressor topology of ferroptosis, because there is no second route from the speck to the pore. The two places where the biology is genuinely alternative are handled differently from each other. NEK7 licensing is an optional regulatory part rather than a core step, because human myeloid cells can activate NLRP3 without it when IKKbeta has recruited NLRP3 to PI4P (PMID:36384135) and because raising NLRP3 abundance makes potassium-efflux-driven activation independent of both NEK7 and priming (PMID:42378282). Interleukin-1 beta and interleukin-18 are recorded as caspase-1 substrates inside the cleavage step and are deliberately given no annoton of their own: they are what the protease acts on, they perform none of the work of their own maturation, and their cytokine activity belongs to the receptor pathways downstream of this module.

Necroptosis (RHIM-dependent RIPK3-MLKL lytic cell death) moduleMODULE:necroptosisCONCRETE A decomposition of the necroptotic process (GO:0070266): the caspase-8-restrained, RIPK3- and MLKL-dependent form of programmed necrosis. The...
[more...][less] A decomposition of the necroptotic process (GO:0070266): the caspase-8-restrained, RIPK3- and MLKL-dependent form of programmed necrosis. The module follows GO's own partition of the process into a signaling phase (GO:0097527 necroptotic signaling pathway), the assembly of the RIPK1/RIPK3 RHIM platform that licenses the effector kinase (GO:1901026 ripoptosome assembly involved in necroptotic process; complex GO:0097342 ripoptosome), and an execution phase (GO:0097528) carried out by MLKL at the plasma membrane. Design intent: the committing chemistry is a single linear hand-off - an upstream RHIM-bearing sensor or adaptor nucleates a RHIM amyloid core with RIPK3, activated RIPK3 phosphorylates MLKL, and phosphorylated MLKL destabilizes the membrane - so the module is one ordered chain of parts rather than the redundant-suppressor topology used for ferroptosis. The branch point that makes necroptosis a distinct program sits upstream: three alternative initiators converge on the same RIPK3 core and are modelled as a variant set along the axis of which receptor supplies the RHIM (RIPK1 downstream of TNFR1 and other death receptors; TICAM1/TRIF downstream of TLR3 and endosomal TLR4; ZBP1 downstream of Z-form nucleic acid sensing). The caspase-8/FADD/cFLIP brake is modelled as an optional regulatory part that negatively regulates the chain, not as a core step: its proteolysis is what normally keeps the module off, and the same complex is the apoptotic alternative.

[more...][less] The vertebrate neural crest gene regulatory network: the transcriptional program by which signals at the edge of the neural plate are converted, through a neural plate border layer and a crest specifier layer, into migratory multipotent crest cells, of which the cranial population forms skeletogenic ectomesenchyme. A parallel competence layer, shared with pluripotent blastula cells, keeps progenitors undifferentiated. Border specifiers (Gbx2, Msx1, AP-2alpha, Pax3, Zic1) are largely ancestral chordate genes already expressed at the amphioxus neural plate border; most crest specifiers were recruited at the base of vertebrates, mainly by changes in where they are expressed, and some cranial circuit components (Ets1) were added later in jawed vertebrates. Neural ectoderm anteroposterior specification moduleMODULE:neural_ectoderm_anteroposterior_specificationABSTRACT The developmental program that, during gastrulation, subdivides newly induced neural ectoderm along the anteroposterior axis into two parallel,...
[more...][less] The developmental program that, during gastrulation, subdivides newly induced neural ectoderm along the anteroposterior axis into two parallel, lineage-committed brain progenitors: an OTX2-positive anterior neural ectoderm that generates the forebrain and midbrain, and a GBX2/HOX-positive posterior neural ectoderm that generates the hindbrain. The module begins where germ-layer specification ends - with SOX2-positive neural ectoderm established under combined BMP, TGF-beta and WNT inhibition - and is driven by a graded posteriorising input of FGF together with retinoic acid. That input is read out by a pair of mutually repressive homeodomain selectors, OTX2 and GBX2, whose shared border is the site at which the midbrain-hindbrain (isthmic) organizer forms; displacing the border displaces the organizer. The two territories are already committed rather than merely differently positioned: challenged with the opposite region's inducing signals they do not interconvert, and they carry diverging accessible-chromatin landscapes that foreshadow their regional identities. Downstream, the anterior territory resolves into FOXG1/SIX3 forebrain and EN1 midbrain progenitors, and the posterior territory into MAFB/HNF1B/HOXA3 rhombomere 5/6 hindbrain progenitors. Grounded in GO:0021999 (neural plate anterior/posterior regionalization). Upstream neural-versus-epidermal ectoderm allocation is supplied by modules/germ_layer_specification.yaml and modules/body_axis_specification.yaml; the signalling machinery is detailed in the fgfr_signaling, retinoic_acid_receptor_signaling, wnt_signaling, bmp_signaling and tgfb_smad_signaling modules; the cerebellar program that continues from the posterior territory's rhombomere 1 is in modules/cerebellum_development.yaml.

Neurexin-centred trans-synaptic adhesion complexesMODULE:neurexin_transsynaptic_adhesion Neurexins are presynaptic type I transmembrane proteins that act as a hub for trans-synaptic adhesion. Their extracellular LNS domains bind a set...
[more...][less] Neurexins are presynaptic type I transmembrane proteins that act as a hub for trans-synaptic adhesion. Their extracellular LNS domains bind a set of structurally unrelated postsynaptic or secreted partners, forming protein bridges that span the synaptic cleft, hold the pre- and postsynaptic membranes together, and signal in both directions to organize synaptic properties. The best-established partners are the neuroligins, which are catalytically inactive esterase-fold transmembrane proteins; the leucine-rich-repeat LRRTM proteins; and a tripartite bridge in which secreted cerebellin hexamers link neurexin to the amino-terminal domain of delta-family ionotropic glutamate receptors (GluD1/GluD2). Which partner a neurexin engages is controlled in large part by alternative splicing, notably at neurexin splice site 4. OUT OF SCOPE: the intracellular scaffolds recruited by the neurexin and partner cytoplasmic tails (CASK, Mint, PSD-95, gephyrin), the synaptic vesicle release machinery, and the many other neurexin ligands (dystroglycan, neurexophilins, latrophilins, calsyntenins, GABA-A receptor, cerebellin-independent C1q-like proteins). Each of these can be added as further partner variants or as a separate module.

Neurotransmitter loading into synaptic vesiclesMODULE:synaptic_vesicle_neurotransmitter_loadingCONCRETE The vesicle-filling stage of the synaptic vesicle cycle. The vacuolar-type H+-ATPase on the synaptic vesicle membrane hydrolyses ATP to pump...
[more...][less] The vesicle-filling stage of the synaptic vesicle cycle. The vacuolar-type H+-ATPase on the synaptic vesicle membrane hydrolyses ATP to pump protons into the lumen, generating a proton electrochemical gradient (a pH gradient plus a lumen-positive membrane potential). A vesicular neurotransmitter transporter then uses that gradient to concentrate transmitter into the vesicle against a steep concentration gradient. The transporter identity sets the transmitter phenotype of the terminal: VGLUT1/2/3 (SLC17A6/7/8) for glutamate, VGAT (SLC32A1) for GABA and glycine, VMAT2 (SLC18A2) for monoamines, and VAChT (SLC18A3) for acetylcholine. The module is modeled with human exemplars but the acidify -> load topology is conserved across metazoan chemical synapses. Grounded in GO:0098700 (neurotransmitter loading into synaptic vesicle) and GO:0097401 (synaptic vesicle lumen acidification).

Nicotine biosynthesis module (Nicotiana / Solanaceae)MODULE:nicotine_biosynthesis A plant-scoped, recursively decomposable decomposition of nicotine biosynthesis as it operates in Nicotiana (tobacco / wild tobacco). Nicotine is...
[more...][less] A plant-scoped, recursively decomposable decomposition of nicotine biosynthesis as it operates in Nicotiana (tobacco / wild tobacco). Nicotine is an alkaloid built by condensing two separately made rings: a PYRIDINE ring supplied by the aspartate-derived NAD/quinolinate (pyridine nucleotide) branch, and a PYRROLIDINE ring (the N-methyl-Delta1-pyrrolinium cation) supplied by the polyamine/ornithine branch. The module separates these two upstream supply branches from the late "nicotine synthase" cascade that joins the rings, and from the vacuolar transport/metabolon step. This module is intentionally NOT a flat gene list (that lives in the per-gene NICAT reviews and the NICOTINE_BIOSYNTHESIS project). Its purpose is to capture the pathway-level structure that the individual gene reviews cannot: the two-branch convergence, the recently revised late steps, and the co-clustered transport component. The late steps are phrased to reflect the 2025-2026 revision of the pathway. In the classical model the N-methylpyrrolinium cation condensed with a nicotinic acid derivative directly. The new model ("complete biosynthesis of nicotine", Cell 2026, PMID:41928514; "nicotine biosynthesis completed by cryptic activating glucosylation", Nat Commun 2026, PMID:42151135) routes nicotinic acid through a hidden N-glucosylation/reduction/condensation/deglucosylation relay: a UDP-glucosyltransferase (UGT1/NaGT) glucosylates nicotinic acid to nicotinic acid N-glucoside, an A622/NaGR reductase and a BBL oxidase act on the activated glucoside during condensation with the pyrrolidine ring, and a beta-glucosidase (beta-GD1/NicGH) removes the sugar to release nicotine. A vacuolar-membrane MATE transporter (MATE1) co-clusters with A622 and beta-GD1 and is required for high heterologous production. This activating-glucosylation relay and the A622-MATE1-beta-GD1 metabolon are the parts of the pathway that GO biological-process and molecular-function terms flatten away.

Notch signaling pathway in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_notch_signalingCONCRETE Notch signaling is a juxtacrine pathway in which the transmembrane ligands Delta and Serrate on one cell bind the Notch receptor on a neighbouring...
[more...][less] Notch signaling is a juxtacrine pathway in which the transmembrane ligands Delta and Serrate on one cell bind the Notch receptor on a neighbouring cell. Ligand binding, together with ligand endocytosis in the signal-sending cell, exposes Notch to cleavage by the ADAM10 metalloprotease Kuzbanian (S2 cleavage), after which the gamma-secretase complex (Presenilin, Nicastrin, Aph-1 and Pen-2) cleaves within the transmembrane domain (S3 cleavage) and releases the Notch intracellular domain. The intracellular domain enters the nucleus and forms a transcriptional activation complex with the CSL DNA-binding protein Suppressor of Hairless and the coactivator Mastermind, switching Su(H) target genes such as the Enhancer of split complex genes from repression to activation. The pathway controls lateral inhibition, boundary formation and binary cell-fate decisions throughout development.

Nuclear auxin signaling (TIR1/AFB-Aux/IAA-TOPLESS-ARF module)MODULE:auxin_nuclear_signalingCONCRETE Nuclear auxin signaling converts intracellular auxin (indole-3-acetic acid, IAA) levels into changes in gene transcription through a short,...
[more...][less] Nuclear auxin signaling converts intracellular auxin (indole-3-acetic acid, IAA) levels into changes in gene transcription through a short, derepression-based pathway. At low auxin, AUXIN RESPONSE FACTOR (ARF) transcription factors sit on auxin-response elements (AuxREs) in target promoters through their B3 DNA-binding domains, but activator ARFs (class A, e.g. ARF5/MONOPTEROS, ARF7/NPH4 and ARF19) are kept inactive by Aux/IAA repressors. Aux/IAAs bind the ARF C-terminal PB1 domain through their own PB1 domain and recruit the Groucho/Tup1-type co-repressor TOPLESS (TPL) and its TPL-related paralogs through an EAR (LxLxL) motif in domain I; TPL represses transcription by engaging the Mediator complex and histone deacetylases. Auxin is perceived by a co-receptor formed by an LRR F-box protein of the TIR1/AFB family and the domain II degron of an Aux/IAA: auxin binds the bottom of the TIR1/AFB pocket and acts as molecular glue that stabilizes Aux/IAA binding. Because the TIR1/AFB protein is the substrate-recognition subunit of an SCF (ASK1-CUL1-RBX1) E3 ligase, co-receptor assembly leads to Aux/IAA polyubiquitination and rapid proteasomal degradation, which removes the Aux/IAA-TPL repressor from ARFs and allows ARF-dependent activation of early auxin-responsive genes, including Aux/IAA genes themselves (negative feedback). Specific responses arise from combinations of co-expressed pairs, such as BODENLOS/IAA12 with MONOPTEROS/ARF5 in embryonic root initiation, and IAA14/IAA18/IAA19 with ARF7 and ARF19 in lateral root formation and tropic growth. Auxin biosynthesis, polar auxin transport (a separate module), non-transcriptional auxin responses and the downstream developmental programs are outside this module's boundary.

[more...][less] The nuclear pore complex (NPC) is a large assembly of about 30 different nucleoporins, each present in multiple copies, that spans the nuclear envelope and controls traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm. A symmetric core of stacked rings (two outer rings built from the Nup107-160 Y-complex, an inner ring, and a transmembrane ring) anchors a central channel filled with phenylalanine-glycine (FG) repeat nucleoporins that form the permeability barrier. Asymmetric cytoplasmic filaments and a nuclear basket attach to the core and act in mRNA export and in docking of transport receptors. Several Drosophila nucleoporins also act off the pore, for example in gene regulation and in mitosis.

Nucleokinesis (motor-driven nuclear translocation) moduleMODULE:nucleokinesisABSTRACT Nucleokinesis is the directed translocation of the nucleus within a cell that is migrating or changing shape, most prominently in migrating neurons...
[more...][less] Nucleokinesis is the directed translocation of the nucleus within a cell that is migrating or changing shape, most prominently in migrating neurons and in the interkinetic nuclear migration of neuroepithelial and radial glial progenitors. In migrating neurons it follows a two-stroke cycle: the centrosome and Golgi first advance into a swelling of the leading process, and the nucleus then moves forward toward them in a saltatory step. The nucleus is coupled to cytoplasmic motors through its envelope, either by LINC complexes (inner-nuclear-membrane SUN proteins bound to outer-nuclear-membrane KASH nesprins, with nesprin-2 recruiting dynein and kinesin through the adaptor BICD2) or, in G2 radial glial progenitors, by nuclear-pore-anchored dynein adaptors (RANBP2-BICD2 and NUP133-CENPF-NDE1/NDEL1). Cytoplasmic dynein, with dynactin and the LIS1-NDEL1/NDE1 regulatory module, pulls the nucleus toward microtubule minus ends at the centrosome along a perinuclear microtubule cage stabilized by doublecortin. Non-muscle myosin II contraction at the rear of the soma assists forward nuclear movement, and in progenitors the kinesin-3 KIF1A drives the opposite, basally directed nuclear movement. CDK5/p35 phosphorylation of NDEL1 links the core machinery to migration signaling. The same dynein-driven program also operates outside the central nervous system: trunk neural crest cells use it to pull their nucleus through confined tissue spaces. Loss of LIS1 or DCX causes lissencephaly, reflecting the dependence of cortical neuronal migration on this machinery.

Both isoforms share a set of non-catalytic scaffold subunits - ribophorin I (RPN1), ribophorin II (RPN2), OST48 (DDOST) and DAD1 - required for complex integrity and substrate presentation. Defects in individual subunits cause congenital disorders of glycosylation (STT3A-, STT3B-, DDOST-CDG), X-linked immunodeficiency with magnesium defect (MAGT1/XMEN) and autosomal-recessive intellectual disability (TUSC3).

Oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) moduleMODULE:oxidative_phosphorylation A taxon-neutral decomposition of oxidative phosphorylation: the coupled process by which a respiratory electron transport chain (ETC) oxidizes...
[more...][less] A taxon-neutral decomposition of oxidative phosphorylation: the coupled process by which a respiratory electron transport chain (ETC) oxidizes reduced cofactors and uses the released free energy to pump protons across a coupling membrane, and an F1Fo-ATP synthase uses the resulting proton-motive force to phosphorylate ADP. The module is deliberately phrased in terms of functional modules, protein complexes, and pathway segments rather than a fixed gene list, so it can represent the mitochondrial inner-membrane chain of eukaryotes and the plasma-membrane respiratory chains of aerobic bacteria. Design intent for complexes (the central modelling question): each respiratory complex is represented as a single PROTEIN_COMPLEX node whose emergent, complex-level catalytic activity is carried by ONE complex-level annoton (the redox half-reaction it performs), with its functionally important subunits exposed as `active_units` on the complex descriptor rather than as separate per-subunit annotons. This mirrors the GO `contributes_to` philosophy: an individual subunit contributes to but does not independently enable the complex activity. Large, internally modular complexes (Complex I; the F1Fo-ATP synthase) are additionally decomposed with `parts` into their functional sub-modules (the N/Q/proton-pumping arms of Complex I; the F1 catalytic head and Fo proton turbine of ATP synthase) — this recursive decomposition is the payoff of the module representation over a flat subunit list. Lineage- and chemistry-specific alternatives that bypass the proton-pumping complexes (type-II NADH dehydrogenase, the alternative oxidase, bacterial bd-type oxidases) are captured as `variant_sets` along explicit axes, so OXPHOS reads as one conserved energy-conservation plan with multiple implementations. Complex assembly/biogenesis is treated as a distinct process from chain operation and kept as an optional sub-module.

P granule assembly and asymmetric segregation in Caenorhabditis elegansMODULE:c_elegans_p_granule_assembly_segregationCONCRETE P granules are the germline ribonucleoprotein condensates of Caenorhabditis elegans. In adult germ cells they sit on the cytoplasmic face of...
[more...][less] P granules are the germline ribonucleoprotein condensates of Caenorhabditis elegans. In adult germ cells they sit on the cytoplasmic face of nuclear pore clusters, where newly exported mRNAs pass through them. In oocytes and embryos they are cytoplasmic and are inherited by the germline founder cell. The condensate is built in layers. The PGL proteins PGL-1 and PGL-3 (with PGL-2 after embryogenesis) self-associate and bind RNA to form the liquid core. The Vasa-family DEAD-box helicases GLH-1 and GLH-4 (with GLH-2) gather at nuclear pores independently of the PGLs and are needed for the PGLs to reach the nuclear periphery. DEPS-1 is a perinuclear P granule protein that is needed for PGL-1 localization and GLH-1 accumulation, and that binds the Piwi protein PRG-1. In the zygote, the intrinsically disordered proteins MEG-3 and MEG-4 condense with mRNA on the surface of PGL droplets. This shell stabilizes the granules, recruits about 500 mRNAs, and makes the granules co-segregate with the germline. Segregation to the posterior blastomere uses two regulatory inputs. First, PAR polarity sets up an anterior-high gradient of the RNA-binding proteins MEX-5 and MEX-6. MEX-5 competes with PGL-3 and MEG-3 for RNA, so granules dissolve in the anterior and condense in the posterior. Second, the DYRK kinase MBK-2 phosphorylates MEG-1 and MEG-3 to promote granule disassembly, and the PP2A phosphatase with its PPTR-1/PPTR-2 B56 regulatory subunits reverses this to promote assembly. MEG-1 and MEG-2 scaffold a second germ plasm condensate. These germline P-bodies carry the DDX6 helicase CGH-1 and other decapping and deadenylation regulators, and they are needed to specify the germline founder cell. Loss of P granule components causes temperature-sensitive or complete sterility, and germ cells that lack P granules can switch to somatic fates.

PAPS biosynthesis and Golgi import (sulfate activation) (PAPSS1/2 -> SLC35B2/3)MODULE:paps_sulfate_activation Sulfation of biomolecules requires an activated sulfonate donor, 3'-phosphoadenosine 5'-phosphosulfate (PAPS), the universal substrate of every...
[more...][less] Sulfation of biomolecules requires an activated sulfonate donor, 3'-phosphoadenosine 5'-phosphosulfate (PAPS), the universal substrate of every cytosolic and Golgi-lumenal sulfotransferase (sulfation of glycosaminoglycans/proteoglycans, glycolipids, steroids and DHEA, thyroid hormone, catecholamines, tyrosine residues and xenobiotics). PAPS is made in two steps by a single bifunctional enzyme, PAPS synthase (PAPSS1, ubiquitous; PAPSS2, predominant in cartilage): an ATP sulfurylase (sulfate adenylyltransferase) domain condenses inorganic sulfate with ATP to adenosine 5'-phosphosulfate (APS) + pyrophosphate, and an APS kinase (adenylyl-sulfate kinase) domain phosphorylates APS with a second ATP to PAPS + ADP. The cytosolic PAPS pool feeds cytosolic sulfotransferases directly, and is imported into the Golgi lumen by the antiporters SLC35B2 (PAPST1) and SLC35B3 (PAPST2), which exchange cytosolic PAPS for lumenal PAP (adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate, the spent product), supplying the Golgi sulfotransferases that sulfate secreted and membrane glycoconjugates. Defects illustrate the pathway's importance: biallelic PAPSS2 mutations cause spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia (Pakistani-type brachyolmia) and androgen excess through defective proteoglycan and DHEA sulfation.

PMK-1 p38 MAPK intestinal innate immunity in Caenorhabditis elegansMODULE:c_elegans_pmk1_intestinal_immunityCONCRETE In the Caenorhabditis elegans intestine, a conserved p38 MAPK cassette is the main signaling route by which infection and other physiological...
[more...][less] In the Caenorhabditis elegans intestine, a conserved p38 MAPK cassette is the main signaling route by which infection and other physiological stresses induce antibacterial defense genes. The TIR-domain protein TIR-1, the nematode ortholog of SARM1, oligomerizes into puncta in intestinal epithelial cells under pathogen or non-pathogen stress. Its NAD+ glycohydrolase activity, which oligomerization strongly potentiates, is required to activate the cascade. TIR-1 acts upstream of the ASK1-family MAP3K NSY-1, which activates the MKK3/6-family MAP2K SEK-1, which in turn phosphorylates and activates the p38 MAPK PMK-1. PMK-1 phosphorylates the CREB/ATF bZIP transcription factor ATF-7. Unphosphorylated ATF-7 represses PMK-1-regulated genes, and phosphorylation switches it to an activator. ATF-7 occupies regulatory regions of pathogen-induced genes in a PMK-1-dependent manner and controls most genes induced by Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection. These outputs include secreted proteins such as C-type lectin domain proteins, lysozymes, CUB-like proteins and ShK-toxin-domain peptides, most of which have not been shown to act against microbes. The ShKT gene sysm-1 (T24B8.5) is the standard transcriptional reporter of pathway activity, but its only demonstrated function is as a secreted intestinal signal that promotes DNA damage-induced germ cell apoptosis. The pathway acts cell-autonomously in the intestine, cooperates with the GATA factor ELT-2, and is required for resistance to Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. The same TIR-1/NSY-1/SEK-1 module also has neuronal roles in AWC asymmetry and serotonin-dependent behavior, and PMK-1 has a second transcriptional target, SKN-1, in the oxidative stress response.

[more...][less] PVR is the single Drosophila receptor tyrosine kinase related to vertebrate PDGF and VEGF receptors. It is activated by three secreted ligands, Pvf1, Pvf2 and Pvf3. PVR signaling guides the migration of border cells in the ovary and of other cells during development, and supports the survival, proliferation and migration of embryonic and larval hemocytes, and acts in dorsal closure and thorax closure. [more...][less] A taxon-neutral decomposition of Hedgehog (Hh) signaling, the metazoan cell-cell communication system in which a dually lipidated Hedgehog ligand released by a signal-sending cell controls the activator/repressor balance of Ci/GLI zinc-finger transcription factors in a receiving cell. The module is written around the segments that are shared from cnidarians and insects to vertebrates: autocatalytic cholesterol-coupled processing and N-terminal palmitoylation of the ligand; reception by the twelve-pass Patched receptor and its Ig/fibronectin-domain co-receptors; relief of Patched-mediated restriction of sterol access to the class-F receptor Smoothened; kinase-driven proteolytic processing of Ci/GLI into a transcriptional repressor when the pathway is off; and Smoothened-dependent conversion of Ci/GLI into an activator through Suppressor of fused, Fused-family kinases, and a kinesin-4 scaffold. Where lineages differ they are modeled as variants on an explicit axis rather than as separate pathways: the vertebrate implementation runs the activation step in the primary cilium with GPR161, intraflagellar transport, and KIF7, while the Drosophila implementation runs the equivalent step on a cytoplasmic Hedgehog signaling complex nucleated by the Costal-2 kinesin at the plasma membrane. Sonic hedgehog (SHH) is the vertebrate exemplar ligand, but it is one of three vertebrate paralogs of the single ancestral Hedgehog ligand and is used here only as a representative member.
