Pantoate-derived coenzyme A biosynthesisMODULE:coenzyme_a_biosynthesis Synthesis of coenzyme A (CoA) from pantoate and beta-alanine. The pantoate branch transfers a hydroxymethyl group to 3-methyl-2-oxobutanoate,...
[more...][less] Synthesis of coenzyme A (CoA) from pantoate and beta-alanine. The pantoate branch transfers a hydroxymethyl group to 3-methyl-2-oxobutanoate, reduces 2-dehydropantoate to (R)-pantoate, and reaches 4'-phosphopantothenate by one of two reaction-order variants. Bacteria and eukaryotes generally use PanC to form pantothenate and then one of three unrelated pantothenate kinase families. Most archaea instead phosphorylate pantoate with PoK before PPS condenses 4-phosphopantoate with beta-alanine, so free pantothenate is not an intermediate. Four subsequent reactions add and decarboxylate cysteine, adenylylate 4'-phosphopantetheine, and phosphorylate dephospho-CoA. CoaB and CoaC may be separate or fused, and the final CoaD and CoaE activities may be separate or fused in CoA synthase. The phosphopantothenoylcysteine decarboxylase may be a homo-oligomeric flavoprotein or, in budding yeast, a heterotrimer in which two paralogous subunit types each contribute an essential catalytic residue. Beta-alanine is supplied by lineage-specific routes and is modeled as an optional supply part with two characterized enzymatic variants: PanD-dependent decarboxylation of L-aspartate in bacteria, and the polyamine-oxidation route of Saccharomyces-type yeasts, in which a flavin polyamine oxidase cleaves spermine to spermidine and 3-aminopropanal and cytosolic aldehyde dehydrogenases oxidize 3-aminopropanal to beta-alanine. Pyrimidine degradation and uptake are further sources that are not modeled here. CoA salvage, phosphopantetheine release from acyl carrier proteins, and downstream CoA-dependent metabolism are outside the module boundary.

Pentose phosphate pathwayMODULE:pentose_phosphate_pathwayCONCRETE A reusable central-carbon module for the pentose phosphate pathway, covering the oxidative conversion of glucose 6-phosphate to ribulose...
[more...][less] A reusable central-carbon module for the pentose phosphate pathway, covering the oxidative conversion of glucose 6-phosphate to ribulose 5-phosphate, the non-oxidative interconversion of pentose phosphates with fructose 6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, and the activation of ribose 5-phosphate to 5-phospho-alpha-D-ribose 1-diphosphate (PRPP). The oxidative branch generates NADPH through glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase, with 6-phosphogluconolactonase hydrolyzing the intermediate lactone; its first step is irreversible and rate-limiting. The reversible non-oxidative branch uses ribose-5-phosphate isomerase, ribulose-phosphate 3-epimerase, transketolase, and transaldolase to balance ribose 5-phosphate, xylulose 5-phosphate, sedoheptulose 7-phosphate, erythrose 4-phosphate, fructose 6-phosphate, and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate according to the demand for NADPH, nucleotide precursors and glycolytic intermediates. Ribose 5-phosphate leaves the pathway mainly through ribose-phosphate diphosphokinase, whose product PRPP feeds nucleotide, histidine and tryptophan biosynthesis. In eukaryotes the pathway is cytosolic. Yeast and bacterial proteins are used as concrete exemplars.

Pentose phosphate pathway — non-oxidative branch + PRPP synthesis; transaldolase/RPIA deficiency, PRPS1 disordersMODULE:pentose_phosphate_nonoxidative_branch The non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway is a set of reversible sugar-phosphate rearrangements that interconvert the five-carbon...
[more...][less] The non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway is a set of reversible sugar-phosphate rearrangements that interconvert the five-carbon sugar ribulose-5-phosphate (from the oxidative branch) with ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis and with the glycolytic intermediates fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate — allowing cells to balance their demand for NADPH versus ribose-5-phosphate. Ribose-5-phosphate isomerase (RPIA) interconverts ribulose-5-phosphate and ribose-5-phosphate; ribulose-5-phosphate 3-epimerase (RPE) interconverts ribulose-5-phosphate and xylulose-5-phosphate; transketolase (TKT, thiamine-diphosphate-dependent) transfers two-carbon units, converting xylulose-5-phosphate + ribose-5-phosphate to sedoheptulose-7-phosphate + glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (and, in a second reaction, xylulose-5-phosphate + erythrose-4-phosphate to fructose-6-phosphate + glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate); and transaldolase (TALDO1) transfers a three-carbon unit, converting sedoheptulose-7-phosphate + glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate to erythrose-4-phosphate + fructose-6-phosphate. Finally, phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate synthetase (PRPS1) uses ribose-5-phosphate + ATP to make 5-phospho-alpha-D-ribose 1-diphosphate (PRPP) + AMP — the activated precursor that commits pentose carbon to de novo and salvage synthesis of purine, pyrimidine and pyridine (NAD) nucleotides. Inherited defects: transaldolase (TALDO1) deficiency causes liver disease and hemolytic anemia; ribose-5-phosphate isomerase (RPIA) deficiency is an extremely rare progressive leukoencephalopathy; and PRPS1 loss-of-function causes Arts syndrome / CMTX5 / DFN2 while gain-of-function (superactivity) causes purine overproduction with gout.

Pentose phosphate pathway — oxidative branch (NADPH generation); G6PD deficiency / favismMODULE:pentose_phosphate_oxidative_branch The oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway is the cytosolic route that diverts glucose-6-phosphate away from glycolysis to generate...
[more...][less] The oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway is the cytosolic route that diverts glucose-6-phosphate away from glycolysis to generate NADPH and pentose sugars. In three irreversible steps it converts glucose-6-phosphate to ribulose-5-phosphate, producing two molecules of NADPH and one CO2: glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) oxidises glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconolactone (reducing NADP+ to NADPH) as the committed, rate-limiting step; 6-phosphogluconolactonase (PGLS) hydrolyses the labile lactone to 6-phosphogluconate; and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (PGD) oxidatively decarboxylates 6-phosphogluconate to ribulose-5-phosphate + CO2 (reducing a second NADP+). The NADPH produced is the cell's principal reducing power for reductive biosynthesis (fatty acids, cholesterol, nucleotides) and, critically in erythrocytes, for regenerating reduced glutathione to defend against oxidative stress; the ribulose-5-phosphate feeds the non-oxidative branch (and thence ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis). Inherited G6PD deficiency is the most common human enzyme defect (~400 million people), X-linked, causing acute oxidant-triggered hemolytic anemia (favism, drug/infection-induced), neonatal jaundice, and — in severe class-I variants — chronic nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia.

Peroxisomal fatty-acid beta-oxidationMODULE:peroxisomal_beta_oxidation Peroxisomal beta-oxidation chain-shortens acyl-CoAs two carbons per turn inside the peroxisomal matrix. In fungi such as budding yeast and in...
[more...][less] Peroxisomal beta-oxidation chain-shortens acyl-CoAs two carbons per turn inside the peroxisomal matrix. In fungi such as budding yeast and in plants it is the only fatty-acid beta-oxidation system of the cell, whereas in animals it handles the substrates mitochondria cannot: very-long-chain fatty acids, 2-methyl-branched fatty acids (pristanic acid), the C27 bile-acid intermediates and dicarboxylic acids. Long-chain substrates enter as acyl-CoA through an ABC-D half-transporter dimer, which in yeast hydrolyses the thioester during transport so that the fatty acid is re-activated on the matrix side by an acyl-CoA synthetase; medium-chain fatty acids enter independently and are activated inside. In humans the two peroxisomal ABC-D half-transporters divide the substrates between them: ABCD1 (ALDP) takes straight-chain very-long-chain acyl-CoA, and ABCD3 (PMP70) takes the branched-chain, C27 bile-acid and dicarboxylic acyl-CoAs. Each turn uses four reactions with peroxisome-specific enzymes: an FAD acyl-CoA oxidase that passes electrons directly to O2 (making H2O2, degraded by catalase); hydration and NAD+-dependent dehydrogenation by multifunctional proteins (the D-specific, (3R)-hydroxyacyl-CoA-forming multifunctional enzyme type 2 in fungi and as the main animal enzyme, plus an L-specific bifunctional protein in animals); and thiolytic cleavage by peroxisomal 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolases. Because the peroxisomal membrane is impermeable to NAD(H), NADP(H) and acetyl-CoA, the pathway also depends on matrix redox shuttles (a peroxisomal malate dehydrogenase reoxidising NADH) and on carnitine or glyoxylate-cycle routes that export the acetyl units. Unsaturated fatty acids additionally need auxiliary enzymes: a delta3-delta2-enoyl-CoA isomerase and an NADPH-dependent 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase, whose NADPH is regenerated inside the peroxisome by NADP-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase. In humans, single-enzyme defects (ACOX1, HSD17B4, EHHADH, SCP2, ABCD1) and peroxisome biogenesis disorders cause accumulation of very-long-chain and branched fatty acids and bile-acid intermediates with severe neurological disease.

Phagocytic engulfmentMODULE:phagocytic_engulfment Phagocytic engulfment is the receptor-driven internalization of a large particle (a microbe, an opsonized target, or an apoptotic cell) into a...
[more...][less] Phagocytic engulfment is the receptor-driven internalization of a large particle (a microbe, an opsonized target, or an apoptotic cell) into a plasma-membrane-derived vacuole, the nascent phagosome. A cell-surface receptor recognizes the particle, either directly (beta-glucan, phosphatidylserine) or through a bound opsonin or bridging ligand (IgG, iC3b, GAS6). Receptor engagement then activates Rho-family GTPases, Rac and Cdc42 for Fc-gamma and apoptotic-cell receptors and RhoA for complement receptor 3. The GTPases drive Arp2/3-dependent actin polymerization that extends pseudopods around the particle. Class I PI3K activity and dynamin are then needed to complete pseudopod extension and close the phagocytic cup. The receptor-to-Rac core is conserved between nematodes and mammals: the CED-1/CED-6 and CED-2/CED-5/CED-12 routes of C. elegans correspond to MEGF10/GULP1 and CRK/DOCK1/ELMO1 upstream of Rac1.

Phagophore assembly site (PAS)MODULE:phagophore_assembly_siteCONCRETE The phagophore assembly site (PAS, historically the pre-autophagosomal structure) is the single perivacuolar punctum in budding yeast at which the...
[more...][less] The phagophore assembly site (PAS, historically the pre-autophagosomal structure) is the single perivacuolar punctum in budding yeast at which the autophagy machinery is concentrated and from which the phagophore emerges. It is not a membrane-bounded organelle: the PAS is a liquid-like condensate of Atg proteins, nucleated by phase separation of the Atg1 kinase complex on an Atg17-Atg31-Atg29 scaffold (starvation-induced bulk autophagy) or on an Atg11-cargo scaffold (selective autophagy and the Cvt pathway), and tethered to the vacuolar membrane by Vac8. Membrane is present at the PAS but is a component of it rather than its boundary: a small number of Atg9 vesicles cluster at the site and are incorporated into the outer autophagosomal membrane, and the downstream machinery - the class III PI3K complex I, the Atg2-Atg18 lipid transfer bridge, and the Atg8 conjugation system - is recruited onto the condensate in a defined hierarchy. The site is dismantled from within: Atg1, activated by lipidated Atg8 on the growing phagophore, phosphorylates Atg13 and triggers dissociation and rapid turnover of Atg1 complex subunits at the PAS. This module models the PAS as a cellular component with a nucleation step, a composition, a positioning mechanism, and a turnover step.

Phagophore-organelle membrane contact siteMODULE:phagophore_organelle_contact_siteCONCRETE A phagophore-organelle membrane contact site is the zone of apposition through which a growing phagophore (isolation membrane) is physically held...
[more...][less] A phagophore-organelle membrane contact site is the zone of apposition through which a growing phagophore (isolation membrane) is physically held against a donor or anchor organelle while the autophagosome is built. Canonically this is the phagophore-endoplasmic reticulum membrane contact site: a bridging assembly in which an ATG2-family rod spans the ~10-20 nm gap between the ER and the phagophore rim, an Atg18/WIPI4-family beta-propeller clamps the ATG2 tip onto phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) on the phagophore, and lipid scramblases work on both sides - VMP1 and TMEM41B in the donor ER membrane, and the ATG9 trimer at the phagophore rim - so that glycerophospholipids delivered by ATG2 into one leaflet are equilibrated across the bilayer. The site is nucleated by the Atg1/ULK1 kinase complex together with class III PI3K-derived PI3P, operates as a lipid conduit that drives phagophore expansion, and is taken apart when contacts are dissolved and the phagophore is sealed. Related contact sites use the same bridging logic with a different partner organelle: PI3P-rich endosomes can serve as an alternative ATG2 lipid donor, and in budding yeast Vac8 anchors the phagophore assembly site to the vacuole, giving a positional rather than lipid-donating attachment. This module models the site as a cellular component with an assembly step, a composition, a lipid flux function, and a disassembly step.

Phagosome maturationMODULE:phagosome_maturation Phagosome maturation turns the nascent phagosome, which has no microbicidal or degradative activity, into a phagolysosome. It does so through an...
[more...][less] Phagosome maturation turns the nascent phagosome, which has no microbicidal or degradative activity, into a phagolysosome. It does so through an ordered series of fusion and fission events with endocytic and lysosomal compartments. The sealed phagosome first recruits active Rab5, and the class III PI3K VPS34 makes PI(3)P on its membrane. The Mon1-Ccz1 complex, a Rab5 effector and Rab7 GEF, then hands the vacuole over to Rab7. Rab7 and its effectors, together with LAMP proteins and the HOPS tethering complex, drive microtubule-dependent movement and fusion with late endosomes and lysosomes. The V-ATPase acidifies the lumen as it is delivered. In professional phagocytes the NOX2 NADPH oxidase also assembles on the phagosomal membrane and produces superoxide into the lumen. The same machinery degrades internalized microbes and engulfed apoptotic cells, and its core is conserved between C. elegans and mammals.

Phosphocreatine shuttle / creatine kinase system (human)MODULE:phosphocreatine_shuttle The creatine kinase (CK) / phosphocreatine energy-buffer system, which uses the creatine produced by creatine biosynthesis (see...
[more...][less] The creatine kinase (CK) / phosphocreatine energy-buffer system, which uses the creatine produced by creatine biosynthesis (see MODULE:creatine_biosynthesis) as a spatial and temporal buffer of ATP. This module covers creatine *utilization*, not its synthesis. A single reversible reaction, creatine kinase activity (ATP + creatine <=> ADP + phosphocreatine, GO:0004111), is run in two cellular locations by compartment-specific isozymes to form a shuttle: mitochondrial CK isozymes (CKMT1A/B ubiquitous, CKMT2 sarcomeric) sit in the mitochondrial intermembrane space and use ATP exported from oxidative phosphorylation to phosphorylate creatine, producing phosphocreatine; phosphocreatine, being small and diffusible, moves through the cytosol to sites of high ATP turnover, where cytosolic CK isozymes (CKB brain-type, CKM muscle-type; assembled as CK-BB, CK-MB, and CK-MM dimers) regenerate ATP from phosphocreatine and ADP exactly where it is consumed. The net effect is to shuttle high-energy phosphate from mitochondria to ATPases and to buffer the cytosolic ATP/ADP ratio in tissues with high, fluctuating energy demand (skeletal and cardiac muscle, brain, photoreceptors, spermatozoa). The same enzymes also support a thermogenic "futile creatine cycle" (GO:0140651) in some adipocytes, in which phosphocreatine is hydrolysed back to creatine (releasing heat) rather than donating phosphate to ADP. The catalytic species are oligomers, and the participants here are modelled as protein complexes mirroring Reactome: the mitochondrial limb as alternative homo-octamers and the cytosolic limb as the CK-MM, CK-BB, and CK-MB dimers (the heterodimer being a genuine two-gene-product catalytic unit). This module is distinct from, and downstream of, creatine biosynthesis: it consumes creatine, it does not make it.

Phosphoinositide biosynthesis (PI -> PI3P/PI4P -> PI(3,5)P2/PI(4,5)P2 kinase network)MODULE:phosphoinositide_biosynthesisCONCRETE Phosphatidylinositol (PI) is phosphorylated on the inositol ring by a conserved set of lipid kinases to give the phosphoinositides that mark...
[more...][less] Phosphatidylinositol (PI) is phosphorylated on the inositol ring by a conserved set of lipid kinases to give the phosphoinositides that mark eukaryotic membranes and recruit effector proteins. A class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (Vps34), held on membranes by its regulatory protein-kinase subunit, makes PI 3-phosphate (PI3P) on endosomes and autophagic membranes. Phosphatidylinositol 4-kinases make PI 4-phosphate (PI4P) in distinct places: the type III-beta enzyme (Pik1/PI4KB) on the trans-Golgi, the type III-alpha enzyme (Stt4/PI4KA), recruited by an Efr3-Ypp1 scaffold, at the plasma membrane, and a type II enzyme on plasma and vacuolar/endosomal membranes. Two kinds of PIP kinase add a 5-phosphate: the type I PI4P 5-kinase (Mss4/PIP5K1) converts plasma-membrane PI4P to PI(4,5)P2, the precursor of inositol-trisphosphate signalling and a regulator of the cortical actin cytoskeleton, and the FYVE-domain PI3P 5-kinase (Fab1/PIKfyve), acting in a complex with Vac14 and the Fig4 phosphatase, converts PI3P to PI(3,5)P2 on the vacuole/late endosome, where it controls vacuole size and membrane homeostasis. Because each kinase acts in its own compartment, the network produces membrane-specific lipid identities rather than a linear pathway; lipid phosphatases (Sac1, synaptojanins, Fig4) reverse these steps and are outside this module.

Phosphorylase kinase complex (activates glycogenolysis) — GSD IXMODULE:phosphorylase_kinase_complex Phosphorylase kinase (PhK) is the large (~1.3 MDa) hexadecameric (alpha-beta-gamma-delta)4 holoenzyme that switches on glycogen breakdown by...
[more...][less] Phosphorylase kinase (PhK) is the large (~1.3 MDa) hexadecameric (alpha-beta-gamma-delta)4 holoenzyme that switches on glycogen breakdown by phosphorylating glycogen phosphorylase on Ser14, converting the low-activity phosphorylase b to the active phosphorylase a. It is the key node coupling hormonal and neural/contractile signals to glycogenolysis: the catalytic gamma subunit (muscle PHKG1 / liver-testis PHKG2) is a Ca2+/calmodulin-regulated Ser/Thr protein kinase held in an autoinhibited state by the large regulatory alpha (muscle PHKA1 / liver PHKA2) and beta (PHKB) subunits; phosphorylation of the alpha and beta subunits by cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA, downstream of adrenaline/glucagon) and Ca2+ binding to the delta subunit (calmodulin, which reports muscle contraction) relieve this inhibition and activate the complex. The activated PhK then phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase, triggering the phosphorolysis step of glycogenolysis. Inherited defects cause glycogen storage disease type IX (one of the most common glycogenoses), with tissue-specific subtypes reflecting the subunit isoforms: PHKA2 -> GSD IXa (X-linked liver, most common); PHKB -> GSD IXb (liver + muscle); PHKG2 -> GSD IXc (liver, more severe, cirrhosis risk); PHKA1 -> GSD IXd (X-linked muscle, exercise intolerance).

Photoperiodic (long-day) flowering via the CONSTANS-FLOWERING LOCUS T pathway (Arabidopsis)MODULE:photoperiodic_flowering_co_ftCONCRETE The external-coincidence mechanism by which Arabidopsis measures day length and converts long days into flowering. In leaf phloem companion cells...
[more...][less] The external-coincidence mechanism by which Arabidopsis measures day length and converts long days into flowering. In leaf phloem companion cells the morning-phased Dof repressors (CYCLING DOF FACTORs, represented by CDF1) bind the CONSTANS (CO) and FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT) promoters and repress them, partly by recruiting TOPLESS. In long-day afternoons the clock-phased FKF1 and GIGANTEA (GI) proteins coincide with light; blue-light activation of the FKF1 LOV domain promotes FKF1-GI complex formation on the CO promoter and SCF(FKF1)-dependent degradation of the CDFs, relieving CO repression. CO protein is unstable in the dark because the COP1-SPA E3 ubiquitin ligase targets it for proteasomal degradation; in the light, photoactivated CRY2 (blue) and phyA (far-red) inhibit COP1-SPA and FKF1 binds and stabilizes CO, so CO protein accumulates only when CO mRNA expression overlaps with light at the end of a long day. CO, in an NF-Y-like trimer with NF-YB/NF-YC, binds CORE (CCACA) elements and activates FT transcription in companion cells. FT protein (florigen) moves through the phloem to the shoot apical meristem, where 14-3-3 proteins bridge it to the phosphorylated bZIP transcription factor FD; this florigen activation complex activates floral integrator and floral meristem identity genes such as SOC1 and AP1, committing the meristem to flowering. The circadian oscillator that phases GI, FKF1, CDF and CO expression, phytochrome-mediated photomorphogenesis, FT transport machinery and the vernalization/autonomous pathways are outside this module.

Phytochrome control of photomorphogenesis (phyA/phyB - PIF - COP1/SPA - HY5)MODULE:phytochrome_photomorphogenesisCONCRETE Red and far-red light control seedling de-etiolation and growth in Arabidopsis thaliana through the phytochrome photoreceptors. In darkness two...
[more...][less] Red and far-red light control seedling de-etiolation and growth in Arabidopsis thaliana through the phytochrome photoreceptors. In darkness two repressor systems keep seedlings etiolated: the PIF bHLH transcription factors (PIF1, PIF3, PIF4 and relatives) promote skotomorphogenic growth and repress chlorophyll biosynthesis and germination, and the nuclear CUL4-DDB1-COP1-SPA E3 ubiquitin ligase targets photomorphogenesis-promoting transcription factors such as HY5 for proteasomal degradation. Light converts phytochromes to the active Pfr form, phyB mainly under red light and phyA under far-red light. Pfr phytochromes enter the nucleus and form photobodies, where they act on both repressor systems. (1) They bind PIFs through APB and APA motifs. This triggers rapid PIF phosphorylation, with SPA1 kinase activity contributing in a phyB-PIF1-SPA1 complex, followed by ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation; PIF1 is turned over through the CUL4-COP1-SPA ligase. (2) They bind SPA proteins and disrupt the COP1-SPA interaction, which inactivates the ligase. HY5 then accumulates and, with the loss of PIF activity, drives photomorphogenic gene expression: hypocotyl growth inhibition, cotyledon expansion and greening. In darkness PIF1 also enhances COP1 E3 activity, so the two repressor systems act synergistically. Blue-light cryptochromes (CRY1) inhibit the same COP1-SPA node and are included only as a converging input. UVR8, PIF-independent phyB outputs, thermomorphogenesis (PIF4-temperature), photoperiodic flowering (COP1-SPA-CO) and hormone crosstalk are outside the module boundary.

Plant cellulose biosynthesis moduleMODULE:plant_cellulose_biosynthesis A taxon-neutral decomposition of plant cellulose biosynthesis as a recursively decomposable module. Cellulose is synthesized at the plasma membrane...
[more...][less] A taxon-neutral decomposition of plant cellulose biosynthesis as a recursively decomposable module. Cellulose is synthesized at the plasma membrane by the cellulose synthase complex (CSC, the "rosette"), which polymerizes UDP-glucose into (1->4)-beta-D-glucan chains that coalesce into crystalline microfibrils in the apoplast. The module separates (1) UDP-glucose substrate supply, (2) glucan polymerization by the CSC with distinct primary- and secondary-cell-wall CESA isoform sets, (3) guidance of CSC trajectory by the cortical microtubule cytoskeleton, (4) accessory enzymes/proteins required for productive synthesis (KORRIGAN endoglucanase, COBRA), and (5) microfibril assembly and organization. It is phrased as functions, complexes, and pathway segments rather than a fixed gene list so it can represent angiosperm, grass, and (with substitution) algal implementations. Concrete UniProt members are Arabidopsis exemplars, not species-restricting claims. Cellulose synthase-like (CSL) backbones of hemicelluloses, lignin biosynthesis, and the bacterial BcsA-type machinery are out of scope. As a bioenergy module, the polymerization step and its CESA isoform composition are the principal determinants of biomass recalcitrance and the main engineering targets for improved lignocellulosic saccharification.

Plant chitin perception by LysM receptor complexesMODULE:chitin_perceptionABSTRACT Flowering plants detect chitin oligosaccharides released from fungal cell walls at the plasma membrane with lysin-motif (LysM) pattern recognition...
[more...][less] Flowering plants detect chitin oligosaccharides released from fungal cell walls at the plasma membrane with lysin-motif (LysM) pattern recognition receptors. Perception needs two activities that different plant lineages divide differently between receptor proteins: high-affinity binding of long-chain chitin oligomers, and an active intracellular serine/threonine kinase. In rice, the kinase-less LysM receptor-like protein CEBiP is the chitin-binding subunit; two CEBiP ectodomains sandwich one chitin octamer, and ligand-induced association with the LysM receptor kinase OsCERK1 supplies the kinase, while OsCERK1 itself is not the chitin binder. In Arabidopsis, the LysM receptor kinase LYK5, whose intracellular domain is a catalytically inactive pseudokinase, is the high-affinity chitin binder, and it recruits CERK1, which both binds chitin with low affinity and is the active kinase. The LYK5 paralog LYK4, also a pseudokinase, binds chitin only weakly and acts as a LYK5-associated co-receptor or scaffold that enhances signalling; lyk4 lyk5 double mutants lose chitin responses. In both configurations the activated CERK1 kinase phosphorylates receptor-like cytoplasmic kinases (RLCKs) of the PBL27/OsRLCK185 type, which phosphorylate MAP kinase kinase kinases (MAPKKK5 in Arabidopsis; OsMAPKKKepsilon and OsMAPKKK18 in rice) that activate the MKK4/MKK5 to MPK3/MPK6 relay, driving defence gene expression and callose deposition. In Arabidopsis, RLCK VII-4 kinases such as PBL19 also phosphorylate MAPKKK5 and may carry most of this step, so the genetic weight of PBL27 is disputed. A parallel branch through BIK1 activates the plasma membrane NADPH oxidase RBOHD, which produces the apoplastic burst of reactive oxygen species. The two branches separate genetically: loss of MAPKKK5 or PBL27 does not reduce the ROS burst.

[more...][less] A taxon-neutral decomposition of plant lignin biosynthesis as a recursively decomposable module. Lignin is a phenolic heteropolymer deposited in secondary cell walls that provides mechanical support and water conduction but is the principal determinant of lignocellulosic biomass recalcitrance. The module separates (1) the general phenylpropanoid entry (PAL -> C4H -> 4CL) that converts L-phenylalanine into p-coumaroyl-CoA, (2) the monolignol-specific "metabolic grid" (HCT, C3'H, CCoAOMT, CCR, F5H, COMT, CAD) that reduces and differentially hydroxylates/methylates hydroxycinnamoyl intermediates into the three canonical monolignols (p-coumaryl, coniferyl, and sinapyl alcohol), (3) export of monolignols across the plasma membrane into the apoplast, and (4) oxidative radical coupling of monolignols by cell-wall laccases and class III peroxidases into the growing lignin polymer, whose p-hydroxyphenyl (H), guaiacyl (G), and syringyl (S) unit composition is set by which monolignols are supplied. It is phrased as functions and pathway segments rather than a fixed gene list so it can represent angiosperm, gymnosperm, and grass implementations (gymnosperms make almost no S lignin because they lack F5H/CYP84A activity; grasses additionally incorporate ferulate/coumarate esters, out of scope here). Concrete UniProt members are Arabidopsis exemplars, not species-restricting claims. As a bioenergy module, monolignol supply flux and the S/G ratio are the dominant engineering levers for reducing recalcitrance and improving saccharification and pulping.

Plant miRNA biogenesis and AGO1 RISC loadingMODULE:plant_mirna_biogenesisCONCRETE In Arabidopsis thaliana, microRNAs (miRNAs) are transcribed by RNA polymerase II as capped and polyadenylated primary transcripts (pri-miRNAs) that...
[more...][less] In Arabidopsis thaliana, microRNAs (miRNAs) are transcribed by RNA polymerase II as capped and polyadenylated primary transcripts (pri-miRNAs) that fold into imperfect stem-loop hairpins. Unlike animals, which split processing between nuclear Drosha and cytoplasmic Dicer, plants carry out both cleavage steps in the nucleus with a single RNase III enzyme, DICER-LIKE1 (DCL1). DCL1 works in a microprocessor with the double-stranded RNA-binding protein HYPONASTIC LEAVES1 (HYL1, also called DRB1) and the C2H2 zinc-finger protein SERRATE (SE). The three proteins meet in nuclear dicing bodies (D-bodies) and nucleoplasm. DCL1 alone can cut miRNA precursors, but most of its products are then misplaced. HYL1 and SE raise the rate of DCL1 cleavage and position the cuts, so that the correct 21-nt miRNA/miRNA* duplex is released. The small-RNA methyltransferase HUA ENHANCER1 (HEN1) then adds a 2'-O-methyl group to the 3'-terminal ribose of each strand of the duplex. This methyl mark protects the miRNA from 3' uridylation, trimming and degradation. The guide strand is then loaded into ARGONAUTE1 (AGO1), the main plant miRNA effector. AGO1 cleaves complementary target mRNAs through its PIWI-domain slicer activity and can also repress their translation. The miRNA-AGO1 complex is the output of this module.

It is phrased as functions and pathway segments rather than a fixed gene list so it can represent Arabidopsis and crop oilseeds (soybean, rapeseed/canola, oil palm, camelina); concrete UniProt members are Arabidopsis exemplars, not species-restricting claims. Plastidial de novo fatty acid synthesis, acyl-chain desaturation/modification, and TAG catabolism (lipolysis/beta-oxidation) are upstream/downstream and out of scope. As a bioenergy module, total TAG flux (DGAT/PDAT capacity), the acyl-CoA pool, and oil-body number/size (oleosin dosage) are the principal engineering levers for raising seed-oil yield for biodiesel and oleochemical feedstocks.

[more...][less] A taxon-neutral decomposition of plant heteroxylan biosynthesis as a recursively decomposable module. Xylan is the dominant hemicellulose of the secondary cell wall: a (1->4)-beta-D-xylan backbone decorated with (alpha-1,2)-linked (4-O-methyl)glucuronic acid and O-acetyl groups in eudicots (glucuronoxylan, GX) and additionally with alpha-arabinofuranosyl and feruloyl-arabinose substitutions in grasses (glucuronoarabinoxylan, GAX). Xylan coats and tethers cellulose microfibrils and is covalently and non-covalently associated with lignin in the lignin-carbohydrate complex, so it is a major contributor to biomass recalcitrance and a key acetyl-group source that inhibits downstream fermentation. The module separates (1) Golgi backbone elongation by the IRX9/IRX10/IRX14 xylan synthase machinery, (2) synthesis of the reducing-end oligosaccharide sequence that may prime/terminate the chain in eudicots, (3) alpha-glucuronosyl sidechain addition (GUX), (4) 4-O-methylation of the glucuronic acid (GXM), and (5) O-acetylation (ESK1/TBL29 with RWA acetyl-CoA supply). It is phrased as functions, complexes, and pathway segments rather than a fixed gene list so it can represent eudicot GX and grass GAX implementations; concrete UniProt members are Arabidopsis exemplars, not species-restricting claims. As a bioenergy module, xylan substitution pattern (acetylation, methyl-GlcA) and quantity are principal engineering targets for reducing recalcitrance and acetate-driven fermentation inhibition.

Polar (cell-to-cell) auxin transportMODULE:auxin_polar_transportCONCRETE Polar auxin transport is the directional, cell-to-cell movement of the phytohormone auxin (indole-3-acetic acid, IAA) through plant tissues. It...
[more...][less] Polar auxin transport is the directional, cell-to-cell movement of the phytohormone auxin (indole-3-acetic acid, IAA) through plant tissues. It generates the auxin gradients and maxima that pattern embryos, organs and vasculature and that drive tropic growth. The chemiosmotic model explains its directionality. In the acidic apoplast, protonated IAAH can enter cells by diffusion, but most uptake is carried out by AUX1/LAX proton-coupled influx symporters. In the near-neutral cytosol IAA is trapped as the membrane-impermeant anion and must be exported by carriers. PIN-FORMED (PIN) efflux carriers are polarly localized within the plasma membrane, so their position sets the direction of flow. Examples are PIN1 at the basal (rootward) side of shoot vascular cells and apically in the shoot-apex epidermis, and PIN2 at the apical (shootward) side of root epidermal and lateral root cap cells. Full-size ABCB/P-glycoprotein transporters such as ABCB19 use ATP to export auxin from the plasma membrane largely non-polarly. They maintain long-distance streams by limiting reuptake and lateral leakage, and they act together with PINs. PIN activity and polarity are set by phosphorylation of the PIN central hydrophilic loop by plasma-membrane-associated AGCVIII kinases. PINOID/WAG kinases phosphorylate sites that recruit PINs into apical targeting (a phosphorylation-dependent polarity switch opposed by PP2A/PP6 phosphatases), and both PID and the basally localized D6 PROTEIN KINASE (D6PK) activate PIN-mediated efflux. This module covers the transport and regulatory activities at the plasma membrane. Nuclear auxin perception and signaling (TIR1/AFB-Aux/IAA-ARF), auxin biosynthesis, intracellular auxin compartmentation (short PINs, PILS) and the vesicle-trafficking machinery that recycles PINs (GNOM ARF-GEF) are outside its boundary.

Primordial germ cell specification moduleMODULE:primordial_germ_cell_specification The early-metazoan program that sets aside the primordial germ cells (PGCs) - the lineage that will form the gametes - from the soma. Two...
[more...][less] The early-metazoan program that sets aside the primordial germ cells (PGCs) - the lineage that will form the gametes - from the soma. Two evolutionarily alternative strategies achieve this and are modelled as a variant set along the "specification mode" axis: (1) preformation, in which maternally inherited germ plasm (a specialised cytoplasm rich in germline determinants such as Vasa/DDX4, Nanos, and Piwi-clade proteins) autonomously specifies PGCs in flies, worms, fish, and frogs; and (2) induction, in which BMP signalling from extraembryonic tissue instructs competent epiblast cells to become PGCs via the PRDM1/PRDM14/TFAP2C tripartite network, as in mouse and (inferred) human. Both routes converge on a conserved germline ground state: transcriptional quiescence of the somatic program, retention of pluripotency potential, and protection of the genome by piRNA-guided transposon silencing. Proline-P5C biosynthesis and catabolismMODULE:proline_metabolismCONCRETE Eukaryotic proline metabolism interconverts L-glutamate, L-ornithine, delta-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate (P5C) and L-proline. In the biosynthetic arm,...
[more...][less] Eukaryotic proline metabolism interconverts L-glutamate, L-ornithine, delta-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate (P5C) and L-proline. In the biosynthetic arm, L-glutamate is phosphorylated to L-glutamyl 5-phosphate and reduced with NADPH to L-glutamate 5-semialdehyde, which cyclizes spontaneously to P5C; P5C reductase then forms L-proline. The two glutamate-activating reactions are catalyzed either by two separate enzymes, a glutamate 5-kinase and a gamma-glutamyl-phosphate reductase (as in fungi), or by the kinase and reductase domains of a single bifunctional P5C synthase (as in animals and plants). Ornithine aminotransferase can feed the same semialdehyde/P5C pool from L-ornithine. In the catabolic arm, a FAD-dependent proline dehydrogenase associated with the mitochondrial respiratory chain oxidizes L-proline back to P5C, and a mitochondrial NAD-dependent P5C dehydrogenase oxidizes the semialdehyde to L-glutamate, so that proline can serve as a carbon and nitrogen source. Biosynthesis and degradation are separated by compartment and by regulation (feedback control of glutamate 5-kinase, proline-induced expression of the catabolic enzymes).

Propionyl-CoA catabolism (propionate to succinyl-CoA via the methylmalonyl-CoA pathway)MODULE:propionyl_coa_catabolism The mitochondrial pathway that converts propionyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, the anaplerotic route by which propionate carbon enters the TCA cycle....
[more...][less] The mitochondrial pathway that converts propionyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, the anaplerotic route by which propionate carbon enters the TCA cycle. Propionyl-CoA arises from the catabolism of the branched-chain amino acids isoleucine and valine, of methionine and threonine, of odd-chain fatty acids, and of the cholesterol side chain (and from gut-microbial propionate). Three enzymatic steps: (1) the biotin-dependent propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC), an alpha6-beta6 dodecamer of PCCA (biotin-carboxylase / biotin-carboxyl-carrier alpha subunit) and PCCB (carboxyltransferase beta subunit), carboxylates propionyl-CoA to (2S)-methylmalonyl-CoA (D-methylmalonyl-CoA) using bicarbonate and ATP; (2) methylmalonyl-CoA epimerase (MCEE) racemises this to (2R)-methylmalonyl-CoA (L-methylmalonyl-CoA); and (3) the adenosylcobalamin (AdoCbl / vitamin B12)- dependent methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMUT) performs the carbon-skeleton rearrangement of L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. The mutase step depends on a dedicated cobalamin cofactor-supply system: MMAB (cblB) is the ATP:cob(I)alamin adenosyltransferase that synthesises AdoCbl, and MMAA (cblA) is a mitochondrial G3E-family GTPase that gates AdoCbl loading onto MMUT and protects/reactivates the holo-mutase. Inherited defects map cleanly onto the steps: PCCA/PCCB → propionic acidemia; MCEE → (usually mild) methylmalonic aciduria; MMUT → methylmalonic aciduria (mut type); MMAB → cblB and MMAA → cblA methylmalonic aciduria (both often vitamin-B12-responsive because they act on cofactor supply).

Protein O-glycosylation in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_protein_o_glycosylationCONCRETE O-glycosylation attaches sugars to the hydroxyl groups of serine, threonine or hydroxylysine. Flies use several independent O-glycosylation...
[more...][less] O-glycosylation attaches sugars to the hydroxyl groups of serine, threonine or hydroxylysine. Flies use several independent O-glycosylation pathways, each started by a dedicated transferase. Mucin-type O-GalNAc glycans are initiated by a family of polypeptide GalNAc transferases (Pgant) and extended by core 1 galactosyltransferase (C1GalTA) and glucuronyltransferase. EGF repeats of Notch and other receptors carry O-fucose added by Ofut1 and elongated by the GlcNAc transferase Fringe, and O-glucose added by Rumi and extended with xylose by Shams and Xxylt. Thrombospondin repeats are O-fucosylated by Ofut2. O-mannose glycans are added in the ER by the Rotated abdomen-Twisted (POMT1-POMT2) complex and, on cadherins, by the TMTC transferases. Nuclear and cytosolic proteins are modified by single O-GlcNAc residues by Super sex combs (OGT) and the modification is removed by O-GlcNAcase, while EGF repeats receive extracellular O-GlcNAc from Eogt. Collagen hydroxylysines are galactosylated after hydroxylation by Plod.

Protein prenylation and CAAX processing (FTase/GGTase-I/RabGGTase -> RCE1 -> ICMT)MODULE:protein_prenylation_caax_processing Prenylation is a lipid post-translational modification that irreversibly attaches a farnesyl (C15) or geranylgeranyl (C20) isoprenoid — supplied as...
[more...][less] Prenylation is a lipid post-translational modification that irreversibly attaches a farnesyl (C15) or geranylgeranyl (C20) isoprenoid — supplied as FPP/GGPP from the mevalonate pathway — to C-terminal cysteines of ~300 human proteins (Ras, Rho, Rac, Rab and other small GTPases, nuclear lamins, kinases), anchoring them to membranes and enabling signalling and vesicular trafficking. Three heterodimeric prenyltransferases do the attachment. Farnesyltransferase (FTase = the shared alpha subunit FNTA + the beta subunit FNTB) and geranylgeranyltransferase type I (GGTase-I = FNTA + PGGT1B) recognise a C-terminal CAAX motif directly and prenylate its cysteine — FTase when X is Met/Ser/Gln/Ala, GGTase-I when X is Leu/Phe. Rab geranylgeranyltransferase (GGTase-II / RabGGTase = RABGGTA + RABGGTB) instead double-geranylgeranylates the C-terminal CC/CXC cysteines of Rab GTPases, which must first be presented by the Rab escort protein REP1/REP2 (CHM/CHML). For the CAAX (FTase/GGTase-I) substrates, two further ER-membrane maturation steps follow: the glutamate-type intramembrane protease RCE1 removes the -AAX tripeptide, exposing the prenylcysteine as the new C-terminus, and the SAM-dependent methyltransferase ICMT carboxymethylates that prenylcysteine, maximising hydrophobicity and membrane affinity. The pathway is a major anticancer target (Ras farnesylation; FTIs) and underlies Hutchinson-Gilford progeria (lamin A prenylation). RabGGTase/REP defects cause choroideremia (via CHM), and RCE1/ICMT are Ras-pathway drug targets.

C5 glutamyl-tRNA and C4/Shemin reactions can independently supply 5-aminolevulinate (ALA); many organisms encode one route, while some encode both. A shared tetrapyrrole trunk then feeds independently selected oxygen-dependent or oxygen-independent coproporphyrinogen oxidases and HemJ-, HemG-, or HemY/PPOX-family protoporphyrinogen oxidases. All realizations converge at protoporphyrin IX, which a species-neutral ferrochelatase reaction converts to heme B. This protoporphyrin-dependent (PPD, "classical") route is one of three known routes to heme B; the coproporphyrin-dependent (CPD) route of Firmicutes and Actinobacteria and the siroheme-dependent alternative heme biosynthesis (AHB) route of sulfate-reducing bacteria and archaea share the ALA-to- uroporphyrinogen III core but are outside this module.

Those small RNAs act as decoys for the Hfq/Crc translational repressor pair: when carbon is poor and crcZ/crcY levels are high, Hfq/Crc is sequestered away from the A-rich catabolite-activity motifs near the ribosome-binding sites of catabolic mRNAs, relieving translational repression. Purine base and nucleoside salvage, with oxidation of purine bases to urateMODULE:purine_salvage_and_catabolism The cytosolic handling of purine bases and nucleosides released by nucleic-acid and nucleotide turnover or taken up from outside the cell. A...
[more...][less] The cytosolic handling of purine bases and nucleosides released by nucleic-acid and nucleotide turnover or taken up from outside the cell. A salvage arm recycles them into nucleotides, sparing costly de novo synthesis: phosphoribosyltransferases transfer the phosphoribosyl group of PRPP to adenine (adenine phosphoribosyltransferase, giving AMP), to hypoxanthine and guanine (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, giving IMP and GMP) and, in fungi and bacteria, to xanthine (xanthine phosphoribosyltransferase, giving XMP); adenosine kinase phosphorylates adenosine to AMP. Interconverting deaminations and phosphorolysis route bases between these entry points: adenosine deaminase (animals) or adenine deaminase (fungi, bacteria) converts the adenine moiety to the hypoxanthine level, purine nucleoside phosphorylase releases hypoxanthine and guanine from inosine and guanosine, and guanine deaminase converts guanine to xanthine. An optional catabolic arm oxidises hypoxanthine and xanthine to urate, by molybdenum-dependent xanthine oxidoreductase in animals, plants and many bacteria, or, for xanthine, by an alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent xanthine dioxygenase found only in fungi. Some organisms lack the catabolic arm entirely: budding yeast has no xanthine oxidoreductase, xanthine dioxygenase or urate oxidase and only salvages purine bases. In humans, inherited defects define classic disorders: complete HPRT1 deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and partial deficiency gout/hyperuricemia; APRT deficiency causes 2,8-dihydroxyadenine nephrolithiasis; ADA and PNP deficiencies cause immunodeficiency through lymphotoxic deoxynucleotide accumulation; and XDH deficiency causes xanthinuria type I (XDH is the target of allopurinol and febuxostat).

Purine nucleotide catabolism to urate (5'-nucleotidases / deaminases -> PNP -> XDH)MODULE:purine_nucleotide_catabolism Purine ribonucleotides are catabolised to the excretory end-product uric acid through a converging network of dephosphorylation, deamination and...
[more...][less] Purine ribonucleotides are catabolised to the excretory end-product uric acid through a converging network of dephosphorylation, deamination and phosphorolysis reactions. AMP is either deaminated to IMP by AMP deaminase (AMPD1/2/3) or dephosphorylated to adenosine by a 5'-nucleotidase — the cytosolic AMP-preferring NT5C1A or the GPI-anchored cell-surface ecto-5'-nucleotidase NT5E (CD73), whose extracellular adenosine is also a major purinergic signal. Adenosine is deaminated to inosine by adenosine deaminase (ADA). IMP and GMP are dephosphorylated to inosine and guanosine by the cytosolic 5'-nucleotidase NT5C2. Purine-nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) then removes the ribose from inosine, guanosine and their deoxy forms, giving hypoxanthine and guanine. Guanine is deaminated to xanthine by guanine deaminase (GDA), while hypoxanthine is oxidised to xanthine and xanthine to urate by xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase (XDH). Defects across the pathway cause disease: ADA and PNP deficiencies cause severe combined / T-cell immunodeficiency, XDH deficiency causes xanthinuria, NT5E loss-of-function causes arterial calcification (ACDC), and activating NT5C2 mutations drive relapse in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

Purine ribonucleotide interconversion (IMP to AMP/GMP and their di- and triphosphates)MODULE:purine_nucleotide_interconversion Inosine monophosphate (IMP), the first complete purine nucleotide made by de novo synthesis or by salvage, is the branch point from which the...
[more...][less] Inosine monophosphate (IMP), the first complete purine nucleotide made by de novo synthesis or by salvage, is the branch point from which the adenine and guanine ribonucleotides are made. Toward AMP, adenylosuccinate synthetase condenses IMP with L-aspartate using GTP to form adenylosuccinate, which adenylosuccinate lyase cleaves to AMP and fumarate. Toward GMP, IMP dehydrogenase oxidises IMP to xanthosine monophosphate (XMP) with NAD+ (the committed, rate-limiting step of guanine-nucleotide synthesis) and GMP synthase aminates XMP to GMP using the amide nitrogen of glutamine. The monophosphates are then phosphorylated by adenylate kinase (AMP to ADP) and guanylate kinase (GMP to GDP), and nucleoside-diphosphate kinase transfers the gamma-phosphate of ATP to GDP (and other diphosphates) to make GTP; ADP is converted to ATP mainly by energy metabolism. AMP deaminase hydrolytically deaminates AMP back to IMP; with adenylosuccinate synthetase and lyase this forms the purine nucleotide cycle, which in animal muscle buffers the adenylate energy charge and releases fumarate and ammonia. Because GTP is required to make AMP and ATP to make GMP, these reactions cross-regulate the adenine and guanine nucleotide pools. The enzymes are cytosolic and conserved from bacteria to fungi and animals, with lineage-specific isozymes (for example, muscle and liver adenylosuccinate synthetases and three AMP deaminases in mammals, and three expressed IMP dehydrogenases in budding yeast). Inherited defects of the human enzymes include ADSS1 distal myopathy, IMPDH1 retinitis pigmentosa, IMPDH2 neurodevelopmental dystonia, myoadenylate deaminase (AMPD1) deficiency and AMPD2 pontocerebellar hypoplasia; IMP dehydrogenase is the target of mycophenolic acid and ribavirin.

Pyrenoid-based CO2-concentrating mechanismMODULE:pyrenoid_ccmCONCRETE The pyrenoid-based CO2-concentrating mechanism (PCCM) of green algae, modeled on Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. Rubisco is condensed by a multivalent...
[more...][less] The pyrenoid-based CO2-concentrating mechanism (PCCM) of green algae, modeled on Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. Rubisco is condensed by a multivalent linker protein into a liquid-like matrix (the pyrenoid) inside the chloroplast stroma. Thylakoid membrane tubules traverse the matrix. Bicarbonate accumulated in the stroma enters the thylakoid lumen through bestrophin-like channels and is dehydrated to CO2 by a lumenal carbonic anhydrase within the tubules, releasing CO2 into the Rubisco matrix. A starch sheath around the matrix limits CO2 back-diffusion, and a stromal LCIB/LCIC carbonic anhydrase complex at the pyrenoid periphery recaptures escaping CO2 as bicarbonate. The parts follow the six-step minimal-PCCM decomposition used in modeling and in plans to engineer a pyrenoid into C3 plant chloroplasts. Bicarbonate uptake across the plasma membrane and chloroplast envelope, and transcriptional induction under low CO2, are included as optional upstream parts.

[more...][less] Recycling of preformed pyrimidine bases and ribonucleosides, taken up from the environment or released by RNA and nucleotide turnover, into UMP and CMP. Uracil is converted directly to UMP by uracil phosphoribosyltransferase with PRPP. Uridine and cytidine are phosphorylated by uridine-cytidine kinase to UMP and CMP; alternatively, cytidine is deaminated to uridine by cytidine deaminase, and the ribonucleosides are cleaved to their free bases either by a nucleoside hydrolase (fungi and protists) or by uridine phosphorylase (animals and bacteria). Cytosine is deaminated to uracil by cytosine deaminase, an enzyme present in fungi and bacteria but absent from animals; this is why the antifungal prodrug 5-fluorocytosine is selectively toxic to fungi. CMP made by salvage is phosphorylated to CDP by UMP/CMP kinase, and UMP joins the de novo product for conversion to UTP and CTP. The same enzymes act on some deoxyribonucleosides (deoxycytidine is phosphorylated or cleaved), but thymidine salvage requires thymidine kinase, which animals and many bacteria have and budding and fission yeasts lack. Uptake of pyrimidine bases and nucleosides by plasma-membrane permeases precedes the module.

Pyrimidine nucleotide catabolism (5'-nucleotidase/deaminase/phosphorylase -> DPYD -> DPYS -> UPB1)MODULE:pyrimidine_nucleotide_catabolism Pyrimidine nucleotides are degraded through a sequence of dephosphorylation, deamination and phosphorolysis that liberates the free bases uracil...
[more...][less] Pyrimidine nucleotides are degraded through a sequence of dephosphorylation, deamination and phosphorolysis that liberates the free bases uracil and thymine, followed by the three-step reductive ring-opening pathway that converts them to beta-alanine and beta-aminoisobutyrate. Pyrimidine mononucleotides (UMP, CMP) are dephosphorylated to uridine and cytidine by the erythrocyte-enriched cytosolic pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase NT5C3A. Cytidine (and 2'-deoxycytidine) is deaminated to uridine (2'-deoxyuridine) by cytidine deaminase CDA. Uridine is phosphorolysed to uracil plus ribose-1-phosphate by uridine phosphorylase UPP1 (ubiquitous) or UPP2 (tissue-restricted paralog); thymidine is analogously phosphorolysed to thymine by thymidine phosphorylase TYMP. The liberated uracil and thymine then enter the conserved reductive catabolic pathway: dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase DPYD reduces them (NADPH) to dihydrouracil/dihydrothymine, dihydropyrimidinase DPYS hydrolyses the ring to N-carbamyl-beta-alanine / N-carbamyl-beta-aminoisobutyrate, and beta-ureidopropionase UPB1 releases beta-alanine / beta-aminoisobutyrate (+ CO2 + NH3). This pathway also governs the activation and inactivation of pyrimidine-analog drugs: NT5C3A/CDA/UPP1/TYMP shape the fluoropyrimidine (5-FU, capecitabine) and cytidine-analog (gemcitabine, cytarabine) response, and DPYD loss-of-function causes severe 5-fluorouracil toxicity. Other deficiencies cause pyrimidine-5'-nucleotidase hemolytic anemia (NT5C3A), MNGIE (TYMP), and dihydropyrimidinuria (DPYD/DPYS/UPB1).

Pyruvate dehydrogenase bypass and acetate-dependent acetyl-CoA synthesisMODULE:pdh_bypass_acetyl_coa_synthesisABSTRACT The pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) bypass makes acetyl-CoA in the cytosol without the mitochondrial PDH complex. Acetaldehyde is oxidised by an...
[more...][less] The pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) bypass makes acetyl-CoA in the cytosol without the mitochondrial PDH complex. Acetaldehyde is oxidised by an aldehyde dehydrogenase to acetate, and acetate is ligated to coenzyme A by an AMP-forming acetyl-CoA synthetase. The acetaldehyde comes either from pyruvate decarboxylase during growth on sugars or from alcohol dehydrogenase oxidising ethanol during growth on ethanol. Acetyl-CoA cannot cross organelle membranes, and some fungi, including budding yeast, lack ATP-citrate lyase. In those organisms this route is the main or only source of nucleocytosolic acetyl-CoA for fatty acid and sterol synthesis, lysine synthesis and histone acetylation, and it is essential. The same three reactions carry ethanol and acetate into central metabolism (via the glyoxylate cycle) after the diauxic shift. The acetate-activation step is the conserved acetyl-CoA synthetase found from bacteria to mammals.

Pyruvate fates — pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and pyruvate carboxylaseMODULE:pyruvate_metabolism The two committed eukaryotic fates of pyruvate that feed the TCA cycle. (1) Oxidative decarboxylation by the mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase...
[more...][less] The two committed eukaryotic fates of pyruvate that feed the TCA cycle. (1) Oxidative decarboxylation by the mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) links glycolysis to the TCA cycle: pyruvate + CoA + NAD+ -> acetyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH. Pyruvate enters the matrix through the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier. The PDC is a giant mitochondrial-matrix multienzyme machine built on a 60-mer E2 (dihydrolipoyllysine-residue acetyltransferase) core, with the thiamine-diphosphate-dependent E1 decarboxylase (an alpha2-beta2 heterotetramer), the E3-binding structural subunit (protein X / E3BP) that anchors the dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase E3, and E3 itself, which reoxidises the lipoyl arms and passes electrons to NAD+. The same subunit architecture is conserved from yeasts (PDA1, PDB1, LAT1, PDX1, LPD1) to animals (PDHA1, PDHB, DLAT, PDHX, DLD), and the E3 is shared with the 2-oxoglutarate and branched-chain 2-oxoacid dehydrogenases. PDC flux is switched off by phosphorylation of E1alpha by pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases and on by dephosphorylation by the phosphatases. (2) Carboxylation by the biotin-dependent pyruvate carboxylase (PC): pyruvate + HCO3- + ATP -> oxaloacetate, the principal anaplerotic reaction replenishing oxaloacetate and the committed first step of gluconeogenesis from pyruvate or lactate. PC is a mitochondrial-matrix enzyme in animals, where it is allosterically activated by acetyl-CoA, the PDC product, coordinating the two fates; in budding yeast the two PC isozymes are cytosolic, so the oxaloacetate they make must be imported into mitochondria to replenish the cycle. In humans, inherited defects cause severe lactic acidosis and neurological disease: PDHA1 (X-linked, the commonest), PDHB, DLAT and PDHX deficiencies cause pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency (Leigh syndrome spectrum), PC deficiency causes lactic acidosis with hypoglycemia, and DLD deficiency (the shared E3) gives a combined phenotype.

In G1, the origin recognition complex (ORC) binds replication origins and, with Cdc6 and Cdt1 (Double parked in Drosophila), loads the MCM2-7 helicase core as an inactive double hexamer around double-stranded DNA; this is origin licensing. In S phase, the Dbf4-dependent kinase (Cdc7 with its regulatory subunit Chiffon) and cyclin-dependent kinases trigger the recruitment of Cdc45 and the four-subunit GINS complex onto MCM2-7, forming the active CMG (Cdc45-MCM-GINS) helicase that unwinds DNA at the replication fork. Retinoid visual cycle (11-cis-retinal regeneration across RPE and photoreceptors)MODULE:retinoid_visual_cycle Vision depends on continuous regeneration of the 11-cis-retinal chromophore that photobleaches to all-trans-retinal each time a photon isomerizes a...
[more...][less] Vision depends on continuous regeneration of the 11-cis-retinal chromophore that photobleaches to all-trans-retinal each time a photon isomerizes a visual pigment. The classical (RPE) visual cycle recycles it across the photoreceptor and retinal-pigment-epithelium (RPE) cells. In photoreceptors, light isomerizes 11-cis-retinal bound to opsin to all-trans-retinal, which is released and reduced to all-trans-retinol by NADPH-dependent retinol dehydrogenases (RDH8 in the outer segment, RDH12 in the inner segment; this also detoxifies the reactive aldehyde). All-trans-retinol travels to the RPE, where lecithin:retinol acyltransferase (LRAT) esterifies it to all-trans-retinyl ester (the pathway's storage/committed form). The central RPE enzyme RPE65 then carries out the coupled ester-hydrolysis and trans-to-cis isomerization, producing 11-cis-retinol, which the NAD+-dependent 11-cis-retinol dehydrogenase RDH5 oxidizes to 11-cis-retinal for return to photoreceptors and recombination with opsin. The cellular retinaldehyde-binding protein RLBP1 (CRALBP) chaperones the hydrophobic 11-cis-retinoids through these steps, and RGR, an opsin-family photoisomerase in RPE/Muller cells, provides a light-driven route regenerating 11-cis-retinal from all-trans-retinal. RDH11 contributes broad retinaldehyde-reductase activity, and DHRS3 buffers retinaldehyde/retinoic-acid levels. Defects across the cycle cause inherited retinal dystrophies: RPE65 and LRAT (Leber congenital amaurosis, the RPE65 form treated by voretigene neparvovec gene therapy), RDH12 (LCA13), RDH5 (fundus albipunctatus), RLBP1 (retinitis punctata albescens / Bothnia dystrophy) and RGR (retinitis pigmentosa).

[more...][less] Riboflavin (vitamin B2) is the precursor of the flavin coenzymes FMN and FAD, which are the redox cofactors of dozens of flavoenzymes in mitochondrial fatty-acid and amino-acid oxidation, the respiratory chain, one-carbon and folate metabolism, and many oxidoreductases. Humans cannot synthesise riboflavin and must take it up from the diet, then convert it intracellularly to the active cofactors. Dietary and cellular riboflavin uptake is mediated by the three plasma-membrane SLC52 riboflavin transporters: SLC52A3 (RFVT3), the principal intestinal apical absorptive transporter; SLC52A2 (RFVT2), broadly expressed including brain; and SLC52A1 (RFVT1), important in placenta for maternal-fetal transfer. In the cytosol riboflavin kinase (RFK) phosphorylates riboflavin (ATP) to flavin mononucleotide (FMN), and FAD synthase (FLAD1) then adenylylates FMN (ATP) to flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD). Defects in the transporters cause riboflavin transporter deficiency: SLC52A2/SLC52A3 loss-of-function causes Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome / Fazio- Londe disease (childhood sensorimotor neuronopathy with deafness and bulbar palsy, treatable with high-dose riboflavin), and maternal SLC52A1 deficiency causes transient neonatal multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency; FLAD1 deficiency causes a riboflavin-responsive lipid-storage myopathy / MADD-like disorder.

Root ground-tissue radial patterning by the SHORT-ROOT-SCARECROW-BIRD moduleMODULE:root_radial_patterning_shr_scrCONCRETE Radial patterning of the Arabidopsis root ground tissue is organised by a mobile GRAS-domain transcriptional regulator. SHORT-ROOT (SHR) is...
[more...][less] Radial patterning of the Arabidopsis root ground tissue is organised by a mobile GRAS-domain transcriptional regulator. SHORT-ROOT (SHR) is transcribed in the stele but the protein moves through plasmodesmata into the single adjacent cell layer (endodermis, cortex/endodermis initial (CEI) and quiescent centre (QC)). There it is captured in the nucleus by the related GRAS protein SCARECROW (SCR), with which it forms a head-to-head heterodimer, and by BIRD/INDETERMINATE-DOMAIN (IDD) C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factors such as JACKDAW (JKD/IDD10) and MAGPIE (MGP/IDD3). The BIRD zinc fingers ZF1-ZF3 contact DNA while ZF3-ZF4 dock into a groove on SHR, so the SHR-SCR heterodimer acts as a transcriptional coregulator brought to target promoters by BIRD proteins. Nuclear retention limits SHR movement to one layer, and the SHR-SCR-BIRD complex activates SCR itself (a positive feedback loop), MGP and other BIRDs (a feed-forward loop), and the D-type cyclin CYCD6;1. CYCD6;1 binds and activates CDKB1 kinases that phosphorylate RETINOBLASTOMA-RELATED (RBR), relieving RBR repression of SCR; this nested feed-forward loop triggers the formative asymmetric periclinal division of the CEI daughter that produces separate endodermis and cortex layers. SHR-SCR also specify endodermal identity, and SCR is required cell-autonomously for QC identity, providing the niche context in which the QC transcription factor WOX5 maintains the surrounding stem cells. Middle-cortex formation later in development reuses the SHR-SCR-CYCD6;1 module.

S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) cycle — SAM synthesis / transmethylation / SAH hydrolysis (MAT1A/GNMT/AHCY); hypermethioninemiasMODULE:sam_cycle The S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) arm of the methionine cycle generates and recycles the universal biological methyl donor. Methionine...
[more...][less] The S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) arm of the methionine cycle generates and recycles the universal biological methyl donor. Methionine adenosyltransferase (liver MAT1A; extrahepatic MAT2A) condenses L-methionine with ATP to form S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM). SAM then donates its methyl group in the many transmethylation reactions of SAM-dependent methyltransferases — of which glycine N-methyltransferase (GNMT), the abundant hepatic enzyme methylating glycine to sarcosine, is the major regulator of the SAM:SAH ratio (cellular methylation capacity) — each producing S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH). Adenosylhomocysteinase (AHCY, SAH hydrolase) then hydrolyses SAH to L-homocysteine + adenosine, relieving the potent SAH product-inhibition of methyltransferases. Homocysteine is then either remethylated back to methionine (methionine synthase MTR / betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase), closing the cycle, or committed to transsulfuration (CBS) toward cysteine — reactions curated in the homocysteine-metabolism module. Inherited defects of the three SAM-arm enzymes all cause hypermethioninemia: MAT1A (MAT I/III deficiency, usually benign, severe forms with CNS demyelination), GNMT (GNMT deficiency, mild hepatopathy), and AHCY (S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase / SAHH deficiency, with elevated SAH/SAM, myopathy, developmental delay and liver disease).

Salicylic acid biosynthesis (isochorismate route) and NPR1-dependent defence signallingMODULE:salicylic_acid_biosynthesis_npr1_signalingCONCRETE After pathogen attack Arabidopsis makes most of its salicylic acid (SA) from chorismate through isochorismate. In the chloroplast stroma,...
[more...][less] After pathogen attack Arabidopsis makes most of its salicylic acid (SA) from chorismate through isochorismate. In the chloroplast stroma, isochorismate synthase 1 (ICS1, also SID2/EDS16) isomerizes chorismate to isochorismate; this is the committed, pathogen-induced step, and its paralog ICS2 contributes little. The MATE transporter EDS5 exports isochorismate to the cytosol, where the GH3 amidotransferase PBS3 conjugates it with glutamate to isochorismate-9-glutamate, which decomposes, spontaneously or with the help of the acyltransferase EPS1, into SA. SA is perceived by the NPR protein family: the paralogs NPR3 and NPR4 bind SA with high affinity and act as CUL3-ligase adaptors that control NPR1 turnover, while NPR1 itself has been reported to bind SA more weakly, although the relative roles of NPR1 and NPR3/NPR4 as SA receptors are debated. SA-induced changes in cellular redox reduce cytoplasmic NPR1 oligomers to monomers that enter the nucleus, where NPR1 acts as a transcription coregulator. Sumoylated NPR1 switches from WRKY repressors to TGA transcription factors and activates defence genes such as PR1, and NPR1 directly induces a set of WRKY transcription factor genes. One of these, WRKY70, is a sequence-specific transcription factor that promotes SA-induced pathogenesis-related gene expression, represses jasmonate-responsive genes and, together with WRKY54, restrains SA biosynthesis, forming a negative feedback loop. Together these steps drive local resistance and systemic acquired resistance (SAR) against biotrophic pathogens.

Salt Overly Sensitive (SOS) pathway (SOS3/CBL4 - SOS2/CIPK24 - SOS1 Na+/H+ antiporter)MODULE:sos_salt_toleranceABSTRACT The Salt Overly Sensitive (SOS) pathway is a calcium-decoding kinase relay that drives Na+ extrusion from plant cells under salinity. A...
[more...][less] The Salt Overly Sensitive (SOS) pathway is a calcium-decoding kinase relay that drives Na+ extrusion from plant cells under salinity. A salt-induced cytosolic Ca2+ signal is sensed by N-myristoylated calcineurin B-like (CBL) EF-hand calcium sensors: SOS3/CBL4 predominantly in roots and SCaBP8/CBL10 in shoots. The Ca2+-bound CBL binds the C-terminal NAF/FISL motif of the CBL-interacting protein kinase SOS2/CIPK24, relieving its autoinhibition and recruiting it to the plasma membrane. The CBL-CIPK24 complex phosphorylates the C-terminal autoinhibitory domain of SOS1/NHX7, an electroneutral plasma-membrane Na+/H+ antiporter, relieving its autoinhibition so that SOS1 uses the proton-motive force to export Na+ to the apoplast; SOS1 also controls long-distance Na+ partitioning at the xylem/symplast boundary. The module ends at SOS1-mediated Na+ efflux. The salt-sensing upstream step (GIPC-mediated Ca2+ influx), SOS2 regulation by ABI2, 14-3-3 proteins and GI, the vacuolar CBL10-CIPK24 branch and NHX-type vacuolar antiporters, and HKT1-mediated xylem Na+ retrieval are outside this module's boundary.

Its alpha subunit forms an hourglass-shaped pore with a lateral gate through which signal sequences and transmembrane segments of nascent polypeptides enter the lipid bilayer; the small beta and gamma subunits stabilize the channel. Serotonin and melatonin biosynthesis (Trp -> 5-HTP -> serotonin -> N-acetylserotonin -> melatonin)MODULE:serotonin_melatonin_biosynthesis Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) and the pineal hormone melatonin are the indoleamine products of a four-step pathway from the essential amino acid...
[more...][less] Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) and the pineal hormone melatonin are the indoleamine products of a four-step pathway from the essential amino acid L-tryptophan. Tryptophan hydroxylase - the neuronal isoform TPH2 in brainstem raphe serotonergic neurons, the peripheral isoform TPH1 in gut enterochromaffin cells, pineal gland and skin - catalyses the rate-limiting hydroxylation of L-tryptophan to 5-hydroxy-L-tryptophan (5-HTP) using tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), O2 and a non-heme Fe(II) centre. The shared aromatic-L-amino-acid decarboxylase (DDC/AADC, curated with the catecholamine pathway) decarboxylates 5-HTP to serotonin. In the pineal gland (and retina) serotonin is then converted to melatonin in two further steps that are gated by the circadian clock: serotonin N-acetyltransferase (AANAT, the "timezyme") N-acetylates serotonin to N-acetylserotonin using acetyl-CoA - the sharply night-elevated, cAMP/14-3-3-regulated rate-controlling step - and acetylserotonin O-methyltransferase (ASMT/HIOMT) O-methylates N-acetylserotonin to melatonin using S-adenosyl-L-methionine. Serotonin acts as a central and enteric neurotransmitter and platelet mediator, while melatonin signals darkness/photoperiod. Variants across the pathway are studied in mood, autism- spectrum and sleep phenotypes.

Sex-steroid biosynthesis and androgen activation — HSD17B3/CYP19A1/SRD5A2MODULE:sex_steroid_biosynthesis The C19 androgen precursors made in the gonads and adrenal (androstenedione, from the CYP17A1 17,20-lyase reaction) are converted into the active...
[more...][less] The C19 androgen precursors made in the gonads and adrenal (androstenedione, from the CYP17A1 17,20-lyase reaction) are converted into the active sex steroids by three endoplasmic-reticulum-membrane enzymes. The testis-specific 17beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 3 (HSD17B3) reduces the 17-keto group of androstenedione to give testosterone, the principal circulating androgen. Testosterone then has two activation fates in target tissues: the microsomal cytochrome P450 aromatase (CYP19A1) aromatizes the A-ring of C19 androgens to the C18 estrogens (androstenedione -> estrone, testosterone -> 17beta-estradiol), the committed and rate-limiting step of estrogen synthesis; and steroid 5alpha-reductase type 2 (SRD5A2) irreversibly reduces the C4-C5 double bond of testosterone to 5alpha-dihydrotestosterone (DHT), the most potent androgen, in prostate and genital skin. Inherited defects define disorders of sex development and hormone imbalance: HSD17B3 (46,XY DSD, 17beta-HSD3 deficiency), CYP19A1 (aromatase deficiency / aromatase excess syndrome; CYP19A1 is also the aromatase-inhibitor breast-cancer drug target) and SRD5A2 (5alpha-reductase-2 deficiency 46,XY DSD; the finasteride/dutasteride target for benign prostatic hyperplasia and androgenetic alopecia).

Shikimate pathway to chorismateMODULE:bacterial_shikimate_chorismate_biosynthesis Seven-step shikimate pathway that converts phosphoenolpyruvate and D-erythrose 4-phosphate to chorismate in bacteria, fungi, plants and...
[more...][less] Seven-step shikimate pathway that converts phosphoenolpyruvate and D-erythrose 4-phosphate to chorismate in bacteria, fungi, plants and apicomplexan protists. DAHP synthase condenses the two central-carbon precursors and is the main point of feedback control; 3-dehydroquinate synthase, 3-dehydroquinate dehydratase, shikimate dehydrogenase, shikimate kinase and EPSP synthase then build 5-enolpyruvylshikimate 3-phosphate, and chorismate synthase performs a reduced-flavin-dependent elimination to give chorismate. The reaction chain is invariant, but its enzyme architecture differs by lineage: bacteria use separate enzymes (with either type I or type II dehydroquinases), plants fuse dehydroquinase and shikimate dehydrogenase in one polypeptide, and fungi and apicomplexa carry the five central activities on a single pentafunctional AROM polypeptide. In plants the pathway is plastidic; in fungi it is cytosolic. Chorismate is the branch point for phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan, folate, ubiquinone and other aromatic compounds, which are outside this module.

Sialic acid (N-acetylneuraminate) metabolism (biosynthesis, activation, transport, catabolism)MODULE:sialic_acid_metabolism Sialic acids (in humans chiefly N-acetylneuraminate, Neu5Ac) are the negatively charged nine-carbon sugars that cap most cell-surface and secreted...
[more...][less] Sialic acids (in humans chiefly N-acetylneuraminate, Neu5Ac) are the negatively charged nine-carbon sugars that cap most cell-surface and secreted glycoconjugates, governing cell-cell recognition, receptor masking, serum-protein half-life and pathogen interactions. Their metabolism forms a compact cytosol-to- organelle pathway. Biosynthesis starts with the bifunctional, feedback-controlled enzyme GNE, whose epimerase domain converts UDP-N-acetylglucosamine to N-acetylmannosamine (ManNAc) and whose kinase domain phosphorylates ManNAc to ManNAc-6-phosphate. The sialic-acid synthase NANS then condenses ManNAc-6-P with phosphoenolpyruvate to N-acetylneuraminate-9-phosphate, which the HAD phosphatase NANP dephosphorylates to free Neu5Ac. In the nucleus, CMAS activates Neu5Ac with CTP to the sugar-nucleotide donor CMP-Neu5Ac; the Golgi antiporter SLC35A1 imports CMP-Neu5Ac into the Golgi lumen (in exchange for CMP) to supply the sialyltransferases that decorate glycans. CMP-Neu5Ac feedback-inhibits GNE, keeping flux matched to demand. On the catabolic side, the lysosomal sialidase NEU1 (acting within the CTSA/GLB1 lysosomal multienzyme complex) removes terminal sialic acids from glycoconjugates during turnover, the lysosomal H+/sialic acid symporter sialin (SLC17A5) exports the released free sialic acid to the cytosol for reuse by CMAS, and the cytosolic aldolase NPL cleaves free Neu5Ac to ManNAc + pyruvate, recycling the amino sugar. Inherited defects at nearly every step cause disease: GNE myopathy and sialuria (GNE), NANS-CDG, SLC35A1-CDG (CDG-IIf), sialidosis (NEU1), free sialic acid storage disorders (Salla disease and infantile sialic acid storage disease; SLC17A5) and an NPL-related myopathy. Several of these respond to ManNAc or sialic-acid supplementation.

Siroheme biosynthesis from uroporphyrinogen IIIMODULE:siroheme_biosynthesis Biosynthesis of siroheme, the iron-containing isobacteriochlorin prosthetic group of assimilatory sulfite and nitrite reductases, from the common...
[more...][less] Biosynthesis of siroheme, the iron-containing isobacteriochlorin prosthetic group of assimilatory sulfite and nitrite reductases, from the common tetrapyrrole precursor uroporphyrinogen III. Three reactions are required: S-adenosyl-L-methionine-dependent bis-methylation of uroporphyrinogen III at C-2 and C-7 to precorrin-2, NAD(P)+-dependent dehydrogenation of precorrin-2 to sirohydrochlorin, and insertion of ferrous iron into sirohydrochlorin to give siroheme. The chemistry is conserved in bacteria, fungi and plants, but the enzyme architecture differs. In enterobacteria a single multifunctional siroheme synthase (CysG) carries all three activities, with the methylase in its C-terminal region and the dehydrogenase and chelatase sharing an N-terminal region. Fungi split the pathway between a monofunctional uroporphyrinogen-III methyltransferase (Met1-type) and a bifunctional dehydrogenase-ferrochelatase (Met8-type) that uses a single active site for both reactions. Bacillus and plants use separate enzymes for every step, including a small SirB-type sirohydrochlorin ferrochelatase that in plants is located in the plastid. Uroporphyrinogen III synthesis is shared with heme, chlorophyll and cobalamin biosynthesis and lies upstream of this module; incorporation of siroheme into sulfite reductase lies downstream.

Specification of floral meristem identity at the Arabidopsis shoot apexMODULE:floral_meristem_identityCONCRETE After floral induction the Arabidopsis shoot apical meristem becomes an indeterminate inflorescence meristem whose lateral primordia must be...
[more...][less] After floral induction the Arabidopsis shoot apical meristem becomes an indeterminate inflorescence meristem whose lateral primordia must be assigned floral, rather than shoot, fate. Floral integrators supply the input: the florigen FT, a PEBP-family protein made in leaves, reaches the apex and acts as a transcriptional coactivator of the bZIP factor FD to activate APETALA1 (AP1) and the MADS-box integrators SOC1 and FRUITFULL (FUL); SOC1 (as a heterodimer with AGL24) binds the LEAFY (LFY) promoter and activates it, and FUL promotes the reproductive transition partially redundantly with SOC1. LFY, a plant-specific DNA-binding transcription factor, directly induces AP1 in the floral anlagen, and AP1 in turn up-regulates LFY, so the two lock in floral fate through positive feedback. The SQUAMOSA-clade MADS factors AP1, CAULIFLOWER (CAL) and FUL act partially redundantly in this step (ap1 cal ful triple mutants make no flowers); AP1 also acts as a master repressor in the young flower, directly silencing the flowering-time/inflorescence genes SOC1, AGL24 and SVP so that the shoot program does not continue in floral meristems. The F-box protein UNUSUAL FLORAL ORGANS (UFO) binds LFY and DNA to form a LFY-UFO transcriptional complex that redirects LFY to region-specific targets in the young flower. TERMINAL FLOWER1 (TFL1), a PEBP paralog of FT, is expressed in the centre of the inflorescence meristem and acts as an FD-dependent corepressor that keeps LFY and AP1 out of the shoot apex, maintaining indeterminate inflorescence identity; AP1 and LFY reciprocally repress TFL1 in floral primordia. The A-class factor APETALA2 contributes to floral meristem establishment alongside AP1. Floral organ identity (the ABCE program activated later by LFY, UFO and AP1 together with SEP proteins), the leaf-side photoperiod pathway that produces FT, and the age, vernalization and gibberellin pathways converging on the integrators are separate modules.

Sphingomyelin cycle (ceramide <-> sphingomyelin interconversion)MODULE:sphingomyelin_cycle Sphingomyelin (SM) is the most abundant sphingolipid of the plasma membrane and a defining component of lipid rafts and the myelin sheath. The...
[more...][less] Sphingomyelin (SM) is the most abundant sphingolipid of the plasma membrane and a defining component of lipid rafts and the myelin sheath. The "sphingomyelin cycle" is the reversible interconversion of SM and ceramide, which couples membrane-lipid homeostasis to ceramide/diacylglycerol signalling. In the synthetic direction the sphingomyelin synthases SGMS1 (trans-Golgi) and SGMS2 (plasma membrane) transfer a phosphocholine head group from phosphatidylcholine (PC) to ceramide, producing SM + diacylglycerol (DAG) — simultaneously consuming the pro-apoptotic lipid ceramide and generating the pro-mitogenic lipid DAG. In the hydrolytic direction, sphingomyelinases (SM phosphodiesterases) cleave SM back to ceramide + phosphocholine, generating the ceramide second messenger. Human cells use several, distinguished by pH optimum and location: the lysosomal acid sphingomyelinase SMPD1 (turnover and the ASMase/ceramide stress pathway; Niemann-Pick A/B on deficiency), and the Mg2+-dependent neutral sphingomyelinases SMPD3 (nSMase2, the major stress-responsive plasma-membrane/Golgi enzyme controlling ceramide signalling, exosome secretion and bone mineralization), SMPD4 (nSMase3, ER/Golgi/nuclear-envelope) and SMPD2 (nSMase1, ER; note its preferred cellular substrate is lyso-platelet-activating factor, so its bulk-SMase role is limited). The ceramide produced feeds the ceramidase/sphingosine-1-phosphate rheostat and re-acylation pathways. Inherited defects illustrate the pathway: SMPD1 Niemann-Pick disease, SGMS2 and SMPD3 skeletal dysplasias, and SMPD4 a neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly.
