Sphingosine-1-phosphate rheostat (ceramide -> sphingosine -> S1P -> exit)MODULE:sphingosine_1_phosphate_rheostat The "sphingolipid rheostat" is the interconversion of the bioactive sphingolipids ceramide, sphingosine and sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P), whose...
[more...][less] The "sphingolipid rheostat" is the interconversion of the bioactive sphingolipids ceramide, sphingosine and sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P), whose relative levels set the balance between cell death/growth arrest (ceramide, sphingosine) and survival/proliferation/migration (S1P). Ceramide is hydrolysed to sphingosine plus a free fatty acid by ceramidases: the alkaline ceramidases ACER1 (ER, skin), ACER2 (Golgi) and ACER3 (ER/Golgi, broadly expressed) act here, complementing the acid (ASAH1, lysosomal) and neutral (ASAH2) ceramidases curated elsewhere. Sphingosine is then phosphorylated with ATP to S1P by the sphingosine kinases SPHK1 (cytosolic, translocating to the plasma membrane; pro-survival/pro-inflammatory) and SPHK2 (nuclear/ER/mitochondrial; its nuclear S1P inhibits HDAC1/2). S1P has two fates. It is reversibly dephosphorylated back to sphingosine by the ER S1P phosphatases SGPP1 and SGPP2 (recycling sphingosine for re-acylation to ceramide and damping S1P signalling), or it is IRREVERSIBLY cleaved by the PLP-dependent ER lyase SGPL1 to (2E)-hexadecenal + phosphoethanolamine — the sole exit from sphingolipid metabolism, which also builds the tissue-to-blood S1P gradient that governs lymphocyte egress. Inherited defects illustrate the pathway's importance: ACER3 childhood leukodystrophy and SGPL1 sphingosine-phosphate-lyase insufficiency syndrome (steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome with adrenal insufficiency); the S1P axis is also the target of the immunomodulator fingolimod (FTY720, an SPHK2 substrate).

Stomatal lineage progression and spacing (EPF-ERECTA-YODA-MAPK and SPCH/MUTE/FAMA-SCRM)MODULE:stomatal_lineage_developmentCONCRETE In the Arabidopsis leaf epidermis, stomata are produced by a dedicated cell lineage whose successive transitions are driven by three closely...
[more...][less] In the Arabidopsis leaf epidermis, stomata are produced by a dedicated cell lineage whose successive transitions are driven by three closely related group Ia bHLH transcription factors, each acting as a heterodimer with the broadly expressed group IIIb bHLHs SCREAM/ICE1 (SCRM) and SCRM2. SPEECHLESS (SPCH) initiates the lineage by driving the asymmetric entry division of a meristemoid mother cell, MUTE terminates the self-renewing asymmetric divisions of the meristemoid and converts it into a guard mother cell (GMC), and FAMA drives the single symmetric GMC division and guard cell differentiation, then locks in guard cell fate with RETINOBLASTOMA-RELATED. Lineage entry and spacing are restrained by cell-cell signalling: the secreted cysteine-rich peptide EPF2, produced by early lineage cells, binds the leucine-rich-repeat receptor kinase ERECTA in a complex with the non-catalytic co-receptor TOO MANY MOUTHS (TMM); ligand binding recruits SERK co-receptor kinases and activates the MAPKKK YODA, which phosphorylates MKK4/MKK5, which in turn activate MPK3/MPK6. MPK3/MPK6, docked onto SCRM through its KiDoK motif and recruited with YODA to the cortex by the polarity scaffold BASL, phosphorylate SPCH and SCRM and promote their degradation, limiting lineage entry. Because SPCH-SCRM directly activates EPF2 and TMM, the circuit forms a negative feedback loop that self-organizes stomatal density and the one-cell spacing rule. The related peptide EPF1, perceived mainly by ERL1, acts later on spacing divisions, and the positive peptide stomagen (EPFL9) competes with EPF2 for ERECTA-TMM. Brassinosteroid (via BIN2 inhibition of YODA), CO2 (via CRSP cleavage of EPF2) and other environmental inputs converge on this module.

Streptococcus pyogenes FbaB covalent surface-adhesin module (CnaB2 isopeptide domain; SpyTag/SpyCatcher origin)MODULE:spytag_spycatcher This module describes the multidomain group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) surface adhesin FbaB (gene fba2; UniProtKB:Q8G9G1) and, in...
[more...][less] This module describes the multidomain group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) surface adhesin FbaB (gene fba2; UniProtKB:Q8G9G1) and, in particular, its CnaB2 / SpaA-like prealbumin-fold domain, which autocatalytically forms an intramolecular Lys-Asp isopeptide bond. FbaB is a major virulence factor of invasive M3/M18 GAS strains: it is covalently anchored to the peptidoglycan cell wall via a C-terminal LPXTG sortase motif, binds host fibronectin through C-terminal fibronectin-binding repeats to mediate adhesion to and invasion of host cells, carries an N-terminal thioester (TED) domain of the kind that covalently captures host proteins in related streptococcal adhesins, and uses the CnaB2 isopeptide bond to gain the mechanical, thermal and chemical stability inferred to be needed for force-bearing engagement of host fibronectin during invasion. The CnaB2 domain (residues ~462-541; the region crystallized in PDB 9OJ3 and earlier FbaB-CnaB2 structures) is the natural scaffold that was split and engineered into the widely used SpyTag/SpyCatcher covalent protein-conjugation system (SpyTag = reactive Asp-bearing peptide; SpyCatcher = Lys-bearing protein partner; catalytic Glu), with SpyTag003/SpyCatcher003 being the third-generation variant in PDB 9OJ3. The module is grounded in a single natural gene product, FbaB; SpyTag and SpyCatcher are engineered fragments of this one protein, not separate genes.

Strigolactone perception and D14-MAX2-SMXL signalling in shoot-branching controlMODULE:strigolactone_signaling_shoot_branchingCONCRETE Strigolactones (SLs) are carotenoid-derived hormones that inhibit axillary bud outgrowth. In Arabidopsis thaliana, SL is perceived by the...
[more...][less] Strigolactones (SLs) are carotenoid-derived hormones that inhibit axillary bud outgrowth. In Arabidopsis thaliana, SL is perceived by the alpha/beta-hydrolase receptor DWARF14 (D14), which binds and slowly hydrolyses the butenolide D-ring. SL binding changes the conformation of D14 so that it associates with the F-box protein MORE AXILLARY GROWTH2 (MAX2) in an SCF(MAX2) E3 ubiquitin ligase and with the SMAX1-LIKE co-repressors SMXL6, SMXL7 and SMXL8. The SMXLs are then polyubiquitinated and degraded by the proteasome, and D14 itself is degraded as negative feedback. In the absence of SL, the nuclear SMXL6/7/8 proteins repress target genes by recruiting TOPLESS-related co-repressors through an EAR motif, and SMXL6 can also bind target promoters itself. Their removal de-represses the bud-expressed TCP transcription factor BRANCHED1 (BRC1), which keeps buds dormant, in part by activating HD-ZIP genes that raise abscisic acid in the bud. SL-triggered SMXL degradation also reduces PIN1 accumulation and auxin transport in the stem, which inhibits bud activation in parallel with BRC1. The sister karrikin pathway uses the same F-box protein, MAX2, with the D14 paralog KAI2 and the SMAX1/SMXL2 repressors. That pathway, SL biosynthesis (D27, MAX3, MAX4, MAX1) and the auxin-transport branch are outside this module.

Synaptic vesicle cycle (umbrella)MODULE:synaptic_vesicle_cycleCONCRETE The life cycle of the synaptic vesicle at a presynaptic terminal, modeled as an organelle lifecycle with five stages: (1) neurotransmitter loading,...
[more...][less] The life cycle of the synaptic vesicle at a presynaptic terminal, modeled as an organelle lifecycle with five stages: (1) neurotransmitter loading, in which the V-ATPase acidifies the lumen and a vesicular transporter fills the vesicle; (2) reserve-pool clustering, in which synapsins tether loaded vesicles into a phase-separated cluster from which they are mobilised on demand; (3) exocytosis, in which vesicles are recruited to the active zone, primed by Munc13/Munc18-1, and fused by the SNARE machinery when synaptotagmin senses Ca2+ entering through Cav2 channels; (4) endocytosis, in which vesicle membrane and proteins are retrieved by clathrin-dependent or ultrafast/bulk routes and re-formed by dynamin fission and auxilin/HSC70 uncoating; and (5) maturation, in which the regenerated vesicle regains its full protein complement and is returned to the loading stage. Stages 1, 3 and 4 are elaborated in separate modules; this umbrella carries the cycle topology and the hallmark machinery of each stage. Exemplars are human; the cycle is conserved at metazoan chemical synapses. Grounded in GO:0099504 (synaptic vesicle cycle).

Synaptic vesicle endocytosis and vesicle regenerationMODULE:synaptic_vesicle_endocytosisCONCRETE The retrieval stage of the synaptic vesicle cycle, in which vesicle membrane and resident proteins deposited in the presynaptic plasma membrane by...
[more...][less] The retrieval stage of the synaptic vesicle cycle, in which vesicle membrane and resident proteins deposited in the presynaptic plasma membrane by exocytosis are recovered and re-formed into release-competent vesicles at the presynaptic endocytic zone. In the classical clathrin-mediated route, the AP-2 adaptor complex, the neuron-specific assembly protein AP180 and the synaptotagmin-sorting adaptor stonin-2 recognise vesicle cargo and PI(4,5)P2 and nucleate a clathrin coat; BAR-domain proteins (endophilin, amphiphysin, syndapin) shape the invaginating membrane and recruit the GTPase dynamin, which constricts and severs the neck; synaptojanin-1 hydrolyses PI(4,5)P2 and auxilin recruits HSC70 to strip the clathrin coat, yielding a naked vesicle ready for re-acidification and loading. The same coat, curvature, fission and uncoating machinery is reused when membrane is first retrieved by clathrin-independent ultrafast or bulk endocytosis and vesicles are then regenerated by clathrin-dependent budding from a synaptic endosome. The module conforms, with stated deviations, to the generic MODULE:vesicle_coat_budding motif. Exemplars are human. Grounded in GO:0048488 (synaptic vesicle endocytosis).

Synaptic vesicle exocytosis (docking, priming, Ca2+-triggered fusion)MODULE:synaptic_vesicle_exocytosisCONCRETE The release stage of the synaptic vesicle cycle at the presynaptic active zone. Loaded vesicles are recruited to the active zone by the vesicle...
[more...][less] The release stage of the synaptic vesicle cycle at the presynaptic active zone. Loaded vesicles are recruited to the active zone by the vesicle GTPase Rab3 and its effector RIM, which together with ELKS scaffolds tether vesicles and position them near voltage-gated Ca2+ channels. Munc13 and Munc18-1 then prime the vesicle by opening syntaxin-1 and templating assembly of the trans-SNARE complex (syntaxin-1 / SNAP-25 / synaptobrevin-2). An action potential opens Cav2 channels; the resulting Ca2+ microdomain is sensed by synaptotagmin-1, which relieves the complexin clamp and drives full SNARE zippering and fusion-pore opening, releasing transmitter. NSF with alpha-SNAP finally disassembles the cis-SNARE complex so the SNAREs can be reused. The inner pair -> fuse -> recycle bundle conforms to the generic MODULE:snare_fusion_cycle motif. Exemplars are human; the machinery is conserved across metazoan chemical synapses. Grounded in GO:0016079 (synaptic vesicle exocytosis).

T cell receptor signaling pathway moduleMODULE:t_cell_receptor_signaling The proximal T cell receptor (TCR) signaling pathway, from antigen engagement at the plasma membrane to calcium/NFAT-driven transcription....
[more...][less] The proximal T cell receptor (TCR) signaling pathway, from antigen engagement at the plasma membrane to calcium/NFAT-driven transcription. Peptide-MHC binding by the clonotypic TCR alpha/beta chains is transmitted by the invariant CD3 and CD3 zeta subunits, whose ITAMs are phosphorylated by the Src-family kinase LCK, carried to the complex by the MHC-matched coreceptor (CD4 or CD8) and kept primed by the phosphatase CD45. Doubly phosphorylated ITAMs dock the tandem SH2 domains of ZAP70, which LCK then activates. ZAP70 phosphorylates the transmembrane scaffold LAT and the cytosolic adaptor SLP-76 (LCP2), which the adaptor GADS bridges into the TCR signalosome; the signalosome recruits PLC gamma 1 and the Tec kinase ITK that activates it. PLC gamma 1 hydrolyses PIP2 to IP3 and DAG; IP3-driven calcium entry activates calcineurin, which dephosphorylates NFAT so that it enters the nucleus and activates target genes. The Ras-MAPK/AP-1 and PKC-theta/NF-kappaB branches that also leave the LAT signalosome are outside this module and are modelled in their own modules. Leaf molecular functions follow the ADAPTIVE_IMMUNITY gene reviews of each member.

Taurine / hypotaurine biosynthesis and transport (CDO1 -> CSAD / ADO; SLC6A6)MODULE:taurine_biosynthesis_and_transport Taurine is one of the most abundant free amino acids in mammalian tissues, essential for bile-salt conjugation, osmoregulation, membrane...
[more...][less] Taurine is one of the most abundant free amino acids in mammalian tissues, essential for bile-salt conjugation, osmoregulation, membrane stabilisation, calcium handling and mitochondrial tRNA modification; it is supplied both by endogenous biosynthesis from cysteine and by cellular uptake. The main biosynthetic route starts with cysteine dioxygenase (CDO1), which oxidises L-cysteine to 3-sulfino-L-alanine (cysteinesulfinate) using O2 and a non-heme Fe(II) centre — the committed, rate-limiting step of cysteine catabolism. Cysteinesulfinic acid decarboxylase (CSAD), a PLP-dependent enzyme, then decarboxylates cysteinesulfinate to hypotaurine. A parallel route is provided by 2-aminoethanethiol (cysteamine) dioxygenase (ADO), which oxidises cysteamine (derived from coenzyme A / pantetheine turnover) directly to hypotaurine; ADO is additionally the N-terminal cysteine dioxygenase of the Cys/N-degron oxygen-sensing pathway. Hypotaurine from either route is oxidised to taurine. Cells that synthesise little taurine rely on the plasma-membrane Na+/Cl- -coupled taurine transporter SLC6A6 (TauT) to import it. Defects illustrate the pathway's importance: SLC6A6 loss-of-function causes taurine-deficiency retinal degeneration and cardiomyopathy, and CDO1 is frequently epigenetically silenced in cancer.

Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) biosynthesis and regenerationMODULE:tetrahydrobiopterin_metabolism Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4, (6R)-L-erythro-5,6,7,8-tetrahydrobiopterin) is an essential reduced-pteridine cofactor for the aromatic amino acid...
[more...][less] Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4, (6R)-L-erythro-5,6,7,8-tetrahydrobiopterin) is an essential reduced-pteridine cofactor for the aromatic amino acid hydroxylases (phenylalanine hydroxylase PAH, tyrosine hydroxylase TH, and the tryptophan hydroxylases TPH1/TPH2), for the nitric oxide synthases, and for alkylglycerol monooxygenase. This module covers the two arms of BH4 homeostasis. (1) De novo biosynthesis, a short cytosolic three-step pathway from GTP: GTP cyclohydrolase I (GCH1) opens the imidazole ring of GTP to give 7,8-dihydroneopterin 3'-triphosphate (the committed, feedback-regulated step); 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin synthase (PTS/PTPS) converts this to 6-pyruvoyl-5,6,7,8-tetrahydropterin; and sepiapterin reductase (SPR) carries out the NADPH-dependent reductions that yield BH4. (2) Regeneration (recycling), which is required because each turn of an aromatic amino acid hydroxylase oxidises BH4 to pterin-4a-carbinolamine (4a-hydroxy-BH4): pterin-4a-carbinolamine dehydratase (PCBD1/PCD) dehydrates this to quinonoid dihydrobiopterin, and dihydropteridine reductase (QDPR/DHPR) reduces the quinonoid dihydrobiopterin back to BH4 using NADH. Because the hydroxylases turn over far faster than de novo synthesis, the PCBD1-QDPR salvage loop supplies most of the BH4 used at steady state. Inherited defects of GCH1, PTS, SPR, PCBD1 or QDPR all cause BH4 deficiency, presenting as BH4-deficient hyperphenylalaninemia (atypical/"malignant" PKU) and/or monoamine-neurotransmitter deficiency (dopa-responsive dystonia, catecholamine and serotonin deficiency), a distinct and separately treatable group of disorders from PAH-deficient classical PKU. PCBD1 additionally moonlights as DCoH, the dimerization cofactor / transcriptional coactivator of the HNF1 transcription factors.

Thiamine (vitamin B1) uptake and diphosphate activation (SLC19A2/A3 -> TPK1 -> SLC25A19; THTPA)MODULE:thiamine_uptake_and_activation Humans cannot synthesise thiamine (vitamin B1) and must take it up from the diet, then convert it to its active cofactor form thiamine diphosphate...
[more...][less] Humans cannot synthesise thiamine (vitamin B1) and must take it up from the diet, then convert it to its active cofactor form thiamine diphosphate (ThDP, also called thiamine pyrophosphate, TPP), which is required by pyruvate dehydrogenase, 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain 2-oxoacid dehydrogenase and transketolase. Free thiamine is imported across the plasma membrane by the two high-affinity SLC19 thiamine transporters THTR1 (SLC19A2) and THTR2 (SLC19A3). In the cytosol thiamine pyrophosphokinase TPK1 transfers a diphosphate group from ATP (physiologically UTP is the preferred donor) to thiamine, producing ThDP. ThDP is then delivered to the mitochondrial matrix by the inner-membrane carrier SLC25A19 to supply the matrix dehydrogenases. Cellular thiamine triphosphate (ThTP), a minor phosphorylated form, is hydrolysed back to ThDP by the cytosolic thiamine triphosphatase THTPA, contributing to phosphothiamine homeostasis. Defects in this module cause thiamine-responsive megaloblastic anaemia (SLC19A2 / Rogers syndrome), biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease (SLC19A3), thiamine metabolism dysfunction syndrome 5 / episodic encephalopathy (TPK1) and Amish lethal microcephaly / THMD4 (SLC25A19).

Thymidylate (dTMP -> dTTP) synthesis; thymidylate synthase / dUTPase / dTMP kinaseMODULE:thymidylate_synthesis Thymidylate synthesis is the route that makes the DNA-specific precursor dTTP, distinguishing DNA (thymine) from RNA (uracil) precursors. dUTP...
[more...][less] Thymidylate synthesis is the route that makes the DNA-specific precursor dTTP, distinguishing DNA (thymine) from RNA (uracil) precursors. dUTP diphosphatase (DUT) hydrolyses dUTP to dUMP + diphosphate, which both keeps the cellular dUTP:dTTP ratio low (preventing mutagenic uracil misincorporation into DNA) and supplies dUMP as substrate. Thymidylate synthase (TYMS) then reductively methylates dUMP to dTMP, using 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate as the one-carbon donor (oxidised to dihydrofolate, regenerated by DHFR) — the sole de novo source of dTMP. Thymidylate kinase (DTYMK) phosphorylates dTMP to dTDP, the essential step common to both the de novo and salvage routes; nucleoside diphosphate kinase then makes dTTP. This pathway is a central target of chemotherapy — TYMS is inhibited by the 5-fluorouracil metabolite FdUMP and by antifolates (raltitrexed, pemetrexed), and the folate cofactor supply is targeted by methotrexate — because rapidly dividing cells depend on de novo dTTP for DNA replication. Perturbing the balance (e.g. DUT loss, TYMS inhibition) causes dUTP accumulation, uracil misincorporation and DNA damage.

Toll signaling pathway in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_toll_signalingCONCRETE The Toll pathway is activated when an extracellular serine protease cascade cleaves the pro-domain of the cytokine-like ligand Spaetzle, allowing...
[more...][less] The Toll pathway is activated when an extracellular serine protease cascade cleaves the pro-domain of the cytokine-like ligand Spaetzle, allowing it to bind the Toll receptor. In the early embryo, a maternally supplied cascade (Gastrulation defective, Snake and Easter), spatially restricted by the Pipe sulfotransferase in the ventral follicle cells, generates ventral Spaetzle and establishes the dorsal-ventral axis. In the immune response, pattern-recognition proteins (PGRP-SA, GNBP1, GNBP3) and the virulence sensor Persephone activate ModSP, Grass and Hayan, converging on the Spaetzle-processing enzyme. Activated Toll recruits the adaptors MyD88 and Tube and the kinase Pelle, which lead to degradation of the IkB protein Cactus and nuclear entry of the NF-kappaB factors Dorsal and Dif. Related Toll receptors such as Toll-7, bound by neurotrophin-like Spaetzle family ligands, act in the nervous system.

Tricarboxylic acid cycleMODULE:tca_cycleCONCRETE A taxon-neutral module for the oxidative tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, covering acetyl-CoA entry through citrate synthase, citrate/isocitrate...
[more...][less] A taxon-neutral module for the oxidative tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, covering acetyl-CoA entry through citrate synthase, citrate/isocitrate interconversion by aconitase, oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate to 2-oxoglutarate and of 2-oxoglutarate to succinyl-CoA, substrate-level phosphorylation by succinyl-CoA ligase, succinate oxidation by respiratory complex II, fumarate hydration, and malate oxidation to regenerate oxaloacetate. The chemistry is conserved between bacteria, where the cycle runs in the cytoplasm and complex II sits in the plasma membrane, and eukaryotes, where it runs in the mitochondrial matrix and complex II sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane. The enzyme implementations differ at several steps: citrate synthase is a hexameric type II enzyme in many Gram-negative bacteria and a dimeric type I enzyme in mitochondria; the isocitrate step uses NADP-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenases in many bacteria but an allosterically regulated NAD-dependent hetero-oligomeric isocitrate dehydrogenase in eukaryotic mitochondria; the eukaryotic 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex carries an extra adaptor subunit that recruits the E3 component; and malate can be oxidized by NAD-dependent malate dehydrogenase or by membrane-associated malate:quinone oxidoreductases. Paralogous isozymes in other compartments (peroxisomal or cytosolic citrate synthase, malate dehydrogenase and NADP-isocitrate dehydrogenase) serve the glyoxylate cycle, NADPH supply or redox shuttles rather than the oxidative cycle.

Troponin complex in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_troponin_complexCONCRETE Troponin is the calcium sensor of the thin filament in striated muscle. It is a complex of three subunits bound to tropomyosin: troponin C binds...
[more...][less] Troponin is the calcium sensor of the thin filament in striated muscle. It is a complex of three subunits bound to tropomyosin: troponin C binds calcium, troponin I inhibits actomyosin interaction at rest, and troponin T anchors the complex to tropomyosin. When calcium binds troponin C, the inhibition by troponin I is relieved and tropomyosin moves to expose myosin-binding sites on actin, allowing contraction. Drosophila has single genes for troponin I (wings up A, wupA) and troponin T (upheld, up), each producing many muscle-specific isoforms by alternative splicing, and five troponin C genes expressed in different muscles; in the indirect flight muscle TpnC4 and TpnC41C are used, with TpnC4 linked to stretch activation.

Type-II (dissociated) fatty-acid synthesis, bacterial and mitochondrialMODULE:type_ii_fatty_acid_synthesis A reusable dissociated fatty-acid synthase (FAS II) pathway in which each reaction is catalysed by a separate enzyme acting on acyl chains carried...
[more...][less] A reusable dissociated fatty-acid synthase (FAS II) pathway in which each reaction is catalysed by a separate enzyme acting on acyl chains carried by a free acyl carrier protein (ACP). Malonyl-CoA formed by acetyl-CoA carboxylase is loaded onto ACP, an acyl-ACP chain is initiated, and the chain is iteratively elongated through condensation, beta-keto reduction, dehydration, and enoyl reduction. The same architecture operates in bacteria (and plastids) and, as a conserved, endosymbiont-derived system, in the mitochondrial matrix of eukaryotes, where it is independent of the cytosolic type I FAS and its best-defined product is octanoyl-ACP, the precursor of lipoic acid. Mitochondrial FAS II uses a homomeric multidomain acetyl-CoA carboxylase, a mitochondrial ACP and partly unrelated reductase and dehydratase families. An optional FabA/FabB branch introduces and extends cis unsaturation in bacteria. Enzyme-family, cofactor and compartment variants are represented explicitly rather than collapsed into a type-I fatty-acid synthase.

A dedicated trans-prenyltransferase sets the tail length (homomeric IspB or Coq1, or a heterotetrameric Dps1/Dlp1 or PDSS1/PDSS2 enzyme). The aromatic head group comes from chorismate via UbiC in bacteria, and from tyrosine in fungi, where aminotransferases form 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate and an aldehyde dehydrogenase (Hfd1) oxidizes 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde to 4-hydroxybenzoate. UbiA-family prenyltransferases (UbiA in the bacterial membrane, Coq2 in the mitochondrial inner membrane) attach the tail. The ring then undergoes one decarboxylation, three hydroxylations, two O-methylations and one C-methylation, in lineage-specific order: bacteria decarboxylate first with prFMN-dependent UbiD (cofactor from UbiX) and use UbiI/UbiH/UbiF or Coq7 hydroxylases, whereas the mitochondrial CoQ synthome hydroxylates C5 with Coq6, O-methylates with Coq3, performs a C1 oxidative decarboxylation with Coq4, then C-methylates (Coq5), hydroxylates C6 (Coq7) and O-methylates again (Coq3). Accessory factors (UbiJ, UbiK and UbiB in bacteria; Coq8, Coq9 and the mitochondrial ferredoxin system in eukaryotes) organize the hydrophobic intermediates or supply electrons. Oxygen-independent UbiT/UbiU/UbiV implementations, C5-C20 prenyl diphosphate synthesis, and coenzyme Q transport and use are outside the module.

Urea cycle (vertebrate hepatic ureagenesis, Krebs-Henseleit cycle)MODULE:urea_cycle The urea cycle (ornithine cycle / Krebs-Henseleit cycle) is the principal pathway for the detoxification of waste nitrogen in ureotelic...
[more...][less] The urea cycle (ornithine cycle / Krebs-Henseleit cycle) is the principal pathway for the detoxification of waste nitrogen in ureotelic vertebrates, converting ammonia (arising largely from amino-acid catabolism) plus bicarbonate and aspartate-derived nitrogen into urea for renal excretion. In mammals it operates predominantly in periportal hepatocytes and spans two compartments: the first two committed steps are mitochondrial and the last three are cytosolic, so the pathway is physically split across the inner mitochondrial membrane and requires two dedicated mitochondrial carriers. The cycle proper comprises six enzymes. N-acetylglutamate synthase (NAGS) produces N-acetyl-L-glutamate (NAG), the obligate allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 and therefore the regulatory gate of the whole pathway. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS1) condenses ammonia, bicarbonate and two ATP into carbamoyl phosphate in the matrix. Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) transfers the carbamoyl group to L-ornithine to give L-citrulline. Citrulline is exported to the cytosol in exchange for ornithine by the mitochondrial ornithine/citrulline carrier SLC25A15 (ORNT1). In the cytosol argininosuccinate synthase (ASS1) condenses citrulline with L-aspartate (the second nitrogen donor, supplied to the cytosol by the citrin aspartate/glutamate carrier SLC25A13) at the expense of ATP to form argininosuccinate; argininosuccinate lyase (ASL) cleaves this to L-arginine and fumarate; and arginase 1 (ARG1) hydrolyses arginine to urea and L-ornithine, regenerating the ornithine that re-enters mitochondria to close the cycle. The fumarate released by ASL links the urea cycle to the TCA cycle and, via aspartate regeneration, to the "aspartate-argininosuccinate shunt". Inherited deficiency of any of the six enzymes, of the two transporters (SLC25A15, SLC25A13), or of NAGS causes a urea cycle disorder presenting with hyperammonemia. The same enzyme chemistry, used biosynthetically rather than for nitrogen disposal, also produces arginine de novo (the arginine biosynthetic pathway) in tissues and organisms lacking a complete ureotelic cycle.

Ureide pathway - nitrogen recovery from allantoin via urea to ammoniaMODULE:ureide_urea_catabolism The ureide pathway recovers the four nitrogen atoms of the purine ring as ammonium. In organisms that keep urate oxidase, urate made by purine...
[more...][less] The ureide pathway recovers the four nitrogen atoms of the purine ring as ammonium. In organisms that keep urate oxidase, urate made by purine catabolism is oxidised to 5-hydroxyisourate, which 5-hydroxyisourate hydrolase and 2-oxo-4-hydroxy-4-carboxy-5-ureidoimidazoline (OHCU) decarboxylase convert to (S)-allantoin. Organisms without these enzymes, such as budding yeasts, can import allantoin from outside and enter the pathway at this point. Allantoinase opens the hydantoin ring to give allantoate. The allantoate is then split along one of two chemical routes. In the first, allantoicase releases urea and (S)-ureidoglycolate, and ureidoglycolate lyase releases a second urea and glyoxylate. In the second, used by plants and many bacteria, allantoate amidohydrolase and ureidoglycine aminohydrolase release ammonium directly, and ureidoglycolate is either split by the lyase or fully hydrolysed by ureidoglycolate amidohydrolase without making urea. The urea is then broken down in one of two ways. Most fungi, plants and many bacteria use a nickel-dependent urease, which hydrolyses urea in one step. Saccharomycetes yeasts instead use urea amidolyase, a biotin-dependent enzyme with two domains: urea carboxylase makes allophanate from urea, bicarbonate and ATP, and allophanate hydrolase converts allophanate to ammonium and CO2. The glyoxylate carbon goes to the glyoxylate cycle. In fungi and animals the enzymes are soluble, and in some organisms the urate oxidase steps are peroxisomal; in plants the steps after allantoin take place in the endoplasmic reticulum.

Vacuolar H+-ATPase in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_vacuolar_atpaseCONCRETE The vacuolar H+-ATPase (V-ATPase) is a rotary proton pump that acidifies lysosomes, endosomes, the Golgi and secretory vesicles, and in specialized...
[more...][less] The vacuolar H+-ATPase (V-ATPase) is a rotary proton pump that acidifies lysosomes, endosomes, the Golgi and secretory vesicles, and in specialized epithelia such as the Malpighian tubules and midgut energizes the plasma membrane for transport. The cytosolic V1 domain hydrolyses ATP at three catalytic sites in an A3B3 hexamer, and the central rotor (subunits D, F and d) transmits rotation to a ring of proteolipid c subunits in the membrane V0 domain. The V0 a subunit provides the proton path together with the c ring, and peripheral stalks of E and G subunits, with C and H, hold the stator. Reversible dissociation of V1 from V0 regulates activity. In Drosophila many subunits are encoded by paralogous genes, some with tissue- or testis-restricted expression, and the accessory proteins Ac45 and ATP6AP2 associate with V0.

Valine and isoleucine distal catabolism (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase -> propionyl-CoA)MODULE:valine_isoleucine_distal_catabolism After the shared, mitochondrial branched-chain aminotransferase (BCAT2) and branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKDH) steps deaminate and...
[more...][less] After the shared, mitochondrial branched-chain aminotransferase (BCAT2) and branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKDH) steps deaminate and oxidatively decarboxylate the three branched-chain amino acids to their acyl-CoA thioesters, valine and isoleucine follow their own distal degradation routes in the mitochondrial matrix that converge on propionyl-CoA. In the VALINE route, isobutyryl-CoA is dehydrogenated by isobutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase (ACAD8, an FAD enzyme feeding electrons to ETF) to methacrylyl-CoA; the crotonase ECHS1 (curated elsewhere) hydrates this to (S)-3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA, which the crotonase-superfamily hydrolase HIBCH deacylates to free 3-hydroxyisobutyrate + CoA (a step thought to detoxify the reactive methacrylyl-CoA). 3-Hydroxy- isobutyrate dehydrogenase (HIBADH, NAD+) then oxidises it to (S)-methylmalonate semialdehyde, and the CoA-acylating aldehyde dehydrogenase ALDH6A1 (methylmalonate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase) oxidatively decarboxylates that to propionyl-CoA. In the ISOLEUCINE route, 2-methylbutyryl-CoA is dehydrogenated by the short/branched-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase ACADSB (FAD -> ETF) to tiglyl-CoA; ECHS1 hydrates it, and HSD17B10 (the moonlighting SDR protein MRPP2/HADH2, in its 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase role, NAD+) oxidises 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA to 2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA, which the thiolase ACAT1 (curated elsewhere) cleaves to propionyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA. The propionyl-CoA produced by both routes enters the propionyl-CoA -> methylmalonyl-CoA -> succinyl-CoA anaplerotic pathway (PCC/MUT). Inherited defects at each step cause distinct organic acidurias (ACAD8: isobutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency; ACADSB: 2-methylbutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency; HIBCH and ALDH6A1: valine-pathway neurometabolic disease; HSD17B10: X-linked MHBD deficiency, which also impairs the protein's separate mitochondrial RNase P role).

Viral factory (virus-induced replication microcompartment)MODULE:viral_factoryABSTRACT A viral factory (VF) is a virus-induced intracellular microcompartment that concentrates the viral genome, the replication and transcription...
[more...][less] A viral factory (VF) is a virus-induced intracellular microcompartment that concentrates the viral genome, the replication and transcription machinery, and the structural proteins of the progeny virion into one place, raising the local concentration of every reactant in the replication cycle while screening replication intermediates from host nucleic-acid sensors and nucleases. The module is deliberately mechanism-neutral at its core and taxon-spanning: what makes a VF a VF is the compartment boundary plus the co-localised replication, transcription, and assembly programme, not any one way of drawing the boundary. Three boundary mechanisms are modelled as variants along a single axis - a host-membrane-derived boundary (spherules, tubes, double-membrane vesicles, convoluted ER), a membraneless biomolecular condensate formed by liquid-liquid phase separation, and a self-assembled proteinaceous shell - because the same downstream programme runs inside all three. Around that core the module places the recruitment of host systems the factory depends on (cytoskeleton, mitochondria, donor membranes, host lipid kinases, in some lineages host transcription machinery), the shielding of replication intermediates from host defences, non-lytic egress, and the antagonists that act on the factory itself.

Vitamin B6 (pyridoxal 5'-phosphate) supply by PdxS/PdxT synthesis or vitamer salvage, and PLP homeostasisMODULE:vitamin_b6_plp_metabolism Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) is the active form of vitamin B6 and the cofactor of a large set of enzymes, including transaminases, decarboxylases...
[more...][less] Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) is the active form of vitamin B6 and the cofactor of a large set of enzymes, including transaminases, decarboxylases and racemases of amino-acid, one-carbon, heme and neurotransmitter metabolism. Cells obtain PLP in two ways. Fungi, plants, archaea and many bacteria can make PLP de novo with the two-subunit PLP synthase: the PdxT (SNO) subunit hydrolyses glutamine and passes the ammonia to the PdxS (SNZ/PDX1) subunit, which builds PLP directly from ribose 5-phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate. This route does not use deoxyxylulose 5-phosphate; the separate DXP-dependent route of some bacteria is described in modules/pyridoxal_5_phosphate_biosynthesis.yaml. All cells can also salvage the B6 vitamers. Pyridoxal kinase (PDXK; BUD16 in budding yeast) phosphorylates pyridoxal, pyridoxine and pyridoxamine with ATP to PLP, pyridoxine 5'-phosphate (PNP) and pyridoxamine 5'-phosphate (PMP), and the FMN-dependent PNP/PMP oxidase (PNPO; PDX3 in yeast) oxidises PNP and PMP to PLP. Animals cannot make PLP de novo and depend on salvage of dietary vitamers. In mammals, PLP levels are also tuned by the magnesium-dependent pyridoxal phosphatase PDXP (chronophin), which dephosphorylates PLP back to pyridoxal and also dephosphorylates the actin regulator cofilin. Inherited PNPO deficiency causes a PLP-responsive neonatal epileptic encephalopathy.

[more...][less] Vitamin D (cholecalciferol from skin or diet, or ergocalciferol) is a prohormone that must be hydroxylated twice before it can act. A microsomal cytochrome P450 25-hydroxylase, principally CYP2R1 in the liver, converts vitamin D to 25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol), the abundant circulating storage form. The mitochondrial cytochrome P450 CYP27B1, whose renal proximal-tubule expression is induced by PTH and suppressed by calcitriol and FGF23, then performs the rate-limiting 1-alpha-hydroxylation to 1-alpha,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol). Calcitriol binds the nuclear vitamin D receptor (VDR), which heterodimerises with RXR on vitamin D response elements and recruits coactivators to regulate target genes driving intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, skeletal mineralization and feedback on vitamin D metabolism: liganded VDR represses CYP27B1 and induces the 24-hydroxylase CYP24A1, which inactivates both calcidiol and calcitriol. Loss of each step causes a vitamin D-dependent rickets: CYP2R1 (VDDR1B, low 25-hydroxyvitamin D), CYP27B1 (VDDR1A, low calcitriol) and VDR (VDDR2A, hereditary 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D-resistant rickets with high calcitriol).

ZIP-2/CEBP-2 translation-surveillance immunity in Caenorhabditis elegansMODULE:c_elegans_translation_surveillance_immunityCONCRETE Caenorhabditis elegans can detect a pathogen by the damage it does to a core host process instead of by recognizing a microbial molecule. The best...
[more...][less] Caenorhabditis elegans can detect a pathogen by the damage it does to a core host process instead of by recognizing a microbial molecule. The best defined case is translation surveillance in the intestine. Pseudomonas aeruginosa Exotoxin A (ToxA) is endocytosed and ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2, which inhibits host mRNA translation. Chemical translation inhibitors such as cycloheximide, and loss of other core host functions, trigger the same response. Enzymatically inactive ToxA does not. So the host senses the block in translation, not the toxin itself. Translation inhibition raises the level of the bZIP transcription factor ZIP-2 through a conserved upstream open reading frame (uORF) in the zip-2 mRNA. This fits a model in which a general fall in translation derepresses ZIP-2 synthesis. ZIP-2 acts with the C/EBP-gamma ortholog CEBP-2, a bZIP partner that binds it, to induce a set of intestinal infection-response genes. These include irg-1 and irg-2, which are induced independently of the PMK-1 p38 MAPK, DBL-1 TGF-beta and KGB-1 JNK pathways. zip-2 and cebp-2 mutants are more susceptible to P. aeruginosa and to ToxA. The molecular functions of the IRG-1 and IRG-2 proteins are unknown. Mitochondrial surveillance through ATFS-1 and the mitochondrial UPR is a parallel, separately regulated surveillance pathway.

cGMP-dependent sensory transduction in Caenorhabditis elegans ciliated neuronsMODULE:c_elegans_cgmp_sensory_transductionCONCRETE Many Caenorhabditis elegans sensory neurons turn an environmental stimulus into an electrical signal through the second messenger cGMP. A guanylyl...
[more...][less] Many Caenorhabditis elegans sensory neurons turn an environmental stimulus into an electrical signal through the second messenger cGMP. A guanylyl cyclase in or near the sensory cilium makes cGMP. The cGMP then opens a cyclic nucleotide-gated (CNG) cation channel made of the pore-forming alpha subunit TAX-4 and the modulatory beta subunit TAX-2. The resulting cation and Ca2+ influx changes the activity of the neuron. The channel is the same in different neurons, but the cyclase differs with the stimulus. In the AWC olfactory neurons, odorant receptors act through the stimulatory Galpha ODR-3, and the transmembrane guanylyl cyclases ODR-1 and DAF-11 act downstream and are required for responses to AWC-sensed odors. In the AFD thermosensory neurons, the receptor guanylyl cyclases GCY-8, GCY-18 and GCY-23 sit in the microvilli of the sensory ending and together are required for temperature-evoked currents. GCY-8 is the one needed to carry out isothermal tracking, GCY-18 is the main cyclase at 20-25 C, and GCY-23 is modulatory; all three help set the temperature range of tracking. In the URX and BAG gas-sensing neurons, heme-containing soluble guanylyl cyclases are both the cyclase and the O2 sensor: GCY-35/GCY-36 respond to rises in O2 and GCY-31/GCY-33 to falls. tax-4 and tax-2 are expressed in the thermosensory, gustatory and olfactory neurons. tax-4 mutants fail to respond to temperature and to soluble or volatile attractants, and they are defective in oxygen responses. A separate set of C. elegans sensory neurons, including AWA and ASH, uses OSM-9/OCR-2 TRPV channels instead of this cGMP-CNG pathway.

eRF1-eRF3 translation termination complex in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_erf1_erf3_termination_complexCONCRETE Eukaryotic translation termination is carried out by the release factors eRF1 and eRF3. eRF1 recognizes all three stop codons in the ribosomal A...
[more...][less] Eukaryotic translation termination is carried out by the release factors eRF1 and eRF3. eRF1 recognizes all three stop codons in the ribosomal A site and triggers hydrolysis of the peptidyl-tRNA bond through its conserved GGQ motif. eRF3 is a translational GTPase that delivers eRF1 to the ribosome as a ternary complex with GTP; GTP hydrolysis by eRF3 accommodates eRF1 and accelerates peptide release.

mRNA 3' end cleavage and polyadenylation machinery in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_cleavage_polyadenylationCONCRETE Most eukaryotic mRNAs acquire their 3' end by endonucleolytic cleavage of the pre-mRNA followed by addition of a poly(A) tail. The cleavage and...
[more...][less] Most eukaryotic mRNAs acquire their 3' end by endonucleolytic cleavage of the pre-mRNA followed by addition of a poly(A) tail. The cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor (CPSF) recognizes the AAUAAA polyadenylation signal through Cpsf160, Wdr33 and Clp (CPSF30), and Fip1 recruits poly(A) polymerase. The cleavage stimulation factor (CstF; CstF50, CstF64 and Su(f), the CstF77 homolog) binds GU-rich sequences downstream of the cleavage site. The core cleavage complex of Cpsf73, Cpsf100 and the scaffold Symplekin (Sym) carries out cleavage, with Cpsf73 as the endonuclease. Cpsf73, Cpsf100 and Sym are shared with the histone pre-mRNA processing machinery.

mRNA m6A methyltransferase complex in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_m6a_methyltransferase_complexCONCRETE N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is deposited on mRNA co-transcriptionally by a methyltransferase complex. Its catalytic core is the Mettl3-Mettl14...
[more...][less] N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is deposited on mRNA co-transcriptionally by a methyltransferase complex. Its catalytic core is the Mettl3-Mettl14 heterodimer, in which Mettl3 is the active methyltransferase and Mettl14 an inactive partner that supports RNA binding. A regulatory subcomplex (MACOM) of Fl(2)d, Virilizer (vir), the E3 ligase Hakai, Flacc and the RNA-binding protein Spenito (nito) is required for m6A deposition and specificity. In Drosophila, m6A modification by this complex regulates Sex-lethal pre-mRNA splicing in sex determination and contributes to neuronal function.

mRNA nuclear export machinery in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_mrna_nuclear_exportCONCRETE Bulk export of mRNA from the nucleus is coupled to transcription and processing. The TREX complex, consisting of the THO subcomplex with the...
[more...][less] Bulk export of mRNA from the nucleus is coupled to transcription and processing. The TREX complex, consisting of the THO subcomplex with the DEAD-box helicase Hel25E (UAP56) and the adaptor Ref1 (ALY), is loaded onto nascent mRNA and hands it to the export receptor heterodimer formed by sbr (NXF1) and Nxt1, which carries the mRNP through the nuclear pore complex by interacting with FG-repeat nucleoporins. TREX-2 (xmas, PCID2 and e(y)2) associates with the nuclear pore and couples transcription with export; in Drosophila it links actively transcribed genes to the nuclear periphery and shares e(y)2 with the SAGA deubiquitinase module.

myo-Inositol and inositol (pyro)phosphate biosynthesis (MIPS/IMPase and the PLC-IPMK-IPK1-IP6K-PPIP5K route)MODULE:myo_inositol_and_inositol_phosphate_biosynthesisCONCRETE myo-Inositol is made de novo from glucose 6-phosphate in two cytosolic steps: myo-inositol-3-phosphate synthase (MIPS), an NAD+-dependent...
[more...][less] myo-Inositol is made de novo from glucose 6-phosphate in two cytosolic steps: myo-inositol-3-phosphate synthase (MIPS), an NAD+-dependent isomerase, cyclises glucose 6-phosphate to 1D-myo-inositol 3-phosphate, and a lithium-sensitive inositol monophosphatase (IMPase) removes the phosphate to release free myo-inositol. Free inositol is used to make phosphatidylinositol and, through the phosphoinositides, the higher soluble inositol phosphates. In the lipid-dependent route, phospholipase C cleaves phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate to diacylglycerol and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3). An inositol polyphosphate multikinase (IPMK; yeast Arg82/Ipk2) phosphorylates IP3 to inositol 1,4,5,6-tetrakisphosphate and then to inositol 1,3,4,5,6-pentakisphosphate (IP5), and inositol-pentakisphosphate 2-kinase (IPK1) completes inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6, phytate). IP6 is further pyrophosphorylated to the high-energy inositol pyrophosphates by two unrelated kinase families: IP6 kinases (yeast Kcs1, mammalian IP6K) make 5-diphosphoinositol pentakisphosphate (IP7), and the PPIP5K/Vip1/Asp1 kinases add a further diphosphate to make IP8. IP6 and the inositol pyrophosphates act in mRNA export, phosphate homeostasis, vacuole biogenesis and stress responses. Some fungi, including fission yeast, lack the de novo branch and rely on imported inositol.

p38 stress-activated MAPK cascade moduleMODULE:p38_cascade A taxon-neutral decomposition of the p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase cascade, the stress- and cytokine-activated concrete realization of the...
[more...][less] A taxon-neutral decomposition of the p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase cascade, the stress- and cytokine-activated concrete realization of the generic three-tier MAP kinase relay (MODULE:mapk_relay). Environmental stresses (UV, osmotic and oxidative stress) and inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-1) signal through upstream MAP3Ks (ASK1/MAP3K5, TAK1/MAP3K7, MLK family) to the dual-specificity MAP2Ks MKK3 (MAP2K3) and MKK6 (MAP2K6), which dually phosphorylate the p38 MAPKs (p38 alpha/beta/gamma/delta) on their TGY activation-loop motif. Active p38 phosphorylates substrate kinases (MK2/MAPKAPK2) and transcription factors (ATF2, MEF2), driving stress-response and inflammatory gene programs. The RAF-analogous kinase relay - MAP3K -> MKK3/6 -> p38 - is declared as an inner bundle that `conforms_to` mapk_relay, while the stress/cytokine input and the p38 effector output and DUSP-mediated feedback are this cascade's free extensions around the conforming core. Grounded in GO:0038066 (p38MAPK cascade) / GO:0051403 (stress-activated MAPK cascade).

piRNA-mediated germline silencingMODULE:pirna_mediated_germline_silencingCONCRETE Animal germ cells use PIWI-clade Argonautes loaded with PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) to recognize transposon transcripts and other foreign or...
[more...][less] Animal germ cells use PIWI-clade Argonautes loaded with PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) to recognize transposon transcripts and other foreign or unwanted RNAs and to silence them. The module has three conserved steps. First, a cytoplasmic PIWI-piRNA complex in perinuclear nuage recognizes a target RNA by base pairing. Second, recognition is converted into an amplified pool of secondary small RNAs. Third, a nuclear Argonaute carries small RNAs into the nucleus and silences complementary loci co-transcriptionally. How the second and third steps are carried out differs between lineages. In insects and vertebrates, amplification is the ping-pong cycle: piRNA-guided slicing by cytoplasmic PIWI proteins (fly Aubergine and Ago3, mammalian PIWIL2/MILI) cuts target and precursor transcripts, and the cleavage products become new piRNAs. Nematodes lack ping-pong. In Caenorhabditis elegans the PIWI protein PRG-1 does not need to slice; its targets are instead used as templates by RNA-dependent RNA polymerase to make secondary 22G-RNAs, which are loaded into nematode-specific WAGO Argonautes. The nuclear step is also carried out by different, non-slicing effectors: fly Piwi directs H3K9me3 heterochromatin, mammalian PIWIL4/MIWI2 directs de novo DNA methylation of transposons, and in nematodes the WAGO HRDE-1 recruits the nuclear RNAi factor NRDE-2 and directs H3K9me3. In C. elegans the silenced state can be inherited for many generations without the piRNA trigger, through the nuclear HRDE-1 loop and a cytoplasmic loop in which the helicase ZNFX-1 and WAGO-4 form Z granules. Loss of the core PIWI proteins causes transposon derepression and sterility in flies and mice, and progressive loss of fertility in nematodes.

tRNA-guanine transglycosylase (queuine insertase) in Drosophila melanogasterMODULE:dmel_trna_guanine_transglycosylaseCONCRETE Eukaryotic tRNA-guanine transglycosylase exchanges guanine 34 in the anticodon of tRNA-Asp, tRNA-Asn, tRNA-His and tRNA-Tyr for queuine, forming...
[more...][less] Eukaryotic tRNA-guanine transglycosylase exchanges guanine 34 in the anticodon of tRNA-Asp, tRNA-Asn, tRNA-His and tRNA-Tyr for queuine, forming queuosine. Animals cannot synthesize queuine and obtain it from diet and gut microbes. The enzyme is a heterodimer of a catalytic subunit (QTRT1 ortholog, Tgt) and a catalytically inactive paralogous accessory subunit (QTRT2 ortholog, CG3434) required for activity.
